The error factor is necessary because when an MSHA sample is challenged, it allows the Secretary to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the sample is above the PEL.
MSHA is also proposing to apply an error factor adjustment of 21 percent to operator samples to determine compliance with the requirements of this part and for consistency across all samples, both operator and MSHA samples. While operator samples would not be cited for overexposure, there are still certain actions that operators must take based on their own sampling, such as corrective actions to reduce respirable crystalline silica exposures when sample results are above the PEL. For additional discussion of the error factor model and citing violations of the respirable crystalline silica PEL, see
Section IV.A.2.e. Paragraph (f).
Furthermore, the Agency is proposing that when mine operator samples are at or above the action level but at or below the PEL in § 60.12(a)(3), mine operators would also be required to provide approved respirators to miners. MSHA expects that providing miners with approved respirators, enrolling them in the proposed respiratory protection program in § 60.14 when any sample results indicate that miners are exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, and sampling as frequently as necessary (as proposed in § 60.12) would improve miner safety. By providing miners with respirators in this instance, miners are informed and can take action to protect themselves from respirable crystalline silica exposures and possible overexposures by voluntarily wearing a respirator. However, MSHA emphasizes that nothing in the proposal changes the existing requirements for operators to take corrective actions and ensure miners wear approved respirators when working in exposures above the PEL.
Mine operators can continue to rely on sample results from ISO/IEC 17025-accredited laboratories, including the 21 percent error factor adjustment, to determine their compliance with the PEL and action level. Miners should be confident that the sample results, including the 21 percent error factor adjustment, provide them with appropriate measurements of their exposures to respirable crystalline silica. Mine operators may continue to use any type of sampling device they choose for respirable crystalline silica sampling as long as it meets the characteristics for respirable particle-size selective samplers that conform to the ISO 7708:1995(E) standard and, where appropriate, meets MSHA permissibility requirements.

1. Section 60.11—Methods of Compliance
Existing § 60.11 requires mine operators to install, use, and maintain feasible engineering and administrative controls to keep each miner's exposure to respirable crystalline silica at or below the PEL. Mine operators must use feasible engineering controls as the primary means of controlling respirable crystalline silica; administrative controls must be used, when necessary, as a supplementary control.
Existing § 60.11(b) prohibits mine operators from using rotation of miners as an acceptable method of compliance for
30 CFR part 60
.
MSHA proposes to amend existing paragraph (b) to clarify that mine operators are prohibited from using rotation of miners as a corrective action under existing § 60.13 when miners' exposures are above the PEL. MSHA thinks this clarification is necessary because many mine operators have indicated that they interpret existing paragraph (b) as a total prohibition against the rotation of miners for any reason when miners are exposed to respirable crystalline silica. Existing paragraph (b) was not intended to bar rotation of miners as an administrative control to reduce exposure to other hazards, or for other reasons. For example, operators rotate miners to limit noise exposure, prevent repetitive strain injuries, and reduce fatigue from strenuous tasks.
After consideration of the concerns raised by stakeholders, MSHA concluded that existing paragraph (b) may be difficult to enforce and may cause confusion for the regulated community. The language in existing paragraph (b) results in operator concern that rotation of miners that is typical in operations and implemented for safety or health reasons could be cited as rotation of miners to limit silica exposures. Existing paragraph (b) may inadvertently lead operators to not rotate miners when appropriate, neglecting other critical health and safety hazards. For instance, it might dissuade implementation of rotation to protect miners from excessive noise exposure and occupational hearing loss.
The proposed change would clarify that existing § 60.11(b) is intended to prohibit the rotation of miners as a corrective action for respirable crystalline silica exposure when exposures are above the PEL. This means when exposure levels are above the PEL, operators may not use rotation of miners as a corrective action to bring silica exposures to levels at or below the PEL. Operators may continue to rotate miners in circumstances consistent with current normal work practices. Therefore, the proposed change would clarify that this section does not bar the use of miner rotation as deemed appropriate by the mine operator in circumstances such as, but not limited to, cross-training, allowing miners to alternate physically demanding tasks with less strenuous activities, or limiting exposure to other hazards for which rotation is a suitable corrective action (
e.g.,
noise or musculoskeletal disorders). Operators may not, however, introduce any new or additional rotation for exposures to other hazards (that could result in additional miners working in conditions above the PEL) while corrective actions under § 60.13 are ongoing for an overexposure to silica.
The following examples help explain MSHA's position prohibiting rotation of miners to be used as a corrective action when exposures are above the PEL:
Example A:
At a surface MNM mine, Miner 1 normally operates a haul truck for their entire 8-hour shift. If a silica sample result indicates an exposure above the PEL for Miner 1, MSHA would not allow the operator to rotate another miner for Miner 1 and run the haul truck for any amount of time for the purpose of reducing Miner 1's silica exposure during the shift, as this is not part of current normal work practices. Rather, if the exposure of Miner 1 is above the PEL, the MNM mine operator would be obligated to implement the corrective action for being above the PEL, to protect Miner 1.
Example B:
At an underground coal mine, Miner 1 and Miner 2 rotate the duties of operating the continuous mining machine as part of their current normal work practice. If a silica sample result indicates an exposure above the PEL, MSHA would allow the coal mine operator to rotate Miner 1 and Miner 2 working on the continuous mining machine while taking corrective actions because this is part of their normal work practices. MSHA emphasizes that when a sample indicates exposures are over the PEL, under existing § 60.13,
Corrective actions,
the operator must make approved respirators available to affected miners before the start of the next work shift in accordance with existing § 60.14(b) and (c) and ensure that affected miners wear respirators properly until miner exposures are at or below the PEL. In the example given above, both Miner 1 and Miner 2 would be considered affected, and the mine operator would be required to comply with the requirements of § 60.13 for both miners. MSHA also emphasizes that sampling under § 60.12(e)(2)(ii) requires coal operators to conduct occupational environmental sampling (
i.e.,
the sampling device stays with the occupation during the rotation).
Example C:
At a surface MNM mine, Miner 1 and Miner 2 normally rotate duties operating a stone cutting saw as an administrative control to reduce noise exposure. If a silica sample result indicates an exposure above the PEL, MSHA would allow the MNM mine operator to continue to rotate Miner 1 and Miner 2 operating the saw while taking corrective actions because this is part of their normal work practices. However, MSHA would not allow the mine operator to add Miner 3 to rotate with Miner 1 and Miner 2 for any amount of time operating the stone cutting saw in order to lower each miner's exposure below the PEL. MSHA emphasizes that when a sample indicates a miner's exposure over the PEL, under existing § 60.13,
Corrective actions,
the operator must make approved respirators available to affected miners before the start of the next work shift in accordance with existing § 60.14(b) and (c) and ensure that affected miners wear respirators properly until miner exposures are at or below the PEL. In the example given above, both Miner 1 and Miner 2 would be considered affected, and the mine operator would be required to comply with the requirements of § 60.13 for both miners. MSHA also emphasizes that sampling under § 60.12(e)(2)(i) requires MNM mine operators to conduct personal breathing-zone sampling (
i.e.,
the sampling device stays with the individual). MSHA expects mine operators to conduct personal breathing-zone sampling on both miners in this example when assessing their exposures to respirable crystalline silica.
This proposed change to § 60.11(b) is consistent with the existing protections for miner safety and health in existing § 60.11 and is intended to clarify MSHA enforcement policy in the Agency's standards. As discussed, amending this provision would not reduce protections afforded to miners as MSHA has consistently recognized that rotation is beneficial for miners' health and safety when used for purposes such as cross-training, alternating physically demanding tasks, or limiting exposure
(

2. Section 60.12—Exposure Monitoring
Existing § 60.12 sets forth requirements for conducting respirable crystalline silica exposure monitoring, including requirements for sampling, corrective actions sampling, periodic evaluation, post-evaluation sampling, sampling requirements, methods of sampling analysis, and sampling records. The exposure monitoring requirements facilitate operator compliance with the PEL and standardize MSHA's approach to monitoring and evaluating respirable crystalline silica exposures to better protect miners' health.
Under this proposed rule, MSHA would amend the exposure monitoring requirements in existing § 60.12 to do the following: (1) amend the sampling structure to “as frequently as necessary”, (2) amend the actions mine operators must take when miners' exposure is at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, (3) amend the actions mine operators must take when miners' exposure exceeds the PEL, (4) remove the requirements for periodic evaluation and post-evaluation sampling, (5) establish a uniform error factor adjustment of 21 percent on sample results for determining compliance with the PEL and for determining exposures at or above the action level, and (6) establish that MSHA would issue citations only for MSHA samples of respirable crystalline silica when laboratory analysis results indicate samples exceed the PEL.
a. Paragraph (a)
Existing § 60.12(a),
Sampling,
includes the requirements for sampling conducted by mine operators to assess miners' exposures to respirable crystalline silica. Samples are compared to the action level and the PEL to determine the effectiveness of existing controls and the need for additional controls.
Paragraph (a)(1)
In existing paragraph (a)(1), mine operators are required to commence sampling by the compliance date to assess the full shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica.
Under this proposed rule, MSHA would move the clause “to assess the full shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica” from existing paragraph (a)(1) to proposed paragraph (a)(2). Under existing paragraph (a)(1), MSHA does not propose to amend the existing requirement that mine operators must commence sampling by the compliance date in § 60.1.
Paragraph (a)(2)
Under existing paragraph (a)(2), mine operators must take certain actions when sampling is below the action level, at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, or above the PEL.
MSHA proposes to amend the sampling structure in § 60.12 from a periodic initial and quarterly frequency to an “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure that assesses actual or reasonably likely exposures at or above the action level.
MSHA expects the “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure to be familiar to mine operators because the proposed amendment would be consistent with MSHA's existing requirements for the control of miners' exposures to other health hazards, and the sampling structure could be quickly implemented by mine operators. For example, the proposed “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure is consistent with the existing MNM requirement to conduct dust, gas, mist, and fume surveys (sampling) as frequently as necessary to determine the adequacy of control measures (§§ 56.5002 and 57.5002). A similar sampling structure can also be found in the existing noise exposure assessment requirements for MNM and coal mines, which requires that mine operators establish a system of monitoring that evaluates each miner's noise exposure sufficiently to determine continuing compliance with the noise exposure requirements (§ 62.110). The proposed sampling structure for respirable crystalline silica is also consistent with the existing MNM standard for controlling diesel particulate matter (DPM), which requires that mine operators monitor as often as necessary to effectively determine, under conditions that can be reasonably anticipated in the mine, whether the average personal full-shift airborne exposure to DPM exceeds the DPM limit (§ 57.5071(a)). MSHA's experience has shown that requirements for operators to conduct sampling “as frequently as necessary” are an appropriate means to determine the adequacy of control measures and protect miner health.
MSHA anticipates that under this proposal, mine operators might determine that some miners are not reasonably likely to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level and would therefore not conduct sampling for those miners. MSHA also anticipates that operators may identify certain miners and occupations requiring more frequent sampling than the initial and subsequent quarterly monitoring for exposures exceeding the action level, particularly when mining conditions, processes, or procedures change (
e.g.,
geological factors or the effectiveness of engineering controls).
Mine operators could use objective data to help determine when to sample and what occupations or areas of a mine may need more frequent sampling to assess respirable crystalline silica exposures. This is consistent with the approach for sampling methods discussed in the 2024 Silica Final Rule, which assigned mine operators responsibility for determining which miners to sample for respirable crystalline silica exposures.
Objective data is information such as air monitoring data from industry-wide surveys or calculations based on the composition of a substance that indicates the level of miner exposure to respirable crystalline silica associated with a specific product, material, process, task, or activity. Mine operators utilizing such data should verify that it represents mining conditions that either closely match, or present greater exposure potential than the processes, material types, control measures, work practices, and environmental conditions present in their current operations.
Some examples of objective data include historical MSHA sampling data, NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations and other published scientific reports, and air monitoring data from industry-wide surveys that demonstrate miners' exposure to respirable crystalline silica associated with a particular product or material or a specific process, task, or activity. At a minimum, mine operators relying on objective data should obtain objective data that is current and accurately characterizes miner exposures to respirable crystalline silica.
The 2024 Silica Final Rule did not adopt the proposed use of objective data to confirm sample results below the action level and discontinue sampling. However, the rule was silent on operator use of objective data to determine which miners are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica. MSHA has consistently recognized that mine operators are aware of the extent and degree of miners' exposures to respirable crystalline silica because they
(
printed page 73068)
have been complying with respirable dust standards for over 40 years. Mine operators are also aware of the occupations, work areas, and work activities where exposures to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level are most likely to occur.
Although not explicit in the 2024 Silica Final Rule, it was MSHA's understanding that operators would use their experience and all available data (including objective data) to determine which miners may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica. In this proposed rule, MSHA acknowledges the benefits of reviewing, analyzing, and determining the applicability of objective data for the purpose of making judgments about which miners are at risk of exposure at or above the action level for respirable crystalline silica. Objective data is valuable for helping mine operators decide where and when to focus sampling efforts, ensuring that monitoring is concentrated on miners who are at greater risk of exposure to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level.
MSHA expects that the proposed change to an “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure does not reduce protections afforded to miners because it would provide more timely and targeted information about respirable crystalline silica concentrations in mining environments. Mine operators would be expected to sample upon recognizing a change in mining conditions, practices, and procedures that could result in exposures at or above the action level, rather than waiting until the next 3-month sampling interval or qualitative assessment.
The proposed change to an “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure modifies specific sampling requirements in § 60.12 related to: (1) the action level trigger, (2) initial sampling and scope, (3) sampling frequency, and (4) discontinuation of sampling. The details of these changes are further described in the following paragraphs.
Action Level Trigger
Under the existing standards, when respirable crystalline silica sample results are at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, operators are required to conduct additional sampling within 3 months. Under the proposed rule, in addition to sampling as frequently as necessary, when miners are exposed at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, mine operators would be required to make approved respirators available before the start of the next work shift in accordance with § 60.14(b) and (c). Miners may choose to wear respirators voluntarily in this instance.
MSHA does not think it is appropriate to require only additional sampling on a set timeframe when sampling indicates exposure at or above the action level. Additional sampling alone does not reduce the health risks for miners. Therefore, the proposed requirement for operators to make approved respirators available by the beginning of the next work shift allows miners to take immediate action to reduce their exposure to respirable crystalline silica. Additionally, operators would be required to sample as frequently as necessary (rather than on a set 3-month timeframe) to determine whether discontinuing the provision of approved respirators is warranted. MSHA expects that these proposed changes would provide greater protection for miners' health than merely requiring additional sampling.
For additional details on the proposed requirement to make approved respirators available, please see the description of paragraph (a)(3) later in this section.
Initial Sampling and Scope
Under the existing standards, mine operators are required to commence sampling by the compliance date for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica. Under the proposed rule, the requirement to commence sampling by the compliance date would remain. Mine operators would conduct sampling “as frequently as necessary” after the compliance date. Also, under the proposed rule, mine operators would need to assess exposures for miners who are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level.
Due to the observed variability of silica sample results and MSHA's proposed application of an error factor on sample results, MSHA now considers that a silica exposure approaching the action level would be the appropriate concentration to commence sampling as frequently as necessary rather than a one-time initial sample of any miner reasonably expected to be exposed to silica. Generally, as silica concentration levels approach the limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) in measured results (which fall below the action level), the accuracy and precision of exposure assessments tend to diminish significantly.
[
2
]
At these lower concentrations, the magnitude of measurement error increases, resulting in less reliable and less consistent data, which leads to decreased confidence in drawing accurate conclusions about exposure levels. Values below the quartz LOD of 2 µg for MNM samples analyzed using the MSHA P-2 method and below the quartz LOD of 3 µg for coal samples analyzed using the MSHA P-7 method are not technologically feasible because they are too small to reliably indicate the presence of respirable crystalline silica.
[
3 4
]
Also, values below the quartz LOQ of 10 µg for both MNM samples analyzed using the MSHA P-2 method and coal samples analyzed using the MSHA P-7 are considered unreliable.
[
5
]
This is because the measured quartz mass below the LOQ, despite usually being detectable, is indistinguishable from instrument noise, resulting in high variability.
Because of these limitations, MSHA has determined that the existing requirement in § 60.12(a)(1) to sample each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica is not actually feasible for those miners whose exposures approach levels at or below the established method's quantification
(
printed page 73069)
limits. The Agency considers that assessing exposures for miners who are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level, taking into account the error factor, will ensure the accuracy and precision of sample results so that miners and mine operators can be confident in measuring exposures to respirable crystalline silica.
By focusing monitoring efforts and resources on areas where silica concentrations approach the action level, the proposed rule better ensures that measurements are more dependable and protective actions are accurately targeted. This approach directs health and safety interventions toward miners facing the most significant risks from respirable crystalline silica exposure, enhancing overall protection.
MSHA expects that this proposed change would not diminish protections for miners because it would focus mine operator and MSHA resources on protecting miners who are at the greatest risk of respirable crystalline silica overexposure.
Sampling at Least Every 3 Months (Frequency)
Under the existing standards, mine operators must continue to sample at least every 3 months when sampling indicates that miner exposures are at or above the action level but at or below the PEL. Under the proposed rule, mine operators would no longer be required to sample at least every 3 months. Instead, mine operators would be required to continue sampling as frequently as necessary to assess the full-shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica to each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level. Sampling frequency would be based on mine-specific conditions and mine operators would be expected to sample upon recognizing a change in mining conditions, processes, or procedures that could result in exposures at or above the action level.
MSHA anticipates that, in some instances, this proposed change would require more frequent operator sampling than the currently prescribed 3-month frequency, and in other instances less frequent operator sampling may be appropriate. For example, MSHA anticipates that operators may identify certain miners and occupations requiring more frequent sampling when mining conditions, processes, or procedures change due to geological conditions or changes in the effectiveness of engineering and administrative controls. MSHA expects that this proposed change would not reduce protection for miners because it requires sampling when conditions, processes, or procedures necessitate, rather than on a set frequency.
Discontinuation of Sampling (Two Consecutive Samplings Below the Action Level)
Under the existing standards, mine operators may discontinue sampling (
i.e.,
stop sampling on a regular 3-month frequency) when two consecutive sample results indicate that miners' exposures are below the action level. Under the proposed rule, the “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure would require that mine operators sample as necessary to assess respirable crystalline silica exposures for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level. This is more protective because there is no “discontinuation” of sampling. Rather, mine operators would continue to evaluate their mines and sample those miners who are exposed or who may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level. MSHA expects that this proposed change enhances miner protection by requiring continual evaluation and sampling based on changing conditions, processes, and procedures at the mine instead of allowing operators to discontinue sampling based on two consecutive samples taken 3 months apart.
In existing paragraph (a)(2), MSHA also proposes to add that sampling shall be conducted “to assess the full shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica.” This proposed amendment is an editorial change since it moves the requirement from existing paragraph (a)(1) to existing paragraph (a)(2).
MSHA proposes to delete existing paragraph (a)(2)(i) in its entirety. Existing paragraph (a)(2)(i) includes a requirement to take at least one additional sampling within 3 months when concentrations are below the action level. This proposed change corresponds with the previously described “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure.
MSHA proposes to delete existing paragraph (a)(2)(ii) in its entirety. Existing paragraph (a)(2)(ii) includes a requirement for additional sampling within 3 months when concentrations are at or above the action level but at or below the PEL. This proposed change corresponds with the previously described “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure.
MSHA proposes to delete existing paragraph (a)(2)(iii) in its entirety. Existing paragraph (a)(2)(iii) includes a requirement for taking corrective actions and sampling pursuant to § 60.12(b) when concentrations are above the PEL. MSHA considers this requirement to be redundant because these requirements are covered under existing § 60.12(b) and § 60.13.
Paragraph (a)(3)
In existing paragraph (a)(3), mine operators are required to continue to sample within 3 months of the previous sampling when the most recent sampling analyses show concentrations at or above the action level but at or below the PEL.
MSHA proposes that when sample results reveal concentrations at or above the action level but at or below the PEL, mine operators must “make approved respirators available before the start of the next work shift in accordance with § 60.14(b) and (c).” This proposal provides miners with additional protection from respirable crystalline silica and thereby limits the health effects associated with respirable crystalline silica exposures until conditions, processes, or procedures change and sampling indicates exposures are below the action level. Because of the recently observed variability in silica sample results and the associated potential health risks, MSHA considers that it is safer to provide miners with respirators in conjunction with conducting sampling as frequently as necessary to protect miners' health. MSHA notes that the proposal does not allow mine operators to simply provide respirators while neglecting other protective measures. Mine operators would still be required to implement engineering and administrative controls to maintain silica levels below the PEL and conduct sampling as frequently as necessary. However, instead of relying solely on sampling, the Agency aims to equip miners with respirators as an additional and immediate protective measure because exposure levels at or above the action level indicate that miners might be working in concentrations near the PEL. This approach provides an added layer of protection aligned with the hierarchy of controls and ensures that miners are effectively safeguarded against harmful silica exposures.
This proposed change is also consistent with existing coal standards for respirable coal mine dust (RCMD) in §§ 70.208(e)(1), 70.209(c)(1), 71.206(h)(1) and 90.207(c)(1). Under
(

these existing standards, coal mine operators must make approved respiratory equipment available when one valid RCMD sample, out of the 5 or 15 samples that coal mine operators routinely collect during quarterly sampling, exceeds the excessive concentration value (ECV). In this case, the mine operator is considered to be compliant with the standards because the number of samples in excess of the ECV is less than the number of samples that are noncompliant with the standard. MSHA considers this situation analogous to when mine operators' respirable crystalline silica sample results reach the action level under this proposed rule, as they are not out of compliance with the PEL, but would be required to provide respirators to protect miners' health as exposure levels approach the PEL.
In existing paragraph (a)(3), MSHA also proposes to change the requirement from “continue to sample within 3 months of the previous sampling” to “until sampling indicates exposures are below the action level” in proposed paragraph (a)(3). This proposed change corresponds to the previously described “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure.
Paragraph (a)(4)
In existing paragraph (a)(4), mine operators may discontinue sampling when two consecutive samplings indicate that miner exposures are below the action level. Existing paragraph (a)(4) also states that the second sampling must be taken after the operator receives the results of the prior sampling but no sooner than 7 days after the prior sampling was conducted.
MSHA proposes to remove existing requirements in paragraph (a)(4) in their entirety because it is unnecessary. In the interest of protecting miners' health, MSHA would no longer allow mine operators to discontinue sampling (see the discussion of discontinuation of sampling presented in the description of paragraph (a)(2) earlier in this section).
MSHA proposes to add a requirement for mine operators to immediately report all sample results conducted pursuant to proposed paragraph (a)(2) that show concentrations above the PEL, to the appropriate District Manager or other MSHA official designated by the District Manager. This proposed change is editorial, as it moves the requirement from existing paragraph (b) to paragraph (a)(4). MSHA also notes that when sample results show concentrations above the PEL, the mine operator would still be required to make approved respirators available to affected miners before the start of the next work shift under existing § 60.13(a)(1). MSHA is not proposing to change the respirator requirement in § 60.13(a)(1).
b. Paragraph (b)
Existing § 60.12(b),

requires that where the most recent sampling indicates that miner exposures are above the PEL, the mine operator must conduct sampling after corrective actions are taken, and until sampling indicates that miner exposures are at or below the PEL. The existing requirements do not define a specific sampling frequency when concentrations are above the PEL, but MSHA anticipates that operators will sample once they have taken corrective actions and continue to sample as frequently as needed until corrective actions have resolved the overexposure. Additionally, MSHA proposes to amend paragraph (b) to add the requirement that once operator sampling (conducted as frequently as necessary) indicates that miner exposures are at or below the PEL, the mine operator would be required to contact the MSHA District Manager or any other MSHA official designated by the MSHA District Manager.
This proposed follow-up notification requirement ensures that MSHA is informed once the operator has successfully implemented sufficient corrective actions to reduce concentrations below the PEL. Requiring timely communication after exposure levels are reduced enhances miner safety and health by allowing MSHA to verify that effective protective measures are in place and maintained to prevent future overexposures. Pursuant to the proposed change in § 60.12(b), once the mine operator achieves a sample result below the PEL and reports the sample result to MSHA, the mine operator would not be required to continue reporting every subsequent sample result indicating exposures are at or below the PEL.

Existing § 60.12(f) requires operators to follow specific requirements for respirable crystalline silica sampling. For example, samples must be collected using respirable-particle-size-selective samplers that conform to the ISO 7708:1995(E) standard. Operators must also select a laboratory for analysis of their respirable crystalline silica samples that is accredited to the ISO/IEC 17025 standard. In addition, operators must select a laboratory that evaluates all samples collected and submitted for analysis for compliance with existing MSHA standards related to respirable crystalline silica exposure, using a respirable crystalline silica analytical method specified by one of three entities: MSHA, NIOSH, or OSHA. MSHA does not propose to amend these requirements.
However, MSHA recognizes that any measurement process has inherent variabilities caused by sampling and analytical error. Such variabilities cause individual measurements to deviate above or below a true value by a random but statistically quantifiable amount. The magnitude of the deviation or error depends on the sampling method and analysis technique used. The accuracy of a measurement depends on both precision and bias (NIOSH, 1995). Precision refers to consistency or repeatability of results, while bias refers to a systematic error that is present in every measurement. The NIOSH Accuracy Criterion establishes a standard for acceptance of dependable analytical methods that accurately reflect real workplace exposures. It requires that measurements consistently fall within a specified percentage of the true concentration, setting a maximum acceptable limit for precision and bias errors combined.
For unbiased sampling and analytical methods, a standard statistic called the coefficient of variation (CV) is used to determine if the method meets the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion. The CV, which is expressed as either a fraction (
e.g.,
0.05) or a percentage (
e.g.,
5 percent), quantifies measurement accuracy for an unbiased method. An unbiased method meets the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion if the “true” CV is no more than 0.128 (12.8 percent). However, because it is not possible to determine the true CV with 100 percent confidence, the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion requires 95 percent confidence that measurements by the method fall within 25 percent of the true concentration 95 percent of the time. Stated in mathematically equivalent terms, an unbiased method meets the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion if there is 95 percent confidence that the true CV is less than or equal to 0.128 (12.8 percent).
For MSHA silica sampling, the MSHA laboratory calculates the relative standard deviation (RSD) to define the CV for health enforcement samples. The RSD is also known as the total coefficient of variation (CV
total
). For respirable crystalline silica analysis, MSHA calculates the RSD using three components: (1) analysis precision, (2) sampling pump (flow rate) error, and (3) sampler error.
MSHA analyzes respirable crystalline silica samples using two primary analytical methods: (1) the MSHA P-2 method,
P-2: X-Ray Diffraction Determination Of Quartz And Cristobalite In Respirable Metal/Nonmetal Mine Dust
(analysis by X-ray diffraction, XRD) for MNM mines, and (2) the MSHA P-7 method,
P-7: Determination Of Quartz In Respirable Coal Mine Dust By Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
(analysis by infrared spectroscopy, FTIR or IR) for coal mines. Both of MSHA's silica methods pass the NIOSH Accuracy Criterion; that is, they measure exposures within 25 percent of the true value 95 percent of the time. The MSHA P-2 method has a higher RSD (11 percent analytical error) compared to the MSHA P-7 method (5.3 percent analytical error).

3. Section 60.14—Respiratory Protection
Existing § 60.14 establishes the requirements for the use of respiratory protection for respirable crystalline silica.
a. Paragraph (a)
Existing § 60.14(a),
Temporary use of respirators at metal and nonmetal mines,
states that when MNM miners must work in concentrations of respirable crystalline silica above the PEL while engineering controls are being developed and implemented or it is necessary by the nature of the work involved, the mine operator shall use respiratory protection as a temporary measure.
MSHA proposes to amend paragraph (a) to remove the term “temporary measure” and replace it with “miners may work for reasonable periods of time.” Thus, proposed paragraph (a) would allow affected miners to work for a reasonable period of time using respiratory protection in concentrations of respirable crystalline silica above the PEL while engineering controls are being developed and implemented, or it is necessary by the nature of the work involved. MSHA also proposes to remove the word “temporary” from the paragraph (a) heading to be consistent with the removal of the term “temporary measure” from the text of the paragraph. MSHA proposes to make these changes for clarity.
After publication of the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA became aware that many mine operators interpreted “temporary” to mean a fixed period of time. Additionally, several stakeholders requested that MSHA clarify the meaning of “temporary” and specify time limitations.
In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, the Agency intended for “temporary” use of respirators in exposures above the PEL to mean miners could work in exposures above the PEL for reasonable periods of time depending on the work being performed, or when developing and implementing engineering controls (
89 FR 28336
). For example, MSHA expects that respirators could be used for a longer period of time in exposures above the PEL if installing several, complex engineering controls; however, MSHA would expect that respirators would likely be worn for a shorter duration in exposures above the PEL when installing fewer, less complex engineering controls. Another instance where the Agency would anticipate longer respirator use is when a miner conducts scheduled maintenance on baghouse filters, as opposed to making
(
printed page 73074)
a quick entry into the baghouse for a visual equipment inspection.
Other examples where respirators could be used for reasonable periods of time are when miners are tasked with cleaning a large material spill or circumstances where other applicable laws require a process to be confined to prevent releases of material to the environment, and working within such spaces may necessitate a respirator to control exposure. Also, transient events such as high wind might increase concentrations temporarily, and respirator use might be appropriate to manage exposure in such situations.
Thus, MSHA proposes the change in existing § 60.14(a) to clarify for stakeholders that the use of respirators is not dependent on a specific time limit but is instead determined to be reasonable based on the nature of the work affected miners are performing while wearing respirators given the variability of mining processes, activities, and commodities that are mined. In addition, MNM mine operators should be familiar with the proposed change since the statement that “miners may work for reasonable periods of time” if they are protected by appropriate respiratory protective equipment when working in concentrations of respirable crystalline silica above the PEL was in the previous standard in §§ 56.5005 and 57.5005 before the 2024 Silica Final Rule. The proposed changes would continue to limit the use of respirators while affected miners work in respirable crystalline silica exposures above the PEL, and the Agency expects that the proposed changes would not result in any reduction in safety for miners.
b. Paragraph (c)
Existing § 60.14(c),
Respiratory protection requirements at all mines,
sets forth the requirements for respiratory protection at MNM and coal mines. Existing paragraph (c)(2) requires that when approved respirators are used, mine operators must have a written respiratory protection program in accordance with ASTM F3387-19, “Standard Practice for Respiratory Protection.”
MSHA proposes to revise paragraph (c)(2) to require mine operators to comply with the respiratory protection requirements from OSHA in
29 CFR 1910.134
(OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard). MSHA would adopt by reference the requirements of
29 CFR 1910.134
,
Respiratory protection,
in this section in proposed paragraphs (c)(3)(i) and (ii), with two exclusions.
The first proposed exclusion in paragraph (c)(3)(i) would be for
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(2)(iii)
, the altitude exceptions for respirators for Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health (IDLH) atmospheres. Under
29 CFR 1910.134 (d)(2)(iii)
, all oxygen-deficient atmospheres are considered IDLH. OSHA permits exceptions based on altitude ranges which are listed in Table II to paragraph (c). Instead of adopting these altitude exceptions, MSHA proposes to continue its longstanding practice of classifying all atmospheres below 19.5 percent oxygen as IDLH and would not permit altitude adjustments for oxygen concentrations. MSHA proposes not to adopt this exception because mining operations are inherently unpredictable, with conditions that can rapidly become life-threatening. Additionally, MSHA's approach to IDLH atmospheres is consistent across all mines and is easily implemented by mine operators to ensure miners' safety and health. For a more detailed discussion of this IDLH exclusion, see
Section IV. C. Updating MSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard by Adopting by Reference OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
.
The second proposed exclusion in paragraph (c)(3)(ii) would be for the record retention period for medical evaluations under OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134(m)(1)
, which is for the duration of the miner's employment plus 30 years. MSHA is proposing to exclude the OSHA retention period because it is not enforced under
29 CFR 1910.134
but rather
29 CFR 1910.1020
; therefore, the record retention period would not be adopted by reference in this proposal.
c. Paragraph (d)
Under a new proposed paragraph (d), MSHA would add a record retention requirement for medical evaluations of miners to determine a miner's ability to wear a respirator. This is not a new record retention requirement because both ASTM F3387-19 and the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard require retention of medical evaluation records as part of a written respiratory protection program. MSHA is proposing the record retention requirement in this section so that mine operators would not have to follow OSHA's record retention requirements in
29 CFR 1910.1020
. Thus, in proposed paragraph (d), MSHA would require the mine operator to maintain a record of the medical evaluation received from the physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP) or specialist under paragraph (c) of this section.
d. Voluntary Respirator Use
Under proposed § 60.12(a)(3), mine operators would be required to provide approved respirators for voluntary respirator use to miners exposed at or above the action level but at or below the PEL. The current respiratory protection standard, ASTM F3387-19, does not address voluntary respirator use. MSHA has determined that the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard is more protective and better suited for the mining industry for multiple reasons, including the fact that it explicitly addresses voluntary respirator use and requires operators to implement certain elements of a written respiratory protection program to ensure safe voluntary respirator use. The Agency expects that changing from ASTM F3387-19 to OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard would enhance protections for miners who voluntarily wear respirators when permitted by the operator.
MSHA also understands that the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would provide other safety advantages over the ASTM standard. For example, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard includes a straightforward fixed threshold for oxygen deficiency and a provision for providing powered air purifying respirators (PAPRs) to miners who are not medically cleared for negative-pressure respirator use (
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(6)(ii)
). Further, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard is freely available to the public in the CFR and on the OSHA website, and OSHA has published an extensive catalog of compliance assistance materials to aid workers and employers with understanding the standard. Adoption of the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would reduce administrative complexity and potential for confusion at mining facilities that fall under both OSHA and MSHA jurisdictions.
The existing respiratory protection standard is ASTM F3387-19, a voluntary consensus standard published by ASTM International in 2019. MSHA incorporated the requirements of ASTM F3387-19 into the Agency's standards in the 2024 Silica Final Rule because it provides detailed information on respirator selection that is based on NIOSH's extensive experience in testing and certifying respirators for occupational use as well as OSHA's research and regulatory development in respiratory protection. Thus, in MSHA's experience, the provisions of the ASTM F3387-19 standard and OSHA's requirements in
29 CFR 1910.134
are largely equivalent with respect to
(
printed page 73075)
respiratory protection program practices. For a detailed discussion of OSHA's respiratory protection requirements in
29 CFR 1910.134
, see
Section IV.C, Updating MSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard by Adopting by Reference OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
.
One area that ASTM F3387-19 does not address, and which OSHA's respiratory protection requirements do address, is voluntary respirator use when exposures are below the PEL and miners are not required by the operator to wear a respirator. MSHA's existing requirements do not specify what actions mine operators must take to prevent health or safety hazards when miners choose to wear respirators voluntarily.
Under the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard, respiratory protection is required in any workplace where respirators are necessary to protect the health of the employee or whenever respirators are required by the employer. For example, if a mine operator requires a respirator to be worn in a particular area, even when the miner is working in exposures determined to be below the respirable crystalline silica standard or other recognized exposure limits, any respirator use (including a P100 filtering facepiece respirator) would not be considered voluntary. In this instance, the miner would need to be enrolled in a written respiratory protection program meeting the requirements of
29 CFR 1910.134
.
If respiratory protection is not required and the mine operator does not advise the miner to use a respirator, but the miner requests to use a respirator, the respirator use is considered voluntary under the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard, whether the respirator is provided by the mine operator or the miner is permitted to use their own respirator. If the mine operator determines that voluntary respirator use will not in itself create a hazard and determines respirator use is permissible, the mine operator must provide respirator users with a copy of Appendix D to § 1910.134 titled,
(Mandatory) Information for Employees Using Respirators When Not Required Under the Standard
(Appendix D).
Generally, for voluntary respirator use, Appendix D instructs the user to:
1. Choose respirators that have been certified by NIOSH;
2. Follow the manufacturer's instructions provided with the respirator including information on how to properly use the respirator and maintain and care for the respirator, and also follow warnings on the limitations of the respirator;
3. Wear a respirator appropriate for the contaminant to be protected against; and
4. Keep track of the user's respirator so that the user does not mistakenly use someone else's respirator.
Under
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)(i)
, the mine operator would be required to provide the advisory information on respirators presented in Appendix D to any miners who voluntarily use respirators. MSHA agrees with this approach and expects that Appendix D would provide essential guidance for miners who voluntarily wear respirators to ensure their proper and effective use.
Under these voluntary use conditions, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators to develop a written respiratory protection program and implement those elements necessary to ensure that any miner using a respirator voluntarily is medically able to do so (
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(1)(ii)
), and that the respirator is cleaned, stored, and maintained so that its use does not present a health hazard to the user (
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(1)(v)
). Voluntary use of respirators does not require all elements of the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard to be included in the written program. Mine operators would not be required to include in a written respiratory protection program those miners who voluntarily use only filtering facepiece respirators (
e.g.,
N95 and P100 filtering facepiece respirators).
MSHA proposes adopting the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard by reference for four reasons.
First, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard reflects current respirator technology and best practices for effective respiratory protection. It is freely available to the public in the CFR and on OSHA's website, including guidance on fit testing, medical evaluation, and voluntary use.
Second, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard comprehensively covers all aspects of respiratory protection programs, from establishment through implementation and evaluation. It addresses program administration, standard operating procedures, medical evaluation, respirator selection, training, fit testing, and respirator maintenance, inspection, and storage. Based on MSHA's experience, adopting the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would help mine operators establish and implement effective respiratory protection programs to protect miners. This adoption would enhance miner safety and health since many mine operators already know how to apply the OSHA standard to their mine-specific conditions.
Third, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard recognizes voluntary use of respirators. The standard requires employers to provide information on the voluntary use of respirators (Appendix D to § 1910.134) and develop and implement certain elements of a written respiratory protection program to ensure the safe and effective voluntary use of respirators to protect miner health and safety. Therefore, the standard does not discourage mine operators from allowing the voluntary use of respirators for added protection.
Fourth, OSHA has compiled extensive, freely available general guidance for employers, respirator program administrators, and respirator users to ensure the effective development and administration of respiratory protection programs. The guidance includes web pages, and online tools related to respiratory protection created by OSHA and other agencies, such as NIOSH. For example, OSHA provides employers with guidance on selecting appropriate respirators for workers using Assigned Protection Factors (APFs) and Maximum Use Concentrations (MUCs). Additionally, OSHA's Small Entity Compliance Guide offers a detailed step-by-step resource, featuring checklists and frequently asked questions that enhance both worker and employer understanding of the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard.
[
21
]
Under this proposed rule, mine operators requiring respiratory protection would need to ensure the proper selection, fit testing, medical evaluation, training, use, and maintenance of NIOSH-approved respirators in accordance with
29 CFR 1910.134
, so that no miner is exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level.
MSHA recognizes that OSHA is currently considering revising the medical evaluation requirements for certain types of respirators in the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard. On July 1, 2025, OSHA published the proposed rule titled “
Amending the Medical Evaluation Requirements in the Respiratory Protection Standard for Certain Types of Respirators.”
90 FR 28463
. OSHA's proposed rule, if finalized, would remove medical evaluation requirements for employees
(
printed page 73076)
required to use filtering facepiece respirators and loose-fitting powered air purifying respirators.
90 FR 28471-28472
. MSHA will monitor this rulemaking and may consider whether additional modifications to the standard or supplemental mining-specific requirements would be necessary for unique circumstances found in mining environments.
4. Section 60.15—Medical Surveillance
Existing § 60.15 requires MNM mine operators to provide medical surveillance at no cost to miners.
MSHA is proposing to amend the medical surveillance requirements in existing § 60.15 to: (1) change from mandatory to voluntary medical examinations for miners new to the MNM industry; (2) require mandatory medical examinations for all sampled miners, both MNM and coal miners, when the sampled miner is exposed above the PEL, as indicated by an MSHA sample;
[
22
]
(3) modify the frequency of voluntary medical surveillance for MNM miners; (4) remove the requirement for reporting chest X-ray classifications to NIOSH; and (5) remove the requirement for the PLHCP to provide any recommended limitations on the miner's use of respirators in the PLHCP's written medical opinion.
Existing § 60.15 is titled
Medical surveillance for metal and nonmetal mines.
However, one provision of proposed § 60.15 would apply to both coal mine operators and MNM mine operators. Accordingly, MSHA proposes to change the title of § 60.15 to “
Medical surveillance.
”
a. Paragraph (a)
Existing § 60.15(a),
Medical surveillance,
requires MNM mine operators to provide each MNM miner medical examinations. Existing paragraph (a)(2) outlines the requirements of the medical examination including: medical and work history, physical examination with special emphasis on the respiratory system, chest X-ray, and pulmonary function test. The medical and work history covers a miner's present and past work exposures, illnesses, history of smoking including e-cigarette use and vaping, and any symptoms indicating respirable crystalline silica related diseases and compromised lung function.
Under this proposed rule, MSHA would revise § 60.15(a) to apply to all mine operators, both MNM and coal. The Agency is proposing this change to paragraph (a) because § 60.15(c) would require mandatory medical examinations for all sampled miners, both MNM and coal miners, when the sampled miner (or miners that were part of a representative sample) is exposed above the PEL, as indicated by an MSHA sample.
[
23
]
When a personal breathing-zone air sample result is above the PEL, the mandatory medical examination would be required for the sampled miner. When an occupational environmental sample result is above the PEL, the mandatory medical examination would be required for all sampled miners who rotated through that occupation on the sampled shift.
b. Paragraph (b)
Existing § 60.15(b),
Voluntary medical examinations,
requires MNM mine operators to provide the opportunity to all MNM miners employed at the mine to have voluntary medical examinations during an initial 12-month period and at least every 5 years after the end of the initial 12-month period. MSHA proposes to make an editorial change in the § 60.15(b) paragraph heading to
Voluntary metal and nonmetal medical examinations.
Additionally, MSHA proposes to add the words “metal and nonmetal” to this paragraph to specify that the requirement to offer voluntary medical examinations would continue to apply only to MNM mine operators. This clarification is necessary due to the proposed removal of “for metal and nonmetal mines” in the title of this section.
MSHA proposes to amend § 60.15(b)(1) to expand the initial period for offering medical examinations to a 5-year period for all MNM miners employed at a mine. The existing requirement in § 60.15(b)(2) for MNM mine operators to make periodic medical examinations available at least every 5 years after the end of the initial period in § 60.15(b)(1) is unchanged. MSHA expects that this proposed amendment would allow more miners to successfully participate in the medical surveillance program for the following reasons.
In the preamble to the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA carefully considered comments related to availability of NIOSH-certified B Readers and issues with access to a PLHCP or specialist qualified to perform the medical surveillance examinations, especially for mines in rural locations. MSHA determined that MNM mine operators should not experience any significant issues identifying a PLHCP or specialist to conduct medical examinations and emphasizes that the 2024 Silica Final Rule allows flexibility by not mandating that the medical examinations be conducted by full-time health care professionals employed by mine operators.
MSHA also determined that technological advancements eliminating the need for geographic proximity between patients and technicians such as NIOSH-certified B Readers, combined with the widespread availability of X-ray testing, make obtaining X-rays and having the results classified by NIOSH-certified B Readers technologically feasible. MSHA found that digital X-ray technology enables chest X-rays to be submitted electronically to remotely located NIOSH-certified B Readers for classification and interpretation. Following consultation with NIOSH, MSHA concluded that NIOSH-certified B Readers with remote reading capabilities are available in sufficient numbers to satisfy the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements. Therefore, MSHA determined that the limited number of NIOSH-certified B Readers in certain geographic locations will not be an obstacle for MNM operators. MSHA further concluded that any increase in demand for these services can be addressed by providers.
Since the 2024 Silica Final Rule's publication, MSHA has become aware that state medical licensing rules could impact the availability of NIOSH-certified B Readers in some states. MSHA is now aware that NIOSH-certified B Readers with remote reading capabilities must be medically licensed in the state where they practice remotely. Therefore, a NIOSH-certified B Reader with remote reading capabilities does not guarantee that miners in other states can access that NIOSH-certified B Reader. MSHA is aware that this could limit access for mine operators and miners attempting to complete initial medical examinations within the 12-month period required in existing § 60.15(b)(1). Also, MSHA is aware of the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact, an agreement among participating states and territories designed to streamline the licensing process for physicians who want to practice in multiple states. However, it is unclear how the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact has affected
(
printed page 73077)
the number of multi-state licensed NIOSH-certified B Readers.
MSHA has data on the number of NIOSH-certified B Readers located in each state. However, MSHA does not have information on NIOSH-certified B Readers licensed to practice in additional states. The available information indicates that many states with significant MNM mining employment have few in-state NIOSH-certified B Readers. MSHA requests additional data on the sufficiency of NIOSH-certified B Reader availability to meet the needs of MNM mine operators providing voluntary medical examinations.
In addition, MSHA is aware that demand for critical minerals is expected to continue to increase.
[
24
]
This would likely result in an increase in the number of MNM mines and in the number of miners at existing mines, which would therefore increase the number of MNM miners seeking voluntary medical examinations. MSHA's proposed change in § 60.15(b)(1) to expand the initial period for offering medical examinations to a 5-year period for all MNM miners employed at a mine would smooth out demand over the course of 5 years instead of an initial 12-month period, ensuring mine operators' and miners' access to PLHCPs, certified specialists, and NIOSH-certified B Readers.
MSHA expects that this would facilitate miner access to medical examinations under the existing § 60.15(b)(2) requirement for MNM mine operators to make periodic medical examinations available at least every 5 years after the initial medical examinations. By extending the initial period for medical examinations in § 60.15(b)(1), miners who may otherwise encounter resource constraints when accessing PLHCPs, certified specialists, and NIOSH-certified B Readers under § 60.15(b)(2) due to the demand created when numerous miners seek these same resources within a 12-month timeframe, should find it easier to obtain access to those resources.
Miners should use the information obtained from medical surveillance to establish a baseline for their health status and may use information from periodic medical examinations to make informed decisions regarding their health.
MSHA proposes to revise § 60.15 by adding a new paragraph designated as paragraph (b)(3). The proposed requirements in new paragraph (b)(3) are substantially similar to the requirements for new miners in existing § 60.15(c),
Mandatory medical examinations;
however, medical examinations for MNM miners new to the mining industry would be voluntary instead of mandatory under this proposed change. The proposed addition of new paragraph (b)(3) includes: (i) an initial examination no later than 60 days after starting employment, (ii) a follow-up examination within 3 years of the initial examination, and (iii) a follow-up examination by a specialist no later than 2 years after the follow-up examination in proposed (b)(3)(ii) if the X-ray shows evidence of pneumoconiosis or the spirometry examination indicates evidence of decreased lung function.
MSHA expects that this change would not result in a reduction of safety because MNM miners new to the mining industry would still be provided with the opportunity to voluntarily participate in medical surveillance, with the opportunity for a baseline medical examination provided within 60 days of beginning work in the mining industry and the opportunity for at least one medical examination every 5 years after the initial medical examination. This proposed change would help address concerns about the availability of NIOSH-certified B Readers to ensure those miners, both MNM and coal, exposed above the PEL can access the mandatory exams in proposed § 60.15(c). In the Agency's experience, the coal miners' medical surveillance program (
30 CFR 72.100
) is appropriate to provide coal miners with information needed for early detection of silica-related disease.
MSHA requests comments on whether the Agency should tie voluntary medical examinations for MNM miners to exposure levels at or above the action level. Please provide comments on the potential benefits and challenges of implementing such a measure and its effectiveness in enhancing miner health and safety.
MSHA is considering allowing employers to use pre-employment medical exams required by the mine operator as a condition of employment to satisfy the requirements for initial medical exams under existing § 60.15(c)(1), which is § 60.15(c)(3)(i) in this proposed rule. The changes would allow pre-employment exams that fulfill the requirements of the initial medical exam in existing § 60.15(a)(2) and existing § 60.15(d)(1) to fulfill the requirements of the initial medical exam. The mine operator, or their selected PLHCP or specialist, would provide miners with an authorization form stating that miners' participation in the medical surveillance portion of the exam is voluntary and explaining that detailed results from the medical surveillance portion of the exam would only be provided to the miner. The miner would need to authorize the voluntary medical examination. MSHA anticipates this dual-purpose exam structure would reduce time miners must spend traveling for medical exams and mitigate issues related to access to a PLHCP or specialist qualified to perform the medical surveillance examinations, especially for mines in locations with limited access to health care. MSHA requests comments on adding provisions that would allow pre-employment exams to serve the dual purpose of fit-for-duty examinations and medical surveillance. In particular, MSHA is interested in the potential benefits for miners and the potential cost implications for mine operators (including estimates of increases in paperwork costs). For a more detailed discussion of paperwork costs, see
Section X. Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995.
c. Paragraph (c)
Existing § 60.15(c),
Mandatory medical examinations,
requires MNM mine operators to provide mandatory medical examinations for miners who are beginning work in the mining industry for the first time. As discussed, the proposed addition of § 60.15(b)(3) would make medical examinations voluntary for MNM miners who begin work in the mining industry for the first time.
Proposed § 60.15(c),
Mandatory medical examinations for all miners exposed above the PEL,
would require mandatory medical examinations for all sampled miners (both MNM and coal) who are exposed above the PEL based on an MSHA sample, within 60 days of receiving the sample results, except for miners who have received a medical examination within the past 2 years under § 60.15 or in accordance with
30 CFR 72.100
.
This proposed revision would reflect a risk-based approach to medical surveillance because it involves identifying and prioritizing both MNM and coal miners who have overexposures to respirable crystalline silica for medical examinations. MSHA expects that miners, both MNM and coal miners, who have confirmed overexposures to respirable crystalline silica face the greatest risk of developing silica-related diseases and, therefore, are most in need of mandatory medical examinations. MSHA is aware that a
(
printed page 73078)
single examination at the time of an over-exposure would be unlikely to identify silicosis unless the miner had acute silicosis or the miner had a previous history of exposure over years; however, a mandatory examination would provide a baseline for later comparison and would help indicate disease progression.
MSHA emphasizes that coal mine operators would continue to provide medical examinations for coal miners under
30 CFR 72.100
, which is unchanged by this proposal. The proposed change in this section would apply to coal mine operators only when coal miners have been exposed to respirable crystalline silica above the PEL, as confirmed by an MSHA sample. In this instance, coal mine operators would be required to provide medical examinations in accordance with this section (§ 60.15). Coal mine operators must separately comply with existing § 72.100 for all other required medical examinations in that section for coal miners.
The proposed change to a risk-based mandatory medical examination structure based on exposures above the PEL resolves the concerns raised by stakeholders about the 60-day timeframe for when medical examinations would be required to be offered and the capacity of PLHCPs and NIOSH-certified B Readers to meet the demands for those medical examinations in the existing standards in § 60.15(c). MSHA expects that this proposal addresses concerns about availability of NIOSH-certified B Readers for medical examinations by providing more time for initial voluntary exams and targeting mandatory exams for those miners at greatest risk,
i.e.,
miners with known exposures above the PEL. Furthermore, the Agency expects this proposal to increase safety for all miners compared to the 2024 Silica Final Rule by requiring all miners to get a mandatory medical examination when exposed to respirable crystalline silica above the PEL.
As described in the 2024 Silica Final Rule, commenters requested that the Agency consider a risk-based approach for medical surveillance in which examinations would be triggered for miners exposed to respirable crystalline silica above a specific level of exposure. One commenter stated that the need for medical surveillance depends on the extent of workplace silica exposures and must be coordinated with industrial hygiene exposure monitoring results. Representatives of industry also supported a risk-based approach with a threshold or exposure trigger for medical surveillance. MSHA's proposed change to mandatory medical examinations for miners with exposures above the PEL addresses these stakeholder concerns by requiring mine operators to provide mandatory medical examinations to all miners with documented overexposures based on MSHA samples. This approach ensures that medical examinations occur closer in time to confirmed overexposures, enabling earlier detection of potential health effects and more timely medical intervention, which can lead to improved health outcomes compared to examinations conducted on an arbitrary schedule potentially years after an overexposure event.
MSHA expects that these proposed mandatory medical surveillance requirements would enhance protections for miners because the mandatory medical examinations would be required for all sampled miners who are overexposed, including both miners new to the industry and experienced miners. Additionally, the proposed changes would extend these protections to both MNM and coal miners. The information obtained from a mandatory medical examination for sampled miners exposed to respirable crystalline silica levels above the PEL would allow miners to make informed decisions about their health.
