C. Updating MSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard by Adopting by Reference OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
MSHA is proposing to update the Agency's existing respiratory protection standard to help safeguard the life and health of all miners exposed to respirable airborne hazards at MNM and coal mines. The proposed rule would adopt by reference OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard,
29 CFR 1910.134
, in existing §§ 56.5005T, 57.5005T, 60.14, and 72.710. OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard mandates a comprehensive respiratory protection program whenever respirators are needed for hazardous airborne contaminants, covering respirator selection, medical clearance, fit testing, training, proper use procedures, maintenance, and regular program evaluation to ensure worker safety. A formal respiratory protection program is required by OSHA whenever respirators are necessary to protect employee health or whenever respirators are required by the employer. This includes both air purifying respirators (
e.g.,
filters, cartridges, canisters) and atmosphere-supplying respirators (
e.g.,
self-contained breathing apparatus, airline).
OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard is widely recognized by experts, industry leaders, government, and professional associations as an effective standard for protecting workers' health. The standard requires employers to select NIOSH-approved respirators when effective engineering controls are not feasible, or while they are being implemented. Respirator selection is based on hazard assessments (
e.g.,
contaminant type, concentration, PEL), work-site conditions, respirator limitations, fit testing, and OSHA's Assigned Protection Factors (APFs), ensuring respirators adequately protect workers while allowing for job performance. In sum, the OSHA standard comprehensively addresses all necessary aspects of a respiratory protection program to ensure its effectiveness.
Since its comprehensive revision in 1998 (
63 FR 1152
, Jan. 8, 1998), OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard has been updated several times to reflect advancements in respirator technology and industry best practices.
[
25
]
In particular, in 2006, OSHA revised its respiratory protection standard to incorporate definitions and requirements for APFs and Maximum Use Concentrations (MUCs), providing employers clear guidelines for selecting respirators based on contaminant levels and required protection.
71 FR 50121
,
50122
, Aug. 24, 2006. Most recently in 2019, OSHA updated Appendix A to § 1910.134,
Fit Testing Procedures,
to incorporate advances in quantitative fit testing technology
84 FR 50739
,
50755
, Sept. 26, 2019.
In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA updated the Agency's respiratory protection standard by incorporating by reference the ASTM F3387-19 standard because it provides mine operators with information and guidance on the proper selection, use, and maintenance of respirators. The ASTM F3387-19 standard replaced the American National Standards Institute's ANSI Z88.2-1969, “Practices for Respiratory Protection” (ANSI Z88.2-1969), which was the Agency's respiratory protection standard for more than 40 years.
During the public comment period for the silica proposed rule, one commenter recommended that MSHA align its proposed respiratory protection requirements with OSHA's requirements in
29 CFR 1910.134
. Also, during meetings with stakeholders to discuss the 2024 Silica Final Rule's implementation, many operators stated that they already followed OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard requirements at their mines or in other areas of their operations. Operators with dual MSHA and OSHA jurisdiction raised concerns about having to maintain two separate written respiratory protection programs: one program to meet MSHA's requirements under ASTM F3387-19 and another program to meet OSHA's requirements in
29 CFR 1910.134
.
In response to comments received on the silica proposed rule suggesting that MSHA adopt the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard, MSHA stated that ASTM F3387-19 references OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard including APFs and MUCs, and fit testing.
89 FR 28339
,
28352
. Furthermore, MSHA observed that many operators, in particular larger mine operators, had already implemented many OSHA requirements in their respiratory protection programs, which are substantially similar to the requirements in ASTM F3387-19.
89 FR 28339
. Also, MSHA responded that the Agency considers the mining industry to be already familiar with many requirements in ASTM F3387-19 because of its familiarity with OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard requirements.
Id.
Like the ASTM F3387-19 standard, OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard contains requirements for: program administration; worksite-specific procedures; respirator selection; employee training; fit testing; user seal checks; medical evaluations; respirator use; respirator cleaning, maintenance, and repair; and other similar provisions. However, MSHA is aware that ASTM F3387-19 and OSHA's
29 CFR 1910.134
requirements differ in some areas such as voluntary respirator use, oxygen-deficiency evaluation, and PAPR accommodations for employees who are not medically cleared for negative-pressure respirator use.
During stakeholder meetings to discuss the implementation of the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA emphasized that any miner who wears a respirator must be enrolled in the mine's respiratory protection program. Some stakeholders raised the issue of voluntary respirator use, and the Agency's response was that a miner who uses a respirator voluntarily would have to be enrolled in the full respiratory protection program according to the requirements of the ASTM F3387-19 standard. Some stakeholders asked if this applied to miners who use dust masks (
e.g.,
N95 filtering facepiece respirators) to protect against nuisance dust. MSHA's response was yes, this applied to all voluntary use of respirators since ASTM F3387-19 did not distinguish between required use and voluntary use.
In light of these questions and issues, MSHA has reconsidered the ASTM F3387-19 standard's lack of voluntary use provisions. The Agency has determined that without voluntary use requirements, some miners may not be permitted to use certain respirators voluntarily because of the burden of enrolling these miners in a complete respiratory protection program. MSHA did not intend for the incorporation by reference of ASTM F3387-19 to discourage miners from voluntarily wearing certain respirators such as dust masks. The Agency expects that adopting by reference OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
would protect the health and safety of miners, both those who are required to wear respirators for reasonable periods of time while working in exposures above the PEL and those who choose to voluntarily wear respirators, such as dust masks, in non-hazardous environments.
OSHA's voluntary use requirements in
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)
apply when employers allow employees to use respirators when such use is not
(
printed page 73083)
required by the employer or by the standard. Section
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)(i)
states that employers must first determine that the respirator use will not in itself create a hazard. If the employer allows voluntary respirator use, section
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)(i)
requires the employer to provide the employee with the information contained in Appendix D to 29 CFR 1910.134, titled “
Information for Employees Using Respirators When Not Required Under the Standard.”
OSHA has determined that all the protections in the respiratory protection standard are not necessary in situations where respirator use is not required,
i.e.,
voluntary use when working in exposures below the PEL. In cases where an employee is voluntarily using a respirator, the employer must implement some of the elements of a written respiratory protection program such as the medical evaluation component of the program and the cleaning, storage, and maintenance provisions, as applicable.
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)(ii)
. However,
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(2)(ii)
provides that employers are not required to include in a written respiratory protection program those employees whose only use of respirators involves the voluntary use of filtering facepieces (dust masks).
Both OSHA (
29 CFR 1910.134(b)
) and MSHA (
30 CFR 57.5015
,
75.321
) consider atmospheres with less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume to be oxygen-deficient and IDLH, requiring the most protective level of respiratory protection (
i.e.,
self-contained breathing apparatus). In contrast, ASTM F3387-19 permits lower oxygen concentrations before classifying an atmosphere as IDLH, provided that the source of oxygen reduction is understood and controlled. Reduced-oxygen atmospheres often appear unexpectedly and are rarely stable and controlled in the mining, general, and construction industries. Further, ASTM's complex oxygen-deficiency characterization approach requires atmospheric pressure measurements and calculations to determine the exact oxygen partial pressure (PO
2
) and corresponding safe oxygen percentage for a specific altitude and environment. It involves multiple thresholds and ranges for IDLH and non-IDLH conditions, making it more complex for workplace applications compared to the single MSHA and OSHA percentage that can be directly read from standard gas monitors. MSHA considers that a simple oxygen percentage cut-off is far more direct for compliance and immediate danger recognition and is also less prone to misinterpretation than ASTM's complex situation-dependent calculations.
Additionally, both OSHA and MSHA have recognized that certain underlying health issues can complicate negative pressure respirator use, often necessitating PAPRs for better comfort and protection. Under
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(6)(ii)
, if a PLHCP identifies a health risk with a negative-pressure respirator, the employer must provide a PAPR if the PLHCP confirms the employee can use a PAPR, effectively accommodating the employee's medical needs. MSHA incorporated this and other OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard provisions in its Diesel Particulate Matter Standard under
30 CFR 57.5060
. While the ASTM F3387-19 standard includes medical evaluation as a required element of a compliant respiratory protection program, it does not directly address issues related to respirator medical clearance, which are found in a different voluntary consensus standard, ASTM F3620-22
Standard Practice for Respiratory Protection—Respirator Use—Physical Qualifications for Personnel
(formerly ANSI Z88.6-2006). In the Agency's view, eliminating the need to cross-reference additional standards would be an improvement because it reduces complexity and decreases the potential for confusion in implementing respiratory protection requirements. Therefore, MSHA considers that adopting by reference
29 CFR 1910.134
would improve clarity and reduce confusion for mine operators in implementing their respiratory protection programs.
For these reasons, MSHA expects that OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
provides greater protection for miners' health and safety than the ASTM F3387-19 standard. While the ASTM F3387-19 standard serves as a valuable technical resource for respiratory protection program managers and other health and safety professionals, it is not written in plain language and incorporates by reference numerous other technical standards that are not freely available to the public. In contrast, OSHA provides an extensive collection of free resources and compliance guides for respiratory protection, including its comprehensive
Small Entity Compliance Guide.
As discussed, MSHA expects that the mining industry is already familiar with many requirements in OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard. In fact, ASTM F3387-19 references OSHA's substance-specific regulations, APFs and MUCs, fit testing methods and fit factors, and cartridge/canister service life estimator software. MSHA anticipates that many mine operators will need to make few, if any, changes to their existing respiratory protection programs. Additionally, mine operators with mining and other operations under both MSHA and OSHA jurisdiction have already implemented written respiratory protection programs compliant with OSHA's standard. However, the Agency recognizes that mines using respirators intermittently or infrequently may need to revise their respiratory protection practices in accordance with the requirements, as applicable, of OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard in
29 CFR 1910.134
.
1. Respiratory Protection Program Requirements
The following provisions, as applicable, would be required in each written respiratory protection program including: procedures for proper respirator selection; medical evaluations; fit testing procedures for tight-fitting respirators; procedures for proper respirator use; procedures for cleaning, disinfecting, storing, inspecting, repairing, discarding, and maintaining respirators; procedures for ensuring atmosphere-supplying respirator breathing-air quality; training; and program evaluation. In addition, certain program elements may be required for voluntary respirator use to prevent potential hazards that could result from such discretionary use. The following subsections outline key requirements specified in
29 CFR 1910.134
.
a. Program Administration
Title 29 CFR
1910.134 specifies several practices related to respiratory protection program administration, including the qualifications and responsibilities of a program administrator. The respiratory protection program must be administered by a suitably trained program administrator who is qualified to administer the program.
29 CFR 1910.134(c)(3)
. Because many mines use dangerous chemicals and/or high exposures may be present, or sophisticated respirators are used, the program administrator must have the appropriate knowledge and experience to administer a respiratory protection program at such mines. In these circumstances, it would be necessary for the program administrator to seek out the expertise needed or to obtain appropriate training. For example, a program administrator's qualifications may have been gained through training or experience; however, the qualifications of a program administrator must be commensurate
(
printed page 73084)
with the respiratory hazards present at a mine.
The qualified program administrator would ensure the respiratory protection program is in writing and would include mine-site specific procedures. The written respiratory protection program would be updated as often as necessary to reflect changing conditions at the mine that affect respirator use. The respiratory protection program administrator's responsibilities should include: measuring, estimating, or reviewing information on the concentration of airborne contaminants; ensuring that medical evaluations, training, and fit testing are performed; selecting the appropriate type or class of respirator that will provide adequate protection for each contaminant; maintaining records; evaluating the respirator program's effectiveness; and revising the program, as necessary.
b. Respirator Selection
Proper respirator selection is an important component of an effective respiratory protection program. OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard provides that proper respirator selection considers the following: the nature of the hazard, user activity and workplace factors, use of NIOSH-approved (
i.e.,
certified) respirators, and respirator limitations and compliance requirements.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(1)(i)-(iii)
. The mine operator would also select approved respirators from a sufficient number of respirator models and sizes so that the respirator is acceptable to, and correctly fits, the miner.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(1)(iv)
.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard provides specific requirements for establishing the nature of inhalation hazards, including determining the following: the types of airborne contaminants present in the workplace; the physical state and chemical properties of these contaminants; the likely airborne concentration of the contaminants (by estimate or measurement); the potential for an oxygen-deficient environment, the existence of an IDLH atmosphere; and compliance with applicable health standards for the contaminants.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(1)(iii)
. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard includes other critical information to support the respirator selection process. This includes APFs to ensure selected respirators meet or exceed required protection levels based on exposure and mode of operation, and MUCs that identify the highest contaminant concentration for safe respirator use.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(3)(i)(A)-(B)
and Table 1. Both factors must be considered during the selection process.
Environments containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen are classified as IDLH and necessitate the most protective respiratory protection equipment—specifically, full facepiece pressure demand self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) certified by NIOSH for a minimum service life of 30 minutes, or a combination full facepiece pressure demand supplied-air respirator (SAR) equipped with an auxiliary self-contained air supply.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(2)(i)(A)
and
(B)
. Additionally, respirators provided only for escape from IDLH atmospheres must be NIOSH-certified for escape from the atmosphere in which they will be used.
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(2)(ii)
.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard at
29 CFR 1910.134(d)(2)(iii)
provides a limited exception in IDLH environments—employers may use alternative atmosphere-supplying respirators if they can demonstrate that oxygen concentrations will consistently remain within the safe ranges specified in Table II of this section under all reasonably foreseeable circumstances (these ranges vary based on altitude). In practical terms, this allows the use of less complex atmosphere-supplying systems, such as airline respirators, when employers can verify that oxygen levels will remain stable and within non-IDLH parameters according to altitude-adjusted thresholds.
This exception applies only in tightly controlled environments where conditions are thoroughly understood and predictable, for example, high-altitude operations where oxygen depletion patterns are consistent and manageable. In practice, employers seldom invoke this exception because most oxygen-deficient environments lack such control, and unexpected oxygen drops pose severe risks.
MSHA proposes to continue its longstanding practice of classifying all atmospheres below 19.5 percent oxygen as IDLH and requiring the most protective level of respiratory protection in these environments. While OSHA provides an altitude-based exception, MSHA proposes not to adopt this exception for mining operations. Mining environments are inherently unpredictable, with conditions that can rapidly become life-threatening. Hazards such as sudden methane releases, other gas emissions, ongoing oxidation reactions, or mine fires can cause abrupt oxygen depletion, creating IDLH conditions that require the highest level of respiratory protection.
c. Medical Evaluation
Medical evaluations determine a miner's ability to use a respirator safely.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)
. The mine operator would provide the medical evaluation before the miner is fit tested or is required to use the respirator in the workplace.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(1)
. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard specifies medical evaluation procedures and provides a medical questionnaire to identify general medical conditions that could place miners who use respirators at risk of serious medical consequences.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(2)
; Appendix C to 1910.134. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard provides that a program administrator would advise the PLHCP of the following conditions to aid in determining the need for a medical evaluation: type and weight of the respirator to be used; duration and frequency of respirator use (including use for rescue and escape); expected physical work effort; additional protective clothing and equipment to be worn; and temperature and humidity extremes. The PLHCP would provide a written recommendation regarding a miner's ability to use a respirator.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(6)(i)
. The written recommendation would only specify any limitations on respirator use related to the medical condition of the employee, or relating to the workplace conditions in which the respirator will be used, including whether or not the employee is medically able to use the respirator; the need, if any, for follow-up medical evaluations; and a statement that the PLHCP has provided the employee with a copy of the PLHCP's written recommendation.
The medical questionnaire and examinations would be administered confidentially during the miner's normal working hours or at a time and place convenient to the miner.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(4)(i)
. Additionally, the medical questionnaire would be administered in a manner that ensures that the miner understands its content.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(4)(ii)
.
Additional medical evaluations may be required under the following circumstances: (1) a miner reports medical signs or symptoms that are related to their ability to use a respirator; (2) a PLHCP, supervisor, or the respirator program administrator informs the mine operator that a miner needs to be reevaluated; (3) information from the respiratory protection program, including observations made during fit testing and program evaluation, indicates a need for a miner's reevaluation; or (4) a change occurs in workplace conditions (
e.g.,
physical
(
printed page 73085)
work effort, protective clothing, temperature) that may result in a substantial increase in the physiological burden placed on a miner.
29 CFR 1910.134(e)(7)
.
d. Respirator Fit Testing
A serious hazard may occur if a tight-fitting respirator, even though correctly selected, is not properly fitted. For example, if an adequate face seal is not achieved, the respirator will provide less protection than designed because contaminants can leak into the breathing zone. Fit testing verifies that the selected make, model, and size of a respirator fits adequately and ensures that the expected level of protection is provided. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard specifies the types of fit tests allowed, procedures for conducting them, and how the fit test results must be used. The standard allows both qualitative fit testing (QLFT) and quantitative fit testing (QNFT) to verify that wearers achieve a satisfactory fit with tight-fitting respirators. Acceptable QLFT and QNFT protocols are contained in Appendix A of
29 CFR 1910.134
. QLFT is limited to negative-pressure respirators requiring a fit factor of 100 or less (
i.e.,
half-mask respirator), as it relies on a pass/fail test based on the wearer's ability to detect taste or odor. This method cannot reliably confirm the higher seal integrity necessary for full-facepiece respirators or advanced protection levels, which require QNFT to attain higher fit factors (
e.g.,
500 or greater).
The standard provides for each respirator wearer to be fit tested before being assigned a tight-fitting respirator. Fit testing must be conducted at least once every 12 months or whenever a wearer or observer expresses concern about respirator fit or comfort, or the wearer has a condition that may interfere with the face piece seal.
OSHA permits the use of stannic chloride as an irritant smoke used in its QLFT protocols in Appendix A to § 1910.134—
Fit Testing Procedures (Mandatory).
MSHA is aware of concerns with using stannic chloride as an irritant smoke due to health risks associated with exposure such as coughing, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and mucous membrane burns if inhaled or exposed to the eyes. OSHA acknowledged these concerns in its 1998 rulemaking (
63 FR 1152
) but chose to retain irritant smoke as a permissible qualitative fit testing method for several reasons discussed in the following.
Historical use and familiarity:
Irritant smoke had been in use for decades and was deeply embedded in existing respirator programs, particularly in industries like firefighting and hazmat response. Eliminating it abruptly would have disrupted established programs;
Practical detection advantage:
The involuntary cough/irritation response was seen by some stakeholders as a more objective indicator of fit failure compared to taste- or smell-based methods, which depend on the worker's subjective reporting;
Industry and stakeholder pressure:
During the comment and rulemaking process, some employers and industry groups argued for retaining it as a legitimate option, and OSHA gave weight to that input; and
Conditional safeguards:
OSHA's position was essentially that with proper precautions and procedures—such as not using it on workers with respiratory conditions—the risk could be managed to an acceptable level.
MSHA requests comments on whether the agency should prohibit the use of stannic chloride during fit testing. MSHA is particularly interested in comments that provide information on the advantages and disadvantages in allowing its continued use.
e. Use of Respirators
Written procedures are essential for the proper use of respirators. Specific procedures are required to prevent leaks in the respirator facepiece seal, prevent miners from removing respirators in hazardous environments, ensure that respirators operate effectively throughout the work shift, and protect miners entering IDLH atmospheres. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would mandate that operators prohibit miners from wearing tight-fitting respirators if they have any condition that would interfere with the respirator seal or valve function. For example, facial hair that comes between the facepiece sealing surface and the face, or that interferes with valve operation, is prohibited.
For all tight-fitting respirators, the operator would ensure that miners perform a user seal check, or follow manufacturers' recommended procedures, each time they put on a respirator. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard also specifies procedures for continued respirator effectiveness, including maintaining appropriate surveillance of work area conditions and degree of miner exposure or stress. The standard would require mine operators to ensure miners leave the respirator use area: (1) to wash their faces and facepieces as necessary to prevent eye or skin irritation from respirator use; (2) when they detect vapor or gas breakthrough, changes in breathing resistance, or facepiece leakage; and (3) to replace respirator filters, cartridges, or canister elements. Additionally, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard specifies several requirements for protecting miners in IDLH atmospheres, including standby rescue personnel, communication systems, and appropriate atmosphere-supplying respirators.
f. Maintenance and Care of Respirators
Proper care and maintenance of respirators is necessary to ensure they function as designed and protect miner safety and health. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard includes specific provisions for respirator cleaning, disinfecting, storage, inspection, and repair. For example, the cleaning and disinfecting provisions state that respirators must be disinfected and cleaned using procedures in Appendix B-2 or equivalent manufacturer procedures. The standard specifies different cleaning intervals based on respirator use: exclusive-use respirators must be cleaned as needed to maintain sanitary conditions, shared respirators must be cleaned between users, and emergency respirators must be cleaned after each use.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require that respirators be stored in a manner that will protect them against damage (
e.g.,
contamination, dust, sunlight, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, damaging chemicals) and prevent distortion of the facepiece and exhalation valve. Emergency respirators would be required to be kept accessible to the work area and stored in clearly marked compartments per manufacturer instructions.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require inspection of respirators based on their intended use. Routine use respirators would be inspected during cleaning and disinfection, and before each use to verify proper working condition. Emergency respirators would be required to be inspected at least monthly and in accordance with manufacturer recommendations and checked for proper function before and after each use. Emergency escape-only respirators would be inspected before being carried into the workplace. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard states that mine operators would inspect respirators to ensure function, tightness of connections, and the condition of the various parts including, but not limited to, the facepiece, head straps, valves, connecting tube, and cartridges, canisters or filters, and a check of
(
printed page 73086)
elastomeric parts for pliability and signs of deterioration.
In addition to the general inspection requirements, the OSHA Respiratory Protection standard would require SCBAs to be inspected monthly. Air and oxygen cylinders would be required to be maintained in a fully charged state and recharged when pressure falls to 90 percent of the manufacturer's recommended level. Operators would need to verify that the regulator and warning devices function properly. Operators would be required to document each emergency respirator inspection with the date, inspector's name, findings, any needed repairs, and the respirator's serial number. This documentation would be required to be kept on a tag attached to the respirator or storage compartment, or in inspection files, until the next inspection.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require respirators that fail inspection or are otherwise found to be defective to be removed from service and discarded or repaired in accordance with specific procedures. Repairs would be required to be performed by trained individuals following manufacturer specifications and using NIOSH-approved manufacturer parts.
g. Breathing Air Quality and Use
It is essential that atmosphere supplying respirators, like supplied-air respirators (SAR) and SCBA, operate reliably and deliver high-quality air to avoid serious health hazards. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators to provide high purity breathing air for use in all atmosphere supplying respirators, regardless of whether the air is supplied from purchased cylinders or generated by an on-site compressor. Specifically, compressed or liquid oxygen must meet United States Pharmacopoeia standards for medical or breathing oxygen, while compressed breathing air must meet or exceed the Grade D breathing air specifications of ANSI/Compressed Gas Association (CGA) Commodity Specification for Air, G-7.1-1989.
Grade D breathing air is the most commonly cited standard for industrial breathing air, and its specifications are as follows: an oxygen content ranging from 19.5 to 23.5 percent by volume; a condensed hydrocarbon (oil) content of 5 milligrams (mg) per cubic meter (m
3
) of air or less; a carbon monoxide (CO) content of 10 parts per million (ppm) or less; a carbon dioxide (CO
2
) content of 1,000 ppm or less; and the absence of any noticeable odor.
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators who purchase cylinders for breathing air use to obtain a supplier certificate of analysis indicating that the air meets Grade D breathing air quality. The operator would also need to ensure that cylinder moisture content remains at or below a dew point of minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit (at one atmosphere of pressure) and that cylinders are tested and maintained according to the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations.
Mine operators utilizing respirable air compressor systems would be subject to specific safety and air quality requirements under the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard. These requirements mandate that systems must: be positioned to prevent the intake of contaminated air; maintain a dew point at least 10 degrees Fahrenheit below the ambient temperature; be equipped with filters and sorbent beds to remove oil, odors, and other impurities; and have a display tag indicating the most current filter service date and the signature of the authorized person who performed the change. The standard requires employers to keep CO below 10 ppm, use alarms (CO or high-temp) for oil-lubricated compressors, install incompatible couplings to prevent contamination, avoid introducing asphyxiants into lines, and use only NIOSH-approved, properly maintained breathing-gas containers for respirators.
Lastly, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard addresses specific safety measures regarding oxygen usage in respiratory protection equipment to prevent fire and explosion hazards. Specifically, compressed oxygen must not be used in air-supplied respirators that were previously used with compressed air. Furthermore, oxygen concentrations exceeding 23.5 percent are strictly reserved for specialized oxygen equipment designed for such conditions, and not for use in standard breathing air systems.
h. Training
Employee training is essential for correct respirator use. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators to provide effective training to miners who are required to use respirators. The training must be comprehensive, understandable, and recur annually, and more often if necessary. The standard would also require mine operators to provide specific basic information about respirators to miners who choose to voluntarily wear respirators when such use is not required by an existing MSHA standard nor required by the mine operator.
To ensure the proper and safe use of a respirator, the standard would also require mine operators to cover several specific elements, ensuring that miners can demonstrate knowledge of the following: why the respirator is necessary and how improper fit, usage and maintenance can make the respirator ineffective; the limitations and capabilities of the selected respirator; how to properly select cartridges and canisters and know the assigned cartridge and canister change schedules for the devices selected; how to use the respirator effectively in emergency situations; how to inspect, put on and remove, use and check the seals of the respirator; the respirator maintenance and storage procedures; how to recognize medical signs and symptoms that may limit or prevent effective use of the respirator; and the general requirements of OSHA's respiratory protection standard.
i. Program Evaluation
To ensure that the written respiratory protection program is being effectively implemented, the OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators to conduct evaluations of the workplace as necessary. Additionally, the standard would require operators to regularly consult with miners who use respirators to assess the effectiveness of the respiratory protection program and to identify and correct any problems encountered with respirator use. At a minimum, the assessment must cover respirator fit, appropriate respirator selection, and proper respirator use and maintenance.
j. Recordkeeping
Like ASTM F3387-19, OSHA's Respiratory Protection Standard would require mine operators to establish and retain written information regarding medical evaluations, fit testing, and their respiratory protection programs. Recordkeeping is an important means of verifying operator compliance with respiratory protection program requirements. Records also enhance miner involvement in the program and support operators in their efforts to audit their program's overall effectiveness.
Under
29 CFR 1910.134
, mine operators would be required to maintain a written copy of their current respiratory protection program. Operators would also be required to retain written fit testing records of QLFTs and QNFTs administered to miners in accordance with
29 CFR 1910.134
. These records would include: (1) name or identification of the miner fit tested; (2) type of fit test performed;
(
printed page 73087)
(3) make, model and size of respirator tested; (4) date of the fit test; (5) pass/fail results if QLFT is used, or the fit factor or other test result record if a QNFT is used. Fit test records would be required to be retained until the next fit test is administered.
Under
29 CFR 1910.134(m)(1)
, OSHA requires employers to keep medical evaluation records, including respirator questionnaires and determinations, for the entire period of employment plus 30 years, following the retention rules in the Access to Employee Exposure and Medical Records standard.
29 CFR 1910.1020
. MSHA proposes not to adopt this OSHA requirement. Instead, MSHA would require records of written determinations regarding a miner's ability to wear a respirator to be retained and made available for the duration of the miner's employment plus 6 months under §§ 56.5005T, 57.5005T, 60.16, and 72.710. This requirement is consistent with the existing requirements of § 57.5075 and § 60.16.
MSHA requests comments on these proposed recordkeeping requirements.

B. Miners and the Mining Industry
The proposed rule would affect mine operators and miners. This section provides information on the structure of the MNM and coal mining industries, including the revenue, number of mines and miners, employment by commodity and size, and economic characteristics of MNM and coal mines. The data come from the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS); U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), the MSHA Office of Educational Policy and Development and the MSHA Office of Program Evaluation and Information Resources; the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB); and the Energy Information Administration (EIA).
1. Structure of the Mining Industry
The mining industry can be divided into two major sectors: (1) MNM mines and (2) coal mines, with further distinction made regarding type of operation: (1) underground mines and (2) surface mines. The MNM mining sector is made up of metal mines (
e.g.,
copper, iron ore, gold, silver) and nonmetal mines. Nonmetal mines can be further categorized into four commodity groups: (1) nonmetal (mineral) materials such as clays, potash, soda ash, salt, talc, and rare earth elements; (2) stone, including granite, limestone, dolomite, sandstone, slate, and marble; (3) crushed limestone; and (4) sand and gravel, including industrial sands.
MSHA tracks several characteristics of mines and categorizes mines by employment size. In this industry profile, MSHA has categorized mines into the following size groups: mines that employ: (1) 1 to 20 miners; (2) 21 to 50 miners; (3) 51 to 100 miners; (4) 101 to 500 miners; and (5) 501 or more miners.

]
MSHA also collects data on independent contractor firms and their employed contract miners' hours worked. Contract miners may work at any mine and more than one mine within a year.

The stone mining subsector includes eight different stone commodities. Seven of the eight are further classified as either dimension stone or crushed and broken stone. Crushed limestone mines made up 16.2 percent of all MNM mines and employed about the same percentage (16.0 percent) of all MNM miners. Sand and gravel mines accounted for 52.7 percent of all MNM mines and employed 21.1 percent of all MNM miners. Nearly all (96.7 percent) of these mines employed fewer than 20 employees. In 2019, the MSHA data show that there were 7,512 contract miners in the sand and gravel mining industry.

In the coal sector, 707 mines (63.9 percent) employed fewer than 20 miners. Overall, coal mine employment in 2019 was 52,966. 2. Economic Characteristics of the Metal/Nonmetal Mining Industry
The value of all MNM mining output in 2019 is estimated at $101.1 billion in 2024 dollars (U.S. DOI, 2019), which is measured in 2022 dollars and updated to 2024 dollars using the U.S. GDP Price Deflator. Metal mines, which include iron, gold, copper, silver, nickel, lead, zinc, uranium, radium, and vanadium mines, contributed $32.4 billion. In the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries, nonmetals, stone, sand and gravel, and crushed limestone are combined into one commodity group called industrial minerals. MSHA estimates the production value of each individual commodity by applying the proportion of revenues of each commodity in the SUSB to the 2019 production value for all industrial minerals reported by USGS. This approach yields the following values in 2024 dollars: metal production is valued at $32.4 billion, nonmetal production at $27.0 billion, stone mining at $15.5 billion, sand and gravel at $10.8 billion, and crushed limestone at $15.4 billion.
3. Economic Characteristics of the Coal Industry
Production in the U.S. coal sector amounted to 706.1 million tons in 2019. To estimate coal revenues in 2019, MSHA combines production estimates with prices per ton. 1. Exposure Monitoring (§ 60.12)
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the standards established by the 2024 Silica Final Rule, mine operators are required to conduct five types of exposure monitoring, including: first- and second-time sampling, above-action-level sampling, corrective actions sampling, periodic evaluations, and post evaluation sampling.
ii. Proposed Rule
MSHA models the following changes from the 2024 Silica Final Rule in this PRIA:
First-time Sampling:
Only sample miners who are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level.
Remove mandatory second-time sampling.
Above-action-level Sampling:
(new) Make approved respirators available before the start of the next work shift if sampling falls between the action level and the PEL.
End the required availability of approved respirators if one sample is below the action level.
Corrective Actions Sampling:
No change.
Periodic Evaluations and Post Evaluation Sampling:
Eliminated.
(new) As-needed Sampling:
Conduct sampling as frequently as necessary to assess the full-shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica to each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level.
Under proposed § 60.12, mine operators would conduct first-time sampling, above-action-level sampling, corrective actions sampling, and as-needed sampling. In this section, MSHA presents its analysis and estimated costs attributable to exposure monitoring under the proposed rule.

All active mines would be required to conduct exposure monitoring; however, MSHA expects that the costs for exposure monitoring vary by mine size and the number of quarters they are in operation. Monitoring Costs
MSHA estimates total sampling costs as a function of several factors: the unit cost of sampling, which is made up of labor costs (time and hourly wage of miners and the persons conducting sampling), laboratory costs for analyzing the samples, and clerical costs for recording the results; the number of samples that constitute the required representative fraction, each time the operator conducts sampling; and the frequency with which operators would be assumed to carry out different types of monitoring. Details of the cost components are:
Labor costs:
Sampling time:
time taken to prepare for and take the samples.
Lost work time: time lost from work to equip a miner with a sampling device.
(
printed page 73093)
Recordkeeping time: time to record and report sample results.
Laboratory analysis fees.
The number of samples is determined by evaluating the following factors:
Representativeness: when several miners perform the same tasks on the same shift and in the same work area, the fraction of those miners sampled to obtain a representative sample, which MSHA estimated based on mine employment and occupation profiles.
Type of exposure monitoring (
i.e.,
above-action-level sampling, corrective actions sampling, and as-needed sampling).
Exposure level (
i.e.,
below the action level, between the action level and the PEL, or above the PEL).
To calculate total sampling costs under the proposed rule, MSHA estimates the number of samples taken based on the type of sampling. For example, exposure levels affect sampling costs because under the proposed rule one sample below the action level would be needed to cease above-action-level sampling. The frequency of corrective actions sampling is based on the exposure level, which is determined by previous samples.

Labor Costs
The largest component of sampling cost is the labor time required to conduct the activities. For sampling, this includes the time needed to prepare for sampling, take the samples, and perform recordkeeping tasks on the results. Sampling takes time, which is valued at the hourly wage of the person wearing the sampling equipment and the person conducting the sampling. To err on the side of overestimation, MSHA assumed that in MNM mines, sample preparation and collection would be performed by an industrial hygienist (IH). The IH may be an in-house specialist or an external consultant.
[
33
]
As a national average, the IH consultant is assumed to charge $1,708 per day, including travel and report preparation costs. The time for the in-house IH is valued at their loaded average hourly wage. MSHA assumed that half of MNM mine operators would hire a contract IH, while the other half would use an on-staff IH for sampling. For coal mines, miners certified to perform sampling under §§ 70.202, 71.202, and 90.202 can conduct the sampling required under the proposed rule. MSHA assumed coal mine operators would use certified miners for sample preparation and collection; therefore, the average labor cost for coal mine sampling is less than 40 percent of that for MNM mine sampling.
In addition to the labor time of the person conducting sample preparation and collection, there are other activities associated with sampling which cost labor time. Time miners spend being equipped with a sampling device is time they do not spend working. MSHA assumes time lost to work is one half hour of labor time valued at the average loaded hourly wage of mine “Extraction Workers” (Standard Occupational Code 47-5000).
MSHA assumes that recordkeeping takes 15 minutes per sample, which is valued at the average loaded hourly wage of mine “Occupational Health and Safety Specialists” (Standard Occupational Code 19-5011). MSHA assumes an additional 2 minutes per sample would be needed for the mine operator to report sample results above the PEL to the MSHA District Manager. Because only a fraction of sample results would be reported to the District Manager, the effective time allotted is substantially larger; for example, if 50 percent of sample results are reported to MSHA, this 2-minute estimate effectively allots 4 minutes per sample that is actually reported.
MSHA also assumes the personnel conducting sampling can collect 2, 3, and 4 samples per day at small, medium, and large mines, respectively. This determines the number of days needed to complete sampling at a mine, and therefore directly affects the labor costs of sampling.
The average labor cost of exposure monitoring is summarized in Table VII-5.
Laboratory Fees for Sample Analysis
MSHA estimates that laboratory analysis would cost the mine operator $159 per sample. This includes the cost of packing and shipping the sample to the lab, the laboratory analysis, and reporting sample results to the operator.
Number of Samples—Representative Sampling
Mine operators would be required to conduct sampling systematically to ensure representativeness and sufficient miner coverage. Because this determines the minimum number of samples required each time sampling is carried out, it is a major determinant of sampling costs. Where several miners
(
printed page 73096)
perform the same tasks on the same shift and in the same work area, the mine operator may sample a representative fraction (
e.g.,
at least two) of these miners to meet the sampling requirements. MSHA estimates for the number of miners considered a representative sample are based on the size of the mine. In small mines that employ 20 or fewer miners (including contract miners), MSHA assumes that a sample comprising at least 50 percent of miners would be necessary to collect a representative sample. In medium-sized mines with 20 to 100 miners, the assumption is that a minimum of 25 percent of miners would need to be sampled for the sample to be representative. In large mines with 100 or more miners, the Agency assumes that a minimum of 15 percent of miners would need to be sampled for the sample to be representative.
Frequency of Exposure Monitoring—Number of Samples
Another component of sampling cost is the frequency with which it must be performed as not all mines operate year-round. Except for first-time sampling, MSHA adjusted all types of sampling for mines that operate fewer than four quarters per year. Each mine would be assumed to take sampling with a frequency equal to the number of quarters the mine is open. For example, mines which are open only two quarters per year would conduct sampling twice during a calendar year. Portable mines are not exempt from the requirements. For corrective actions sampling, sampling frequency depends on sample results as specified by MSHA's exposure monitoring requirements.
Trends in Sample Results and Sampling Costs
Under proposed § 60.12, MSHA expects the percentage of samples that exceed the action level or exceed the PEL would decline over the first several years following promulgation. The decline would be due to several factors: first, mine operators would gain experience and incur increased maintenance and repair to reduce exposure levels to below the action level so they may limit above-action-level sampling. Second, some engineering controls are likely to reduce exposures below the PEL and/or the action level. Third, improving the control of respirable crystalline silica dust in part of the mine is likely to reduce exposure elsewhere in the mine. The combination of these effects is especially observable in the coal industry. Although the 2024 Silica Final Rule established a PEL of 50 µg/m
3

Table VII-6
).
MSHA estimates the percentages of samples exceeding the action level and the PEL in the first year of compliance based on its historical exposure profile developed using the Agency's compliance sampling data. Because no available data indicate the yearly rate at which mine operators would reduce miner exposures to levels below the action level, MSHA assumed the percentage of samples exceeding the action level and the PEL would decline linearly until reaching a steady value in Year 7 and subsequent years.
a. First-Time Sampling
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(a)(1) and (a)(2)(i), samples would be taken based on a representative fraction of the miners who are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica. First-time sampling occurs at the start of the 2024 Silica Final Rule's respective compliance date for coal mines and MNM mines. Second-time sampling occurs within 3 months of first-time sampling.
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(a)(2)(ii), if the additional sample is between the action level and the PEL, the mine operator would be required to take another sampling within 3 months, transitioning into the above-action-level sampling as described in the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(a)(3) and (4).
The assumptions used in calculating the number of first- and second-time samples can be found in the FRIA of the 2024 Silica Final Rule.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.12(a)(2), mine operators would not be required to perform second-time sampling. MSHA, however, anticipates that all mines would perform first-time sampling to collect valuable data concerning respirable crystalline silica exposure rates in their mine. Under the proposed rule, mine operators would only need to sample the miners that are or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level, instead of all miners expected to be exposed to any respirable crystalline silica. This decreases the number of miners the operator must sample.
In subsequent years only new mines would be performing first-time sampling. MSHA projects that about 2 percent of mines in any given year
(

would be new entrants to the mining industry.
iii. Summary of Changes
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(a)(1) and (a)(2)(i), MSHA estimates the number of first- and second-time samples for the first 7 years in the top panel of Table VII-7. Under the proposed rule, the number of first-time samples would be halved because mine operators would no longer be required to conduct second-time sampling (bottom panel of Table VII-7).
b. Above-Action-Level Sampling
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(a)(2)(ii), if the sampling under this section is between the action level and the PEL, the mine operator is required to take another sampling within 3 months. This sampling can be discontinued when the two most recent sample results demonstrate exposure below the action level.
Although reducing exposures below the action level is costly for mine operators, repeated sampling is also costly. Mine operators have both a financial incentive and a human resource incentive to reduce exposures not just below the PEL but below the action level. From a human resource standpoint, reducing exposures below the action level would ensure that mine operators have a healthier miner population, thus reducing employee time-off and turnover. Reducing exposures below the action level would also ensure that mine operators can discontinue sampling if exposures consistently remain below the action level.
MSHA expects that the number of above-action-level samples would decline over time as mine operators come into compliance through engineering controls and administrative controls but would not entirely disappear. For the specific assumptions used in calculating the number of above-action-level samples taken each year, see the FRIA of the 2024 Silica Final Rule.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.12(a)(3), if the sampling of any miner who may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level is between the action level and the PEL, the mine operator would be required to make approved respirators available before the start of the next work shift in accordance with § 60.14(b) and (c) until sampling indicates exposures are below the action level. Mine operators would need only one sample result at or below the action level to stop sampling and to discontinue providing respirators to affected miners.

This proposed change would substantially reduce the number of miners being sampled as miners expected to be exposed below the action level are no longer required to be sampled. The mine operator is required to take additional or new corrective actions until sampling indicates miner exposures are at or below the PEL.
ii. Proposed Rule
The proposed rule would keep the requirement to conduct corrective actions sampling.

The proposed rule would make no changes to the 2024 Silica Final Rule requirements concerning corrective

d. Periodic Evaluations and Post Evaluation Sampling
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(c), at least every 6 months after commencing sampling under § 60.12(a)(1) or whenever there is a change in: production; processes; installation or maintenance of engineering controls; installation or maintenance of equipment; administrative controls; or geological conditions; mine operators are required to evaluate whether the change may reasonably be expected to result in new or increased respirable crystalline silica exposures. Once the evaluation is completed, the mine operator is required to: (1) make a record of the evaluation, including the evaluated change, the impact on respirable crystalline silica exposure, and the date of the evaluation; and (2) post the record on the mine bulletin board and, if applicable, by electronic means, for the next 31 days.
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.12(d), if the mine operator determines as a result of the periodic evaluation that miners may be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level, the mine operator is required to perform sampling to assess the full shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be at or above the action level.
ii. Proposed Rule
The proposed rule would remove the requirements to conduct periodic evaluations and post-evaluation sampling.
iii. Summary of Changes
Under the proposed rule, MSHA would remove the requirements for periodic evaluations and post-evaluation sampling. The proposed change to an “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure makes these requirements redundant. Under the “as frequently as necessary” sampling structure, mine operators would continually evaluate their mines for the same conditions, processes, or procedures that triggered a periodic evaluation under the 2024 Silica Final Rule, such as changes in production, installation and maintenance of engineering controls, installation and maintenance of equipment, administrative controls, or geological conditions.

i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
There are no requirements concerning as-needed sampling in the 2024 Silica Final Rule.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.12(a)(2), mine operators would conduct sampling as frequently as necessary to assess the full-shift, 8-hour TWA exposure of respirable crystalline silica for each miner who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed to respirable crystalline silica at or above the action level.
The assumptions MSHA used for the frequency of this type of sampling are based on the number of quarters a mine is active in a year:
4 Quarters: once every 12 months.
3 Quarters: once every 18 months.
1 or 2 Quarters: once every 24 months.
iii. Summary of Changes
Although post evaluation sampling in the 2024 Silica Final Rule is no longer required, the proposed rule introduces as-needed sampling, which would require mine operators to sample as frequently as necessary rather than sampling within three months as required in the 2024 Silica Final Rule. When sample results are between the action level and the PEL, miners would receive better protection when respirators are provided in combination with sampling “as frequently as necessary.” Since as-needed sampling is not currently required, all changes would represent an increase in the number of samples and compliance costs. 3. Respiratory Protection (§ 60.14)
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
The requirements for the use of respiratory protection at MNM mines are presented in the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.14(a). If sample results indicate miners' exposure exceeds the PEL, mine operators are required to use respiratory protection as a temporary measure when miners must work in concentrations of respirable crystalline silica above the PEL while engineering control measures are being developed and implemented or it is necessary by the nature of work involved.
ii. Proposed Rule
MSHA proposes to amend the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.14(a) to clarify the use of respirators at MNM mines. Miners are allowed to work for reasonable periods of time using respiratory protection when they must work in an environment when silica concentrations are above the PEL.
iii. Summary of Changes
This proposed change clarifies that mine operators may allow miners to use respiratory protection for reasonable periods of time, instead of as a temporary measure. Amending provisions in the 2024 Silica Final Rule would not change compliance costs concerning the number of affected miners or required respirators when miners are exposed above the PEL, and the change would not result in any reduction in safety for miners.
The additional costs for respirator use identified in proposed § 60.12(a)(3) are discussed above in above-action-level sampling.
4. Medical Surveillance (§ 60.15)
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, § 60.15 requires MNM mine operators to provide mandatory medical examinations to new miners within 60 days of beginning employment with limited exceptions, and at multiple other intervals. It also requires MNM mine operators to provide voluntary medical examinations to all miners during an initial 12-month period and every 5 years.
ii. Proposed Rule
The proposed rule would require MNM mine operators to provide voluntary medical examinations to new miners within 60 days of beginning employment and at multiple other intervals. MSHA also proposes language that would require MNM mine operators to provide all miners the opportunity for voluntary medical examinations at least every 5 years. Additionally, MSHA proposes that all mine operators (coal and MNM) would be required to provide mandatory medical examinations to sampled miners who are exposed above the PEL based on an MSHA sample, within 60 days of the sample results, except for miners that have received a medical examination within the last 2 years.
The proposed rule changes mandatory medical surveillance to voluntary medical surveillance for new MNM miners and extends the initial time to provide medical examinations under voluntary medical surveillance from 1 year to 5 years. This is not expected to reduce miners' access to medical examinations as operators are still required to provide examinations on a voluntary basis.
The proposed rule adds a new requirement for both MNM and coal mine operators to provide mandatory medical examinations to sampled miners with exposures above the PEL, except for miners who have received a medical examination within the last two years. The proposal requires MNM and coal mine operators to provide medical examinations to sampled miners with overexposures within 60 days of the operator's receipt of the sample results to allow for early detection and help allocate limited medical resources to the most at-risk miners.
In this section, MSHA considers the cost to mine operators for providing medical examinations to MNM and coal miners under the proposed requirements in § 60.15. These examinations include both voluntary and mandatory examinations for MNM miners and mandatory examinations for coal miners. Specifically, MSHA estimates the following medical examinations:
MNM mine operators would provide voluntary medical examinations for new miners who begin work in the mining industry for the first time, including initial, 3-year follow-up, and 2-year follow-up examinations;
MNM mine operators would provide voluntary 5-year examinations for both new and current miners;
MNM mine operators would provide mandatory examinations if an MSHA sample shows that the miner is exposed above the PEL; and
Coal mine operators would provide mandatory examinations if an MSHA sample shows that the miner is exposed above the PEL.
To estimate the compliance costs to mine operators, MSHA estimates the cost of a medical examination, and the number of medical examinations miners would receive.
a. Costs of A Medical Examination
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.15(a), MNM mine operators are required to provide each miner with periodic medical examinations at no cost to the miner. The medical examinations must include the following information: medical and work history, physical examination, chest X-ray, and pulmonary function test. Mine operators are also required to obtain a written medical opinion from the PLHCP or specialist within 30 days of the medical examination that contains any recommended limitations on the miner's use of respirators.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.15(a), each mine operator would be required to provide to each miner periodic medical examinations at no cost to the miner and at specified frequencies. The medical examinations would need to include the following information: a medical and work history; a physical examination; a chest X-ray; and a pulmonary function test, administered by a spirometry technician. Mine operators would also be required to obtain a written confirmation of the medical examination from the PLHCP or specialist within 30 days of the medical examination.
MSHA assumes that a medical examination has the following cost elements: chest X-ray, spirometry test, symptom assessment and occupational history, the physical examination, lost work time while being examined, lost travel time, transportation cost, and recordkeeping of the mine operator.
MSHA calculates the unit cost of an examination using the same method as OSHA's Final Economic Analysis (FEA) of medical surveillance associated with the OSHA Silica Rule (OSHA, 2016).

b. Voluntary Medical Examinations for MNM Miners
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.15(b), MNM mine operators are required to provide mandatory medical examinations to new miners within 60 days of beginning employment with limited exceptions and at multiple other time intervals. These initial medical examinations are mandatory for miners joining the mining industry. MNM operators are also required to provide voluntary medical examinations to all miners during an initial 12-month period and then once every 5 years.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.15(b), each MNM mine operator would provide the opportunity to all miners employed at the mine to take the medical examinations at specified frequencies. These examinations would be provided to new miners within 60 days of beginning employment and at multiple other time intervals (including 3-year follow-up, 2-year follow-up, and 5-year examinations). These examinations would be provided to all miners at least every 5 years. Miners could take voluntary medical examinations if they choose to, but MNM mine operators would be required to offer them to eligible miners.
There is no readily available data on MNM miners' participation rate. For purposes of this analysis, MSHA estimates compliance costs for voluntary examinations using two participation rates to determine the proportion of eligible MNM miners who would choose to take a voluntary examination: low 25% and high 75%. At a 25 percent participation rate, 25 percent of eligible miners would choose to take the voluntary examinations offered by mine operators. MSHA presents the cost estimations for each participation rate in Table VII-30. For illustrative purposes, MSHA presents the calculation using a 25 percent participation rate in the first 11 years of the purposed rule's implementation, while the full analysis period is 60 years. Results from a 75 percent participation rate are reported in Table VII-30.

c. Mandatory Medical Examinations for Exposed MNM and Coal Miners
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
Under the 2024 Silica Final Rule standards, there is no requirement for mine operators to provide medical examinations to miners who have been exposed above the PEL.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under proposed § 60.15(c), both MNM and coal mine operators would be required to provide mandatory medical examinations to miners who are exposed above the PEL based upon an MSHA sample within 60 days of the operator's receipt of the sample results. However, a miner who has been exposed above the PEL, based upon an MSHA sample, would not be provided with a mandatory medical examination if the miner has taken a medical examination within the last two years. The examination taken within the last two years include voluntary examinations offered in proposed § 60.15(b) or mandatory examinations required in proposed § 60.15(c), or in accordance with § 72.100.
Miners who would choose to take voluntary examinations within the last two years would not be provided with a mandatory examination even when they would be found to be exposed above the PEL. For illustrative purposes, MSHA presents the calculation of mandatory examinations in the first 11 years of the proposed rule's implementation, excluding any voluntary examinations (under a 25 percent participation rate) and mandatory examinations in the last two years. This participation rate affects how many miners would be excluded from the requirement to take mandatory medical examinations.
ii-1. Mandatory Medical Examinations for Exposed MNM Miners
Number of Sampled Exposed MNM Miners
Under proposed § 60.15(c), sampled miners would be required to get mandatory medical examinations if an MSHA sample indicates an exposure above the PEL. In this analysis, MSHA uses the samples presented in the FRIA Table 2-5 from the 2024 Silica Final Rule to estimate the number of MNM miners sampled each year by MSHA. 5. Updates to OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard (§ 60.14(c)(2))
i. 2024 Silica Final Rule
In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, § 60.14(c)(2) requires mine operator to have a written respiratory protection program that meets requirements in accordance with ASTM F3387-19,
Standard Practice for Respiratory Protection.
The 2024 Silica Final Rule requires mine operators who would allow or direct miners to use respirators for protection from airborne hazards to develop a written respiratory protection program that meets the requirements of ASTM F3387-19, an industry consensus standard.
ii. Proposed Rule
Under the proposed rule, mine operators would follow the requirements for respiratory protection from OSHA's Respiratory Protection
(
printed page 73116)
Standard, instead of the ASTM F3387-19 standard. The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard includes provisions for voluntary respirator use, which would provide miners with access to greater protection from respirator use when their exposure is between the action level and the PEL. The proposed rule contains language that would require mine operators' written respiratory protection programs to conform to OSHA Respiratory Protection requirements set forth in
29 CFR 1910.134
, rather than ASTM F3387-19.
iii. Summary of Changes
The OSHA Respiratory Protection Standard would be more protective and appropriate for the mining industry. It also explicitly addresses voluntary respirator use and requires operators to implement certain elements of a written respiratory protection program for safe voluntary respirator use. To err on the side of overestimation, MSHA has determined that amending the 2024 Silica Final Rule's requirements in § 60.14(c)(2) would not change mine operators' compliance costs as it does not change requirements for respiratory protection programs, such as written standard operating procedures or fit testing.

MSHA recognizes there are potential one-time and recurring costs associated with the rule for the mining community to get familiar with the rule. Regulatory familiarization costs represent direct costs on businesses for familiarizing themselves with the compliance requirements within the rule.

VIII. Regulatory Alternatives
MSHA examined three regulatory alternatives in the 2024 Silica Final Rule, which comparatively present alternative approaches for lowering
(
printed page 73121)
miners' exposure to respirable crystalline silica and improving respiratory protection for all airborne contaminants (
89 FR 28389
).
The first alternative contains less stringent provisions of lower frequency exposure monitoring but includes no change to the PEL and action level. This regulatory alternative would result in lower costs of compliance. However, MSHA thought that more frequent sampling would provide multiple unquantified benefits, including closely monitored miner exposure trends, higher confidence of continued compliance, and better protection of miners' health. Therefore, this regulatory alternative was not selected.
The second alternative combines less stringent exposure monitoring with a more stringent PEL at 25 μg/m
3
. To meet the PEL of 25 μg/m
3
, mine operators would incur substantially greater engineering control costs when compared to the estimated compliance costs for reaching a PEL of 50 μg/m
3
. This regulatory alternative would increase miner protection, resulting in measurable increases in avoided mortality and other health benefits as compared to a PEL of 50 μg/m
3
. MSHA did not select this regulatory alternative because the net benefits of this alternative would be negative due to much higher compliance costs. Additionally, MSHA determined that meeting a PEL of 25 μg/m
3
is not achievable for all mines. Therefore, MSHA is not selecting this alternative under the proposed rule.
The third regulatory alternative examines a different methodology for calculating miners' exposures and assesses the impact on compliance cost reductions and other effects of using the full-shift TWA instead of the full-shift, 8-hour TWA specified in this proposed rule. In the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA did not select this alternative.
Additionally, the proposal would likely be more burdensome for some operators and less burdensome for others, while maintaining equal or greater protections compared to the 2024 Silica Final Rule standards; therefore, the Agency has not identified a viable alternative to this rule that would provide the desired contrast and analysis, beyond maintaining the status quo of the 2024 Silica Final Rule.
Under the Mine Act, MSHA is not required to use estimated net benefits as the basis for its decision. MSHA requests comments on the assumptions and methodologies of regulatory alternatives and also asks for any data or quantitative information that may be useful in evaluating the estimated costs and benefits associated with the alternatives.
IX. Regulatory Flexibility Analysis
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) of 1980, as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) of 1996, requires preparation of an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) for any rule that by law must be proposed for public comment, unless the agency certifies that the rule “will not, if promulgated, have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.”
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
. The RFA defines small entities to include small businesses, small organizations, including not-for-profit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions.
This proposed rule amends standards established by the 2024 Silica Final Rule. The 2024 Silica Final Rule included a regulatory flexibility analysis that concluded the Agency could certify the standards would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. That regulatory flexibility analysis identified the total number of regulated small entities, evaluated the compliance costs for small entities, and compared the annual compliance costs relative to annual revenue. Compliance costs were found to be less than 0.5 percent of the revenues for all small entities and less for small entities with fewer than 5 employees.
Key inputs for MSHA's identification of small entities have not changed meaningfully in the interim period since the publication of the 2024 Silica Final Rule. MSHA estimated there were 5,462 mine controllers that met the definition of small entity in the 2024 Silica Final Rule analysis.
This proposed rule contains provisions that would affect costs to small mines. MSHA considered the changes in costs to small mines when developing this proposed rule under the provisions of the RFA. The PRIA presented in Section VII of this preamble finds that the estimated cost burdens of this proposed rule are substantially lower than the standards established by the 2024 Silica Final Rule. The annualized compliance costs are projected to comprise less than 0.06 percent of annual estimated industry revenues. Thus, MSHA considers the conclusions of the April 2024 analysis to still be applicable, and compliance costs are expected to remain less than 0.5 percent of revenues for small entities.
MSHA initially concludes that the impacts of this proposed rule would not have a “significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities” and that the preparation of an IRFA is not warranted. MSHA will transmit this certification and supporting statement of factual basis to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration for review under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
.
In keeping with the 2024 Silica Final Rule, MSHA commits to provide compliance assistance (including training and best practice materials) to all mine operators, with an emphasis on small operators.
MSHA requests comments on whether the proposed rule would significantly increase costs for small entities relative to the standards established in the 2024 Silica Final Rule.
