The provision also states that “[t]his divestiture requirement shall not apply to persons or entities that exceed the 39 percent national audience reach limitation through population growth.” This clarifying language merely restates Commission policy adopted when the national cap based on audience reach was first adopted in 1985 and cannot be read as indicating that population growth was the only congressionally-approved method of avoiding divestiture after exceeding the national cap. We note that this sentence does not include the reference, “in paragraph (1)(B),” which some might claim suggests the number is to be unchangeable statutory language. However, given the other references in the CAA to section (c)(1)(B), the second sentence is best understood as also referring to that section (which only directs the Commission to use its rulemaking authority) rather than creating a freestanding statutory cap. Furthermore, as noted earlier, the CAA refers to provisions relating to the national cap as “rules.” CAA § 629(3), 118 Stat. at 100.
100. Finally, we see no independent significance to the CAA's various other references to “the 39 percent national audience reach limitation for television stations in [section 202(c)](1)(B).” CAA section 629(2), (3), 118 Stat. at 99-100 (amending 1996 Act section 202(c), (h), 110 Stat. at 111-12). This language simply reflects that, at the time Congress enacted the CAA, it had directed the Commission in section 202(c)(1)(B) to revise its rules to reset the national cap to that particular level. While they refer to the then-existing cap, they do not freeze the cap at a particular level indefinitely. The references to the 39% number are to its placement “in paragraph (1)(B),” which is the provision of the 1996 Act that directed the Commission to set the cap through its rulemaking authority, which necessarily preserves Commission discretion to adjust its rules as warranted by the public interest.
101. We acknowledge that there are some statements by Members of Congress while the CAA was under consideration, as well as other contemporaneous accounts expressing a
(
printed page 72815)
belief that the statute would preclude the Commission from making further changes to the national cap. But these statements are belied by the terms of the legislation that was adopted. As the Supreme Court has reiterated, “[L]egislative history is not the law. It is the business of Congress to sum up its own debates in its legislation, and once it enacts a statute we do not inquire what the legislature meant; we ask only what the statute means.”
Epic Systems Corp.
v.
Lewis,
584 U.S. 497, 523 (2018). In similar circumstances, the D.C. Circuit in
Fox I
refused to find a statement “by the ranking minority Member of the relevant subcommittee of the House” that the 1996 Act's specification of a 35% cap “should settle the issue for many years to come” to dispose of the statute's meaning.
Fox I,
280 F.3d at 1043.
102. A few commenters assert that the Commission is prevented from repealing the national cap by the Major Questions Doctrine. But that doctrine applies to instances in which an agency claims “extravagant statutory power over the national economy” in the absence of clear authority from Congress. See
Utility Air Regulatory Group
v.
EPA,
573 U.S. 302, 324 (2014). The Commission has held the power to modify or repeal broadcast ownership rules since the Communications Act was passed. It is not regulating outside its area of expertise or invoking expansive power from a narrow statute. And, as we have discussed, nothing in the CAA repeals the Commission's authority to review its rules, even where the “starting point” has been set by Congress.
Fox I,
280 F.3d at 1043.
103. In sum, the best reading of the statute supports the Commission's longstanding position that the Commission retains authority to modify or eliminate the national television audience reach rule upon determining that the rule no longer serves the public interest, and for the reasons we have explained, we have determined that here. We therefore exercise our authority to modify our rules by repealing the national audience reach limitation for television stations in favor of a case-by-case analysis of specific transactions. This, in our judgment, far better serves the public interest in light of the significant changes to the position of television broadcasters in the modern media marketplace.
Procedural Matters
104.
Regulatory Flexibility Act.
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, as amended (RFA), requires that an agency prepare a regulatory flexibility analysis for notice and comment rulemakings, unless the agency certifies that “the rule will not, if promulgated, have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.”
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.,
as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement and Fairness Act (SBREFA),
Public Law 104-121
, 110 Stat. 847 (1996);
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
. Accordingly, the Commission has prepared a Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) concerning the possible impact of the rule and policy changes contained in this Report and Order on small entities. The FRFA is set forth below.
105.
Paperwork Reduction Act.
This Report and Order does not contain proposed new or revised information collection requirements subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,
Public Law 104-13
(
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
). In addition, this Report and Order therefore does not contain any new or modified “information burden for small business concerns with fewer than 25 employees” pursuant to the Small Business Paperwork Relief Act of 2002,
Public Law 107-198
,
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(4)
.
106.
Congressional Review Act.
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs of the Office of Management and Budget has found that this rule is major under the Congressional Review Act,
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. The Commission will send a copy of this Report & Order to Congress and the Government Accountability Office pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 801(a)(1)(A)
.
Final Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis
107. As required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, as amended (RFA), the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) incorporated an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) in
Amendment of Section 73.3555(e) of the Commission's Rules, National Television Multiple Ownership Rule,
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (
NPRM
), released on December 18, 2017. The Media Bureau sought further written public comment in
Media Bureau Seeks to Refresh the Record in the National Television Multiple Ownership Rule Proceeding,
Public Notice (
Refresh Public Notice
), including comment on the IFRA. The comments received are addressed below. This Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) conforms to the RFA and it (or summaries thereof) will be published in the
Federal Register
.
A. Need for, and Objectives of, the Rules
108. In December 2017, the Commission adopted an
NPRM
to seek comment on whether to retain, modify, or eliminate its rule limiting entities from owning or controlling broadcast television stations that, in the aggregate, reach more than 39% of the television audience households in the United States. The
NPRM
also sought comment on a component of the rule, which provides a 50% discount to UHF stations for purposes of calculating compliance with the 39% audience reach cap, often referred to as the “UHF discount.” In June 2025, the Media Bureau issued the
Refresh Public Notice
seeking to refresh the record in this proceeding. In light of the request to refresh the record, the
Refresh Public Notice
invited comment on any potential effect of proposals on small entities and the IRFA. In the
Report & Order,
we repeal the national television multiple ownership rule, an important step towards modernizing our regulation of the media marketplace.
109. We find that the record demonstrates that eliminating the national television multiple ownership rule serves the public interest, as it is no longer necessary to promote competition, viewpoint diversity, and localism. The Commission has found since 2003 that the rule is not needed to promote competition and viewpoint diversity, which is only more true today in the modern, diverse media marketplace that includes the proliferation of online video streaming options for viewers. On localism, we agree that increased scale will open opportunities for broadcasters to attract additional capital and advertising revenue needed to produce local programming and to improve service to their local communities. We find that a case-by-case review of applications for the transfer and assignment of television licenses is a better way to ensure that the Commission's media ownership goals are being met. Accordingly, we eliminate the national television multiple ownership rule.
B. Summary of Significant Issues Raised by Public Comments in Response to the IRFA
110. While no commenter directly responded to the IRFA in this proceeding, one commenter references the RFA process. That commenter contends that the Commission's regulatory flexibility analysis under the RFA is insufficient because, in seeking to refresh the record, the Commission “fails to provide any meaningful analysis of how potential changes to the nationwide audience reach cap or UHF discount might affect small broadcast entities.” The commenter further states that “[t]o address this deficiency, the FCC should conduct a comprehensive
(
printed page 72816)
RFA analysis before proceeding with any modifications to the national audience reach cap or UHF discount.” The arguments raised by the commenter fail to acknowledge that the 2017
NPRM
in this proceeding included the requisite IRFA and that the
Refresh Public Notice
sought further comment on that IRFA. The Commission has reviewed the record in its entirety and has evaluated the impact of this final action on small broadcast entities, and now publishes this FRFA, consistent with the requirements of the RFA.
C. Response to Comments by the Chief Counsel for the Small Business Administration Office of Advocacy
111. Pursuant to the Small Business Jobs Act of 2010, which amended the RFA, the Commission is required to respond to any comments filed by the Chief Counsel for the Small Business Administration (SBA) Office of Advocacy, and also provide a detailed statement of any change made to the proposed rules as a result of those comments. The Chief Counsel did not file any comments in response to the proposed rules in this proceeding. The SBA Office of Advocacy did file comments in another Commission proceeding (GN Docket No. 25-133) that discuss the national television multiple ownership rule,
47 CFR 73.3555(e)
.
D. Description and Estimate of the Number of Small Entities to Which the Rules Will Apply
112. The RFA directs agencies to provide a description of, and where feasible, an estimate of the number of small entities that may be affected by the adopted rules. The RFA generally defines the term “small entity” as having the same meaning as the terms “small business,” “small organization,” and “small governmental jurisdiction.” In addition, the term “small business” has the same meaning as the term “small business concern” under the Small Business Act. A “small business concern” is one which: (1) is independently owned and operated; (2) is not dominant in its field of operation; and (3) satisfies any additional criteria established by the SBA. The SBA establishes small business size standards that agencies are required to use when promulgating regulations relating to small businesses; agencies may establish alternative size standards for use in such programs, but must consult and obtain approval from SBA before doing so.
113. Our actions, over time, may affect small entities that are not easily categorized at present. We therefore describe three broad groups of small entities that could be directly affected by our actions. In general, a small business is an independent business having fewer than 500 employees. These types of small businesses represent 99.9% of all businesses in the United States, which translates to 34.75 million businesses. Next, “small organizations” are not-for-profit enterprises that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their field. While we do not have data regarding the number of non-profits that meet that criteria, over 99% of nonprofits have fewer than 500 employees. Finally, “small governmental jurisdictions” are defined as cities, counties, towns, townships, villages, school districts, or special districts with populations of less than fifty thousand. Based on the 2022 U.S. Census of Governments data, we estimate that at least 48,724 out of 90,835 local government jurisdictions have a population of less than 50,000.
114. The rule changes adopted in the
Report and Order
will apply to small entities in the industries identified in the chart below by their six-digit North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes and corresponding SBA size standard. Based on currently available U.S. Census data regarding the estimated number of small firms in each identified industry, we conclude that the adopted rules will impact a substantial number of small entities. E. Description of Economic Impact and Projected Reporting, Recordkeeping, and Other Compliance Requirements for Small Entities
115. The RFA directs agencies to describe the economic impact of adopted rules on small entities, as well as projected reporting, recordkeeping and other compliance requirements, including an estimate of the classes of small entities which will be subject to the requirement and the type of professional skills necessary for preparation of the report or record.
116. In this
Report and Order,
we repeal the national television multiple ownership rule. Accordingly, small and other entities that want to purchase or control broadcast television stations that, in the aggregate, reach more than 39% of the television audience households in the United States will no longer need to make a showing or otherwise calculate and demonstrate compliance with the rule. We find that there are no reporting, recordkeeping, or other compliance requirements for small entities. After reviewing the record in this proceeding, we received no concerns about these types of burdens on small entities. In addition, as the
Report and Order
explains, eliminating the national cap will not permit any more or less consolidation within a local market and so will not reduce the number of voices in the market or increase the concentration among
(
printed page 72817)
stations for small broadcasters in a given market.
F. Discussion of Steps Taken To Minimize Significant Economic Impact on Small Entities, and Significant Alternatives Considered
117. The RFA requires an agency to provide, “a description of the steps the agency has taken to minimize the significant economic impact on small entities . . . including a statement of the factual, policy, and legal reasons for selecting the alternative adopted in the final rule and why each one of the other significant alternatives to the rule considered by the agency which affect the impact on small entities was rejected.
118. The rule change, eliminating the national television multiple ownership rule, is deregulatory in nature and does not impose or increase regulatory burdens on small entities. In the
Report & Order,
the Commission finds that a case-by-case approach to applications for television license transfers and assignments is the best way to promote the Commission's media ownership goals of localism, competition and viewpoint diversity. Notably, in response to the latest request for comment in the
Refresh Public Notice,
broadcast commenters were unified in their advocacy for complete elimination of the rule. As the
Report & Order
explains, elimination of the rule would not result in a loss of viewpoint diversity or competition in the local markets in which broadcast stations operate. Further, the
Report & Order
finds that eliminating the national cap does not permit any more or less consolidation within a local market and therefore has no effect on the number of voices in the market. Similarly, the
Report & Order
finds that competition within a local market will not be harmed by the substitution of one station owner for another, and preservation of the rule is not needed to promote localism.
119. Some commenters believe an alternative approach of maintaining the national ownership cap will encourage competition and local programming. By contrast, the
Report & Order
makes clear that eliminating the rule will enable broadcasters to gain additional scale, which will allow broadcasters to generate additional revenues that can be used to provide broadcast service to the local community. Creating this flexibility for broadcasters is important, as the
Report & Order
details the loss of viewership and revenue that the industry has endured since the time when the Commission last reviewed the need for this rule. The
Report & Order
further finds that scale will give local broadcast affiliates additional leverage vis-à-vis the national networks with which they negotiate for affiliation, thereby improving the ability of broadcast affiliates to resist network demands with respect to compensation and programming decisions. We considered alternative arguments that eliminating the national ownership cap would give broadcasters leverage over multichannel video programming distributors (MVPDs) in retransmission consent negotiations; however, any retransmission consent concerns may be addressed in the context of a specific transaction or in a separate rulemaking proceeding. The
Report & Order
also explains that, for individual stations that are financially struggling, repealing the national cap would give those stations additional options by permitting station groups with healthier balance sheets to expand into new markets, acquire those stations, and provide communities with more robust locally-oriented programming.
G. Report to Congress
120. The Commission will send a copy of the
Report & Order,
including this Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, in a report to Congress pursuant to the Congressional Review Act. In addition, the Commission will send a copy of the
Report & Order,
including this Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the SBA and will publish a copy of the
Report & Order,
and this Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (or summaries thereof) in the
Federal Register
.

AGENCY:
Indian Health Service, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Final notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the Indian Health Service (IHS) has decided to expand the geographic boundaries of the Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area (PRCDA) for Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo (“YDSP” or “Tribe”) to include Dona Ana County, New Mexico. The final PRCDA includes Dona Ana County, New Mexico, and El Paso and Hudspeth Counties, Texas. This expansion will authorize additional YDSP Tribal members and beneficiaries to receive Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) services.
DATES:
This expansion is effective as of the date of publication of this notice.
ADDRESSES:
This notice can be found at
https://www.federalregister.gov
.
Written requests for information should be delivered to: CDR Tracy Sanchez, Acting Director, Office of Resource Access and Partnerships, Indian Health Service, 5600 Fishers Lane, Mail Stop 06SEH03, Rockville, MD 20857.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
CDR Tracy Sanchez, Acting Director, Office of Resource Access and Partnerships by email at
Tracy.Sanchez@ihs.gov
,
or by phone at (301) 443-0969 (This is not a toll-free number).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IHS provides services under regulations in effect as of September 15, 1987, and republished at
42 CFR part 136, subparts A-C
. Subpart C defines a Contract Health Service Delivery Area (CHSDA), now referred to as a PRCDA, as the geographic area within which PRC will be made available by the IHS to members of an identified Indian community who reside in the PRCDA. Residence within a PRCDA by a person who is within the scope of the Indian health program, as set forth in
42 CFR 136.12
, creates no legal entitlement to PRC but only potential eligibility for services. Services needed, but not available at an IHS/Tribal facility, are provided under the PRC program depending on the availability of funds, the relative medical priority of the services to be provided, and the actual availability and accessibility of alternate resources in accordance with the regulations.
The regulations at
42 CFR part 136, subpart C
, provide that, unless otherwise designated, a PRCDA shall consist of a county which includes all or part of a reservation and any county or counties which have a common boundary with the reservation.
42 CFR 136.22(a)(6)
. The regulations also provide that after Consultation with the Tribal governing body or bodies on those reservations included within the PRCDA, the Secretary may, from time to time, redesignate areas within the United States for inclusion in or exclusion from a PRCDA.
42 CFR 136.22(b)
. The regulations require that certain criteria must be considered before any redesignation is made. The criteria are as follows:
(1) The number of Indians residing in the area proposed to be so included or excluded;
(2) Whether the Tribal governing body has determined that Indians residing in the area near the reservation are socially and economically affiliated with the Tribe;
(3) The geographic proximity to the reservation of the area whose inclusion or exclusion is being considered; and
(4) The level of funding which would be available for the provision of PRC.
Additionally, the regulations require that any redesignation of a PRCDA be made in accordance with the procedures of the Administrative Procedure Act (
5 U.S.C. 553
).
42 CFR 136.22(c)
. In compliance with this requirement, the IHS published a notice of proposed redesignation and requested public comments on July 1, 2026 (
91 FR 40009
). The IHS received no comments in response to the notice of proposed redesignation.
In support of this expansion, the IHS makes the following findings:
1. By expanding the PRCDA to include Dona Ana County, New Mexico, the IHS and YDSP estimate that the Tribe's PRC-eligible population would increase by an estimated 500 Tribal members.
2. As part of their expansion request, YDSP submitted a resolution from the Tribe's governing body. The resolution explains that the expansion is intended to serve their Tribal members living in Dona Ana County, New Mexico, and it describes those Tribal members as being socially and economically tied to the Tribe's reservation. The resolution also states that YDSP intends to include other eligible American Indians and Alaska Natives who maintain close economic and social ties with the Tribe, consistent with
42 CFR 136.23(a)(2)(ii)
.
3. The requested expansion would form a contiguous area with the existing PRCDA. Tribal members of YDSP reside in the county proposed for inclusion in the expanded PRCDA. Through their expansion request, the Tribe described how close Dona Ana County, New Mexico, is to their reservation and health clinic, approximately 45 miles. The Tribe explained that it is close enough for their Tribal members residing in Dona Ana County to utilize the YDSP Health Clinic as their primary site of care. For these reasons, the IHS has determined the additional county proposed for inclusion to be geographically proximate, meaning “on or near,” to the Tribe's reservation.
4. Through YDSP's request to expand its PRCDA, the Tribe has indicated that the PRC program can continue providing the same level of care to the PRC eligible population if the PRCDA is expanded as proposed, without requiring additional funding from the IHS or reduction of the current medical priority level.

Indian Health Service
AGENCY:
Indian Health Service, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Final notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the Indian Health Service (IHS) has decided to expand the geographic boundaries of the Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area (PRCDA) for the Kewa Pueblo (“Kewa Pueblo” or “Tribe”) to include Bernalillo County, New Mexico. The final PRCDA includes Bernalillo, Sandoval, and Santa Fe Counties, New Mexico. This expansion will authorize additional Kewa Pueblo Tribal members and beneficiaries to receive Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) services.
DATES:
This expansion is effective as of the date of publication of this notice.
ADDRESSES:
This notice can be found at
https://www.federalregister.gov
.
Written requests for information should be delivered to: CDR Tracy Sanchez, Acting Director, Office of Resource Access and Partnerships, Indian Health Service, 5600 Fishers Lane, Mail Stop 06SEH03, Rockville, MD 20857.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
CDR Tracy Sanchez, Acting Director, Office of Resource Access and Partnerships by email at
Tracy.Sanchez@ihs.gov
,
or by phone at (301) 443-0969 (This is not a toll-free number).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IHS provides services under regulations in effect as of September 15, 1987, and republished at
42 CFR part 136, subparts A-C
. Subpart C defines a Contract Health Service Delivery Area (CHSDA), now referred to as a PRCDA, as the geographic area within which PRC will be made available by the IHS to members of an identified Indian community who reside in the PRCDA. Residence within a PRCDA by a person who is within the scope of the Indian health program, as set forth in
42 CFR 136.12
, creates no legal entitlement to PRC but only potential eligibility for services. Services needed, but not available at an IHS/Tribal facility, are provided under the PRC program depending on the availability of funds, the relative medical priority of the services to be provided, and the actual availability and accessibility of alternate resources in accordance with the regulations.
The regulations at
42 CFR part 136, subpart C
, provide that, unless otherwise designated, a PRCDA shall consist of a county which includes all or part of a reservation and any county or counties which have a common boundary with the reservation.
42 CFR 136.22(a)(6)
. The regulations also provide that after Consultation with the Tribal governing body or bodies on those reservations included within the PRCDA, the Secretary may, from time to time, redesignate areas within the United States for inclusion in or exclusion from a PRCDA.
42 CFR 136.22(b)
. The regulations require that certain criteria must be considered before any redesignation is made. The criteria are as follows:
(1) The number of Indians residing in the area proposed to be so included or excluded;
(2) Whether the Tribal governing body has determined that Indians residing in the area near the reservation are socially and economically affiliated with the Tribe;
(3) The geographic proximity to the reservation of the area whose inclusion or exclusion is being considered; and
(4) The level of funding which would be available for the provision of PRC.
Additionally, the regulations require that any redesignation of a PRCDA be made in accordance with the procedures of the Administrative Procedure Act (
5 U.S.C. 553
).
42 CFR 136.22(c)
. In compliance with this requirement, the IHS published a notice of proposed redesignation and requested public comments on June 25, 2026 (
91 FR 38449
). The IHS did not receive any comments in response to the notice of proposed redesignation.
In support of this expansion, the IHS makes the following findings:
1. By expanding the PRCDA to include Bernalillo County, New Mexico, the Kewa Pueblo estimates that the Tribe's PRC eligible population would increase by an estimated 200 Tribal members.
2. As part of their expansion request, the Kewa Pueblo submitted a resolution from the Tribe's governing body. The resolution indicates that the requested expansion is intended to serve their members living in Bernalillo County, New Mexico. During Tribal Consultation, the Kewa Pueblo verified that those members are socially and economically affiliated with the Tribe.
3. Bernalillo County is approximately 30 miles from the Tribe's reservation. The requested expansion would form a contiguous area with the existing PRCDA. Tribal members of the Kewa Pueblo reside in the county proposed
(
printed page 72882)
for inclusion in the expanded PRCDA. For these reasons, the IHS has determined the additional county proposed for inclusion to be geographically proximate, meaning “on or near,” to the Tribe's reservation.
4. Through the Kewa Pueblo's request to expand its PRCDA, the Tribe has indicated that the PRC program can continue providing the same level of care to the PRC eligible population if the PRCDA is expanded as proposed, without requiring additional funding from the IHS or reduction of the current medical priority level.
An updated listing of the PRCDAs for all federally recognized Tribes may be accessed via the Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Areas link on the IHS PRCDA Redesignation website (
https://www.ihs.gov/​prc/​prcda-expansion
).
Accordingly, the IHS finalizes the redesignation of the Kewa Pueblo PRCDA to include Bernalillo County, New Mexico.
Mark Cruz,
Director, Indian Health Service.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Proposed rule; request for public comment.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA or Department) proposes to amend the regulations governing grazing and livestock use on the National Forest System to modernize grazing administration, improve clarity, codify existing policy, and expand opportunities for stewardship and access. The proposed amendments would update permit issuance, eligibility, and qualification provisions; establish a framework for adaptive response to drought, wildfire, and similar disturbance events; and expand authorities for stewardship-oriented livestock use, including adding the ability to implement stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing) under a temporary grazing permit or livestock use permit. The proposed rule would revise grazing fee provisions to ensure consistent fee-setting across the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands, and establish a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock by permittees. It would consolidate and renumber existing sections in subpart A for clarity and make conforming, technical, and administrative updates throughout part 222. The Department invites public comment on all aspects of the proposed rule.
DATES:
Comments must be received in writing by December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments, identified by RIN 0596-AD75, should be sent via one of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for sending comments; or
Mail:
Hardcopy letters must be submitted to the Director, Natural Resources, National Forest System, 201 14th Street SW, Mailstop 1108, Washington, DC 20250-1124. Hardcopy letters must be postmarked on or before the close of the comment period as shown above in
DATES
.
Comments should be confined to issues pertinent to the proposed rule, should explain the reasons for any recommended changes, and should reference the specific section and wording being addressed, where possible. All timely comments, including names and addresses when provided, will be placed in the record and will be available for public inspection and copying. Comments and a plain language summary of the proposed rule may be viewed on the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
In the search box, enter “RIN 0596-AD75,” and click the “Search” button. For this reason, please do not include in your comments information of a confidential nature, such as sensitive personal information or proprietary information. If you send an email comment, your email address will be automatically captured and included as part of the comment that is placed in the public docket and made available for public viewing. Please note that comments containing any standard confidentiality disclaimer—such as the automatic notices added to some emails—will be treated as public comments that may be made available to the public notwithstanding the inclusion of the routine notice.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Myra Black, Rangeland Program Manager, National Forest System, Natural Resources, USDA Forest Service, by phone at (202) 205-1464. Individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may call 711 to reach the Telecommunications Relay Service, then provide the phone number of the named point of contact for further information.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background and Need
A. Authority
The Forest Service administers livestock grazing on the National Forest System under the authority and direction of the Organic Act of 1897 (
16 U.S.C. 481
,
551
), the Transfer Act of 1905 (
16 U.S.C. 472
), the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act of 1937 (
7 U.S.C. 1010
,
1011
,
1012
), the Granger-Thye Act of 1950 (
16 U.S.C. 572
,
580d
,
580g
,
580h
,
580l
), the Multiple-Use Sustained-Yield Act of 1960 (
16 U.S.C. 528-531
), the Forest and Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act (RPA) of 1974, as amended by the National Forest Management Act (NFMA) of 1976 (
16 U.S.C. 1600-1605
,
1609
,
1613
), the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (
43 U.S.C. 1740
,
1751-1752
), the Public Rangelands Improvement Act of 1978 (
43 U.S.C. 1901-1908
), the Agricultural Credit Act of 1987 (
7 U.S.C. 5101-5106
), the Wilderness Act of 1964 (
16 U.S.C. 1133
), and Public Law 97-258 (
31 U.S.C. 9701
), as well as various appropriations provisions and executive orders. The Forest Service issues grazing permits and other livestock use authorizations on the National Forest System lands. Regulations for administration of livestock grazing and rangeland management on National Forest System lands are set forth at 36 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 222.
B. Existing Regulatory Framework
Part 222 is organized into four subparts. Subpart A (Grazing and Livestock Use on the National Forest System) establishes the substantive and procedural framework for the issuance, modification, suspension, and cancellation of grazing permits, as well as for cooperation in management. Subpart B (Mediation of Term Grazing Permit Disputes) provides for the mediation of disputes regarding term grazing permits in States with mediation programs certified by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Subpart C (Grazing Fees) governs the calculation and collection of grazing fees on the National Forest System. Subpart D (Management of Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros) is not affected by this rulemaking.
The substantive regulations governing the issuance and administration of grazing permits in subpart A have not been comprehensively revised since 1977, with limited amendments in 1979, 1981, 1990, and 2022. Subpart C has remained largely unchanged since 1979, with adjustments to the grazing fee formula and to the assessment of fees for excess and unauthorized use most recently codified in 2022 (
87 FR 35097
, June 9, 2022). In the intervening decades, livestock grazing on the National Forest System has continued to be a vital component of rural livelihoods, food and fiber production, and the management of forage, fuels, and other vegetation across about 96 million acres of allotments. Grazing practices have evolved, ranching workforce demographics have shifted, drought and wildfire frequency and intensity have increased, and the framework for cooperation with neighboring Federal land managers, States, Tribes, and conservation partners has matured.
C. Need for Amendments
Many considerations prompt the Department to propose these amendments to part 222. Below, the Department groups the proposed changes into clear categories, explains the current status quo under existing
(
printed page 73035)
regulations or directives, and describes why specific updates are necessary.
1. Modernize and Codify Long-Standing Practices Reflected in Forest Service Directives
On December 18, 2020, the Forest Service published in the
Federal Register
proposed directives to revise Forest Service Manual 2200 and Forest Service Handbooks 2209.13 and 2209.16 (
85 FR 82432
, December 18, 2020). These directives received and incorporated public input and were finalized between 2022 and 2025. The revisions replaced dated terminology (such as substituting “range” with “rangeland”), updated temporary non-use policies to provide greater management flexibility during climatic events and for resource management needs, added flexibilities to reduce barriers to entry into the agricultural industry, and provided greater clarity and consistent interpretation for policies and procedures that were reflective of how practices were being implemented on the ground. This proposed rule updates terminology and delegations to the “authorized officer,” and places long-standing administrative practices from Forest Service Manual 2200 and Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 into regulation where rights and obligations are clearer; no substantive change is intended except where expressly noted in the paragraphs below.
In 2021 the Rangeland Management program embarked on a strategic and futuristic exploration called “Rangeland Futuring,” consisting of brainstorming exercises and listening sessions with employees, stakeholders (17 different interest groups including industry, environmental groups, federal agencies, and advocacy), Tribes, and permittees. The intent of Rangeland Futuring was to gain perspective on how the Agency should manage its rangelands into the future and focus on actions such as improving access to term grazing permits, providing greater flexibilities in term grazing permits, improve overall livestock management, improve program transparency, improve monitoring consistency, implement modernized rangeland management technologies and coordination, implement employee development, enhance Tribal engagement, and other ideas related to rangeland management. The input received through the workshops and webinars was developed into implementable actions leading to modernization of the existing regulations and the need to better align with the Bureau of Land Management.
The existing regulations are also being modernized to align the Rangeland Management program to legislation, such as the Carl Levin and Howard P. “Buck” McKeon National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2015 (
Pub. L. 113-291
), and reflect current agency policies and practices, that came out of the Rangeland Futuring effort over the past six years.
2. Establish Explicit Adaptive Tools for Rangeland Disturbance and Emergency Response
Under current regulations, authorized officers and permittees address events such as drought, wildfire, and sudden reductions in forage or water availability through case-by-case decisions relying on annual operating instructions, permit letters, and directive guidance. This ad hoc approach can delay actions and lead to inconsistent documentation. This proposed rule therefore codifies a rangeland disturbance planning and emergency response framework (new section222.2(e) and section222.5(d)) with clear criteria; consultation, cooperation, and coordination steps; and documentation requirements (for example duration, affected pastures, and termination criteria). This structure makes temporary response actions predictable and transparent, so they can be invoked promptly and consistently when ground conditions change. It also provides for grazing flexibility of up to 21 days early before the beginning date specified in the permit or not to extend grazing more than 21 days after the end date specified on the permit (222.5(c)(7)), to account for annual fluctuations in climate, and water and forage availability when needed to reduce fine fuels or adjust grazing due to drought conditions.
3. Update Eligibility and Qualification Provisions To Reflect Contemporary Ranching Pathways
Existing regulations emphasize outright ownership of base property and livestock and do not fully account for common, lawful arrangements used by beginning ranchers and successors (for example, successional base property, extended purchase agreements, leases of livestock or property, or mentor/mentee arrangements). Consistent with recently finalized directives and codifying the policies, the proposed rule clarifies that “owned or leased” base property and livestock qualify (section222.3(h)(2)), adds exceptions for documented successional and mentor/mentee arrangements, and recognized certain family succession circumstances. These changes formalize pathways that have reduced barriers to entry in practice and better match the realities of ranch transitions, workforce demographics, and the scale of community ranching operations. In addition to these added flexibilities to reduce barriers, the Forest Service is adding the opportunity to allow leasing of base property and livestock to better align with Bureau of Land Management (BLM) base property and livestock leasing policies and further diversify opportunities for the various business transactions that transpire in the ranching industry.
4. Replace Dated Permit-Cap Provisions With a Flexible Anti-Consolidation Framework
Current upper and special limits in section 222.3(c)(1)(vi)(E) are phrased in terms that do not provide authorized officers the discretion needed to address two opposite trends: (1) excessive accumulation of multiple permits by a single-family unit or related group of entities, and (2) proliferation of inefficiently small split permits that are difficult to administer, diminish livestock production ranches and viable market supplies, as well as fragment herd management across an allotment. The proposed rule authorizes denial of applications that would produce either extreme based on documented local factors such as reduced opportunities for local or beginning ranchers, diminished on-the-ground oversight, or impaired economic viability of community-scale ranching (section 222.6(h)). This modern, criteria-based approach allows field units to tailor decisions to local conditions and staffing realities while maintaining fair access to grazing capacity.
5. Address Livestock Leasing Through Targeted Surcharge
Current fee provisions in subpart C do not expressly address situations where livestock owned by non-permittees are lawfully leased by the permittee and grazed on the permittee's allotment. To recover the government's incremental administrative costs, capture a portion of the larger profit associated with pasturing livestock, and to promote parity with the Bureau of Land Management, this proposed rule would create a surcharge for such authorized leasing (section 222.50(d), section 222.52(d), section 222.53(i)), consistent with the long-standing concept used by the Bureau of Land Management at
43 CFR 4130.8-1(f)
. See
31 U.S.C. 9701
. The surcharge does not prohibit leasing, but may provide incentive to maintain owned livestock, which are familiar with grazing the allotment and promoting long-term stewardship of the land. The surcharge would capture a
(
printed page 73036)
portion of the larger profit associated with pasturing livestock and prices the additional administrative burden exempting properly documented mentees, beginning ranchers, permittee successors, immediate or extended family members under section 222.3(h)(2)(v), and operators receiving relief due to drought, fire, or other natural causes. This targeted instrument supports mentoring and succession objectives while discouraging arrangements that would bypass permittee responsibilities or obscure ownership.
6. Consolidate and Clarify Fee-Setting Across Western National Forests and National Grasslands
Although the existing formula at section 222.51 governs fee calculation on Western forests and informs grassland fees, it is split across sections 222.51 and 222.52. The proposed rule would consolidate fee-setting, while retaining the existing fee formula, for the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands into a single section (section 222.51), set forth the grazing fee formula explicitly without change, and codifies the fee-reduction and fee-credit provisions historically administered through Forest Service Manual 2240 and Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, chapters 20 and 80, and other related guidance. Codification increases transparency, reduces confusion for operators who graze across forest and grassland units, and preserves established caps.
7. Streamline Eastern States' Competitive Bidding Procedures
Current section 222.54 requires each bidder to deposit 10 percent of the total bid amount, with refunds processed for unsuccessful or unqualified bidders. Field units report that this deposit-and-refund cycle imposes an administrative burden disproportionate to its purpose. The proposed rule would remove the deposit requirement and retain qualification checks and minimum bid setting (section 222.53), reducing administrative burden, speeding award timelines, and lower up-front barriers without changing how fair market value is established.
8. Align With the Bureau of Land Management and Inter-Department Initiatives Where Appropriate
Many operators hold authorizations on both National Forest System lands and adjacent BLM lands. Divergent definitions and tools can impose compliance costs and complicate administration. In 2025 the Secretaries of Agriculture and Interior coordinated an initiative to develop a USDA-DOI Grazing Action Plan to streamline and modernize livestock grazing on federal lands, with key goals of strengthening rancher resilience, reducing barriers to ranchers through modernization, supporting herd rebuilding, and maintaining working rangelands while sustaining rangeland health and supporting rural economies. In March 2026, Forest Service and BLM signed the Advancing Grazing on Forest Service and BLM Lands Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), which commits the two agencies to coordinated actions, including prioritizing vacant and closed allotments, maximizing grazing flexibilities, streamlining permitting, improving data transparency, expanding targeted and outcome-based grazing, enhancing wildlife liaison functions, and modernizing grazing management practices. The Forest Service has coordinated with the BLM throughout the development of this proposed rule and has incorporated structural and substantive elements that align with the BLM rulemaking, including the surcharge concept and certain policies such as extending temporary non-use for personal convenience from 3 years to 4 years.
At the Department's direction, the Forest Service initiated its collaborative work with the BLM on this proposed rule in January 2026. From the outset, consistency between the Departments' regulations was a key objective. In the early development of this proposed rule the Forest Service and BLM met to identify and discuss consistency on key policy issues such as ensuring livestock grazing increased livestock production, leasing of base property and livestock, expanding opportunities for beginning ranchers, and broadening the definition of base property. From January to June 2026, BLM assisted with the review and participated in development of this rule by integrating BLM rule language to improve consistency in permit administration and rangeland management across administrative boundaries. Development of this proposed rule in its entirety was collaborative and coordinated to improve consistency for livestock operators who graze across both systems. For example, key provisions in this proposed rule reflecting an intentional effort to improve consistency include:
Allowing leasing of base property and livestock consistent with BLM regulation (
36 CFR 222.1
,
222.3(h)(2)
);
Redefining “base property” to include water rights consistent with BLM regulations (
36 CFR 222.1
); and
Providing additional opportunities to consult, cooperate, and coordinate with permittees before taking permit action (
36 CFR 222.5(c)
,
(d)
,
(e)
).
Extending temporary non-use for personal convenience from 3 to 4 years (
36 CFR 222.5(d)(1)(ii)
).
Although the agencies have different authorities, the Department has endeavored to achieve consistency regarding policy issues to the benefit of shared livestock operators. The Department seeks public comment on this proposed rule as to whether these objectives have been met, and where even greater consistency and equalization may be achieved. The Department will consider these comments in the development of a final rule.
D. Overview of Proposed Rule
This proposed rule would amend subparts A, B, and C of
36 CFR part 222
. Subpart D (Management of Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros) is not affected. The principal elements of the proposed rule are summarized below. A section-by-section explanation follows.
The title of part 222 would be revised from Range Management to Rangeland Management to reflect contemporary terminology and to better align the part heading with current agency usage and statutory context.
Subpart A would be reorganized and revised to modernize the framework for issuing and administering grazing permits. Section 222.3 would be revised in full to consolidate the categories of permits, eligibility and qualification requirements, and codify the grant priority process for available grazing capacity. Notable substantive changes include:
Livestock use permits.
Extend the maximum term from one year to up to five years to reduce repeat paperwork for research, transportation stock, and targeted vegetation management while preserving their non-renewal priority status (section 222.3(j)(2)). Livestock use permits would also be expanded to include stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing and targeted grazing).
Discretionary priority and qualification exceptions.
Codify, for existing policies and use of the prospectus-based offerings process, discretionary priority for qualified beginning ranchers and permittee mentees, and add four exceptions that reflect directive-based pathways now common in practice (section 222.3(g), (h), (k)). This formalizes tools used to
(
printed page 73037)
reduce barriers and support family and workforce succession.
Section 222.4 would be amended with a revised heading and targeted updates to paragraph (a) to reflect delegation to the authorized officer and maintain current cancellation grounds. Routine adjustments would be addressed in the new section 222.5.
A new section 222.5 would consolidate and codify the framework for changes in permitted, authorized use, and active use including codifying procedures and limits for temporary non-use and permit modifications currently found in Forest Service manual and handbook, including:
Temporary non-use for personal convenience.
Clarify limits (up to 4 consecutive years, not to exceed 4 years in a 10-year rolling period when less than 90 percent of permitted numbers are grazed), keeping the concept but adding guardrails to prevent extended temporary non-use from eroding management objectives.
Temporary non-use for resource management needs.
Make explicit documentation and monitoring requirements; preserve emergency authority for immediate closures or temporary changes when needed to protect resources.
Temporary increases/decreases and forage reserve use.
Clarify written request requirements and a 21-day window for short-term changes within existing permit terms; specify how additional forage is apportioned, including for stewardship outcomes and forage reserves.
Sections 222.6 and 222.7 would each be revised in full. Current section 222.9 would be redesignated as section 222.8 and completely revised to consolidate and update the provisions currently found in sections 222.6, 222.9, and 222.10. Current section 222.7 would be redesignated as section 222.9 and fully revised to update the existing requirements contained in section 222.7. Finally, current section 222.8 would be redesignated as section 222.10 and revised in full to update the provisions of the existing section 222.8.
Subpart B would be amended to revise the heading and introductory text of section 222.20 to clarify that mediation is available in States with a USDA certified mediation program, the heading and paragraph (b) of section 222.21 to clarify the parties to mediation include the authorized officer who made the decision or his or her designee, and section 222.26 in full. These changes would replace references to the “Chief, Forest Service” with references to the “authorized officer” to reflect current delegations and would clarify the parties to mediation as being the authorized officer or the authorized officer's designee while keeping the scope of ex parte communications the same as the current section.
Subpart C would be amended to revise sections 222.50 and 222.51 in full; remove existing section 222.52 (National Grasslands), the substance of which would be incorporated into revised section 222.51; and redesignate sections 222.53 and 222.54 as sections 222.52 and 222.53, respectively, with conforming and substantive amendments.
Substantive policy changes would (1) expand base property definition from `land and improvements owned and used by the permittee for a farm or ranch operation and specifically designated by the permittee to qualify for a term grazing permit' to include crop lands and stockwater rights, which provides greater flexibility for applicants to qualify for a term grazing permit, while better aligning with BLM regulations; (2) reduce barriers to permit acquisition for beginning ranchers and mentees through targeted exceptions and discretionary priority in prospectus-based offerings, as these policies are already being widely implemented through Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, chapter 10; (3) expand stewardship-oriented authorities, including adding the ability to implement stewardship projects under a temporary grazing permit or livestock use permit, due to the increasing need for a permit to facilitate implementation of targeted grazing and stewardship agreements; (4) clarify and expand the procedures for temporary non-use, increases and decreases in permitted use, and permit modifications to codify existing practices; (5) codify the rangeland disturbance planning framework for drought, wildfire, and other events; (6) codify a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock; (7) consolidate fee-setting for the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands; (8) codify fee-reduction and fee-credit provisions for grazing on the national grasslands and land utilization projects; (9) replace outdated permit-cap provisions with a more flexible anti-consolidation framework; and (10) improve consistency with BLM livestock grazing regulations and practices.
II. Section-by-Section Explanation of the Proposed Rule
A. Subpart A—Grazing and Livestock Use on the National Forest System
1. Section 222.1 Authority and Definitions
The Department proposes to revise section 222.1 in full. Paragraph (a) would be updated to reflect that the Chief, Forest Service, may redelegate the authority to develop, administer, and protect rangeland resources to the authorized officer through Forest Service Manual 2200, consistent with current practice. The reference to “range resources” would be updated to “rangeland resources” throughout to align with contemporary usage in directives and planning.
Paragraph (b) would replace the existing list of definitions with an updated, expanded list presented in alphabetical order. New definitions would be added for terms used elsewhere in the proposed rule or as found in the Forest Service Manual and Handbooks, including active allotment; actual use; adjusted grazing value; authorized officer; active use; authorized use; beginning rancher; conservation practice; consultation, cooperation, and coordination; current grazing management; eleven Western States; unauthorized use rate; fair market value; fee credit; forage reserve allotment; grant process; grazing agreement; grazing association; land use practices; lessee of base property; lessee of livestock; livestock use permit; maintenance of rangeland improvements; mentee; monitoring; nine Great Plains States; non-permittee; temporary non-use; permitted use; preferred applicant; rules of management; small farm or ranch; stocking rate; succeeding family member; successional base property; successional livestock arrangement; supplemental feed; targeted grazing; temporary grazing permit; term grazing permit consolidation; term grazing permit with on-and-off provisions; term private land grazing permit; trend; unauthorized livestock; vacant allotment; and waiver of term grazing permit. Most defined terms exist in recently updated Forest Service directives, which went through public notice and comment, and are carried into regulations for transparency and ease of administration, while other terms are being added for consistency with BLM.
Existing definitions would be updated where necessary to reflect current terminology, statutory references, and Forest Service practice. The definition
(
printed page 73038)
of range betterment fund would be updated to reflect that the fund consists of 50 percent of all monies received as fees for grazing livestock on the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States or $10,000,000 per annum, whichever is greater, consistent with title IV, section 401(b)(1), of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act.
2. Section 222.2 Allotment Management
The Department proposes to revise section 222.2 in full and incorporate into this section the provisions on allotment management plans, changes to allotment boundaries, and rangeland disturbance planning.
Paragraph (a) would establish that forage-producing National Forest System lands are managed for livestock grazing in a manner consistent with land management plans. Paragraph (a) has similar wording to the current paragraph (c) of this section. Forest plans guide multiple-use management, and grazing authorizations have long been issued to conform with plan direction; this codifies existing practice.
Paragraph (b) has similar wording and the same intent as the current paragraph (a), carrying forward the existing direction on the designation of allotments. Paragraph (c) would make allotment management plans optional to align with wording in Section 402(d) of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act, whereas the current paragraph (b) makes development of an allotment management plan mandatory. Paragraph (c) carries forward the provisions on allotment management plans, including the consultation, cooperation, and coordination process; if an allotment management plan is developed it will include elements such as prescribe the livestock grazing practices necessary to meet specific resource objectives defined in existing environmental analysis, specify any operational flexibility that can be approved by the authorized officer, and include a monitoring plan; the treatment of private and State lands; and revision and termination procedures. Under current practice, authorized officers frequently use annual operating instructions or functionally equivalent instruments to implement site-specific direction where a full allotment management plan is not necessary. Making allotment management plans optional eliminates duplicative documentation in routine cases and allows allotment management plans to be prepared where they add value. When an allotment management plan is prepared, the content requirements remain mandatory.
Paragraph (d) would codify the provisions on changes to allotment boundaries, such as when the conditions under which a realignment may be considered a technical correction, the procedures for combining vacant allotments, and the requirements applicable when a boundary modification is not appropriately handled as a technical correction. Paragraph (e) would establish the rangeland disturbance planning framework, which provides considerations for the authorized officer to navigate, providing for temporary response actions, such as temporary changes in livestock numbers, season of use, pasture rotation, timing of use, area of use, water use, supplemental feeding locations, targeted grazing, temporary non-use or other actions necessary to maintain rangeland resources and livestock health during drought, wildfire, or other events that materially reduce forage or water availability. Authorized officers and permittees currently navigate disturbance events through case-by-case tools. Codifying a clear, repeatable framework reduces uncertainty, improves timeliness, and delineates documentation and notice expectations. The framework also clarifies that targeted grazing may be used, when appropriate and consistent with applicable law and plan direction, as a tool within wildfire decisions (see section 222.5 for related authorities).
3. Section 222.3 Issuance of Grazing Permits
The Department proposes to revise section 222.3 in full and incorporate into this section the provisions on eligibility and qualification requirements, permits with priority for renewal, permits with no priority for renewal, and grant priority for available grazing capacity. Paragraph (a) retains components of the current wording and further identifies the categories of permits available for grazing and livestock use, including term grazing permits, temporary grazing permits, and livestock use permits. Paragraphs (b) through (e) would describe the substantive content and effect of term grazing permits, including the elements that must be specified on the permit, that grazing is by production-oriented livestock, the treatment of variable-use authorizations, the subjection of all permits to cancellation, suspension, or modification, and the longstanding principle that permits convey no right, title, or interest in any lands or resources. Paragraph (f) would update existing paragraph (c) to allow the authorized officer (rather than the Chief, Forest Service) to issue permits. Paragraph (g) would carry forward the existing direction at paragraph (c)(1)(vi) on the issuance, renewal, and administration of term permits, and would codify a discretionary priority for qualified beginning ranchers or permittee mentees when a term grazing permit is issued through a prospectus, together with four categories of exceptions to the qualification requirements (phased acquisition of base property or livestock; successional base property arrangements; permittee mentor/mentee arrangements; and successional livestock arrangements). This discretionary priority for qualified beginning ranchers or permittee mentees is a policy from Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10, that is being codified to align with the Department's direction to expand opportunities for beginning ranchers. The prospectus process has historically been used across the Eastern States and National Grasslands when soliciting applicants for a term grazing permit when long term forage is available. The process of prioritizing applicants, the grant priority process, has historically been utilized throughout National Forest System lands. Paragraph (h) would codify eligibility and qualification requirements that are not currently in part 222 but have been long standing policies in the Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10. Paragraph (h) also includes codifying six exceptions to the base property and livestock ownership requirement. Paragraph (i) would carry forward the framework for permits with priority for renewal at the existing paragraph (c)(1), including the 10-year permit term and the priority position of the existing permit holder. Paragraph (j) would carry forward the framework for permits with no priority for renewal at the existing paragraph (c)(2), with two notable updates: it would add a sixth ground for issuing a temporary grazing permit (use on a forage reserve allotment by a non-permittee and use for stewardship and targeted grazing projects), and it would extend the term of livestock use permits from one year to up to five years and expand its use to include stewardship and targeted and grazing projects. Paragraph (j) would also codify the term private land permit. Paragraph (k) would codify the grant priority process for available grazing capacity, including a prospectus-based priority order that favors qualified beginning ranchers, mentees, and small business ranchers. Historically, the grant priority process has been used when grazing capacity becomes available on a permanent sustained-yield basis for grazing across
(
printed page 73039)
the Forest Service, giving first priority to existing permittees when unresolved resource or management concerns exist and then to permittees who have invested in the allotment and the increase in available forage is due to their efforts. These priorities remain as they historically have been. However, if these situations are not present when the opportunity for available forage arises, the next order in the grant priority process is to issue a prospectus and solicit applicants, giving priority to a beginning rancher, mentee, or small business rancher; whereas historically this priority was given to owners of livestock currently authorized on ranges administered by the BLM to the extent that the BLM ranges need adjustments and then to a new applicant (not an existing term permittee) who is eligible and qualified. Nearly all grant priority process decisions were issued to existing Forest Service permittees due to unresolved resource or management concerns and rarely came down to the process of seeking new applicants. Thus, the policies rarely provided opportunities to allow new ranchers into the public lands grazing system.
Compared to the current regulation, these changes include the following:
Issuance authority.
The authorized officer—rather than the Chief—may issue permits (updates existing paragraph (c)).
Eligibility/qualification.
The section codifies eligibility and qualification exceptions (successional arrangements, mentor/mentee, phased acquisition, extended livestock purchase), making transparent practices that have been administered via Forest Service directives.
Grant priority for available capacity.
Codifies a prospectus-based priority order that favors qualified beginning ranchers, mentees, and small business ranchers when no preferred applicant exists, while maintaining first priority for renewal with the existing permit holder under
43 U.S.C. 1752(c)
.
Prioritizing beginning ranchers and mentees for newly available capacity may place other qualified applicants behind those categories in prospectus order. The rule preserves first priority for renewal and does not alter existing permit holders' status on their current allotments.
4. Section 222.4 Cancellation or Suspension of Grazing Permits
The Department proposes to amend section 222.4 by revising the section heading, paragraph (a) introductory text, and paragraph (a)(2)(iv). The section heading would be amended from “Changes in grazing permits” to “Cancellation, modification, or suspension of grazing permits” to more accurately describe the section's content, which is principally directed at the grounds and procedures for cancellation, modification, and suspension of grazing and livestock use permits. The introductory text of paragraph (a) would be revised to refer to the “authorized officer” rather than the “Chief, Forest Service,” consistent with the substitution made throughout part 222 to reflect current delegations. Paragraph (a)(2)(iv) would be revised to refer to “the allotment” rather than “the allotted range,” consistent with the defined term “allotment” at section 222.1(b); no substantive change to the grounds for cancellation is intended. The remaining provisions of section 222.4 would not be amended. Routine adjustments to permitted and authorized use—including temporary non-use for permittee personal convenience, temporary non-use for resource management needs, emergency closures, and permit modifications—would be governed by new section 222.5.
5. Section 222.5 Changes in Permitted, Authorized, and Active Use
The Department proposes to add a new section 222.5 to better align wording with BLM, consolidate, codify, and modernize the policies governing changes in the use of National Forest System lands for livestock grazing. This includes adopting common terminology regarding the amount of livestock grazing that may occur in a given year, as “authorized use.” To provide clarity across agencies, the Forest Service will use the term “active use” when describing the amount of grazing that can be permitted and available for use. Section 222.5 does not currently exist in
36 CFR part 222
; the substance of this new section has been administered through Forest Service Manual 2200 and 2230 and Forest Service Handbooks 2209.13 and 2209.16. The components of paragraph (a) have been interwoven throughout policies in the Forest Service Manual 2200 and 2230 and Forest Service Handbooks 2209.13 and 2209.16; by codifying the policies in paragraph (a) it makes the policies more concise. Paragraph (b) would require that any further modifications to permitted use be based on site-specific analysis informed by monitoring data, documented field observations, ecological site inventories, or other updated information that was included during the site-specific analysis deemed acceptable by the authorized officer, which is consistent with policies in the Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapters 10 and 90, as well as consistent with BLM regulation at 4110.3-2. Paragraph (c) would codify current Forest Service Handbook policies and procedures found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 for increasing permitted, authorized, and active use, including authorizations to fill in behind approved temporary non-use; the conditions for forage reserve use; the apportionment of additional forage for stewardship outcomes as found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 and 30 policies; add the new written-request requirement and 21-day timing window for temporary changes within existing permit terms; and the apportionment of additional forage available on a permanent or sustained-yield basis through the grant process in section 222.3(l), consistent with policies in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10. Paragraph (e) would codify, with minor changes, current Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 policies and procedures for permit modifications, including a new consult, cooperate, and coordinate requirement, written documentation through a letter with appropriate attachments, the one-year advance notice requirement for changes in season of use, livestock numbers, kind, class, or allotment (carried forward from existing section 222.4(a)(8), with an emergency exception), and eight enumerated

categories of permit modification purposes.
All frameworks above have been utilized through Forest Service directives Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 and local program administration. Codification increases transparency, consistency, and efficiency while keeping on-the-ground discretion where needed.
6. Section 222.6 Term Grazing Permit Waivers and Applications
The Department proposes to revise section 222.6 to codify, with minor changes, the procedures for waivers of term grazing permits and applications for term grazing permits as found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10. The waiver and application procedures have historically been administered through Forest Service Manual 2230 and the corresponding Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10; codifying them in regulation provides transparency and increased certainty for permittees and applicants. The section would address the circumstances under which a waiver must be submitted by retaining the existing policies found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 and adding language to address the new ability to lease base property that has a term grazing permit associated with it; the requirements applicable to waivers by retaining the existing policies found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10 and adding a 90-day complete and execution requirement when the sale or lease occurs; the effect of approval; the special procedures applicable to inheritance is added to be consistent with BLM language while also codifying language consistent with Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 10; new language added to address base property leases, and entity name change policies remain unchanged; the consequences of failure to comply with the requirements; modernization of the upper and special limits concept, as found in existing 222.3 (1)(vi)(E), by focusing on the criteria authorized officers may use to deny an application that would result in excessive consolidation or in an inefficiently small permit; the circumstances under which an application must be submitted following a waiver of term grazing permit; and adding a 90-day complete and execution requirement for applications to be files following a sale or lease.
Bringing waiver and application procedures from Forest Service directives into regulation standardizes expectations nationwide and reduces administrative burden, while providing consistencies with the BLM.
