These provisions consolidate and clarify practices historically addressed in Forest Service directives to make them easier to find and apply. The compensation provision reflects the statutory framework in
43 U.S.C. 1752(g)
regarding two-year notice and reasonable compensation.
9. Section 222.9 Cooperation in Management
The Department proposes to redesignate existing section 222.7 as section 222.9 and to revise the redesignated section in full. The section is being revised because the existing section on Cooperation in management was confusing and did not clearly articulate the difference between formally recognized grazing associations and local, county, State, national, or Tribal livestock associations. The revision provides more depth and details for formal recognition and cooperation with grazing associations and codifies Forest Service Handbook 2209.13 Chapter 20. The substantive provisions on cooperation with grazing associations would be reorganized into paragraphs addressing the authority to recognize associations, the requirements for recognition, when withdrawal of recognition is warranted, and rules of management which describe how an association will administer the grazing program for its members on the lands covered by their forest Service grazing agreement, and the purpose is to provide clear and consistent rules that will be applied to each member and to distribute livestock grazing privileges in a fair manner to all qualified members. References to the “Chief, Forest Service” would be replaced with references to the “authorized officer” to reflect current delegations. Paragraphs on cooperation with national, State, and county livestock organizations adds recognition of Tribal livestock organizations; interagency cooperation; and cooperation with others would be carried forward with minor wording updates.
Reorganization of this section improves clarity without changing substantive policy.
10. Section 222.10 Cooperation in Control of Estray or Unbranded Livestock, Animal Diseases, Noxious Weeds, and Use of Pesticides
The Department proposes to redesignate existing section 222.8 as section 222.10 and to revise the redesignated section. The section heading would be amended to refer to “noxious weeds” rather than “noxious farm weeds.” References to the “Chief, Forest Service” would be replaced with references to the “authorized officer.” The substantive provisions governing cooperation with State, county, and Federal agencies on livestock diseases, sanitation, and noxious weeds; with the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service on pesticide spray programs; and with State cattle and sheep sanitary or brand boards on control of estray and unbranded livestock would be carried forward without substantive change.
B. Subpart B—Mediation of Term Grazing Permit Disputes
1. Section 222.20 State Mediation Program
The Department proposes to revise section 222.20 to update the section heading from “Decisions subject to mediation” to “State mediation program” and to remove redundant phrasing in the body of the section. The substantive scope of the section—which provides that the holder of a term grazing permit issued in a State with a mediation program certified by the U.S. Department of Agriculture may request mediation of a dispute relating to a decision to suspend or cancel the permit—would not change. However, mediation of a dispute relating to a decision to deny development of a stockwater improvement has been added to the section in order to provide a process for permittees to seek relief from a decision which would prevent them from proving beneficial use of their filed water right application and obtaining the water right.
2. Section 222.21 Parties and Participation
The Department proposes to amend section 222.21 by revising the section heading, the introductory text, and paragraph (b). The section heading would be updated to refer to “Parties and participation” rather than “Parties.” The introductory text would be revised to clarify that the listed individuals are the parties and participants who may attend mediation of a term grazing permit dispute. This change would replace the current language, which narrows participation to “parties” and may imply that only the authorized officer and permittee may participate, when participation is often expanded to include legal counsel, and the permittee's creditors. Paragraph (b) would be revised to identify “the authorized officer who made the decision being mediated or his or her designee” as the participating Forest Service representative, replacing the more specific reference to the Chief, Forest Service or other Forest Service employee. Paragraphs (a), (c), (d), and (e) would not be amended.
3. Section 222.26 Ex Parte Communications
The Department proposes to revise section 222.26 in full to update the reference from “the Chief of the Forest Service or other Forest Service employee who made the decision being mediated, or his or her designee” to “the authorized officer or his or her designee.” The substantive prohibition on ex parte communications between the participating Forest Service official and the Appeal Deciding Officer would not change. Sections 222.22 (Stay of appeal), 222.23 (Confidentiality), 222.24 (Records), and 222.25 (Costs) would not be amended.
C. Subpart C—Grazing Fees
1. Section 222.50 Grazing Fees
The Department proposes to revise section 222.50 in full. The section heading would be amended from “General procedures” to “Grazing fees.” Paragraph (a) would carry forward the requirement that fees be charged for all livestock grazing or livestock use of National Forest System lands, with cross-references updated to reflect the consolidation of free-use authorities into revised section 222.3. Paragraph (b) would carry forward the policy basis for fee establishment under Office of Management and Budget Circular A-25, as revised in 1993. Paragraphs (c) and (d) would clarify the animal unit month (AUM) definition for fee-calculation purposes by stating that one animal unit month is a month's use of forage and occupancy of rangeland by one cow, bull, steer, heifer, bison, horse (ancillary to livestock production), burro, or mule, or five sheep or goats; and provide expressly that the Forest Service will not charge grazing fees for animals less than 6 months of age that are the progeny of animals upon which fees are paid. Paragraph (e) would establish a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock owned by persons other than the permittee, equal to 35 percent of the difference between the current year's Federal grazing fee and the prior year's private grazing land lease rate per animal unit month for the appropriate State, as determined by the National Agricultural Statistics Service. The surcharge concept aligns with the Bureau of Land Management's surcharge at
43 CFR 4130.8-1(f)
. Targeted exemptions that exist in current Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, Chapter 10, and being codified here would be available for livestock owned by
(
printed page 73042)
properly documented mentees, beginning ranchers, permittee successors, immediate or extended family members, and operators receiving relief from drought, fire, or other natural causes. Paragraphs (f) through (q) would carry forward and reorganize the provisions on lambing, transportation livestock, billing and rounding, due dates and late fees, fee credits, refunds, fee year, data year, and the unauthorized grazing use rate, including the conditions under which the authorized officer may waive monetary fees for unauthorized grazing use as provided in the 2022 final rule (
87 FR 35097
, June 9, 2022).
The fee policy at Circular A-25 remains current and aligning surcharge structure with the BLM simplifies program administration for operators that graze across systems.
2. Section 222.51 National Forests in 16 Western States and National Grasslands
The Department proposes to revise section 222.51 in full to consolidate fee-setting for the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States and the national grasslands. Paragraph (a) would expand the scope from National Forests and Land Utilization Projects in the 16 contiguous Western States of Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming to also include all national grasslands because the fee formula is the same and this consolidation of sections reduces redundancy found by separating out the national grasslands. Paragraph (b) would set out the grazing fee formula expressly, in the form GF = BV × (FVI + (BCPI−PPI))/100, with definitions for each variable carried forward from existing section 222.51(b) and clarified for ease of administration. Paragraph (c) would carry forward the existing 25-percent annual change limit, and paragraph (d) would carry forward the existing $1.35-per-animal unit month floor. Paragraph (e) would codify the long standing fee-reduction provisions found in the Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, Chapters 20 and 80 and Forest Service Manual 2200, Chapter 40 for authorized land use practice expenditures on the national grasslands and land utilization projects. Land use practices include conservation practices and certain administrative costs incurred by grazing associations for routine administration of the livestock grazing activities of its members under a grazing agreement issued by the Forest Service. Fee reductions have been used on National Grasslands and land utilization projects since the late 1930s, when these lands began to be managed for rehabilitation and sustainable use. This practice was reaffirmed by the Comptroller General's 1950 decision, which confirmed the Secretary's authority under Section 32(c) of the Bankhead-Jones Farm Tenant Act of 1937 to lease lands “with or without consideration” and to establish terms that best accomplish the purposes of the Act. Fee reductions continue to be applied when permittees incur required conservation or administrative expenditures.
Paragraph (f) would modernize and codify fee credit language found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, Chapters 20 and 80, and Forest Service Manual 2200, Chapter 40 to reflect the long-standing practice of using fee-credits when a permittee or grazing association funds an approved rangeland improvement up-front and receives fee credits in future years to replenish the contributed funds. Fee credits have been long articulated within
36 CFR 222.53(c)(3)(ii)
and
36 CFR 222.54(g)(2)
for the Eastern States as a mechanism to facilitate required rangeland improvements to maintain and improve rangeland conditions, however fee credits have only been described in policy on the National Grasslands.
These provisions reflect long-standing Forest Service grasslands program practices in Forest Service directives. Consolidation makes the formula and reductions easier to administer across lands where operators often participate in both National Forest and grassland programs.
3. Removal of Section 222.52 (National Grasslands)
The Department proposes to remove existing section 222.52 (National Grasslands), which provides that grazing fees for national grasslands will be established under concepts and principles similar to those in section 222.51(b). Because revised section 222.51 would directly govern fee-setting on the national grasslands, this one-sentence section is no longer necessary.
4. Section 222.52 Grazing Fees in the Eastern States—Noncompetitive Procedures
The Department proposes to redesignate existing section 222.53 as section 222.52 and to revise the redesignated section. Paragraph (a) would be revised to enumerate the Eastern States to which the noncompetitive procedures apply, replacing the existing reference to “the Eastern and Southern Regions.” Paragraph (b) would be revised to cross-reference paragraph (a) and to update the cross-reference to the redesignated competitive bidding section. Paragraph (c) would be revised to replace references to “the Chief, Forest Service, or an authorized officer to whom such authority has been delegated” with references to the “authorized officer.” Paragraphs (c)(2) (Annual Adjustment of Base Grazing Value), (c)(3) (Computation of Annual Grazing Fee), and (c)(4) (Implementation) would not be substantively amended.
5. Section 222.53 Grazing Fees in the Eastern States—Competitive Bidding
The Department proposes to redesignate existing section 222.54 as section 222.53 and to revise the redesignated section. Paragraph (a)(1) would be revised to enumerate the Eastern States to which the competitive bidding procedures apply. Paragraph (a)(2) would be revised to add limited liability companies to the list of allowable bidders because longstanding Forest Service policy found in Forest Service Handbook 2209.13, Chapter 10, recognizes limited liability companies as a legal entity that is eligible to apply for and hold a term grazing permit. Modernization of these regulations is warranted because limited liability companies are more common today, operating in the agricultural industry, than they were the last time
36 CFR 222.54
was updated. Paragraph (b) would be revised to update the cross-reference to the redesignated noncompetitive section. Paragraph (d) would be revised to remove the requirement that each applicant submit a bid deposit equal to 10 percent of the total amount of the bid, eliminating the deposit-and-refund cycle currently required for unsuccessful or unqualified bidders. Eastern States staff indicate that the practice of requiring a deposit for all bidders, processing the deposits, then refunding the deposits for the unsuccessful bids is a burdensome process for employees, as well as bidders. The cost of providing a bid deposit for beginning ranchers, who are trying to establish themselves in the industry, with minimal capital and funding, presents a barrier. Paragraph (e) would be revised conformingly to remove the requirement that the authorized officer refund the deposit. Paragraph (h) would be revised to update the cross-reference to the redesignated noncompetitive section. Paragraphs (c) (Prospectus), (f) (Permit Issuance), and (g) (Computation of Successful Bidder's Annual Fee) would not be substantively amended.

III. Regulatory Certifications
A. Regulatory Planning and Review
Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 provides that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) in the Office of Management and Budget will determine whether a regulatory action is significant as defined by
E.O. 12866
and will review significant regulatory actions. OIRA has determined that this proposed rule is significant as defined by
E.O. 12866
.
E.O. 13563
reaffirms the principles of
E.O. 12866
while calling for improvements in the Nation's regulatory system to promote predictability, to reduce uncertainty, and to use the best, most innovative, and least burdensome tools for achieving regulatory ends. The Department has developed the proposed rule consistent with
E.O. 13563
.
B. Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
E.O. 14192
requires that an agency, unless prohibited by law, identify at least ten existing regulations to be repealed when the agency publicly proposes for notice and comment or otherwise promulgates a new regulation with total costs greater than zero.
E.O. 14192
further requires that new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least ten prior regulations. While there are modest administrative costs, the proposed rule is expected to lower barriers to entry for beginning ranchers and small operations, modernize grazing administration, increase flexibility for permittees, and align more closely with contemporary ranching practices and Bureau of Land Management regulations. Accordingly, this proposed rule is anticipated to be a deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
.
C. National Environmental Policy Act
The proposed rule would amend the regulations governing grazing and livestock use on the National Forest System. Departmental regulations at
7 CFR 1b.4(c)(20)
exclude from documentation in an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement “rules, regulations, or policies to establish servicewide administrative procedures, program processes, or instructions.” The Department's preliminary assessment is that this proposed rule is administrative and procedural, falls within this categorical exclusion, and that no extraordinary circumstances exist that would require preparation of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement. Any subsequent, site-specific grazing authorizations or rangeland actions will undergo National Environmental Policy Act review, as appropriate under Forest Service procedures at
36 CFR part 220
and Departmental regulations at
7 CFR part 1b
. A final determination will be made upon adoption of the final rule.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Department has considered this proposed rule under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 602
et seq.
). Most Forest Service grazing permittees would be considered small entities under Small Business Administration size standards. The proposed rule would expand eligibility for term grazing permits to include applicants who own or lease (rather than only own) base property and livestock; would establish discretionary priority for qualified beginning ranchers and mentees; would codify a surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock; and would streamline the Eastern State's competitive bidding process by removing the current 10-percent bid deposit requirement. In the aggregate, the proposed rule is expected to reduce barriers to entry for beginning and small business ranchers by prioritizing them for available forage and by providing opportunities to phase into securing a term grazing permit, a process that better aligns with modern economic constraints experienced by beginning and small ranchers, and to lower compliance costs and increasing consistency in practice by aligning the Forest Service framework with that of the Bureau of Land Management for operators who graze on both Federal land systems. The Department does not currently anticipate that this proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, as defined by the Regulatory Flexibility Act. However, the Department will consider public comments and any information submitted regarding potential impacts on small entities before making a final certification. The Department specifically invites comment on the potential economic effects of this proposed rule on small entities.
E. Federalism
The Department has considered this proposed rule under the requirements of
E.O. 13132
, Federalism. The Department has determined that the proposed rule conforms with the federalism principles set out in this E.O., would not impose any compliance costs on the States, and would not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, the Department has concluded that this proposed rule would not have federalism implications.
F. Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
E.O. 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, requires Federal agencies to consult and coordinate with Tribes on a government-to-government basis on policies that have Tribal implications, including regulations, legislative comments or proposed legislation, and other policy statements or actions that have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes. Departmental Regulation 1350-002 establishes the Department's policy on Tribal consultation.
The Department has reviewed this proposed rule in accordance with the requirements of
E.O. 13175
and Departmental Regulation 1350-002 and has determined that this proposed rule has Tribal implications. Consistent with that determination, the Forest Service has notified Tribal governments about the opportunity to engage in government-to-government consultation. The Forest Service will continue to engage with Tribal governments—and when requested, consult with affected Tribes—throughout the rulemaking process and will fully consider Tribal views in the final rule. The Forest Service specifically invites comment from Tribes on the proposed rule and any aspect of the rule that may affect Tribes, Tribal lands, treaty rights, or trust resources.
G. Family Policymaking Assessment
Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999 (
Pub. L. 105-277
), requires Federal agencies to issue a Family Policymaking Assessment for a rule that may affect family well-being. The proposed rule would have no impact on the autonomy or integrity of the family as an institution. Accordingly, the Department has concluded that it is not

necessary to prepare a Family Policymaking Assessment for the proposed rule.
H. Takings Implications
The Department has analyzed the proposed rule in accordance with the principles and criteria in
E.O. 12630
, Governmental Actions and Interference with Constitutionally Protected Property Rights. The Department has determined that the proposed rule would not pose the risk of a taking of private property. Term grazing permits, temporary grazing permits, and livestock use permits convey no right, title, or interest held by the United States in any lands or resources, and the proposed rule expressly preserves the longstanding right to reasonable compensation for a permittee's interest in authorized permanent rangeland improvements when permits are cancelled to devote lands to another public purpose.
I. Energy Effects
The Department has reviewed the proposed rule under
E.O. 13211
, Actions Concerning Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use. The Department has determined that the proposed rule would not constitute a significant energy action as defined in
E.O. 13211
.
J. Civil Justice Reform
The Department has analyzed the proposed rule in accordance with the principles and criteria in
E.O. 12988
, Civil Justice Reform. Upon publication of the proposed rule, (1) all State and local laws and regulations that conflict with the proposed rule or that impede its full implementation would be preempted; (2) no retroactive effect would be given to this proposed rule; and (3) it would not require administrative proceedings before parties may file suit in court challenging its provisions.
K. Severability
The Department intends for the provisions of this rule to be considered separately. If any portion of this rule were stayed or invalidated by a reviewing court, the remaining elements would continue to provide the agency with important and independently effective tools to manage livestock grazing on the National Forest System lands. If a court prevents any provision of this proposed rule from taking effect, it is the Department's intent that the other parts of the rule would not be affected. The remaining provisions would remain in force.
L. Unfunded Mandates
Pursuant to Title II of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Department has assessed the effects of the proposed rule on State, local, and Tribal governments and the private sector. The proposed rule would not compel the expenditure of $100 million or more, adjusted annually for inflation, in any 1 year by State, local, and Tribal governments in the aggregate or by the private sector. Therefore, a statement under section 202 of the Act is not required.

This proposed rule contains information collection requirements subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act (

§ 222.1
Authority and definitions.
(a)
Authority.
The Chief, Forest Service, shall develop, administer, and protect the rangeland resources, and permit and regulate the grazing use of all kinds and classes of livestock on all National Forest System lands and on other lands under Forest Service control. The Chief's authority may be redelegated to the authorized officer through these regulations and Forest Service Manual 2200 Zero Code.
(b)
Definitions.
For purposes of this subpart—
Active allotment
means an allotment with a term grazing permit issued authorizing grazing or for which a transition between term grazing permits is occurring.
Active use
means that portion of the permitted use within an allotment that
(
printed page 73045)
is: (1) Available for livestock grazing use under a permit or lease; (2) Not approved for temporary non-use; and (3) Not in suspension.
Actual use
means where, how many, and what kind or class of livestock graze on an allotment, or on a portion or pasture of an allotment, and how long they graze. Actual use may be expressed in terms of animal unit months.
Adjusted grazing value
means the total grazing fee calculated as authorized animal unit months (AUMs) multiplied by the grazing fee, minus land use practices on national grasslands or fee credits on eastern national forests. The adjusted grazing value is the amount due shown on the bill for collection. This applies to national grasslands and eastern forests.
Allotment
means an area of land designated and managed for grazing and livestock.
Allotment management plan
means a document prepared in accordance with
43 U.S.C. 1702(k)
.
Animal unit month (AUM)
means one month's use of forage and occupancy of rangeland by one (1) cow, bull, steer, heifer, bison, horse (ancillary to livestock production), burro, or mule, or five (5) sheep or goats.
Authorized officer
means a Forest Service line officer with the authority to take certain actions related to rangeland management on National Forest System lands and other lands under Forest Service control.
Authorized use
means the part of active use that is available for grazing in a given year. It is specified on the annual bill for collection and verified by the permittee's payment of fees.
Base property
means:
(i) Private land, owned or leased by a permittee or permit applicant, that contains livestock operation facilities capable of serving as a base of operations for the livestock use of National Forest System lands; or
(ii) Private land, owned or leased by a permittee or permit applicant, that has the capability to produce crops or forage that can be used to support authorized livestock for a specific period of the year; or
(iii) Stockwater rights that are vested in the permittee or permit applicant pursuant to State law and appurtenant to National Forest System lands, or private lands owned or leased by a permittee or permit applicant.
Beginning rancher
means a permittee's children, grandchildren, or other individuals who has not owned or served as an officer, managing partner or member, or any other deciding individual of a farm or ranching business for a period of 10 or more years;
Cancel or cancellation
means action taken through a final written decision to permanently invalidate a term grazing permit in whole or in part.
Carrying capacity
means the average number of livestock, wildlife, or both that may be sustained on a management unit, compatible with management objectives for the unit. In addition to site characteristics, carrying capacity is a function of management goals and management intensity.
Class of livestock
means an age or sex group of a kind of livestock.
Conservation practice
means a type of land use practice consisting of structural and nonstructural rangeland improvements that may be implemented by grazing associations and permittees on national grasslands and land utilization projects, subject to the approval of the authorized officer.
Consultation, cooperation, and coordination
means interaction for the purpose of obtaining advice or exchanging opinions on issues, plans, or management actions.
Current grazing management
means grazing in accordance with the terms and conditions of an existing permit, including any modifications that are consistent with an applicable Department of Agriculture land management plan.
Direct permittee
means, in the context of National Grasslands, an individual or organization that holds a grazing permit (temporary or term) issued directly by the U.S. Forest Service for use of National Grasslands for livestock production. This is distinct from an indirect permittee, who may be a member of a grazing association or other group that holds the permit on behalf of its members.
Eleven Western States
means the States of Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, New Mexico, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming, which are used to calculate the forage value index.
Fair market value (FMV)
means the monetary amount that is reasonably expected for use of rangeland, and that applies only to grazing fees. Expressed as an amount per month, fair market value is usually established by competitive conditions. For grazing on National Forest System lands, fair market value is the difference between the total costs associated with livestock grazing on privately leased grazing lands and the total non-fee costs of livestock grazing National Forest System lands.
Fee credit
means the value of rangeland improvements required by an authorized officer on eastern national forests, or as conservation practices on national grasslands and land utilization projects, that are credited against the annual grazing value in the determination of a grazing fee.
Forage reserve allotment
means an allotment (such as a grass bank or swing allotment) that is used for a short-term (less than three years) when needed and for which a project-level environmental analysis and decision has been made to authorize use of the allotment forage resource. Forage reserves can be used to facilitate landscape-level management by improving flexibility in responding to needs (such as drought, fire, or restoration) or resource management opportunities (such as vegetative manipulation). Intermittent use of forage reserves should occur to ensure they remain in a ready-to-use state to avoid the forage reserve declining into decadent overgrowth or rangeland improvements falling into disrepair.
Grant process
means the procedure for identifying an applicant or applicants to receive a term grazing permit when grazing capacity becomes available and there is no preferred applicant.
Grazing agreement
means a type of term grazing permit that authorizes eligible grazing associations and grazing districts organized under State or Tribal law to graze livestock on National Forest System lands. It includes provisions to allow the association to distribute its allotment use among its members and administer its members' use in conformance with applicable law, regulation, land management plan and allotment management plan direction, the terms and conditions of the grazing agreement, and the association's rules of management and bylaws.
Grazing association
means a cooperative of National Forest System grazing users to which a grazing agreement has been issued. Grazing associations are organized under State or Tribal statutes for the purpose of cooperative management of permitted livestock and to administer the livestock grazing use distributed to its members. Grazing associations may also be referred to as grazing districts.
Grazing permit
means a document authorizing livestock to use National Forest System or other lands administered by the Forest Service for the purpose of livestock production (such as the production of meat, milk, fiber, or other products) and includes animals used in support of livestock production operations, such as pack and saddle stock.
Grazing preference or preference
(see also
Preferred applicant
) means a
(
printed page 73046)
superior or priority position against others for the purpose of receiving or renewing a grazing permit. This priority is attached to base property that is owned or leased by the permittee or it may be attached to permitted livestock owned by the permittee.
Land use practices
means practices contained within the conditions of a grazing permit that is issued on national grasslands. The costs of these practices are deducted from the annual grazing value to determine the annual grazing fee. Land use practices include:
(i)
Conservation Practices.
The protection, planning, and land treatment and rangeland improvement measures (structural and nonstructural) that the Forest Service requires in carrying out the provisions of a grazing permit or grazing agreement. Some examples include fences, water developments, and prescribed fire.
(ii)
Administrative Activities.
Allowable administrative and program management activities carried out by a grazing association functioning under a grazing agreement, which would otherwise be an expense incurred by the Forest Service. Examples include billing and oversight of approved rangeland improvement projects.
Lessee of base property
means an individual or entity that has a possessory interest under a lease for the base property associated with a grazing permit. A grazing permit can only be issued to a lessee who leases base property that is associated with a grazing permit and meets the other eligibility requirements. To obtain a permit the lessee of base property must prove a possessory interest in the leased base property, that has a grazing permit associated with it, through a formal lease agreement. When a term grazing permit is associated with permitted livestock, an individual or entity may lease property that meets the base property requirements, so they are eligible for a grazing permit.
Lessee of livestock
means a permittee that has a possessory interest under a lease agreement for livestock that will be managed by the permittee on the allotment. The permittee must prove a possessory interest in the leased livestock through a formal lease agreement.
Livestock
means production oriented animals of any kind kept or raised for the use or production of meat, milk, fiber, or other products, and includes animals used in support of the production operation (such as horses used as permittee pack and saddle stock).
Livestock use permit
means a permit issued for purposes other than livestock production (such as research, leased sires, or targeted grazing). The issuance term shall not exceed five years, and the permit has no priority for renewal.
Maintenance of rangeland improvements
means the timely repair of rangeland facilities to a condition adequate to ensure proper functioning of the facility, perpetuate its life, and protect or improve the rangeland resource. Satisfactory maintenance of improvements is a mandatory term and condition of the permit for grazing on National Forest System lands.
Mentee
means someone who is mentored by an existing permittee and enters into a mentor/mentee agreement approved by the authorized officer.
Monitoring
means the observation and orderly collection of data over an appropriate time-period to evaluate:
(i) Effects of management actions; and
(ii) Effectiveness of actions (such as land health).
National forests in the 16 contiguous Western States
means lands designated as national forest within the boundaries of Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming (national grasslands are excluded) (
43 U.S.C. 1902(i)
).
National Forest System lands
means the national forests, national grasslands, land utilization projects, other Federal lands for which the Forest Service has administrative jurisdiction, and all other lands and interests mentioned in
16 U.S.C. 1609(a)
.
Nine Great Plains States
means the States of Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, in which the indices are collected to determine the annual grazing value on the 17 national grasslands in those States.
Non-permittee
means a person who owns or leases livestock and does not have a grazing permit to graze livestock on National Forest System lands.
Other lands under Forest Service control
means non-Federal public and private lands over which the Forest Service has been given control through lease, agreement, waiver, or otherwise.
Outcome-based grazing
means the incorporation of pre-authorized grazing plan modifications, called flexibilities, into grazing authorizations to better respond to changing conditions to achieve vegetation objectives.
Permitted livestock
means livestock owned or leased by the permittee that has been identified by brand or other markings as requested on the application for a term grazing permit, temporary grazing permit, or term private land permit.
Permitted use
means the forage allocated for grazing by production-oriented livestock in an allotment under a permit and is expressed in AUMs. Permitted use includes authorized use and active use and suspended use AUMs. See also
Active use.
Permittee
means any person who has been issued a grazing permit.
Preferred applicant
(see also
Grazing preference
) means an individual who has priority position against others for the purpose of receiving (through waiver or grant) or renewing a grazing permit. The entity remains in preferred applicant status until all required documentation is submitted within the time limit agreed upon by the authorized officer, reviewed, and it is determined that the applicant meets all eligibility and qualification requirements.
Rangeland betterment
means rehabilitation, protection, and improvement of National Forest System lands to arrest rangeland deterioration and improve forage conditions, fish and wildlife habitat, watershed protection, and livestock production.
Range betterment fund
means the fund established by title IV, section 401(b)(1), of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976. This fund consists of 50 per centum of all monies received by the United States as fees for grazing livestock on the national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States or $10,000,000 per annum, whichever is greater.
Rangeland improvement
means any authorized activity, physical modification, or treatment designed to improve production of forage; change vegetation composition; control patterns of use; provide water; stabilize soil and water conditions; restore, protect, and improve the health of rangeland ecosystems to benefit production-oriented livestock, wild horses and burros, and fish and wildlife. The term includes, but is not limited to structures, treatment projects (
i.e.,
prescribed fire), and use of mechanical devices or modifications achieved through mechanical means (
i.e.,
inter-seeding, pitting).
Rules of management
means a set of policies, procedures, and practices, including eligibility requirements, developed by a grazing association or grazing district and approved by the authorized officer, that govern the grazing use both on National Forest System lands covered by a grazing agreement and on private, State, Tribal, or other agency lands under the management of a grazing association.
(
printed page 73047)
Small farm or ranch
means a business that is classified as a small family farm according to the farm typology maintained and periodically updated by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service, based on gross cash farm income categories and family ownership criteria. The term small business farm or ranch is synonymous with small farm or ranch.
Stocking rate
means the number of specific kinds and classes of animals grazing a given area over a specific time period per acre. Stocking rate is usually expressed in AUMs per acre.
Succeeding family member
means child, grandchild, niece, or nephew of a permit holder. The term grazing permit may be waived to such family member.
Successional base property
means base property that is leased for the purpose of facilitating the lessee's ability to transition to owning the leased base property within a specified period of time.
Successional livestock arrangement
means an approved written agreement between a permittee and the permittee's successor that allows the successor to build a herd by incrementally acquiring the current permittee's permitted livestock operation over a declared period of time, during which the permittee's livestock will be replaced by livestock owned by the successor.
Supplemental feed
means a feed or nutritional supplement that augments the forage available from the National Forest System lands and is provided to improve livestock nutrition or rangeland management.
Suspend or suspension
means the temporary withholding from active use, through a decision issued by the authorized officer or by agreement, of part or all of the term grazing permit, provided however, such withholding shall not exceed a period of 3 years or until the violation is remedied, or until specified objectives or actions have been met, whichever is earlier.
Sustained yield
means the achievement and maintenance, in perpetuity, of a high-level, annual or regular periodic output from the various renewable resources of the National Forest System lands, consistent with multiple use.
Targeted grazing
means using livestock as a tool to create strategic linear fuel breaks, to reduce fine fuel height and fuel loading, and to maintain fine fuels reduction for a specified period under, or to address other resource issues such as control of undesirable plant species.
Temporary grazing permit
means a type of grazing authorization issued in certain circumstances to allow use of forage available on National Forest System lands (either within or outside of an allotment) when issuance or modification of a term grazing permit is not appropriate or needed, or authorizes the use of livestock to meet other resource objectives (for example, outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing).
Temporary non-use
means that portion of active use that the authorized officer approves in writing to not be used temporarily. Temporary non-use may be in response to a request made by the permittee for personal convenience or it may result from resource management needs required by the authorized officer.
Term grazing permit consolidation
means the consolidation of two or more term grazing permits for the same entity when the entity obtains qualified base property or permitted livestock, or both, which have been historically associated with separate livestock operations on grazing allotments, and applies to obtain the term grazing permits and consolidate them under a single permit.
Term grazing permit with on-and-off provisions
means a type of term grazing permit with a provision that may be issued to a qualified applicant who holds a term grazing permit and who owns or leases non-National Forest System land that is intermingled with, or adjacent to, and used in conjunction with, a Forest Service grazing allotment.
Term private land grazing permit
means a permit issued to a person who owns or leases unfenced private, State, or other rangeland parcels that are intermingled with, or adjacent to, a Forest Service grazing allotment, and who does not hold a term grazing permit for grazing on the National Forest System lands on the allotment.
Trend
means the measurable direction of change over time, either toward or away from desired management objectives.
Transportation livestock
means livestock used as pack and saddle stock for travel on the National Forest System.
Unauthorized leasing and subleasing
means:
(i) The lease or sublease of a Federal grazing permit, associated with the lease or sublease of base property, to another party without a required transfer approved by the authorized officer;
(ii) The lease or sublease of a Federal grazing permit to another party without the assignment of the associated base property;
(iii) Allowing another party, other than sons, daughters, and grandchildren of the grazing permittee or beginning ranchers meeting the requirements of § 4130.7(f), to graze on public lands livestock that are not owned or controlled by the permittee; or
(iv) Allowing another party, other than sons, daughters, and grandchildren of the grazing permittee or beginning ranchers meeting the requirements of § 4130.7(f), to graze livestock on public lands under a pasturing agreement without the approval of the authorized officer.
Unauthorized livestock
means any cattle, sheep, goat, hog, bison, or equine not defined as a wild free-roaming horse or burro or feral animal (one that is abandoned or unbranded), or any other livestock or exotic ungulate, that is not authorized by a Forest Service permit and bill for collection. Noncommercial pack and saddle stock used by recreationists, travelers, and other forest and grassland visitors for occasional trips, and livestock trailed over an established driveway when there is no overnight stop on National Forest System land, do not fall under this definition.
Unauthorized use rate
means the annual fee charged for unauthorized livestock use.
Utilization
means the portion of the current year's growth removed during a specified period. The term is also used to refer to the pattern of such use. For guidance on utilization, see
Utilization Studies and Residual Measurements: Interagency Technical Reference
(Technical Reference 1734-3) (Bureau of Land Management et al. 1996, revised 1997, 1999), or subsequent updates.
Vacant allotment
means an allotment for which no term grazing permit is currently issued.
Waiver of term grazing permit
means a form completed by the holder of a term grazing permit that surrenders all privileges provided under the permit back to the United States. If the holder of the term permit has sold base property or permitted livestock to another individual or entity, the waiver may be executed in favor of the purchaser to apply for the permit.

Revise § 222.2 to read as follows:
§ 222.2
Allotment management.
(a) Consistent with land management plans, forage-producing National Forest System lands may be managed for livestock grazing.
(b) Allotments shall be designated on the National Forest System and on other lands under Forest Service administration where the land is available for grazing. Associated private and other public lands may be considered in such designation, with the consent of the landowner, lessee, or agency, to form logical rangeland management units.
(
printed page 73048)
(c)
Allotment management plans.
An allotment management plan may be developed for each allotment. If the authorized officer elects to develop an allotment management plan, the plan shall be developed in consultation, cooperation, and coordination with affected permittees, landowners, and any State or Tribe with lands covered by such allotment management plan. The allotment management plan shall be implemented, reviewed periodically, and revised as needed.
(1) Permits may incorporate an allotment management plan for managing livestock grazing.
(2) Allotment Management Plans will:
(i) Prescribe the livestock grazing practices necessary to meet specific resource objectives defined in any existing environmental analysis;
(ii) Specify any operational flexibility that can be approved by the authorized officer; and
(iii) Include a monitoring plan to evaluate the effectiveness of management actions in achieving the specific resource objectives of the plan.
(3) Private, Tribal, and State lands may be included in allotment management plans, dealing with rangeland management, with the consent or at the request of the parties who own or lease those lands.
(4) A requirement to conform with completed allotment management plans shall be incorporated by reference into the terms and conditions of the grazing permit for the allotment.
(5) Allotment management plans may be revised or terminated by the authorized officer. When revisions or terminations occur, the authorized officer shall inform through written notification affected permittees, landowners involved, and any State or Tribe having lands within the area covered by the plan.
(d)
Changes to allotment boundaries.
After consultation, cooperation, and coordination with the affected grazing permittee(s) and any States or Tribe having lands within the allotment to be covered by such allotment management plan, the authorized officer may designate and adjust grazing allotment boundaries. The approach used to modify allotment boundaries shall be determined on a case-by-case basis. In some instances, modifying an allotment boundary may be considered a technical correction, while in other instances, modification may require environmental analysis and decision.
(e)
Rangeland disturbance response actions.
The authorized officer may implement temporary response actions to address drought, wildfire, flood, insect or disease outbreak, loss of water availability, or other events that materially reduce forage or water availability or otherwise threaten rangeland resources or livestock health.
(1) Temporary response actions may include temporary changes in livestock numbers, season of use, pasture rotation, timing of use, area of use, water use, supplemental feeding locations, targeted grazing, temporary non-use, or other actions necessary to protect rangeland resources or livestock health.
(2) Before implementing a temporary response action, the authorized officer shall, to the extent practicable, consult, cooperate, and coordinate with affected permittees and consider reasonable alternatives proposed by affected permittees.
(3) The authorized officer shall document the basis for the temporary response action, including the conditions prompting the action, the expected duration, the affected allotments or pastures, and the criteria for terminating or revising the action.
(4) A temporary response action under this paragraph does not modify the term grazing permit unless the authorized officer separately modifies the permit in accordance with § 222.5(e).
(5) In an emergency, the authorized officer may make a temporary response action effective immediately or on a date specified in the decision. The authorized officer shall provide written notice to affected permittees as soon as practicable.
(6) The authorized officer may determine that vegetation, soil, or other resources on National Forest System lands are at substantial risk of wildfire due to drought, fuels buildup, or other causes, or at immediate risk of erosion or other damage due to wildfire. The authorized officer may include targeted grazing as a component of a wildfire management decision, consistent with applicable law, the applicable land management plan, and agency procedural requirements.

Revise § 222.3 to read as follows:
§ 222.3
Issuance of grazing permits.
(a) Unless otherwise specified by the Chief, Forest Service, all grazing and livestock use on National Forest System lands and on other lands under Forest Service control must be authorized by a term grazing permit, a term grazing permit with on-and-off provisions, grazing agreement, term private land grazing permit, a temporary grazing permit, or a livestock use permit.
(b) Term grazing permits (including term grazing permit, term grazing permit with on-and-off provisions, grazing agreement, and term private land grazing permit) authorize grazing by production-oriented livestock on the National Forest System lands, consistent with land management plans as available. Permits must specify the permitted use, the kind and number of livestock, the period of use, the allotment to be used, and the terms and conditions, and must identify the appropriate land management plan and the site-specific analysis and decision associated with the permit.
(c) The number and season of use, and designated areas permitted in a term grazing permit (including term grazing permit, term grazing permit with on-and-off provisions, grazing agreement, and term private land grazing permit) may be changed on an annual basis, through the authorized use, to address resource needs or respond to drought, fire, or other situations.
(d) All permits shall be made subject to cancellation, suspension, or modification for any violation of federal law, these regulations or any terms or conditions of the permit, or Allotment Management Plan.
(e) Term grazing permits, temporary grazing permits, term grazing permits with on-and-off provisions, grazing agreement, and term private land grazing permits, and livestock use permits convey no right, title, or interest held by the United States in any lands or resources.
(f) The authorized officer may issue permits for livestock grazing and other use by livestock, such as for vegetation control or invasive species management, on the National Forest System and on other lands administered by the Forest Service.
(g) The Chief, Forest Service, shall prescribe provisions and requirements under which term permits will be issued, renewed, and administered, including:
(1) The amount and character of base property and livestock that the permit holder shall be required to own or lease.
(2) Conditions for the approval of temporary non-use of the permit for specified periods.
(3) Discretionary priority for a qualified beginning rancher or permittee mentee when issuing a term grazing permit through a prospectus. Beginning ranchers and permittee mentees must meet all eligibility and qualification requirements intended to reduce barriers to entry into the agricultural industry, or demonstrate that they meet the exceptions prescribed by the Chief. Exceptions to the qualification requirements for beginning ranchers and permittee mentees may be approved
(
printed page 73049)
singularly or in combination and include:
(i) Allowing for the phased acquisition of base property or livestock, or both, under limited circumstances.
(ii) Allowing for a successional base property arrangement, which essentially sets up an extended purchase and sale agreement. This means that the base property owner agrees to sell the described base property, and the successor agrees to purchase the property by the date specified in the arrangement.
(iii) Allowing a beginning rancher or a mentee to be mentored by a permittee. When a permittee mentor/mentee arrangement is approved by the authorized officer, the mentee is not issued a term grazing permit; instead, the mentee may run up to 50 percent of the permitted livestock numbers under the permittee mentor's term grazing permit.
(iv) Allowing successional livestock arrangements to provide the opportunity for an entity seeking to acquire the current permittee's livestock operation to build a herd by incrementally acquiring livestock from the current permittee.
(h)
Eligibility and qualification requirements.
Term grazing permits may be issued only to individuals or entities who meet the eligibility and qualification requirements.
(1) To be considered eligible to hold a term grazing permit, an applicant must be:
(i) A citizen of the United States who has reached the age of majority by the State where the permitted grazing activity would occur, except for individuals who have not reached the age of majority and have a parent, guardian, or trustee who cosigns the permit; a minor who has obtained the status of legal adulthood before reaching the legal age of majority by court order for emancipation; or a citizen of a foreign country who has demonstrated intent to become a citizen by having filed for naturalization;
(ii) An entity formed and recognized as a legal entity in accordance with applicable Federal and State statutes; or
(iii) An American Indian Tribe, Tribal Organization, or Tribal member.
(2) To be considered as qualified to hold a term grazing permit, an eligible applicant must own or lease base property, as defined in § 222.1, and own or lease the livestock to be permitted. However, when any of the excepted conditions described below apply, an entity may be approved to meet those requirements:
(i) An exception to the base property ownership/lease requirement is provided to allow for successional base property arrangements, providing the opportunity for an entity to incrementally acquire ownership of a current permittee's described base property.
(ii) An exception to the livestock ownership/lease requirement is provided to allow current permittees to mentor an aspiring small business rancher or beginning rancher. When a beginning rancher or mentor/mentee arrangement is approved by the authorized officer, the beginning rancher or mentee is not issued a term grazing permit; instead, the beginning rancher or mentee may run up to 50 percent of permitted livestock numbers under the permittee's term grazing permit.
(iii) An exception to the livestock ownership/lease requirement is provided to allow for successional livestock arrangements, providing the opportunity for an entity seeking to acquire the current permittee's livestock operation to build a herd by incrementally acquiring livestock from the current permittee.
(iv) An exception to the livestock ownership/lease requirement is provided to allow beginning ranchers to enter into extended livestock purchase and sale arrangements when additional time is needed for the beginning rancher to acquire enough livestock to fully stock the term grazing permit.
(v) An exception to the requirement that base property ownership/lease and permitted livestock be held by the same precise legal entity is provided to facilitate estate planning and family livestock operation. Under limited circumstances, one entity may own the base property and a second entity composed of the same individuals may own or lease the livestock to be permitted. The authorized officer may allow up to 50 percent of the permitted livestock to be owned by the permit holder's immediate or extended family members and grazed under the permit holder's term grazing permit, provided the permit holder annually identifies the number, ownership, and brands of such livestock.
(vi) Under instances where a ranch becomes associated with a permanent conservation easement that prohibits subdividing it into parcels, the Forest Service may recognize this one property as the base property qualifying multiple different entities to hold grazing permits associated with that land.
(i)
Permits with priority for renewal.
Term grazing permits authorized in this paragraph have priority for renewal and may be in the form of term grazing permits, grazing permits with on-and-off provisions, or grazing agreements. Permittees and applicants must be eligible and qualified to hold such permits in accordance with paragraph (h) of this section. Permits issued under this paragraph may be issued as follows:
(1) On national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States, 10-year term permits will be issued unless the land is pending disposal, will be devoted to other uses prior to the end of 10 years, or it will be in the best interest of sound land management to specify a shorter term in accordance with
43 U.S.C. 1752(b)(3)
.
(2) On National Forest System lands other than national forests in the 16 contiguous Western States, the permit term shall be for periods of 10 years or less. Term grazing permits in the form of grazing agreements may be issued to cooperative grazing associations or similar organizations incorporated or otherwise established pursuant to State or Tribal law.
(3) A term permit holder has first priority for receipt of a new permit at the end of the term period, provided the permit holder has fully complied with the terms and conditions of the expiring permit.
(4) To update terms and conditions, term grazing permits may be cancelled at any time, provided a new permit is issued to the existing permit holder for a new term of the appropriate number of years for a new permit, per paragraphs (1) and (2) above.
(5) New term permits may be issued to an eligible and qualified purchaser of a permittee's permitted livestock or base property, or to a lessee of a permittee's base property, provided the permittee waives the term permit to the United States in favor of the purchaser of base property or livestock, or the base property lessee.
(6) When a permit expires or is waived, the authorized officer shall renew an existing permit or issue a new permit to reallocate the use from the expiring/waived permit with terms and conditions consistent with the supporting environmental analysis and decision.
If a permit expires or is waived, and there is no current environmental analysis or a new environmental analysis is necessary, the authorized officer shall:
(i) for the National Forests in the 16 contiguous Western States, issue a permit with the same terms and conditions until the environmental analysis and documentation required under NEPA and other applicable laws is complete. After completion of this process the permit may be canceled, suspended, or modified accordingly.
(
printed page 73050)
(ii) for lands other than the National Forests in the 16 contiguous Western States, issuance of the permit shall be consistent with appropriations language, if available, and all applicable laws.
If a permit is cancelled, this paragraph does not apply. See 222.4(c).
(7) If the permittee chooses to dispose of all or part of the permittee's base property or permitted livestock (not under approved temporary non-use), but does not choose to waive the term permit, the authorized officer shall give written notice that the permittee is no longer qualified to hold a permit. The permittee shall be given up to one year to reestablish qualifications before cancellation action is final.
(j)
Permits with no priority for renewal.
Permits with no priority for reissuance are subject to terms and conditions as prescribed by the authorized officer and are authorized as follows:
(1) Temporary grazing permits for periods not to exceed one year, on a charge basis, may be issued provided this use is consistent with multiple-use objectives and does not interfere with existing livestock operations on the National Forest System lands. The authorized officer shall consult, cooperate, and coordinate with affected permittees on common allotments prior to issuance of temporary grazing permits:
(i) to allow for the use of rangelands while a term grazing permit is held in suspension;
(ii) to use additional forage created by unusually favorable climatic conditions;
(iii) to use the permitted rangelands when the permit holder's livestock is in temporary non-use status for reasons of personal convenience;
(iv) to allow a person to continue to graze livestock for the remainder of the grazing season where base property has been sold or the lease cancelled, the permit waived, and a new term permit issued;
(v) to allow grazing use in the event of drought or other emergency of National or Regional scope where such use would not result in permanent resource damage;
(vi) to allow for vegetation control or invasive species management, as well as stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing); or
(vii) to allow use on a forage reserve allotment by an entity who does not have a term grazing permit.
(viii) The permittee or individual who acquires a temporary permit shall perform annual rangeland improvement maintenance prior to turning livestock out on the allotment.
(2) Livestock use permits shall not exceed five years and may be issued consistent with applicable laws and under terms and conditions prescribed by the authorized officer as follows:
(i) paid permits for transportation livestock;
(ii) paid or free permits for research purposes and administrative studies;
(iii) paid or free permits to trail livestock across National Forest System lands;
(iv) free permits to persons who reside on ranch or agricultural lands within or contiguous to National Forest System lands, not to exceed 10 head of livestock owned or kept whose products are consumed or whose services are used directly by the family of the resident, and who distinctly need such National Forest System lands to support such animals;
(v) free permits to campers and travelers for the livestock actually used during the period of occupancy. This may be authorized without a written permit;
(vi) paid or free permits for horses, mules, or burros used by permittees to support management of permitted livestock when they are not included in the term grazing permit;
(vii) free permits for horses, mules, or burros to cooperators who use pack and saddle stock to support research, administration, or other work being conducted. This may be authorized without a written permit;
(viii) paid or free permits for livestock used as a management tool to manipulate or control vegetation or invasive species, as well as implement stewardship projects (such as outcome-based grazing or targeted grazing) on a given parcel of National Forest System land; or
(ix) paid permits to holders of grazing permits for breeding animals used to service livestock permitted to graze on lands administered by the Forest Service.
(3) Term private land permits may be issued to an applicant who owns or leases unfenced private, State, or other rangeland parcels that are intermingled with, or adjacent to, a Forest Service-administered grazing allotment but does not hold a term grazing permit for use of the National Forest System lands, under the following conditions:
(i) The applicant shall provide proof of ownership or lease of the offered land for grazing purposes.
(ii) Issue this permit only if it is in the best interest of the United States, considering the management of National Forest System lands and resources within the allotment, and whether the owned or leased lands should be managed with the National Forest System lands as a logical grazing unit.
(iii) Term private land permits may be issued for a period that coincides with the term of their land lease or other agreement that allows their use, or for a period of up to 10 years, whichever is less.
(iv) The authorized officer shall estimate the grazing capacity for the offered lands identified in the application for a term private land grazing permit.
(v) The applicant must agree to all terms and conditions of the term private land grazing permit, including the overall season of use and the number of livestock on the owned or leased lands.
(vi) Livestock that access National Forest System lands without authorization are unauthorized livestock.
(k)
Grant priority for available grazing capacity.
When grazing capacity becomes available on a permanent sustained-yield basis for grazing, the authorized officer may authorize grazing use of such land or forage on the basis of this section, § 222.5, § 222.7(a), or any of the following factors:
(1) When unresolved resource or management concerns exist on a district or forest, priority consideration shall be given to impacted permittees first. Authorized officers shall document the rationale for determining which permittee will be granted the unobligated capacity when addressing unresolved resource or management concerns.
(2) When no unresolved resource or management concerns exist:
(i) When the available grazing capacity is associated with an allotment with existing permittees and is a direct result of permittees' direct contributions to the completion of rangeland improvements, development programs, or enhanced livestock grazing and rangeland management, the capacity shall be allocated in a proportional manner relative to the contributions made by each permittee leading to the increased capacity;
(ii) When grazing capacity is added through a land exchange, and that land is incorporated into an existing allotment, priority shall be given to existing permittees on the allotment who grazed the acquired land prior to the land exchange; or
(iii) When the available grazing capacity is not associated with paragraph (l)(2)(i) or (ii) of this section, the authorized officer shall solicit applicants by issuing a prospectus in the following priority order:
(A) to a beginning rancher or mentee with a permittee mentor/mentee
(
printed page 73051)
agreement who is a small business rancher;
(B) to existing permittees on adjacent allotments who are small business ranchers;
(C) to owners of livestock who are not current Forest Service permittees but are currently in good standing and authorized on rangeland administered by the Bureau of Land Management to the extent provided in the memorandum of understanding between the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management; and then
(D) to a solicited applicant who has applied in response to a prospectus and is eligible and qualified.
