§ 222.5
Changes in permitted, authorized, and active use.
(a) The authorized officer shall periodically review the permitted use specified in a grazing permit and shall make changes in the permitted use, authorized use, or active use as necessary, when supported by site-specific analysis from monitoring, documented field observations, ecological site inventory, or other data acceptable to the authorized officer to:
(1) Manage, maintain, or improve rangeland health or productivity; or
(2) Assist, if necessary, in making progress toward restoring riparian ecosystems to properly functioning conditions; or
(3) Conform to land management plans.
(b) If sufficient improvement cannot be achieved through adjustments to authorized use, modifications to permitted use may be necessary and should be based on a site-specific analysis, which shows active grazing use is causing an unacceptable level or pattern of utilization, or when use exceeds the livestock carrying capacity as determined through monitoring data, documented field observations, ecological site inventories, or other information deemed acceptable by the authorized officer.
(c)
Allocation of additional forage.
Apportioned forage shall be consistent with multiple-use and sustained-yield management objectives.
(1) Additional forage available on a permanent or sustained-yield basis for grazing by production-oriented livestock shall be apportioned to eligible and qualified applicants in accordance with the grant process in § 222.3(k). The authorized officer shall apportion the available forage after consultation, cooperation, and coordination with affected permittees on a common allotment, and any State having lands within the allotment.
(2) Additional forage temporarily available for grazing by production-oriented livestock may be apportioned on an annual temporary basis, depending on the need by permittees or individuals who acquire a temporary permit, or based on resource management needs.
(3) When additional forage is temporarily available due to temporary non-use for personal convenience by a permittee, the authorized officer may authorize grazing to fill in behind the approved temporary non-use. The use may be made temporarily available to an existing permittee through a bill for collection or to an individual who acquires a temporary permit.
(4) Forage reserve use by existing permittees shall be authorized on the bill for collection. Forage reserve use by a non-permittee shall be authorized by a temporary permit.
(5) When livestock management activities are needed temporarily to achieve identified rangeland condition outcomes, such as invasive species control, vegetation management, or fuels treatments), additional forage may be apportioned to permittees or others in accordance with § 222.3(c), § 222.3(f), § 222.3(j)(1), § 222.3(j)(2), or § 222.3(k).
(6) Permittees who seek temporary changes in grazing use within the terms and conditions of their permit must request the changes in writing from the Forest Service before the requested change in grazing use would be authorized.
(7) The authorized officer may approve temporary changes in livestock number, period of use, or both, provided that any temporary change in the authorized period does not begin more than 21 days before the beginning date specified in the permit and does not extend more than 21 days after the ending date specified on the permit, unless otherwise authorized in an allotment management plan.
(d)
Personal or required non-use.
(1)
Temporary non-use for the permittee's personal convenience.
(i) Temporary non-use for the permittee's personal convenience occurs when a permittee requests to graze less than 90 percent of the permitted number of livestock on a specified allotment for a given grazing year. Temporary non-use applies only to the number of animals and can be requested for partial numbers of permitted livestock or for all of the permitted livestock.
(ii) Temporary non-use for the permittee's personal convenience may only be authorized for up to 4 consecutive years and may not exceed 4 years in a 10-year rolling period.
(iii) Temporary non-use for the permittee's personal convenience must be requested in writing by the permittee for each year. Approval or denial shall be documented by the authorized officer in writing.
(2)
Temporary non-use for resource management needs.
(i) When the authorized officer determines that temporary non-use for resource management needs is necessary, the authorized officer would initiate consultation, and coordination with affected permittees and the State or Tribe having lands within the allotment.
(ii) Permitted use may be placed into temporary non-use for resource management needs, in whole or in part, on a temporary basis due to drought, fire, or other natural causes; or to facilitate installation, maintenance, or modification of rangeland improvements. The temporary non-use shall be implemented and documented through the annual bill for collection.
(iii) Temporary non-use for resource management needs may be requested by the permittee and must be requested in writing for each year it is desired.
(iv) The authorized officer may require temporary non-use for resource management needs or temporarily modify management practices when review of site-specific monitoring shows that current grazing use is causing an unacceptable level or pattern of utilization, or when use exceeds the carrying capacity. Only monitoring methods and data approved by the Forest Service and collected at sites identified in the allotment management
(
printed page 73052)
plan, land management plan, or site-specific analysis shall be used.
(v) Where permitted use is reduced under this section, it will be placed in temporary non-use for resource management needs until the authorized officer has determined that the specific objectives that were expected to be met by implementing the temporary non-use for the resource management needs have been met, and livestock can return to the area. The need for temporary non-use should be identified on an allotment-by-allotment basis. When establishing the need for temporary non-use for resource management, the authorized officer shall document the following in a memorandum to the file and a letter to the permittee:
(A) The period and amount of temporary non-use being approved or required must be identified;
(B) The objectives to be achieved, such as how the temporary non-use would enable or support the implementation of vegetation treatments (such as prescribed fire or seeding); the specific resource conditions that are expected to be met, enhanced, or how the temporary non-use will enable progress to be made toward achieving the specific resource conditions;
(C) How the temporary non-use is expected to achieve the described objectives; and
(D) The monitoring that will be conducted (the type, frequency, and so forth), and when the data will be reviewed to determine if the temporary non-use is achieving the described objectives.
(vi) When the temporary non-use is a result of an emergency (such as for drought, fire, flood, or animal disease outbreaks/transmissible livestock disease) and there is a need to immediately protect the soil, vegetation, or other resources, the authorized officer should issue notices of emergency closure and decisions requiring modification of authorized grazing use. The notices may be effective upon issuance or on a date specified in the decision.
(vii) The authorized officer shall not authorize qualified applicants to graze forage made available as a result of temporary non-use for resource management needs.
(3) Temporary non-use for rangeland research may be available under a written agreement between the Forest Service, the permittee, and the entity conducting the research on an allotment, or portion of an allotment, as needed for a study area, and must be requested in writing.
(4) Temporary non-use of grazing association-issued term grazing permits shall be administered as follows:
(i) Associations may approve member requests for temporary non-use for personal convenience and for resource management needs.
(ii) Associations may require their members to take temporary non-use for resource management needs if, in coordination with the Forest Service the Forest Service determines the temporary non-use is needed (such as due to wildfire and drought).
(iii) Grazing associations shall ensure that the implementation of their temporary non-use policy is consistent with the Forest Service temporary non-use policies.
(iv) The Forest Service authorized officer may approve requests by the grazing association for temporary non-use for personal convenience, resource management needs, or require temporary non-use for resource management needs.
(v) Grazing associations must graze at least 90 percent of the number of livestock under their association-issued grazing permit each year, unless the Forest Service approves or requires temporary non-use.
(vi) The need for resource management temporary non-use should be identified on an allotment-by-allotment basis and should include specific objectives that are expected to be met by implementing temporary non-use.
(vii) The grazing association shall be responsible for working with its members to carry out temporary non-use for resource management needs on the associated allotments.
(viii) A member's failure to place livestock on the National Forest System lands without approved or required temporary non-use may be subject to non-compliance actions as described in the association's rules of management.
(ix) A grazing association is authorized to allow association members or temporary non-members to fill in behind a member's temporary non-use for personal convenience. If an association decides not to fill in behind the member's temporary non-use for personal convenience, the association must contact the Forest Service and request that the temporary non-use be approved and reflected on the annual bill for collection issued by the Forest Service to the association.
(e)
Permit modifications.
The authorized officer may make modifications to the terms and conditions of a grazing permit when livestock use or related management practices are not meeting the land management plan, allotment management plan, management objectives, or are not in conformance with the results of the monitoring data. Before any modifications are made to the term grazing permit, the authorized officer will consult, cooperate, and coordinate the need for such action with the permittee, the State, and Tribe having lands or responsibility for managing resources on the allotment. To the extent practical, the authorized officer will provide the permittee and State having lands or responsibility for managing resources in the allotment an opportunity to review, comment and give input during the preparation of reports that evaluate monitoring and other data that are used as a basis for making decisions to increase or decrease grazing use, or to change the terms and conditions of a permit. Permit modifications are issued through a letter to the permittee. Permit modifications may be for purposes such as:
(1) Achieve resource management objectives or adapt to changed rangeland resource conditions.
(2) Comply with requirements of or changes to applicable laws, regulations, land management plans, decisions, agency policies and procedures, and other legally binding documents. Other management needs could include amendments or revisions to a land management plan, or to conservation recommendations provided in a new biological opinion.
(3) Respond to permittee requests within the parameters of the land management plan, grazing permit terms and conditions, and site specific environmental analysis.
(4) Increase or decrease livestock numbers, period of use or change the kind or class of livestock.
(5) Changes in the area to be grazed, including modification of allotment boundary changes to or inclusion of an allotment management plan.
(6) Modify other terms and conditions of the permit, including provision for construction or reconstruction, and/or maintenance, of rangeland improvements.
(7) Devote lands to other public purposes and provide 2 years notice to permittee if the modification includes a partial cancellation.

§ 222.6
Term grazing permit waivers and applications.
(a) A waiver of the term grazing permit shall be submitted when one of the following occurs:
(1) Sale of base property that has a term grazing permit associated with it;
(
printed page 73053)
(2) Lease of base property that has a term grazing permit associated with it;

(3) The waiver of the term grazing permit shall note that the permittee agrees to reasonable compensation as calculated per 222.8(h) for contributions to rangeland improvements and does not hold, and never has, any ownership interest in rangeland improvements constructed, installed, or maintained by the seller on National Forest System lands associated with the waiver.
(4) The authorized officer may modify the terms and conditions of a permit during the permit waiver process when such modifications are needed to conform to current situations brought about by changes in law, regulations, executive orders, allotment management plans, land management planning, resource conditions or management needs, or preferred applicant requests.
(c) At the date of approval of a waiver of term grazing permit, the existing grazing permit shall terminate automatically.
(d) When an individual or entity inherits base property and/or permitted livestock through operation of law or testamentary disposition, and they are otherwise eligible and qualified to hold a term grazing permit, process a waiver of term grazing permit in the same manner as waivers for term grazing permits due to the sale and purchase of base property or permitted livestock.
(1) In the event a will, estate settlement agreement, or probate provides for different owners of the base property and permitted livestock, the opportunity to apply for the term grazing permit is usually provided to the entity that inherits the base property unless otherwise specified or agreed to by the parties.
(2) Strict compliance with the qualification requirements may not be appropriate during the settlement of an estate. The estate shall be required to meet all qualification requirements within three years, unless the administrator of the estate can document why it would be inequitable to do so or why a longer time period is required.
(3) If the individual or entity does not meet the eligibility and qualification requirements in accordance with § 222.3(h) by the end of the three-year period, or as agreed upon by the authorized officer, then the term grazing permit shall be subject to cancellation.
(4) Once a waiver of term grazing permit is received, the individual or entity that inherited the base property should submit an application for a term grazing permit.
(e) When a waiver for a term grazing permit is received due to a base property lease, the following conditions apply:
(1) The base property owner (lessor) must complete and execute a waiver for a term grazing permit within 90 days of signing the lease agreement.
(2) The base property lessee must complete and execute an application for a term grazing permit within 90 days of signing the lease agreement.
(3) Once the application for a term grazing permit is processed, the term grazing permit will be issued for a term that coincides with the expiration of the base property lease agreement or up to 10 years, whichever is shorter. If the permit is issued for a term of less than 10 years, the authorized officer should determine that approving the waiver and issuing the permit will be in the best interest of sound land management to specify a shorter term.
(4) If the base property lease agreement is not renewed, the term grazing permit will be waived back to the base property lessor.
(5) If the term grazing permit is cancelled due to permit violations by the lessee, the grazing preference may be held by the Forest Service for up to one year, while waiting for the lessor to become qualified to hold a term grazing permit. The lessor's term grazing permit application shall be held in preferred applicant status.
(6) If the lessor sells the base property associated with the grazing preference before re-qualifying to hold the term grazing permit, the authorized officer may approve waiving the grazing preference to the base property purchaser. If the grazing preference is not waived with the sale of the base property, then the authorized officer may offer it in accordance with the grant process in section § 222.3(k).
(7) When base property is under lease, a lessee's request for a waiver of the term grazing permit will not be accepted, unless the waiver is waiving the term grazing permit back to the lessor, or unless the lessor agrees, in writing, to allow the lessee to waive the permit to a different entity.
(f) If an entity wishes to change its name on a term grazing permit, it must execute a waiver of the term grazing permit and submit an application for a term grazing permit with all the supporting documents. Term grazing permits cannot be modified to update the name change. Regardless of how many years remain on the old permit, a new 10-year term grazing permit is issued in the name of the new entity.
(g) Following the waiver of a term grazing permit, the authorized officer may consult, cooperate, and coordinate with the preferred applicant, the State or Tribe having lands within the allotment, and affected permittees if the application is for use on a common allotment, before issuing the grazing permit.

(1) Limitations on term grazing permit consolidation should be based on whether the consolidation would result in excessive accumulation of term grazing permits by a single family unit or related group of entities, including circumstances where consolidation would:
(i) Reduce opportunities for local or beginning ranchers or permittee mentees;
(ii) Undermine locally based livestock operations;
(iii) Diminish on-the-ground oversight; or
(iv) Impair the economic viability of community scale ranching.
(2) The authorized officer may deny an application for a term grazing permit when approval would result in issuing and administering a small term grazing permit deemed inefficient for the government to administer, does not align with the local livestock industry for the production of food and fiber, or is not in the best interest of the government.
(i) An application for a term grazing permit must be submitted when one of the following occurs:
(1) Purchase of base property that has a term grazing permit associated with it;
(2) Lease of base property that has a term grazing permit associated with it;
(3) Purchase of permitted livestock that have a term grazing permit associated with the livestock;
(
printed page 73054)
(4) Permittee requests to reassign or change the base property parcel's legal description; or the name of the permitted entity; or
(5) Expiration of the current term grazing permit. The application for a term grazing permit should be submitted at least 1 month prior to the term grazing permit expiration date to ensure timely processing of the renewal.
(j) The purchaser of base property or permitted livestock must complete and execute the application for a term grazing permit within 90 days of purchasing the base property or permitted livestock, or they will lose their priority for obtaining preferred applicant status. Add § 222.7 to read as follows:
§ 222.7
Changes in National Forest System land acreage.
(a) When lands are added to the National Forest System or existing National Forest System lands are newly designated as available for livestock grazing under the administration of the Forest Service, the authorized officer may make the forage for livestock available to eligible and qualified applicants through the grant process described in § 222.3(k).
(b) Where there is a decrease in National Forest System land acreage available for livestock grazing within an allotment:
(1) Grazing permits may be cancelled or modified as appropriate to reflect the changed area of use.
(2) Grazing permits may be cancelled in whole or in part. Cancellations determined by the authorized officer to be necessary to protect the National Forest System lands shall be apportioned by the authorized officer based on the level of available forage and the magnitude of the change in National Forest System land acreage available, or as agreed to among the permittees and the authorized officer.
(c) When National Forest System lands are disposed of or devoted to a public purpose that precludes livestock grazing, permittees shall be given two years' prior notification, except in cases of emergency (such as national defense requirements in time of war, natural disasters, or national emergency needs), before grazing permits may be cancelled. A permittee may unconditionally waive the two-year prior notification. Such a waiver shall not prejudice the permittee's right to reasonable compensation for, but not to exceed the fair market value of, the permittee's interest in authorized permanent rangeland improvements located on these National Forest System lands (see § 222.8(h)).

Revise the newly redesignated § 222.8 to read as follows:
§ 222.8
Rangeland improvements.
(a) The authorized officer may authorize installation and maintenance of structural and nonstructural rangeland improvements as needed to manage the rangeland resource on National Forest System lands and other lands under Forest Service control.
(b) Rangeland improvements shall be constructed, installed, used, maintained, modified, and removed from National Forest System lands in a manner consistent with multiple-use management, optimal effectiveness, and cost efficiency by permittees or other cooperators (including individuals, organizations, or agencies other than the Forest Service), subject to the following:
(1) All rangeland improvements to be installed, constructed, or modified by the permittee on National Forest System lands and other lands under Forest Service control must be authorized by a term grazing permit modification, the provisions of which become part of the term grazing permit. Term grazing permits require the holder to maintain their assigned rangeland improvements.
(2) All rangeland improvements completed by other cooperators, individuals, organizations, or agencies shall be authorized for construction and maintenance through agreements, contracts, memorandums of understanding, or other appropriate documentation or authorization where the Forest Service is a party. The Forest Service will consult, cooperate, and coordinate with the permittee prior to allowing work by a third party to commence. The Forest Service shall keep a copy of the documentation in the rangeland improvement project file.
(3) If the permittee hires a third party to complete the permittee's required contributions to the rangeland improvement project, the permittee must inform the authorized officer of their decision and secure approval from the authorized officer before work begins on the project.
(4) Title to permanent structural and nonstructural rangeland improvements shall rest in the United States.
(5) Title to temporary and removable structural rangeland improvements (such as corrals, creep feeders, loading chutes, and troughs for hauled water) may be retained by the cooperator if no part of the cost for the rangeland improvement is borne by the United States. Once the use for the season has concluded, the temporary and removable structures will be removed from National Forest System lands.
(6) Rangeland improvement work performed by a cooperator or permittee on National Forest System lands shall not confer the exclusive right to use the improvement or the land influenced; nor does it convey to the permittee or cooperator any right, title, or interest in any lands or resources held by the United States.
(c) The authorized officer will review proposed rangeland improvement projects under applicable laws to determine if the proposed action is subject to the requirements of NEPA, as outlined at
7 CFR part 1b
, and to determine whether additional analysis or documentation is required under NEPA and applicable implementing procedures. If the authorized officer determines that the proposed action
(
printed page 73055)
may proceed consistent with
7 CFR part 1b
and other applicable requirements, then a term grazing permit modification is initiated to authorize the project. The permittee may voluntarily accept the modification or appeal the modification under
36 CFR 214
.
(d)
Term grazing permit modifications for rangeland improvements.
(1) A modification to part 3 of the term grazing permit must be completed to authorize and document the work to be completed for rangeland improvement projects with permittees.
(2) Permit modifications for rangeland improvements must include construction specifications, location, estimated cost and degree of cost-sharing, the specific contributions (such as labor, materials, and funding) that will be made by the permittee and the Forest Service, and a timeline for required completion.
(3) Permittees shall contribute the agreed-upon contributions of money, labor, equipment, or materials for new, modified, or reconstructed rangeland improvements on National Forest System lands when the rangeland improvement is used for livestock management purposes. All permittee contributions shall be documented through the permit modification, case files, and database of record.
(4) Once the construction of the rangeland improvement is complete and the authorized officer determines that the rangeland improvement meets the required specifications, part 3 of the term grazing permit must be modified to add the rangeland improvement(s) to the list of improvements assigned to the permittee for maintenance.
(5) Permittees are required to maintain all assigned rangeland improvements related to livestock grazing on National Forest System lands or other lands under Forest Service control and to keep them in standard operable condition throughout their normal life expectancy. This includes periods during temporary non-use and suspension. Permittees are responsible for all maintenance costs associated with rangeland improvements. The permittee will only be assigned maintenance for improvements that they benefit from.
(e)
Non-permittee cooperators for rangeland improvements.
(1) The authorized officer shall evaluate non-permittee proposals to construct rangeland improvements under the same criteria that apply to permit holders, to determine if the improvements contribute toward accomplishing the overall resource management objectives for the area. Before any work is completed by a non-permittee, the Forest Service will consult, cooperate, and coordinate with any existing permittees, States, and Tribes that have lands within the allotment.
(2) The authorized officer shall ensure that rangeland improvements financed by non-Federal contributions are cost-effective and that they are located and built to Forest Service specifications.
(3) The authorized officer should use a collection agreement for any funds that non-Federal parties deposit with the Forest Service for rangeland improvements.
(4) The authorized officer should use a Challenge Cost Share Agreement when cooperation is between the Forest Service and a non-permittee, involves an exchange of funds, materials, or services that is mutually beneficial, and enhances the Forest Service's activities.
(5) The authorized officer should use a Memorandum of Understanding when cooperation is between the Forest Service and a non-permittee, does not involve an exchange of funds, materials, or services, and the agreement is non-binding.
(6) The authorized officer should use an interagency agreement when an agreement is between the Forest Service and other Federal agencies, including those instances that involve sharing of costs, equipment, and expertise.
(7) If the rangeland improvement is an authorized restoration service with a State, county, or Tribe, and is not excluded, a Good Neighbor Agreement may be appropriate.
(8) The authorized officer should use a Cooperative Agreement when the Forest Service provides materials or funds to the cooperator to complete the project and the cooperator is a non-permittee and non-Federal entity or individual.
(9) The authorized officer should consult with a Grants and Agreements specialist to determine whether a different agreement is available for the type of work being desired.
(f)
Removal of rangeland improvements.
(1) Rangeland improvements shall not be removed from National Forest System lands without authorization.
(2) The authorized officer may require permittees to remove rangeland improvements when the improvements are no longer helping to achieve land management plan or allotment goals and objectives, or if the improvements fail to meet the criteria under this section.
(g)
Water rights for the purpose of livestock grazing on National Forest System lands.
(1) Any right asserted by the United States in accordance with State law to use water on National Forest System land for the purpose of livestock watering shall be acquired, perfected, maintained, and administered under the laws of the State where such land is located, as authorized by applicable Federal waivers of sovereign immunity. Any stock water right shall be acquired, perfected, maintained, and administered in the name of the United States, including joint ownership between the United States and permittee where required by State law, expressed or implied principal-agent relationships, or any other legal arrangements recognized under State law and in coordination, consultation, and cooperation with the holder or holders of a valid grazing permit on the allotment.
(2) The Forest Service will not change the purpose of use, place of use, or place of diversion of a water right acquired, perfected, maintained, or administered under paragraph (1) of this section except in accordance with State law. The Forest Service must give a minimum of 30 days' notice and the opportunity to object to any grazing permittees who utilize the subject water for their livestock before making any such application for a change with the State.
(3) The United States shall not condition the authorization of a cooperative range improvement project on the permittee placing the name of the United States on a permittee's water right authorized under State law.
(h)
Compensation for permittees' interest in authorized permanent rangeland improvements.
(1) A current permittee may be entitled to reasonable compensation for the adjusted value of the permittee's investment in authorized permanent rangeland improvements, as listed in the term grazing permit, in situations where the permit has been cancelled, in whole or in part, to devote the permitted grazing land to another public purpose that precludes livestock grazing. Such compensation shall not exceed the fair market value of the terminated portion of the permittee's interest in such improvements.
(i) This compensation for permittees' interest in authorized permanent rangeland improvements only applies when the current permittee made a quantifiable and verifiable investment of money, labor, or materials to construct one or more permanent improvements on the subject land. Former permittees who contributed to an improvement but lost or waived their term grazing permit prior to the subject lands being devoted to another public purpose are not eligible for compensation, nor are permittees who are grazing their
(
printed page 73056)
livestock on the National Forest System lands but did not contribute to the improvement. Investments towards the maintenance of improvements are not eligible for compensation.
(ii) Compensation may be authorized when:
(A) A term permit for grazing on all National Forest System lands in the 16 contiguous Western States is cancelled, in whole or in part, to devote the land to another public purpose that precludes livestock grazing; or
(B) A term permit for grazing on National Forest System lands in the Eastern States is cancelled, in whole or in part, to devote the land to another public purpose that precludes livestock grazing; or
(C) A grazing agreement on National Grasslands is cancelled, in whole or in part, to devote the land to another public purpose that precludes livestock grazing, and the improvements have been constructed by a grazing association or grazing district on a national grassland, entitling the association or district to compensation; provided that the portion of the improvement funded through fee reductions for conservation practices shall not be eligible for compensation. The grazing association has responsibility to distribute any compensation paid by the Forest Service back to the member who contributed funds to the improvement.
(2) Compensation to permittees for their contributions in authorized permanent rangeland improvements does not apply to administrative decisions that temporarily reduce livestock numbers or seasons of use due to resource conditions, or that require a change in the timing of use for compatibility with other resource needs. It also does not apply to permit cancellations due to noncompliance by the permittee.
(3) Pursuant to
43 U.S.C. 1752(g)
, except in cases of emergency, no term grazing permit shall be cancelled to devote the lands covered by the permit to another public purpose without two years' prior notification. It is the responsibility of the Forest Service to notify the permittee that the permittee is eligible for compensation and to identify the amount of compensation.
(4) Reasonable compensation for the adjusted value of the permittee's investment may not exceed the fair market value of the permittee's investment at the time of permit cancellation.
(5) Any portion of improvement funding contributed by the Forest Service from appropriated funds, including range betterment funds, is not eligible for compensation.
(6) Cooperative construction funds provided by State or other Federal agencies (such as Environmental Quality Incentives Program funds through the Natural Resources Conservation Service) shall not be considered part of the permittee's investment.
(7) A Forest Service appraiser, or the services of a qualified third-party appraiser managed by a qualified Forest Service employee, shall use Forest Service-accepted appraisal methods to determine the adjusted value based on the national and local conditions that influence costs where the improvements are located. Generally, amortization schedules are not to be used to determine adjusted value; the appraisal states the present value, which includes an assessment of the condition of the improvement due to regular maintenance or lack thereof. Only the value of the improvement will be considered for compensation, not how much the improvement may have increased the value of the land for grazing.
(8) Compensation may not exceed the amount of the original investment by the permittee in the construction or reconstruction of the improvement.
(9) Completed permit modifications for rangeland improvement work, electronic improvement records, and other documentation and records from the agency and permittee shall be used to verify the costs incurred by both parties to construct the improvements.
(10) Payments for compensation for the adjusted value of the permittee's investment in authorized permanent rangeland improvements shall be handled as obligations of the United States in conformance with current agency policy.
(11) Compensation cannot be made to persons who are no longer permittees, nor to permittees presently using the allotment and associated permanent rangeland improvements that were placed or constructed by former permittees. When a term grazing permit holder executes a permit waiver, and the waiver is accepted by the authorized officer, all interest in the rangeland structural improvements to which the permittee has contributed, and any potential right to compensation upon permit cancellation, cease to exist.
(i)
Range betterment fund.
In addition to rangeland development accomplished through funds from the rangeland management budget line item, the Granger-Thye Act, and deposited and non-deposited cooperative funds, rangeland development may also be accomplished through use of the range betterment fund as follows:
(1) On national forests within the 16 contiguous Western States, the authorized officer shall implement rangeland improvement programs where necessary to arrest rangeland deterioration and improve forage conditions, with resulting benefits to wildlife, watershed protection, and livestock production. One-half of the available funds shall be expended on the national forest where derived. The remaining one-half of the fund shall be allocated for rangeland rehabilitation, protection, and improvements on National Forest System lands as the Chief, Forest Service, directs. During the planning process, consultation shall be held with grazing permittees affected by the rangeland rehabilitation, protection, and improvements.
(2) The funds may be used for activities associated with on-the-ground improvements, including the planning, design, layout, contracting, modification, maintenance for which the Forest Service is responsible, and monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness of specific rangeland improvement projects.
(3) During the assessment needs for the rangeland development or rangeland improvement programs, the authorized officer shall consult, cooperate, and coordinate with the affected permittees.

Revise the newly redesignated § 222.9 to read as follows:
§ 222.9
Cooperation.
(a)
Cooperation with grazing associations.
(1)
Authority.
The authorized officer is authorized to recognize, cooperate with, and assist grazing associations in the management of the livestock and rangeland resources on a single grazing allotment, associated groups of allotments, or other association-controlled lands on which the members' livestock are permitted to graze.
(2)
Requirements for recognition.
The requirements for receiving recognition are:
(i) A grazing association must be established as a co-operative pursuant to State or Tribal law as a precursor to being recognized by the Forest Service and considered for the issuance of a grazing agreement. An established grazing association may contact the authorized officer in writing, requesting that the grazing association be formally recognized and issued a grazing agreement;
(ii) The members of the association constitute a majority of the grazing
(
printed page 73057)
permittees on the grazing allotment or allotments involved;
(iii) The officers of the association are elected by a majority of the association members or of a quorum as specified by the association's constitution and bylaws;
(iv) The officers other than the Secretary (primary officer) and Treasurer must be grazing permittees on the grazing allotment or allotments involved;
(v) The association's activities must be governed by a constitution and bylaws acceptable to and approved by the authorized Forest Service officer; and
(vi) Rules of management are needed to ensure proper resource management.
(3)
Withdrawing recognition.
The authorized officer may withdraw recognition of the association whenever it is dissolved in accordance with the State or Tribal law where it was established.
(4)
Rules of management.
(i) Rules of management are developed by the board of directors of a grazing association and used in administering the grazing program for its members on all association-administered lands.
(ii) Grazing associations are responsible for developing their initial rules of management, which are then provided to the Forest Service authorized officer for review and concurrence.
(iii) An association's rules of management may be more restrictive than applicable Federal law, regulation, or Forest Service policy, but they cannot be less restrictive. The authorized officer will not concur with any rules that are less restrictive or are otherwise in conflict with applicable Federal law, regulation, and Forest Service policy.
(iv) The rules of management describe how an association will administer the grazing program for its members on the lands covered by their respective grazing agreements. The purpose of the rules of management is to provide clear and consistent rules that will be applied to each member and to distribute livestock grazing privileges in a fair manner to all qualified members.
(b)
Cooperation with national, State, Tribal and county livestock organizations.
The appropriate authorized officer shall endeavor to establish and maintain close working relationships with national livestock organizations that have an interest in the administration of National Forest System lands and shall work cooperatively with State and county livestock organizations having similar interests. The policies and programs of national, State, Tribal and county livestock organizations give direction to, and reflect in, the practices of their members. Good working relationships with these groups are conducive to the betterment of rangeland management on both public and private lands.
(c)
Interagency cooperation.
The appropriate authorized officer shall cooperate with other Federal agencies that have a jurisdictional interest during development of allotment management plans, and management plans, or site-specific plans on National Forest System lands, as well as coordinate with State and local governments pursuant to
16 U.S.C. 1604(a)
as appropriate.

§ 222.10
Cooperation in control of estray or unbranded livestock, animal diseases, noxious weeds, and use of pesticides.
(a) Insofar as it involves National Forest System lands and other lands under Forest Service control, or the livestock that graze thereon, the authorized officer shall cooperate with:
(1) State, county, and Federal agencies in the application and enforcement of all laws and regulations relating to livestock diseases, sanitation, and noxious weeds;
(2) The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service and other Federal or State agencies and institutions in surveillance of pesticide spray programs; and
(3) State cattle and sheep sanitary or brand boards in control of estray and unbranded livestock to the extent it does not conflict with the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971.
(b) The authorized officer shall cooperate with county or other local weed control districts in analyzing noxious weed problems and developing control programs in areas of which the national forests and national grasslands are a part.

Revise § 222.50 to read as follows:
§ 222.50
Grazing fees.
(a) Fees shall be charged for all livestock grazing or livestock use of National Forest System lands, or other lands under Forest Service control. An exception applies to livestock use authorized free of charge under § 222.3 (j)(2)(ii)-(viii).
(b) Except as provided in § 222.3 (j)(2)(ii)-(viii) and § 222.50(k), the full
(
printed page 73058)
fee shall be charged for each animal unit month of grazing use. For the purposes of calculating the fee, an animal unit month is defined as one month's use of forage and occupancy of range by one (1) cow, bull, steer, heifer, bison, horse (ancillary to livestock production), burro, or mule, or five (5) sheep or goats.
(1) Over the age of 6 months at the time of entering the public lands or other lands administered by the Forest Service;
(2) Weaned regardless of age; or
(3) Becoming 12 months of age during the authorized period of use.
(c) The Forest Service shall not charge grazing fees for animals that are less than 6 months of age at the time of entering National Forest System lands, provided that they are the progeny of animals upon which fees are paid, and provided that they will not become 12 months of age during the authorized period of use.
(d) A surcharge shall be added to the grazing bill for authorized leasing of livestock. The surcharge shall be over and above any other fees that may be charged for livestock grazing on National Forest System lands. Surcharges shall be paid prior to grazing use. The surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock owned by persons other than the permittee shall be equal to 35 percent of the difference between the current year's Federal grazing fee and the prior year's private grazing land lease rate per animal unit month for the appropriate State as determined by the National Agricultural Statistics Service. This surcharge shall be charged per animal unit month.
(e) No additional charge will be made for the privilege of lambing upon National Forest System lands, or other lands under Forest Service control.
(f) In calculating the bill for collection, the authorized officer will round charges to reflect the nearest whole number of animal unit months.
(g) Transportation livestock may be charged at a special rate, and at a minimum established for such use. Fees for horses, mules, or burros associated with management of permitted livestock on an allotment, or for research purposes and administrative studies, and authorized on a charge basis, are determined under provisions of paragraph (b) of this section.
(h) The fees for trailing livestock across National Forest System lands will conform with the rates established for other livestock. Where practicable, fees for trailing permitted livestock will be covered in the regular grazing fee, and the crossing period will be covered in the regular grazing period.
(i) Fees are due on the due date specified on the bill for collection. Payment shall be made prior to grazing use, unless otherwise approved by the authorized officer, as in cases of split billing and actual use billing. Grazing use that occurs prior to payment of a bill, except where specified in an allotment management plan or functional equivalent, is unauthorized use and may be dealt with under § 222.50(k) of this part. If allotment management plans, or the functional equivalent, provide for billing after the grazing season, fees will be based on actual grazing use and will be due upon issuance. Repeated delays in payment of actual use billings, or noncompliance with the terms and conditions of the grazing permit and allotment management plan, or the functional equivalent, shall be dealt with through non-compliance procedures and be cause to revoke provisions for actual use billing.
(j) The unauthorized grazing use rate shall be determined by establishing a base value without giving consideration for those contributions normally made by the permittee under the terms of the grazing permit. This rate is charged for unauthorized forage or forage in excess of authorized use and is separate from any penalties that may be assessed for a violation of a prohibition issued under
36 CFR part 261.7
or from an administrative permit action. This rate shall apply to, but not be limited to, the following circumstances: excess number of livestock grazed; livestock grazed outside the permitted grazing season; livestock grazed in areas not authorized under a grazing permit and a bill for collection; or livestock grazed without a permit. Pursuant to paragraph (a) and (c) of this section, a grazing fee shall be charged for each animal unit month of livestock grazing or use, unless the use is calculated at less than one animal unit month, in which case a minimum of one animal unit month shall be charged. This includes any unauthorized grazing use. The authorized officer may waive monetary fees for unauthorized grazing use only when all three of the following conditions are met:
(1) The unauthorized use was a result of unforeseen or uncontrollable circumstances on behalf of the permittee or non-permittee, and the livestock associated with such use were removed by the permittee or non-permittee within the timeframe required by the authorized officer;
(2) The forage consumed by the unauthorized use is not significant; and
(3) National Forest System lands have not been damaged significantly by the unauthorized use.
(k) Credits on a bill for collection may be allowed under justifiable conditions and circumstances as the authorized officer may specify.
(l) Refunds may be approved at the discretion of the authorized officer unless the request for refund is necessary due to a duplicate or overpayment.
(m) The fee year for the purpose of charging grazing fees will be March 1 through the following February.
(n) The data year for the purpose of collecting beef cattle price data for computing indexes will be November 1 through the following October and apply to the following fee year.
(o) For annual billing prior to the turn-on date and the first bill for collection in a split-billing schedule, bills for collection should be sent to the permittee at least 40 days, but not more than 60 days, before the authorized on-date.
(p) Failure to pay the bill for collection within 15 days of the due date specified in the bill shall result in a late fee assessment of $25.00 or 10 percent of the grazing bill, whichever is greater, but not to exceed $250.00. Payment made later than 15 days after the due date shall include the appropriate interest, administrative fee, and penalty. Failure to make payment within 30 days after the due date is a violation of the term grazing permit and shall result in permit action in accordance with § 222.4(a)(3).

Revise § 222.51 to read as follows:
§ 222.51
National Forests in 16 Western States and National Grasslands.
(a) Grazing fees are established on lands designated as national forests and land utilization projects in the 16 contiguous Western States: Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, Wyoming, and on all national grasslands.
(b) Notwithstanding the provisions of § 222.50(b) of this part, the calculated grazing fee shall be equal to the $1.23 base established by the 1966 Western Livestock Grazing Survey multiplied by the result of the Forage Value Index (computed annually from data supplied by the National Agricultural Statistics Service) added to the Combined Index (Beef Cattle Price Index minus the Prices Paid Index) and divided by 100, as follows:
GF = BV × (FVI + (BCPI − PPI))/100
Where:
(
printed page 73059)
GF =
Grazing Fee,
the estimated economic value of livestock grazing, defined by Congress as the fair market value of the forage.
BV =
Base Value
of $1.23, the base economic value of grazing on public rangeland established by the 1966 Western Livestock Grazing Survey.
FVI =
Forage Value Index,
the weighted average estimate of the annual rental charge per animal unit month for pasturing cattle on private rangelands in the eleven Western States (Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, and California), computed by the National Agricultural Statistics Service from the June Enumerative Survey, divided by $3.65 and multiplied by 100.
BCPI =
Beef Cattle Price Index,
the weighted average annual selling price for beef cattle (excluding calves) in the eleven Western States (Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, Nevada, Washington, Oregon, and California) for November through October, computed by the National Agricultural Statistics Service, divided by $22.04 per hundredweight and multiplied by 100.
PPI =
Prices Paid Index,
the following selected components from the National Agricultural Statistics Service's Annual National Index of Prices Paid by Farmers for Goods and Services, adjusted by the weights indicated in parentheses to reflect livestock production costs in the Western States: Fuels and Energy (14.5); Farm and Motor Supplies (12.0); Autos and Trucks (4.5); Tractors and Self-Propelled Machinery (4.5); Other Machinery (12.0); Building and Fencing Materials (14.5); Interest (6.0); Farm Wage Rates (14.0); and Farm Services (18.0).
(c) Any annual increase or decrease in the grazing fee for any given year shall be limited to not more than plus or minus 25 percent of the previous year's fee.
(d) The grazing fee for any year shall not be less than $1.35 per animal unit month.
(e)
Fee reductions for authorized land use practice expenditures.
(1) The authorized officer may authorize fee reductions on national grasslands and land utilization projects when the permittee incurs approved expenditures for authorized land use practices, including conservation practices and, when applicable, administrative costs. To qualify for a fee reduction, expenditures for approved land use practices must be documented in writing and verified by the authorized officer. Fee reductions apply only to national grasslands and land utilization projects and are not available on national forests.
(2) Fee reductions for administrative activities are only available to grazing associations and grazing districts (“associations”) for routine costs incurred by the association to administer the livestock grazing activities of its members under a grazing agreement issued by the Forest Service. There is no fee reduction for administrative costs for grazing permits issued directly by the Forest Service to individuals, since the Forest Service still performs these administrative functions.
(i) Administrative costs are costs that would otherwise be borne by the Forest Service if it were directly administering the grazing permits of the association members. These costs must be approved in advance by the authorized officer and may include routine administrative and clerical expenses related to issuing association-issued permits, collecting grazing fees, monitoring livestock use, enforcing permit terms and conditions, recordkeeping, and other expenses such as salaries and benefits, payroll taxes, postage, copying, depreciation, office space, utilities, legal and accounting fees, and directors' expenses necessary to administer the agreement.
(ii) Administrative costs shall not include any expenses related to legal challenges or fees of any kind. Association costs for memberships in, dues for, or contributions to advocacy groups are not allowable administrative expenses.
(f)
Fee credits.
A permittee can fund an approved rangeland improvement up-front, then receive fee credits in future years as compensation for the government's cost-share portion of the project. Fee credits may be used on national grasslands where a direct permittee is involved and, in some situations, when a grazing association is involved.
(1) Credit shall not be allowed, and work plans shall not be approved, for more than the number of years remaining of the permittee's 10-year grazing permit. However, in some cases involving large or expensive projects, it may be prudent to issue a new 10-year permit at the beginning of the project to allow for maximum fee credit toward the expense of the large project.
(2) When grazing associations are involved and they are working in conjunction with all of their benefitting members, associations may secure and obligate larger amounts of money to complete large or expensive conservation practice rangeland improvements (such as drilling a one-time water well or installing a water pipeline system).
(3) When total project costs exceed conservation practice funds available in that one year, fee credits may be allowed in future years under approved work plans to credit the association for its initial advance funding provided to complete the project. Credit shall not be allowed, and work plans shall not be approved, for more than the number of years remaining of the 10-year grazing agreement.

Redesignate § 222.53 as § 222.52, and amend the newly redesignated § 222.52 by revising paragraphs (a), (b), and (c) introductory text, (c)(1) introductory text, (c)(1)(i) through (iii), and adding paragraph (d), to read as follows:
§ 222.52
Grazing fees in the Eastern States—noncompetitive procedures.
(a)
Scope.
Except as provided in § 222.53 of this subpart, the fee charged for commercial livestock grazing use and occupancy on National Forest System lands in the States of New York, Missouri, Vermont, West Virginia, Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Puerto Rico, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia shall be determined through noncompetitive, fair market value procedures. These rules do not apply to grazing fees on National Forest System lands in Oklahoma or national grasslands in Texas. Grazing permits under the noncompetitive fee method in the Eastern States are subject to the rules governing grazing permit administration in subpart A of this part.
(b)
Applicability.
The rules of this section apply to the establishment of grazing fees for existing permittees on the lands identified in paragraph (a) of this section, including grazing associations in New York and Missouri as of March 1, 1990, to any livestock on-and-off permits defined in subpart A of this part, and to any allotments advertised for competitive bidding which were not bid on (§ 222.53(h) of this subpart). Noncompetitive permits vacated or terminated by an existing permittee, and any new allotments created after the effective date of this rule, shall be offered on a competitive bid basis as specified in § 222.53 of this subpart. As provided in subpart A of this part, holders of term permits have first priority for receipt of a new permit.
(c)
Fee system.
The grazing fee charged under this section shall be based on fair market value, as determined by using comparable private grazing lease rates, adjusted for the difference in the costs of grazing comparable private leased lands and National Forest System lands, or by reference to prevailing prices in
(
printed page 73060)
competitive markets for other Federal or State leased or permitted grazing lands that are the same as, or substantially similar to, grazing lands offered or administered by the Forest Service in the Eastern States, with comparability adjustments as appropriate. Rates for grazing on comparable private lands shall be adjusted for the difference between the total costs of operating on private grazing lands and the total costs (other than grazing fee costs) of operating on National Forest System lands.
(1)
Establishing base grazing value.
(i) The authorized officer shall determine an estimated base market value of grazing use and occupancy on National Forest System lands in the Eastern States for the following designated subregions:
(A) Corn Belt (Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, and Ohio);
(B) Lake States (Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin);
(C) Northeast (Maine, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, and Vermont);
(D) Appalachia (Kentucky, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia);
(E) Southeast/Delta (Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Texas); and
(F) Florida.
(ii) The authorized officer shall revise or update estimated market values of grazing use and occupancy as necessary to respond to significant changes in the agricultural economy in the Eastern States, and to ensure that fees represent fair market value.
(iii) The authorized officer, where sufficient market data exist, may establish the base grazing value for grazing allotments using comparable, local rates for leasing private grazing lands.
(d)
Surcharge for leased livestock.
A surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock owned by persons other than the permittee, equal to 35 percent of the non-competitive grazing fee for the Eastern States per animal unit month for the appropriate Subregion, as determined by the National Agricultural Statistics Service. Targeted exemptions would be available for livestock owned by properly documented mentees, beginning ranchers, permittee successors, immediate or extended family members, and operators receiving relief from drought, fire, or other natural causes.
*

*
*
27.
Redesignate § 222.54 as § 222.53, and amend the newly redesignated § 222.53 by revising paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), (b), (d), (e), and (h), and adding paragraph (i), to read as follows:
§ 222.53
Grazing fees in the Eastern States—competitive bidding.
(a)
General procedures.
(1)
Applicability.
The rules of this section apply to grazing fees for any allotment established or vacated on National Forest System lands in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, Maine, Pennsylvania, Vermont, West Virginia, Wisconsin, Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Puerto Rico, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia, after February 26, 1990, as well as to grazing fees for existing allotments for such lands that have already been established under competitive procedures as of the date of this rule. Permits offered for competitive bidding in the Eastern States are subject to the rules governing grazing permit administration in subpart A of this part. The rules of this section do not apply to negotiated livestock use permits or to permits with on-and-off grazing provisions as authorized in subpart A of this part. Holders of term permits have first priority for receipt of a new term grazing permit in accordance with subpart A of this part. These rules also do not apply to grazing fees on National Forest System lands in Oklahoma or national grasslands in Texas.
(2)
Allowable bidders.
Bids for grazing permits shall be accepted from individuals, partnerships, grazing associations (formed after February 26, 1990), joint ventures, corporations, limited liability companies, and other organizations.
(b)
Establishment of minimum bid price.
Authorized officers shall establish a minimum bid price for each available allotment as described in § 222.52 of this subpart.
*

(d)
Submission of bid.
Each applicant shall submit an application for the grazing permit and a sealed bid for the grazing fee.
(e)
Qualifications.
Upon opening applicants' bids, the authorized officer shall determine whether each bidder meets the qualifications to hold a permit as set forth in subpart A of this part.

(h)
No bids received.
If qualified sealed bids are not received, the authorized officer reserves the right to conduct an oral auction using the minimum bid price established under paragraph (b) of this section, or to establish grazing fees through noncompetitive grazing fee procedures specified in § 222.52 of this subpart.
(i)

A surcharge for authorized leasing of livestock owned by persons other than the permittee, equal to 35 percent of the non-competitive grazing fee for the Eastern States per animal unit month for the appropriate Subregion, as determined by the National Agricultural Statistics Service. Targeted exemptions would be available for livestock owned by properly documented mentees, beginning ranchers, permittee successors, immediate or extended family members, and operators receiving relief from drought, fire, or other natural causes.

ACTION:
Notification of change to telephonic-only public hearing on a proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that the public hearing scheduled for December 15, 2026, at 10 a.m. ET, for the notice of proposed rulemaking and notice of public hearing (REG-117199-25) published in the
Federal Register

.

Concerning the proposed regulations, Constance Chien, (202) 317-7002, or Andrew Fahmy, (202) 317-3840; concerning submissions of comments and the public hearing, the Publications and Regulations Section at (202) 317-6901 (not toll-free numbers) or by email at
publichearings@irs.gov

The rules of
26 CFR 601.601(a)(3)

Individuals who have already sent an email to
publichearings@irs.gov

https://www.regulations.gov

publichearings@irs.gov

title: National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) Projects and Activities
abstract: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) invites organizations to submit letters of interest to participate in NCCoE collaborative research projects through a standing consortia structure. This Federal Register Notice (FRN) notifies interested parties that NIST is establishing a single process through which organizations may express interest in participating in one or more NCCoE project consortia. Rather than issuing a separate FRN for each new NCCoE project, NIST is posting a single partnership announcement in the Federal Register and directing interested parties to SAM.gov for further information. New NCCoE collaborative research projects will be announced on SAM.gov. Additionally, NIST will maintain a publicly available list of active and forming NCCoE projects on the NCCoE website (https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/portfolio), where instructions for letters of interest will also be posted. Organizations may submit letters of interest to participate in one or more consortia on a rolling basis. Selected participants will collaborate with NIST through Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs), and contribute technology, expertise, and products to NCCoE cybersecurity demonstrations. SUMMARY:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) invites organizations to submit letters of interest to participate in NCCoE collaborative research projects through a standing consortia structure. This
Federal Register
Notice (FRN) notifies interested parties that NIST is establishing a single process through which organizations may express interest in participating in one or more NCCoE project consortia. Rather than issuing a separate FRN for each new NCCoE project, NIST is posting a single partnership announcement in the
Federal Register
and directing interested parties to
SAM.gov
for further information. New NCCoE collaborative research projects will be announced on
SAM.gov
. Additionally, NIST will maintain a publicly available list of active and forming NCCoE projects on the NCCoE website (
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​portfolio
), where instructions for letters of interest will also be posted. Organizations may submit letters of interest to participate in one or more consortia on a rolling basis. Selected participants will collaborate with NIST through Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs), and contribute technology, expertise, and products to NCCoE cybersecurity demonstrations. Interested organizations should describe the technical expertise, services, and/or products that they will bring to NCCoE to support the Center's collaborative research activities. Participation is open to all interested organizations that can contribute their expertise, services, and/or products to the NCCoE's projects and activities. Selected participants will be required to enter into a CRADA with NIST. At NIST's discretion, entities that are not legally permitted to enter into CRADAs may be allowed to participate under a separate non-CRADA agreement.
DATES:
NCCoE collaborative research projects operate on an ongoing basis. New NCCoE collaborative research projects will be announced on
SAM.gov
and the NCCoE website (
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov
). The current list of NCCoE projects seeking collaborators will be maintained on the NCCoE website and updated as new projects are initiated. The timeframe for submissions will be shared on the NCCoE website as new projects are announced. NIST will periodically review submissions and notify applicants if they are selected to participate in NCCoE projects.
ADDRESSES:
Interested parties can access the letter of interest request for a consortium by visiting
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​CRADA
and completing the letter of interest webform. Completed letters of interest may be submitted to the email address listed for the consortium, by email to
nccoe@nist.gov
,
or with a hardcopy to: National Institute of Standards and Technology, NCCoE; 9700 Great Seneca Highway, Rockville, MD 20850. Organizations whose letters of interest are accepted in accordance with the process outlined in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this notice will be asked to sign a CRADA with NIST. The CRADA template will be made available to selected applicants by NIST's Technology Partnerships Office (TPO).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Contact the NCCoE by email at
NCCoE@nist.gov
,
by phone at (301) 975-0200, or by mail to National Institute of Standards and Technology, NCCoE; 9700 Great Seneca Highway, Rockville, MD 20850. For questions related to CRADAs please contact J'aime Maynard, Consortia Agreements Officer, NIST's Technology Partnerships Office (TPO), by email to
agreements@nist.gov

inquiry@nist.gov
or by phone at (301) 975-2762.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background:
The NCCoE, part of NIST, is a public-private collaboration for accelerating the widespread adoption of secure technologies. The NCCoE brings together experts from industry, government, and academia to develop practical, interoperable cybersecurity and privacy approaches that address the real-world needs of complex Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) systems.
NCCoE projects are selected based on their alignment with NIST and government and industry priorities. For example:
National Priorities:
The challenge addresses a nationwide cybersecurity challenge.
NIST Mission and Available Resources:
The work builds on NIST standards and technology expertise in areas such as cryptography, identity, risk management, privacy, trustworthy systems, and more.
NCCoE Mission Alignment:
The work addresses a real-world challenge using commercial technology.
Industry Signals:
The topic is consistently identified by industry participants as a priority.
NCCoE's project portfolio (
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​portfolio
) evolves in response to emerging cybersecurity challenges, national priorities, and stakeholder input. As new projects are initiated, they will be posted on
SAM.gov
and the NCCoE website (
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov
), without issuing an additional
Federal Register
Notice.
Process:
NIST is soliciting responses from all sources of relevant technical capabilities (see below) to enter into a CRADA to provide technical expertise, technology products, and other capabilities as necessary to build and demonstrate integrated approaches in support of NCCoE's projects and activities, as described in the previous section.
Interested parties can submit a letter of interest to participate in NCCoE projects by visiting the NCCoE website (
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov
), and then navigating to
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​CRADA
and completing the letter of interest webform; alternatively, parties can provide the information detailed in LETTER OF INTEREST, below, and send via email or hardcopy (for reference, see
ADDRESSES
section above). NIST will contact interested parties if there are questions regarding the responsiveness of the letters of interest to the project objective or requirements identified below. NIST evaluates complete letters of interest on a first-come, first-served basis and determines technical acceptability based on fit within the project's scope and satisfaction with the project's technical requirements. Selected participants will be required to enter into a CRADA with NIST. At NIST's discretion, entities that are not legally permitted to enter into CRADAs may be allowed to participate pursuant to separate non-CRADA agreements.
Objective of NCCoE Projects:
NCCoE projects demonstrate integrated cybersecurity solutions using
(
printed page 72854)
commercially available technologies. Collaborators contribute products, technical expertise, and implementation expertise that enable NIST to build and evaluate reference architectures addressing real-world technology transition challenges. This will help enable projects that are aligned with U.S. industry and government needs, promote secure-by-design technologies and applications, and ensure that the U.S. Government is at the forefront of managing national security risks in technology environments. NCCoE's work is open and transparent, and it invites interested parties to provide insights into emerging cybersecurity challenges and solutions, and to accelerate the adoption of cybersecurity processes and tools.
Building upon its long track record of working with the private and public sectors and its history of reliable and practical measurement and standards-oriented solutions, NCCoE seeks research collaborators who can support this vital undertaking. Specifically, NCCoE looks to:
Create a convening space for collaborators to engage in dialogue and strive for open and transparent collaborations.
Bring together stakeholders from industry and academia to work collaboratively to build and mature cybersecurity processes and tools for IT systems.
Demonstrate the ability to secure IT systems using commercially available technologies.
Participation in NCCoE projects provides organizations with the opportunity to collaborate directly with NIST and other industry leaders to address significant cybersecurity challenges. Collaborators contribute technologies and expertise to build integrated reference architectures that demonstrate practical implementations of standards, best practices, and commercially available technologies. These demonstrations inform NIST guidance and help accelerate the adoption of secure technologies across government and industry.
NCCoE projects and activities are subject to change based upon current NCCoE, NIST, and U.S. Government priorities and as advances in the technical state of the art open new avenues for scientific inquiry and collaboration. These changes may result in the addition or removal of measurement science, technologies, and support areas listed above.
Requirements for Letters of Interest:
Interested Parties must use NCCoE's Letter of Interest form (OMB Control No. 0693-0075) to submit their interest in participating in NCCoE projects. A sample of the current version of the form is available at
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​get-involved/​collaborate-us-technical-contributions
.
Each NCCoE project announcement will contain specific instructions on how to request and submit a letter of interest for that project.
A Federal agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, nor shall a person be subject to a penalty for failure to comply with an information collection subject to the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 unless the information collection has a currently valid OMB Control Number. The approved OMB Control Number for this information collection is 0693-0075. Without this approval, NCCoE could not conduct this information collection. Public reporting for this information collection is estimated to be approximately 2 hours per response, including the time for reviewing instructions, searching existing data sources, gathering and maintaining the data needed, and completing and reviewing the information collection. All responses to this information collection are voluntary. Send comments regarding this burden estimate or any other aspect of this information collection, including suggestions for reducing this burden to NCCoE using the information in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section above.
Letters of interest should not include proprietary information. NIST will not treat any information provided in response to this notice as proprietary information.
NIST cannot guarantee that all submissions will be utilized or that the products proposed by respondents will be used in NCCoE's activities. Each prospective participant will be expected to work collaboratively with NIST staff and other project participants under the terms of the NCCoE project agreement.
Additional details about the NCCoE's project portfolio are available at:
https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/​portfolio
For additional information on the NCCoE governance, business processes, and NCCoE operational structure, visit the NCCoE website
https://nccoe.nist.gov/​
.

Title:

OMB Number:

Expiration Date of Approval:
January 30, 2027.
Type of Request:
Extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
The Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) (
7 U.S.C. 2321
et seq.
) was established: “To encourage the development of novel varieties of sexually reproduced plants and make them available to the public, providing protection available to those who breed, develop, or discover them, and thereby promote progress in agriculture in the public interest.”
The PVPA is a voluntary user-funded program that grants intellectual property rights protection to breeders of new, distinct, uniform, and stable sexually reproduced, tuber propagated, and asexually reproduced plant varieties. To obtain these rights the applicant must provide information which shows the variety is eligible for protection and that it is indeed new, distinct, uniform, and stable as the law requires.
Application forms, descriptive forms, and ownership forms are furnished to applicants to identify the information which is required to be furnished by the applicant to legally issue a certificate of protection (ownership). The certificate is based on claims of the breeder and cannot be issued based on reports in publications not submitted by the applicant. Regulations implementing the PVPA appear at
7 CFR part 92
.
Applicant's Ownership ST-470, Application for Plant Variety Protection Certificate; ST-470 A, Origin and Breeding History; ST-470 B, Statement of Distinctness; Form ST-470 series, Objective Description of Variety (Exhibit C);
and
Form ST-470-E, Basis of Applicant's Ownership
are the basis by which the determination, by experts at PVPO, is made as to whether a new, distinct, uniform, and stable seed reproduced or tuber-propagated variety in fact exists and is entitled to protection. The ST-470 application form combines Exhibits A, B, and E into one form. The information received on applications, with certain exceptions, is required by law to remain confidential until the certificate is issued (
7 U.S.C. 2426
).
The information collection requirements in this request are essential to carry out the intent of the PVPA, to provide applicants with certificates of protection, to provide the respondents with the type of service they request, and to administer the program.

Public reporting burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 1 hour per response.

2,132.

(1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology. Comments may be sent to the Plant Variety Protection Office (PVPO), Science and Technology, Agricultural Marketing Service, USDA, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Room 2915-S, Stop 0274, Washington, DC 20250 or by email to
AMS.PVPOForms@usda.gov

All responses to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record.

I. Table of Abbreviations
