II. Background and Authority
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded a contract for the dismantling, recycling, and disposal of EX ENTERPRISE. Under this contract, EX ENTERPRISE will be dismantled in its entirety, and all resulting materials will be recycled or disposed of. Specifically, hazardous materials, including low-level radioactive waste, will be packaged and safely transported for disposal at authorized licensed sites. The vessel will be towed to its designated dismantlement location and has no capability to maneuver under its own power. Work will be performed in Mobile, Alabama, and is expected to be completed by December 2030. The receiving facility for the EX ENTERPRISE is on the west side of the Mobile River, located at 701 South Royal Street, in Mobile, AL.
To support the project, the U.S. Coast Guard was asked to establish a temporary fixed safety zone on portions of the Mobile Bay and Mobile River channels to address risks associated with its transit into Mobile, and a second temporary fixed safety zone around the EX ENTERPRISE to address risk associated with the dismantling operation. These risks include the fact that EX ENTERPRISE has no propulsion, limited maneuverability, and contains regulated materials requiring controlled handling. When moored, the vessel will undergo prolonged dismantling operations involving the removal of hazardous materials and regulated waste, including radiological materials. Work crews,
(
printed page 72797)
equipment, and response assets will be actively engaged on and around the hull. The Captain of the Port Sector Mobile (COTP) has determined that the transit and dismantling operations present safety concerns for the EX ENTERPRISE, personnel involved with the operations, and the public. Therefore, the COTP is establishing this rule under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
, which is needed to protect personnel and vessels in the navigable waters within these zones.
The Coast Guard published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) on October 1, 2026 (
91 FR 62368
), proposing temporary moving and fixed safety zones to support the transit and dismantling of EX ENTERPRISE and soliciting public comments. After publication of the NPRM, the U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard agreed that the Naval Vessel Protection Zone regulation described in
33 CFR 165.2025
will be enforced around the EX ENTERPRISE during the voyage, in place of a moving safety zone regulation. Therefore, the USCG is removing the moving safety zone that was proposed in that NPRM. The two fixed zones will remain in place. Accordingly, the Coast Guard is issuing this temporary final rule (TFR), which establishes safety zones that mirror the locations, dimensions, and enforcement periods of the fixed safety zones proposed in the NPRM.
Because of the hazards associated with this event, the Coast Guard finds that under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. We must establish this safety zone by November 11, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
III. Discussion of Comments and the Rule
During the comment period that ended on October 16, 2026, we received two comments. Both commenters recommended clearer parameters for the fixed zone described in paragraph (a)(3) of that NPRM. The Coast Guard agrees and amended the rule to describe the fixed safety zone using specific geographic coordinates rather than a radius around the vessel. This change also addresses one commenter's question concerning the units of measurement used in the NPRM by replacing the radius-based description with a boundary defined by geographic coordinates.
One commenter also requested clarification concerning a potential change in the vessel's mooring location. The U.S. Navy is making arrangements to moor EX ENTERPRISE at a precise location. If the mooring location changes, the Coast Guard will amend this temporary final rule, as appropriate, and provide notice to the public through appropriate means.
Following publication of the NPRM, the U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard agreed that the Naval Vessel Protection Zone regulation described in
33 CFR 165.2025
will be enforced around EX ENTERPRISE during its transit. Accordingly, the proposed moving safety zone is no longer necessary and has been removed from this temporary regulation. The two fixed safety zones will remain in effect.
Additionally, the temporary fixed safety zone around the EX ENTERPRISE once it is moored at the receiving facility will remain in effect throughout the dismantling operations, for an estimated period of four years, not five years as mistakenly stated in section III of the NPRM. This Safety Zone will also not impact the federal channel. This zone is necessary due to the extensive dismantling work, removal of hazardous and regulated materials, and the continuous presence of personnel and equipment on and around the hull, all of which create elevated risks to nearby traffic.
The duration and enforcement periods for the temporary fixed safety zone, and the temporary fixed moored safety zone have been tailored to ensure protection of personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in these navigable waters while minimizing impacts on other waterway users to only what is necessary.
The COTP will provide specific notice of the enforcement date and time through Broadcast Notice to Mariners and other public advisories. Enforcement of the fixed safety zone on the navigational channel would terminate once the EX ENTERPRISE is moored at the receiving facility.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analysis based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. Section 605 of the RFA allows an agency to certify a rule, in lieu of preparing an analysis, if the rulemaking is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Coast Guard certifies that, although some small entities may intend to transit the safety zone above, this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. Vessel traffic will be able to safely transit around both fixed safety zones, and may enter the zones with the authorization of the COTP. The temporary fixed safety zone in the channel will impact the designated area for a few hours on one day. In addition, the Coast Guard will issue a Broadcast Notice to Marines via VHF FM marine channel 16, which will allow small entities to adjust their transit plans, and the rule allows vessels to request permission to enter the zone from the COTP.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247).
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
(
printed page 72798)
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment.
This rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1. A Record of Environmental Consideration supporting this determination is available in the docket.

33 CFR part 165
as follows:
PART 165—REGULATED NAVIGATION AREAS AND LIMITED ACCESS AREAS
1.
The authority citation for part 165 continues to read as follows:
Authority:
46 U.S.C. 70034
,
70051
,
70124
;
33 CFR 1.05-1
,
6.04-1
,
6.04-6
, and
160.5
; DHS Delegation No. 00170.1, Revision No. 01.4.
2.
Add § 165.T08-1214 to read as follows:
§ 165.T08-1214
Safety Zone; Sector Mobile Captain of the Port Zone, Mobile, AL
(a) Locations.
(1) The following area is a fixed safety zone: all navigable waters within any Federal channel from the Mobile Bar Channel, beginning at the Mobile Bar Lighted Buoy 1 (LLNR 6100), extending northward to the Mobile River Channel ending at the Cochrane Bridge.
(2) The following area is a fixed moored safety zone: All navigable waters of the Mobile River bound by the following approximate coordinates 30°40′34″ N, 088°02′16″ W, east to 30°40′33″ N, 088°02′13″ W on the west edge of the Mobile River Channel, south along the west edge of the Mobile River Channel to 30°40′18″ N, 088°02′05″ W, to 30°40′19″ N, 088°02′16″ W, then north along the shoreline back to the point of origin while the EX ENTERPRISE is moored at the receiving facility on the west side of the Mobile River, located at 701 South Royal Street, in Mobile, AL.
(b) Definitions.
As used in this section, designated representative means a Coast Guard Patrol Commander, including a Coast Guard coxswain, petty officer, or other officer operating a Coast Guard vessel and a Federal, State, and local officer designated by or assisting the Captain of the Port Sector Mobile (COTP) in the enforcement of the safety zone.
(c) Regulations.
(1) Under the general safety zone regulations in subpart C of this part, you may not enter the safety zones described in paragraphs (a)(1) and (2) of this section unless authorized by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(2) To seek permission to enter, contact the COTP or the COTP's representative on VHF-FM channel 16 or by telephone at (251) 266-5888. Those in the safety zone must comply with all lawful orders or directions given to them by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(d) Enforcement periods.
This temporary regulation is effective from November 11, 2026, until May 11, 2030. The zones described in paragraph (a) of this section will be enforced during the periods described below.
(1) The fixed safety zone described in paragraph (a)(1) of this section will be enforced beginning when the EX ENTERPRISE arrives at the entrance of the Mobile Bar Channel at the Mobile Bar Lighted Buoy 1 (LLNR 6100), and will remain in effect, until the vessel is moored at the receiving facility.
(2) The fixed safety zone described in paragraph (a)(2) of this section will be enforced once the EX ENTERPRISE is moored at the receiving facility and will remain in effect until the dismantlement project has progressed to a stage deemed safe for nearby vessel traffic by the Captain of the Port (COTP). The dismantlement project is expected to be completed by December 2030, and all radioactive material is expected to be removed before May 2030, at which time the fixed safety zone around the EX ENTERPRISE will no longer be required. If the fixed safety zone is no longer required before May 11, 2030, enforcement of the fixed safety zone described in paragraph (a)(2) of this section will be terminated, and notice given via Local Notice to Mariners. The USCG Heartland District Local Notice to Mariners can be found at:
http://www.navcen.uscg.gov
.
(4) For each enforcement period generally described above, the Captain of the Port (COTP) will issue a Marine Safety Information Bulletin (MSIB) and Broadcast Notice to Mariners via marine channel 16 (VHF-FM), and Local Notice to Mariners announcing the exact dates and times of the enforcement periods in advance to the local maritime community.
M.O. Vega,
Captain, U.S. Coast Guard, Captain of the Port Sector Mobile.

[EPA-R05-OAR-2026-4753; FRL-9802.1-01-R5]
AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to withdraw the Federal Implementation Plan (FIP), promulgated on October 12, 2022 (the “2022 FIP”), for attaining the 2010 1-hour primary sulfur dioxide (SO
2
) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) in the Detroit area. On May 19, 2025, the EPA approved a revision to Michigan's State Implementation Plan (SIP) for attaining the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS in the Detroit area, rendering the 2022 FIP duplicative. The EPA is proposing this action pursuant to Clean Air Act (CAA) section 110.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before December 28, 2026.
Virtual Public Hearing.
If anyone contacts the EPA requesting to present at a virtual public hearing on or before November 27, 2026, the Agency will hold a virtual public hearing on December 14, 2026.
To request to present at a virtual public hearing, or to pre-register to attend the hearing, if one is held, please use the online registration form available at
https://www.epa.gov/​mi/​detroit-so2-federal-implementation-plan
or contact Abigail Teener at (312) 353-7314 or by email at
teener.abigail@epa.gov
.
The EPA is asking all hearing attendees to register, even those who do not intend to present. The last day to request to present at the hearing will be November 27, 2026. If no request to present at the virtual public hearing is received by 11:59 p.m. Central Time (CT) on November 27, 2026, the EPA will not hold the hearing. If a virtual hearing is held, the EPA will accept registration until the start of the hearing.
The EPA will announce the status of the hearing on November 30, 2026 on the public hearing website at
https://www.epa.gov/​mi/​detroit-so2-federal-implementation-plan
.
Alternatively, interested parties may contact Abigail Teener at (312) 353-7314 or by email at
teener.abigail@epa.gov
to find out if the hearing is being held.
(
printed page 72839)
If a request to present at the virtual public hearing is received by November 27, 2026, the EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on December 14, 2026. The EPA will post a general agenda for the hearing on December 10, 2026. The agenda will be available at
https://www.epa.gov/​mi/​detroit-so2-federal-implementation-plan
and will list pre-registered presenters in approximate order. The hearing will convene at 9:00 a.m. CT and will conclude at 1:00 p.m. CT, or 15 minutes after the last pre-registered presenter in attendance has presented if there are no additional presenters. The EPA will announce further details on the virtual public hearing website at
https://www.epa.gov/​mi/​detroit-so2-federal-implementation-plan
.
The EPA will make every effort to follow the schedule as closely as possible on the day of the hearing; however, please plan for the hearing to run either ahead of schedule or behind schedule. Each commenter will have five minutes to provide oral testimony. The EPA encourages commenters to provide the Agency with a written copy of their oral testimony electronically by including it in the registration form or emailing it to
teener.abigail@epa.gov
.
The EPA may ask clarifying questions during the oral presentations but will not respond to the presentations at that time. Written statements and supporting information submitted during the comment period will be considered with the same weight as oral comments and supporting information presented at the virtual public hearing.
Please note that any updates made to any aspect of the hearing will be posted online at
https://www.epa.gov/​mi/​detroit-so2-federal-implementation-plan
.
Please monitor our website or contact Abigail Teener at (312) 353-7314 or
teener.abigail@epa.gov
to determine if there are any updates. The EPA does not intend to publish a document in the
Federal Register
announcing updates concerning the virtual public hearing.
If you require the services of a translator or a special accommodation such as audio description/closed captioning, please pre-register for the hearing with Abigail Teener at (312) 353-7314 or
teener.abigail@epa.gov
and describe your needs by November 27, 2026. The EPA may not be able to arrange accommodations without advance notice.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R05-OAR-2026-4753 at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
or via email to
arra.sarah@epa.gov
.
For comments submitted at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from the docket. The EPA may publish any comment received to the Agency's public docket. Do not submit to the EPA's docket at
https://www.regulations.gov
any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI), Proprietary Business Information (PBI), or other information the disclosure of which is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. The EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission (
i.e.,
on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). For additional submission methods, please contact the person identified in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. For the full EPA public comment policy, information about CBI, PBI, or multimedia submissions, and general guidance on making effective comments, please visit
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​commenting-epa-dockets
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about this proposed rule, please contact Abigail Teener, Air and Radiation Division (AR-18J), U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 5, 77 West Jackson Boulevard, Chicago, Illinois 60604, telephone number: (312) 353-7314, email address:
teener.abigail@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Throughout this document, the use of “we,” “us,” or “our” is intended to refer to the EPA. We use multiple acronyms and terms in this preamble. While this list may not be exhaustive, to ease the reading of this preamble and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here:
CAA—Clean Air Act
CBI—Confidential Business Information
CT—Central Time
DIG—Dearborn Industrial Generation
EPA—Environmental Protection Agency
FIP—Federal Implementation Plan
NAAQS—National Ambient Air Quality Standard
NSR—New Source Review
OMB—Office of Management and Budget
PBI—Proprietary Business Information
PRA—Paperwork Reduction Act
RACM—Reasonably Available Control Measures
RACT—Reasonably Available Control Technology
RFA—Regulatory Flexibility Act
RFP—Reasonable Further Progress
SIP—State Implementation Plan
SO
2
—Sulfur Dioxide

Organization of this document.
The information presented in this preamble is organized as follows:
I. Background
II. Detroit SO
2
FIP
III. Michigan's Revised SIP for the Detroit SO
2
Area
IV. FIP Withdrawal
V. What action is the EPA taking?
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
I. Background
On August 5, 2013, the EPA designated the Detroit area, a portion of Wayne County, Michigan, as nonattainment for the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS based on ambient air quality data collected at the Detroit SW monitoring site (AQS ID 26-163-0015) from 2009 to 2011.
[
1
]
The nonattainment area designation became effective on October 4, 2013. CAA section 191 directs States to submit a SIP for an area designated as nonattainment for the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS to the EPA within 18 months of the effective date of the designation,
i.e.,
in this case, by no later than April 4, 2015. Under CAA section 192, the SIP must demonstrate attainment of the NAAQS as expeditiously as practicable, but no later than five years from the effective date of designation, which was October 4, 2018, for the Detroit nonattainment area.
On March 18, 2016, the EPA published an action finding that Michigan had failed to submit the required SO
2
attainment plan by the submittal deadline.
[
2
]
Under CAA section 110(c), the finding triggered a requirement that the EPA promulgate a FIP within two years of the finding unless, by that time, (a) the State had made the necessary complete submittal, and (b) the Agency had fully approved the submittal as meeting all applicable requirements.
On May 31, 2016, and June 30, 2016, Michigan submitted a Detroit SO
2
attainment plan and associated final enforceable measures, respectively. Michigan's submission of a complete attainment plan terminated the deadlines for imposing sanctions, pursuant to
40 CFR 52.31(d)(5)
, but it did not terminate the EPA's FIP obligation. On March 19, 2021, the EPA partially approved and partially disapproved Michigan's SO
2
plan as submitted in 2016 (the “March 2021
(
printed page 72840)
Action”).
[
3
]
The March 2021 Action approved the enforceable control measures for two facilities, approved the base-year emissions inventory, and affirmed that the New Source Review (NSR) requirements for the area had previously been met in the SIP. In the same March 2021 Action, the EPA disapproved the SIP attainment demonstration, as well as the requirements for meeting reasonable further progress (RFP) toward attainment of the NAAQS, reasonably available control measures/reasonably available control technology (RACM/RACT), contingency measures, and control measures for two facilities. The partial disapproval started a new sanctions clock under CAA section 179(a), but it did not have any impact on the FIP clock.
II. Detroit SO
                    2
                     FIP
On October 12, 2022, the EPA promulgated the 2022 FIP for the Detroit SO
2
nonattainment area.
[
4
]
In accordance with CAA section 172, the 2022 FIP includes an attainment demonstration for the Detroit area and addresses requirements for RFP, RACM/RACT, enforceable emission limitations and control measures, and contingency measures. The 2022 FIP did not address emissions inventory or NSR requirements, as they had already been approved in the SIP as part of the March 2021 Action.
The 2022 FIP, codified at
40 CFR 52.1189
, includes emission limits and associated requirements for United States Steel Corporation (“U.S. Steel”), EES Coke Battery (“EES Coke”), Cleveland-Cliffs Steel Corporation, and Dearborn Industrial Generation (DIG). The 2022 FIP also relies upon emission limits for Carmeuse Lime and DTE Trenton Channel, which had already been incorporated into Michigan's SIP at the time the 2022 FIP was promulgated.
The 2022 FIP satisfied the Agency's duty to promulgate a FIP for the area under CAA section 110(c) that resulted from the previous finding of failure to submit. However, the 2022 FIP did not affect the sanctions clock started under CAA section 179 resulting from the EPA's partial disapproval of the prior SIP, which would be terminated by an EPA rulemaking approving a revised SIP.
III. Michigan's Revised SIP for the Detroit SO
                    2
                     Area
On December 20, 2022, Michigan submitted a revised attainment plan for the Detroit SO
2
nonattainment area mirroring the 2022 FIP. Michigan's submittal relied in part upon permits that had not yet been issued but would include limits and associated requirements for U.S. Steel, EES Coke, and DIG facilities no less stringent than those set forth in the 2022 FIP. On February 21, 2023, Michigan submitted a clarification letter committing to submit the necessary permits by April 30, 2024. On March 23, 2023, the EPA proposed to conditionally approve Michigan's plan, conditioned upon the issuance, and submission for incorporation into the SIP, of the applicable permits for the U.S. Steel, EES Coke, and DIG facilities.
[
5
]
On December 14, 2023, Michigan submitted three applicable permits for the U.S. Steel, EES Coke, and DIG facilities. On April 2, 2024, Michigan submitted the final applicable permit for the DIG facility, along with a request that the EPA approve the State's revised plan. On May 19, 2025, the EPA fully approved Michigan's revised SIP submission, which the State submitted to the Agency on December 20, 2022, and supplemented on February 21, 2023, December 14, 2023, and April 2, 2024, for attaining the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS for the Detroit area and for meeting other nonattainment area planning requirements of CAA sections 110, 172, 179, and 192.
[
6
]
The EPA approved Michigan's demonstration that these requirements provide for attainment of the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS in Detroit and concluded that Michigan had satisfied the other applicable requirements for nonattainment areas.
On May 5, 2025, Michigan submitted a redesignation request and maintenance plan for the Detroit nonattainment area for the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS, which relies on the State's approved attainment plan for the area. On April 2, 2026, the EPA determined that the Detroit, Michigan area is attaining the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS and took action in accordance with Michigan's request to redesignate the area to attainment of the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS and approve the State's maintenance plan for the area.
[
7
]
The maintenance plan, designed to ensure the area will continue to maintain attainment of the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS, does not rely on the 2022 FIP and instead relies on the permanent and enforceable SO
2
emission limits and associated requirements in Michigan's SIP.
IV. FIP Withdrawal
The EPA is now proposing to withdraw the 2022 FIP because the Agency has since taken subsequent SIP actions such that Michigan's SIP for the Detroit SO
2
area now satisfies the requirements of the March 2021 Action. As is explained in section III of this preamble, the EPA approved Michigan's complete submittal into the State's SIP, rendering it federally enforceable. As a result, the 2022 FIP is no longer necessary for attainment of the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS in the Detroit area.
Under CAA section 110(l), the EPA cannot approve a plan revision if the revision would interfere with any applicable requirement concerning attainment and maintenance of the NAAQS, RFP, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. Michigan's SIP for the Detroit SO
2
area mirrors the 2022 FIP and contains SO
2
emission limits and associated requirements that are equally as stringent as those set forth in the 2022 FIP. Therefore, the withdrawal of the 2022 FIP will not interfere with attainment or maintenance of the NAAQS, RFP, or any applicable requirements under the CAA, and the EPA proposes to find that the withdrawal of the 2022 FIP is consistent with CAA section 110(l).
V. What action is the EPA taking?
The EPA is proposing to withdraw the 2022 Detroit SO
2
FIP by removing
40 CFR 52.1189
and all provisions therein because Michigan's SIP for attaining the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS in the Detroit area, which the Agency approved on May 19, 2025, satisfied the requirements of the March 2021 Action. The maintenance plan for the Detroit area, designed to ensure the area will continue to maintain attainment of the 2010 1-hour primary SO
2
NAAQS, does not rely on the 2022 FIP and instead relies on the permanent and enforceable SO
2
emission limits and associated requirements in Michigan's SIP. The EPA is proposing this action pursuant to CAA section 110.
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders can be found at
https://www.epa.gov/​laws-regulations/​laws-and-executive-orders
.
(
printed page 72841)
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review and
Executive Order 13563
: Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review
This action is exempt from review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review because it is deemed to be a rule of particular applicability. This action affects and is limited to four specific facilities in the Detroit area.
B.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
Executive Order 14192
does not apply because rules of particular applicability are exempted from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
This rule does not impose an information collection burden under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). This action does not contain any information collection activities.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
I certify that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). This action will not impose any requirements on small entities. This action merely proposes to remove duplicative requirements and imposes no new requirements.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
This action does not contain any unfunded mandate as described in UMRA,
2 U.S.C. 1531
through
1538
, and does not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. The action imposes no enforceable duty on any State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector.
F.
Executive Order 13132
: Federalism
This action does not have federalism implications. It would not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
G.

AGENCY:
Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of Safety Advisory.
SUMMARY:
FRA is issuing Safety Advisory 2026-02 to alert the passenger rail industry to the severe safety risks associated with advanced chemistry batteries, such as lithium-ion battery (LiB) power sources, carried aboard passenger railcars within electric micromobility vehicles (EMVs). Recent full-scale testing shows that thermal runaway in these battery systems poses rapid and potentially catastrophic thermal, toxicological, and visibility hazards inside passenger railcars. This Safety Advisory recommends specific operational, training, and emergency planning and response mitigations to protect passengers and crew members.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Michael Hunter, Staff Director, Passenger Rail Division, Office of Railroad Safety, FRA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590, (202) 579-5508,
Michael.Hunter@dot.gov
.
Disclaimer:
This Safety Advisory is considered guidance pursuant to
49 CFR part 5, subpart C
. Except when referencing laws, regulations, policies, or orders, the information in this Safety Advisory does not have the force and effect of law and is not binding in any way. This document does not revise or replace any previously issued guidance.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Electrochemical Failure Mechanisms
Underwriters Laboratories Fire Safety Research Institute (UL FSRI) Test Report
[
1
]
EMVs, which encompass e-bicycles, e-scooters, e-unicycles, and hoverboards, have experienced a surge in popularity for first- and last-mile transit connectivity. The rapid integration of passenger transit with EMV travel has introduced high-energy-density electrochemical storage systems (
i.e.,
the LiB power sources on the EMVs) directly into occupied passenger railcars. While these vehicles provide notable societal benefits, their power systems represent a unique hazard in enclosed transport environments. The primary safety vulnerability stems from the potential for one of the high-energy-density electrochemical storage systems, such as a LiB pack, to undergo thermal runaway, an uncontrolled, self-sustaining exothermic reaction that occurs when internal heat generation exceeds the battery's ability to dissipate that heat.
LiB failures are typically initiated by three distinct abuse modes:
Electrical Abuse:
Overcharging, over-discharging, or experiencing internal or external electrical short-circuits.
Thermal Abuse:
Exposure to high temperatures, environmental overheating, or external fire exposure.
Mechanical Abuse:
Physical damage, structural crushing, shock or impact, or localized penetration of individual battery cells.
To quantify these hazards, researchers at the UL FSRI conducted full-scale experiments inside an 85-foot, 72-passenger railcar to evaluate the dangers of EMV battery fires. They triggered thermal runaway (an uncontrollable, self-heating battery failure) in four common EMVs (a standing e-scooter, an e-bicycle, and two seated e-scooters) placed in standard passenger storage locations to measure heat, smoke, and toxic gas buildup.
UL FSRI Findings
The UL FSRI report uncovered two main immediate threats to passengers: (1) extreme heat experienced within 10 feet of the device; and (2) toxic asphyxiant gases filling the passenger car. The UL FSRI report explained that when the devices were forced into thermal runaway, the failing batteries suddenly vented flammable gas that
(
printed page 72944)
ignited into a fireball with little to no warning. Extreme heat within 10 feet (3 meters) created life-threatening conditions for nearby passengers in 20 to 60 seconds. Also, hot smoke traveled end-to-end through the 85-foot railcar in just 19 to 34 seconds. Complete loss of visibility occurred across the car between 1 minute 48 seconds and 4 minutes 6 seconds, which can severely hinder passenger and crew egress speeds. In addition to loss of visibility, the researchers found that dangerous asphyxiant gases accumulated quickly. Based on fractional effective dose, a standard fire safety engineering calculation used to estimate human incapacitation, the air throughout the entire railcar became toxic to breathe in 3 minutes 37 seconds to 7 minutes 8 seconds.
The test report demonstrates that failing LiBs create severe, life-threatening conditions very quickly. Occupants (passengers and crew members) within 10 feet of a failing LiB that enters thermal runaway are exposed to both threats immediately (toxic gas and extreme heat) that can overcome an individual within 20 to 60 seconds. But what is more concerning is that the majority of occupants are exposed to toxic asphyxiant gas without immediately recognizing the threat. Those located away from the immediate proximity of a LiB entering thermal runaway will be exposed to those gases and incapacitated quickly.
FRA Regulations
Fire Safety
Under
49 CFR 238.103
, railroads are required to execute a written fire safety analysis (FSA) utilizing a formal safety methodology, such as MIL-STD-882, to identify inherent design hazards, evaluate emergency egress and ventilation systems, assess overheat protection, and determine the necessity of automatic fire suppression and smoke detection systems.
[
2
]
Further, railroads must adopt and strictly adhere to written procedures for the inspection, testing, and maintenance of all onboard fire safety systems and equipment to maintain continuous compliance.
[
3
]
When a passenger railroad permits transportation of EMVs powered by LiB onboard passenger equipment, it introduces high-energy combustible fuel loads and severe thermal runaway ignition sources into the passenger car environment.
[
4
]
Because LiB failures can trigger rapid self-sustaining thermal reactions, intense heat generation, and toxic gas release that exceed baseline interior material flammability assumptions, accommodating these devices alters the overall risk profile and available ignition sources.
[
5
]
Under § 238.103(c) and (d), the railroad must conduct or update its FSA to re-evaluate whether existing mitigations remain sufficient to ensure safe passenger evacuation during a battery-initiated fire.
[
6
]
If the FSA indicates that the risk of personal injury from onboard LiB hazards is non-negligible or unacceptable within that operating environment, the railroad is required under § 238.103(c)(2) and (d)(1)(ii) to implement effective remedial safety measures, such as establishing fire-isolated containment areas, prohibiting onboard battery charging, enforcing capacity thresholds, or instituting operational restrictions, to mitigate the fire risk to an acceptable level.
Passenger Train Emergency Preparedness
Under
49 CFR part 239
, FRA prescribes minimum safety standards requiring passenger railroads and host railroads to adopt, implement, and comply with a written passenger train emergency preparedness plan (PTEPP) designed to reduce the magnitude and severity of casualties during emergency situations.
[
7
]
To manage effectively the unique hazards associated with onboard EMVs, passenger railroads should leverage their required PTEPP as a flexible, proactive tool. By voluntarily integrating micromobility risk mitigation procedures, such as designated stowage locations, LiB fire hazard training for onboard personnel, and tailored emergency response protocols, into their written plans, railroads can enhance overall system safety and operational readiness.
[
8
]
Recommended Actions
Considering the above discussion, FRA recommends that railroads providing passenger rail service:
1.
Review Safety Research:
Review the UL FSRI report, “Recommendations to Improve Passenger Railcar Safety During Electric Micromobility Vehicle Fires”
available at
https://doi.org/​10.60752/​102376.32136697
.
2.
Update FSAs:
Update their FSA under
49 CFR 238.103
to account for the increased on-board fire load if the railroad permits EMVs containing a LiB power source. Railroads should also implement mitigations developed as part of updating the FSA that reduce the level of risk to acceptable levels. For example, railroads could install non-combustible liners in designated storage locations to help mitigate the spread of fire to adjacent material.
3.
Prohibit Seat and Underseat Storage:
Prohibit storage of these devices at seat or underseat locations where devices are in proximity to interior materials that may contribute to the spread and severity of any potential onboard fire and where devices cannot be easily monitored by train crews or passengers for signs of overheating.
4.
Update Emergency Plans and Conduct Training:
Update written PTEPPs under
49 CFR part 239
with specific procedures for dealing with devices that appear to be overheating or have entered thermal runaway, especially while trains are operating in tunnels or on elevated structures. Those procedures should include instructions to crew members and other onboard employees to prioritize emergency egress of passengers away from the threat over attempting to extinguish or otherwise fight the thermal event. Once updated, conduct training for employees.
5.
Prohibit LiB-Powered Devices in End Cars:
Prohibit lithium-ion powered devices in the forward- or rear-most cars as a localized fire or thermal runaway event in these end cars could severely impede or entirely block critical egress vestibules and end-frame doors.
6.
Prohibit Onboard Battery Charging:
Prohibit the charging of these devices during passenger operations to eliminate a potential thermal runaway ignition source.
FRA encourages the railroad industry to take actions consistent with the preceding recommendations, and to take all actions that help ensure the safety of the Nation's railroad employees and the public. Nothing in this Safety Advisory alters any existing regulatory requirements, operating rules, or obligations under Federal law. FRA may modify this Safety Advisory 2026-02, issue additional safety advisories, or take other appropriate actions it deems necessary to ensure the highest level of safety on the Nation's railroads, including pursuing enforcement or other corrective measures under its rail safety authority.
Issued under authority delegated in
49 CFR 1.89
.
John Karl Alexy,
Associate Administrator for Railroad Safety and Chief Safety Officer.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Under
5 CFR 1320.8(d)
, PHMSA must provide interested members of the public and affected agencies with the opportunity to comment on information collection and recordkeeping requests before the agency submits them to OMB for approval. In accordance with this requirement, PHMSA published a
Federal Register
notice providing a 60-day comment period on its intent to request OMB approval of the information collection requests described below.
[
1
]
During the 60-day comment period, PHMSA received 10 comments—a joint comment from the American Gas Association (AGA) and the American Public Gas Association (APGA); a joint comment from the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Liquid Energy Pipeline Association (LEPA); a joint comment from the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (INGAA) and API; a comment from GPA Midstream Association (GPA Midstream); a comment from Summit Utilities Inc. (SUI); a comment from Environmental Defense Fund (EDF); a comment from National Association of Pipeline Safety Representatives (NAPSR); a comment from Pipeline Safety Trust (PST); and two comments from individual stakeholders.
[
2
]
Below is a summary of the comments received and PHMSA's responses.
[
3
]
A. Form PHMSA F 7100.1-1 Annual Report for Gas Distribution Pipeline Systems
1. Diameter-Based Reporting
PHMSA proposed eliminating diameter-based reporting of main miles and the number of services. Instead, operators would report cast and wrought iron pipelines six inches or less in diameter and two types of plastic pipe widely regarded as having poor material properties: polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS). The proposal would simplify parts B2 and B3 to focus only on higher-risk materials.
Comments Received
AGA and APGA support PHMSA's broader data revitalization effort and recommend that PHMSA remove terms and definitions from the instructions that are no longer relevant under the proposed amended report fields. AGA and APGA assert that such amendments will reduce confusion.
NAPSR, EDF, and PST do not support the proposed amendments and believe that there is still value in collecting distribution pipe diameter data. NAPSR asserted that larger-diameter pipes pose higher safety risks because they are easier for third parties to strike, carry more gas, and take longer to isolate during a shutdown. NAPSR further commented that comparing annual diameter data helps target inspections toward recent construction activity. EDF commented that diameter data is valuable to understand the scope of an operator's overall system and potential safety risks. PST commented that PHMSA's claim that pipe diameter is not a significant risk factor to pipeline integrity is unsubstantiated as American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) B31.8S, incorporated by reference in
49 CFR part 192
, lists pipeline diameter as a data element necessary for risk assessment.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to eliminate diameter-based reporting of main miles and the number of services. PHMSA notes that the Federal Pipeline Safety Regulations governing distribution integrity management programs (DIMP) under part 192, subpart P, do not reference ASME B31.8S. Though it is important for pipeline operators to know the diameter of individual gas distribution pipelines, gas distribution integrity decisions are not strongly influenced by pipeline diameter. Commenters did not raise additional pipeline materials that PHMSA should include in parts B2 and
(
printed page 72950)
B3 of the annual report. In addition to the changes already proposed, PHMSA requests that OMB approve adding “other plastic” to parts B2 and B3. Any plastic other than polyethylene (PE) is considered a higher risk material and warrants individual reporting in part B. B. Form PHMSA F 7100.2-1 Annual Reports for Natural and Other Gas Transmission and Gathering Pipeline Systems
1. Volume of Gas Transported

18 CFR 260.1

Comments Received
INGAA and API support the proposal, echoing PHMSA's underlying justification. GPA Midstream also supports the change, noting further that

EDF opposes the removal, contending that it ignores PHMSA's role as the Federal pipeline safety regulator and its removal will increase the burden on stakeholders who have to consult databases maintained at multiple agencies that have varying disclosure methods and timeframes.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to remove and reserve part C. PHMSA has determined that the aggregate volume of gas transported across a transmission system is not a relevant indicator of pipeline safety. Furthermore, because other Federal agencies already collect this volume data and it remains publicly accessible, retaining part C is duplicative and unnecessary.
2. Number of Anomalies Reported
PHMSA proposed removing the number of anomalies reported from all sections of part F, including the number of anomalies an operator excavates in a given calendar year; the total number of anomalies an operator repairs based on each assessment method; and the number of anomalies repaired or eliminated by pipe replacement based on the class location or high consequence area (HCA) designation of the location of the anomaly.
Comments Received
INGAA and API support the proposal. They also recommend PHMSA remove all references to anomalies in the reporting instructions on pages 8, 10, 16, and 24. SUI supports the change, stating that anomaly count results in inconsistent data and the time and resources required to gather this data does not yield a proportional benefit in enabling meaningful industry-wide comparisons. GPA Midstream also favors the removal, noting that eliminating the requirement aligns with the principles of the PRA.
NAPSR opposes the complete elimination of anomaly counts. NAPSR urged PHMSA to retain high-level anomaly reporting or provide a clear alternative data source, emphasizing that anomaly metrics serve as a vital annual integrity management signal for State regulators to monitor operator performance and prioritize inspections. PST also opposes the proposal, arguing that anomaly data helps gauge the efficacy of different inspection methods. PST questioned the proposal's regulatory consistency, noting PHMSA separately proposed adding anomaly tracking to accident/incident reports.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA proposed to add anomaly questions to accident and incident reports while simultaneously eliminating anomaly tracking from the annual report. Gas transmission pipeline operators are currently required to report the number of anomalies identified and repaired across various pipeline inspection methods. Though Federal Pipeline Safety Regulations do not formally define “anomaly,” the term generally refers to a deviation—or an indication of a deviation—from sound material that requires further investigation. In addition to the number of anomalies, operators also report the number of conditions repaired in part F. Section 192.933(d) defines specific types of conditions inside HCAs, and a single repaired condition may encompass one or multiple anomalies. Outside HCAs, conditions are defined in § 192.714(d). Furthermore, while advancements in inspection technology have improved the detection of anomalies, many of these identified anomalies do not constitute actionable conditions that require repair. As such, PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to remove the reporting of anomaly counts. Part F of the annual report will continue to capture condition repairs, which PHMSA clearly defines in its regulations and provide the needed information to gauge the efficacy of different inspection methods.
3. Pipeline Diameter
Currently, gas transmission pipeline operators submit pipeline diameter data to PHMSA through two mechanisms: part H of the annual report, and as a spatial attribute within the National Pipeline Mapping System (NPMS). To eliminate duplicative reporting, PHMSA proposed removing part H from the annual report. Under the proposal, PHMSA would leverage NPMS submittals to generate tabular diameter data in the same format currently derived from the annual report. The agency would then publish this NPMS-sourced tabular data on its public website to ensure uninterrupted access for stakeholders.
Comments Received
INGAA and API support the proposal and concurred with PHMSA's justification for eliminating duplicative reporting. NAPSR cautioned that removing part H would cause transmission and gathering pipeline diameter data to be reported in separate systems, potentially creating confusion for users attempting to access the data. NAPSR urged PHMSA to ensure that the proposal does not further delay the information becoming publicly available.
EDF opposed the amendment, arguing that PHMSA failed to justify the change and that pipeline diameter is relevant to determine the potential impact radius. EDF also asserted that the current NPMS format makes it difficult for the public to navigate and extract meaningful information about pipeline infrastructure.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to remove part H from the annual report. While processing NPMS submittals may require additional time to update pipeline diameter, PHMSA finds that avoiding this minor delay does not justify retaining duplicative reporting requirements. To maintain public access and continuity, PHMSA will convert NPMS Geographic Information System (GIS) diameter data into tabular format and integrate it directly into the file containing data from the other parts of the annual report.
4. Pipeline Mileage by MAOP
PHMSA proposed modifying the reporting instructions for part Q, where gas transmission operators report pipeline mileage by maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP) determination method. The proposed revision clarifies the proper timing for transitioning mileage from the § 192.619 portion of part Q to the § 192.624 portion as operators implement MAOP reconfirmation.
Comments Received
AGA and APGA recommend that PHMSA remove the rows for “Class 1 (not in HCA or MCA)” and “Class 2 (not in HCA or MCA)” from the § 192.624 table. They noted that mileage not subject to § 192.624(a) should remain under the § 192.619 section of part Q. They further recommended PHMSA strike the words “is completed” from the phrase “Pressure test in accordance with § 192.624(c)(1), and material testing in accordance with § 192.607 is completed.” AGA and APGA expressed concern that the current wording could cause confusion as it implies an operator must fully finalize all material verification activities under § 192.607 before it can report mileage as reconfirmed via pressure testing.
(
printed page 72952)
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is accepting the AGA and APGA recommendation in part. PHMSA will remove the rows for “Class 1 (not in HCA or MCA)” and “Class 2 (not in HCA or MCA)” from the § 192.624 table in part Q, as mileage not subject to § 192.624(a) appropriately belongs in the § 192.619 portion. However, PHMSA will retain the phrase “is completed” regarding material verification under § 192.624(c)(1). PHMSA maintains that an operator must fully finalize material properties records verification in conjunction with pressure testing under § 192.624(c)(1). Operators with traceable, verifiable, and complete records meet the material properties records requirement without testing pipeline facilities. If material properties verification testing is required, the specific required tests are in § 192.607. Operators without traceable, verifiable, and complete records must excavate as needed to obtain material properties test results.
PHMSA has modified the instructions to remove the presumption that material testing is required but retains “is completed.” The new text describing when reconfirmation under § 192.624(c)(1) is completed is “Pressure test in accordance with § 192.624(c)(1) and verification of material property records in accordance with § 192.607 is completed.”

D. Form PHMSA F 7100.3-1, Annual Report for Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Facilities
1. LNG Facility Duplicative Reporting
Currently, operators of LNG facilities report to PHMSA in two places: the annual report and NPMS submittals. PHMSA proposed adding the latitude and longitude of an LNG plant to the annual report. Once this change is implemented, PHMSA intends to eliminate the requirement in § 191.29 for LNG operators to submit to NPMS. These changes would preserve PHMSA's ability to generate maps showing the location of LNG plants and eliminate duplicative reporting.
Comments Received
NAPSR opposes the amendment, stating that NPMS data is used by emergency response officials. EDF commented that NPMS should continue collecting relevant information regarding LNG facilities.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with the proposal to add the latitude and longitude of an LNG plant to the annual report. PHMSA will use data collected through the annual report to construct an LNG GIS layer within NPMS. PHMSA will make this LNG GIS layer available to all stakeholders, including emergency response officials. This process mirrors PHMSA's established practice for underground natural gas storage (UNGS) facilities, ensuring consistent GIS mapping and data integration without imposing additional submittal burdens on operators.
2. Define “Retired”
PHMSA proposed to define “retired” in the annual report instructions and remove the abandoned status code option from the report. An abandoned LNG plant would no longer be included in the annual report. To accommodate the possibility of facilities with varying status codes, PHMSA proposes adding the reporting of status code at the facility level. The operator would not enter the status code for the plant but it will be inferred from the status entered by the operator for each facility comprising the plant. These changes would ensure consistent reporting across the industry.
Comments Received
INGAA and API commented that using both “facility” and “plant” within part B creates confusion and recommends that PHMSA select a single term for reporting purposes. They further recommend adopting the term “out of service” rather than “retired,” commenting that “out-of-service” provides greater granularity and is easier for operators to apply to specific assets.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA will continue using both “plant” and “facility” in its annual report form and accompanying instructions. As per § 193.2007, an “LNG plant” is typically multiple “LNG facilities” functioning as a unit. Operators need to understand the difference between “plant” and “facility” to properly complete the annual report. PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to define “retired” in the instructions, remove the “abandoned” status code, and collect status at the facility level to infer overall plant status. PHMSA disagrees with the recommendation to replace “retired” with “out-of-service.” The term “retired” connotes an intentional decision to no longer use a facility, whereas “out-of-service” is appropriate for a facility temporarily not in service, such as due to waiting for parts or funding.
3. Defining “Maximum Liquefaction Rate” and “Maximum Vaporization Capacity”
Currently, part B of the LNG annual report requires operators to submit data for “maximum liquefaction rate” and “maximum vaporization capacity.” The annual report instructions, however, do not formally define these terms. To eliminate ambiguity and promote uniform, accurate reporting across regulated entities, PHMSA proposed to add explicit definitions for both terms to the reporting instructions.
Comments Received
INGAA and API stated that baseload LNG operators typically measure their liquefaction rate in terms of LNG produced rather than volumetric gas measurements. NAPSR submitted comments supporting defining the terms.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to establish explicit definitions for “maximum liquefaction rate” and “maximum vaporization capacity” in the annual report instructions. While larger LNG plants may measure the liquefaction rate in terms of the liquid produced, PHMSA continues to propose the “maximum liquefaction rate” in cubic feet of gas. However, PHMSA erroneously proposed “of LNG” as part of the instructions for “maximum liquefaction rate.” PHMSA proposes striking “of LNG” from “(MMCF/D) of feed gas of LNG” on the instructions for the liquefaction rate. Specifying “MMCF/D of feed gas” provides a clear, standardized metric for gas volume prior to liquefaction, ensuring consistent reporting across operators while eliminating ambiguity in the instructions.
4. Unit of Measurement Recommendation by Commenter
INGAA and API recommend that PHMSA use cubic meters instead of barrels when measuring liquid, as barrels are used primarily to measure crude oil and other hazardous liquids. INGAA and API also recommended reorganizing part B to position “Type” and “Function” fields directly beneath the location section to streamline data entry and logically group facility identification parameters.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA proposes implementing both recommendations. Grouping all plant data at the beginning of part B may help operators recognize the transition from plant data to facility data. For the same reason, PHMSA proposes replacing the term “Process” with “Facilities” in part B and modifying the instructions to emphasize the transition from plant to facility. As to the barrels versus cubic meters, implementing cubic meters for liquid volume aligns the annual report with standard commercial and operational accounting practices.
5. Vibration and Mechanical Fatigue
Recognizing that vibration and mechanical fatigue are documented causes of LNG piping and weld failures, PHMSA proposed adding “vibration- or fatigue-related” in part C. The amendment will improve root-cause data collection and safety tracking.
Comments Received
INGAA and API request that PHMSA adopt the broader term “operational-related” instead of “vibration- or fatigue-related” to categorize these piping and weld leaks. INGAA and API also recommended removing “Excavation Damage” as a cause category for leaks in part C, arguing that excavation activity within an LNG plant boundary is rare or handled under different operational controls. NAPSR also submitted comments supporting adding “vibration- or fatigue-related” in part C.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to add “vibration- or fatigue-related” as a fourth cause category for
(
printed page 72954)
leaks from piping or welds in part C and is retaining “Excavation Damage” as a cause category for leaks in part C. The agency determined that “vibration- or fatigue-related” provides specific, actionable safety data on known mechanical stress factors unique to plant piping systems, whereas a broad “operational-related” category would be overly generic and could obscure mechanical stress factors. Furthermore, retaining “Excavation Damage” ensures consistency across PHMSA reporting forms and maintains coverage for ground-disturbing activities that could occur within facility boundaries.
6. Emergency Shutdown Actuations
PHMSA proposed removing emergency shutdown (ESD) actuations that resulted from conditions other than an actual emergency from part D. Because a plant shutdown occurring in the absence of a genuine emergency does not directly reflect a safety threat or pipeline integrity issue, PHMSA proposed removing non-emergency ESD actuations from part D to streamline reporting requirements.
Comments Received
INGAA and API commented in support of the proposal, reiterating that non-emergency ESD actuations do not indicate a safety issue.
NAPSR commented in opposition to the proposal, asserting that tracking non-emergency ESD actuations provides a useful reliability indicator for a critical safety system. NAPSR noted that a high frequency of false or non-emergency ESD events can foster operator complacency and lead to dangerous response lags during actual emergency events.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to remove ESD actuations resulting from conditions other than an actual emergency from part D. While PHMSA acknowledges NAPSR's concerns regarding safety system reliability and potential operator complacency, PHMSA maintains that routine or maintenance-related shutdowns do not directly correlate with active safety hazards or operational failures. Removing non-emergency ESD actuations focuses part D data collection on genuine safety events, reducing administrative burden while ensuring PHMSA and State oversight authorities retain visibility over true emergency operations and system performance.
7. Physical Security and Cybersecurity
PHMSA proposed to modify the annual report form and instructions to ensure that only physical security, not cybersecurity, breaches are reported in part D to ensure consistent reporting across the industry.
Comments Received
NAPSR expresses concern over excluding cybersecurity events, asserting that State pipeline safety programs require consistent annual visibility into cybersecurity incidents which could impact the safe operation of LNG facilities.
INGAA and API recommended eliminating the security breach reporting requirement entirely. They stated that operators already report security incidents to other Federal entities—such as the U.S. Coast Guard under the Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA)—and argued that a disaggregated annual count without context does not provide a meaningful indicator of safety. They further recommended that PHMSA limit reporting physical breaches and exempt Coast Guard-regulated facilities if it retains physical security breach reporting.
PHMSA Response
PHMSA is proceeding with its proposal to limit part D security breach reporting to physical security incidents only. PHMSA is not adopting INGAA and API's request to eliminate security breach reporting entirely or exempt facilities regulated under MTSA. Annual tracking of physical security breaches provides PHMSA and State inspection personnel with vital baseline trend data to evaluate physical facility security controls over time. As to NAPSR's concerns, there is an inherent time lag between the occurrence of a cyber event and the submittal of an annual report, rendering an annual metric ineffective for real-time cybersecurity response and oversight. Cybersecurity threats require immediate notification and mitigation, which operators already perform under mandatory reporting protocols established by other Federal authorities, such as the Transportation Security Administration and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. In 2010, TSA issued the initial edition of its Pipeline Security Guidelines to assist operators of gas pipelines and LNG facilities in the development and evaluation of comprehensive security programs at their facilities. TSA's Pipeline Security Guidelines, which have been updated several times (most recently in April 2021), set forth non-binding guidance pertaining to corporate security policies, security vulnerability assessments, physical security measures, and cybersecurity efforts.
[

TSA conducts voluntary visits with pipeline operators as part of its Corporate Security Review Program. TSA personnel work with operator personnel during these visits to analyze FSPs and policies and compare practices against the Pipeline Security Guidelines.
Restricting part D strictly to physical security events eliminates redundant multi-agency reporting burdens while maintaining appropriate physical security visibility.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This document announces the Agency's receipt of and solicits comments on requests by registrants to voluntarily cancel their pesticide registrations of certain products and to amend their product registrations to terminate one or more uses. In accordance with the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), EPA provides a periodic notice of receipt addressing requests received by EPA since the last notice of receipt was issued and uses the month and year in the title to help distinguish one document from the other. EPA intends to grant these requests at the close of the comment period for this announcement unless the Agency receives substantive comments during the comment period that would merit further review of the requests or the requests are withdrawn by the registrant. If these requests are granted, EPA will issue an order in the
Federal Register
cancelling the listed product registrations, after which any sale, distribution, or use of the products listed in this document will only be permitted after the registrations have been cancelled if such sale, distribution, or use is consistent with the terms as described in the final order.
DATES:
Comments and withdrawal requests must be received on or before December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, identified by docket identification (ID) number EPA-HQ-OPP-2026-0067, online at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Additional instructions on commenting and visiting the docket, along with more information about dockets generally, are available at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets
.

Christopher Green, Regulatory & Information Services Division, Office of Mission Critical Operations, Environmental Protection Agency, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460-0001; telephone number: (202) 566-2707; email address:
green.christopher@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary
A. Does this action apply to me?
This action is directed to the public and may be of interest to a wide range of stakeholders including environmental, human health, and agricultural advocates; the chemical industry; pesticide users; and members of the public interested in the sale, distribution, or use of pesticides.
B. What action is the Agency taking?
This document announces receipt by EPA of requests from registrants to voluntarily cancel their pesticide registrations and amend their product registrations to terminate one or more uses of the products listed in Unit II, that are currently registered under FIFRA section 3 (
7 U.S.C. 136a
) or section 24(c) (
7 U.S.C. 136v(c)
). Unless the Agency determines that there are substantive comments that warrant further review of the requests or the registrants withdraw their requests, EPA intends to issue an order in the
Federal Register
canceling and amending the affected registrations.
C. What is EPA's authority for taking this action?
FIFRA section 6(f)(1) (
7 U.S.C. 136d(f)(1)
) provides that a registrant of a pesticide product may at any time request that any of its pesticide registrations be canceled. Before acting on a request for voluntary cancellation, EPA must provide at least a 30-day public comment period on the request. FIFRA further provides that, before acting on a request for voluntary cancellation or termination of any minor agricultural use, EPA must provide an 180-day comment period unless:
1. The registrants request a waiver of the comment period, or
2. The EPA Administrator determines that continued use of the pesticide would pose an unreasonable adverse effect on the environment.
The registrants in Table 3 of Unit II have requested that EPA waive the 180-day comment period. Accordingly, this document provides a 30-day comment period on these requests.
D. What should I consider as I prepare my comments for EPA?
1.
Submitting CBI.
Do not submit this information to EPA through email or
https://www.regulations.gov
.
If you wish to include CBI in your comment, please follow the applicable instructions at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​commenting-epa-dockets#rules
and clearly mark the information that you claim to be CBI. In addition to one complete version of the comment that includes CBI, a copy of the comment without CBI must be submitted for inclusion in the public docket. Information marked as CBI will not be disclosed except in accordance with procedures set forth in
40 CFR part 2
.
2.
Tips for preparing your comments.
When preparing and submitting your comments, see the commenting tips at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​commenting-epa-dockets
.
E. How can a registrant withdraw their request for voluntary cancellation?
Registrants who choose to withdraw their request for voluntary cancellation should submit a withdrawal request in writing to the person listed under

For voluntary cancellations of the registrations listed in Table 1 of Unit II, registrants will be permitted to sell and distribute existing stocks of voluntarily canceled products for 1 year after the effective date of the cancellation order.
