SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
As explained in greater detail in the proposed rule (
91 FR 8151
), Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 (
42 U.S.C. 1436a
) (“Section 214”) prohibits HUD from making certain financial assistance available to persons other than United States citizens or specified categories of eligible noncitizens. The Section 214 requirements apply to financial assistance provided under the following HUD programs (collectively referred to in this preamble as “Section 214 covered programs” or “covered programs”):
1. Section 236 of the National Housing Act (
12 U.S.C. 1715z-1
) (tenants paying below market rent only) (the Section 236 program); and
2. The United States Housing Act of 1937 (
42 U.S.C. 1437
et seq.
) which covers: HUD's Public Housing programs, the Section 8 rental assistance programs, and the Housing Development Grant programs (with respect to low-income units only).
[
1
]
HUD's current regulations implementing Section 214 require that each family member applying for assistance under a Section 214 covered program either: (1) submit a declaration declaring that he or she is a U.S. citizen, as defined in
24 CFR 5.504(b)
(which specifies that citizen means a citizen or national of the United States), or a noncitizen with eligible immigration status;
[
2
]
or (2) elect not to contend eligible immigration status and, therefore, not submit documentation for verification.
[
3
]
HUD's regulations also cover how a family with individuals whose eligibility has not been established or who are not eligible for assistance may still receive assistance: through prorated assistance, based on the number of individuals in the family for whom eligibility has been affirmatively established,
[
4
]
or in limited circumstances, through a temporary deferral of termination of assistance.
[
5
]
II. The Proposed Rule
On February 20, 2026, HUD published the “Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status” proposed rule (the proposed rule) in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 8151
). This proposed rule sought to bring the agency's regulations into greater alignment with the wording and purpose of Section 214, and to align with the current Administration's priorities and regulatory reform efforts, by revising HUD's regulations to require the verification of U.S. citizenship or the eligible immigration status of all applicants and recipients of assistance under a covered program regardless of age, and to make prorated assistance a temporary condition pending verification of eligible status of all family members, where permitted by statute.
HUD proposed numerous changes to
24 CFR part 5
, which included:
—revisions to require all applicants and tenants in Section 214 covered programs to submit evidence of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status regardless of age, replacing outdated terminology;
—redefining or defining important terms;
—removing outdated or unnecessary language or programs;
—changes to regulatory requirements regarding which families may receive which types of assistance to better implement statutory requirements and add clarifying details;
—changes to capture the type of prorated assistance where at least one family member has verified U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status and the remaining family members' verification is pending;
—revisions to require persons who declare themselves to have U.S. citizenship to provide a signed declaration and a verification consent form;
—removing the option for persons to elect “do not contend” to have eligible status of any kind (citizenship or immigration status);
—requiring responsible entities, as defined in
24 CFR 5.504
, to provide notification of Section 214 requirements to certain tenants no later than 30 days after the effective date of the rule;
—providing that Public Housing Agencies (PHAs) or owners, as applicable, may meet reporting requirements by conforming with applicable
Federal Register
Notices, including Interagency Notices (such as the 2000 Interagency Notice at
65 FR 58301
), regarding compliance with section 404 of Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA);
—requiring the verification consent form to notify individuals that PHAs
(
printed page 72979)
or owners, as applicable, must inform DHS immediately whenever personnel determine that any member of a household is present in the U.S. in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act;
—clarifying that families must submit required evidence for a family member only one time during continuously assisted occupancy under any Section 214 program;
—identifying acceptable documentation for evidence of U.S. citizenship (U.S. birth certificate, a naturalization certificate, a consular report of birth abroad (FS-240), a valid unexpired U.S. passport, a certificate of citizenship, or other appropriate documentation that HUD may specify in guidance);
—describing HUD's secondary verification procedures where a responsible entity would need to provide notice of the results of primary verification and include other information in the notice;
—requiring responsible entities to review additional information and acceptable documentation provided by individuals;
—requiring that the responsible entity must request additional verification in the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program within 30 days of notification of the results of primary verification for secondary verification of eligible immigration status;
—clarifying that the notice of denial or termination must specify that individuals may seek a records correction with any agency that issued documents or maintains records relevant to the individual's verification of eligible status; and
—technical changes to the regulations to further conform to Section 214's statutory requirements.
See the proposed rule for a full description of all proposed regulation changes associated with this rulemaking.
III. This Final Rule
HUD reviewed and considered all public comments submitted in response to the proposed rule, which are summarized and addressed below. After considering public comments, this final rule incorporates a majority of the regulatory changes as described in the proposed rule; however, HUD is making certain revisions to Section 214 regulations different from those described in the proposed rule. HUD is also making certain additional non-substantive revisions to provide better clarity.
First, HUD is revising § 5.508(g) to allow responsible entities to grant an additional 30 days (60 days total) for a family to obtain necessary evidence. HUD is also revising
24 CFR 5.508(e)(ii)
to require responsible entities to inform tenants in the notification of Section 214 requirements of the availability of extensions of up to 60 days and their right to request such extensions. HUD acknowledges the barriers individuals may face obtaining documents, so to provide more flexibility, HUD is providing a greater extension based on the circumstances of the individual case. This extension is similar to § 5.216(e)(2)(ii)(B) which provides one additional extension for the disclosure of Social Security numbers for new household members under the age of six. HUD determined that a total 60-day extension was appropriate, rather than a 90-day extension as can be granted for the disclosure of Social Security numbers for new household members under the age of six, because there is a comparatively higher risk of fraud or ineligibility when others in the family have not provided necessary evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status.
Additionally, in § 5.508(f)(3), HUD is clarifying that a new family member must submit required evidence not later than the date the responsible entity performs verification of other aspects of eligibility for assistance, instead of when the responsible entity anticipates or has knowledge that verification of eligibility will occur.
Second, in § 5.216(e)(1)(ii), this rule is revising language to state “Each participant subject to the disclosure requirements under paragraph (e)(1)(i) of this section must submit the following information to the processing entity when providing evidence of citizenship or eligible status under § 5.508(f)(2)(i)-(ii).” This revision will align citizenship and eligible status disclosure at the same time as Social Security number disclosure. HUD also is revising § 5.508(b)(1) to include disclosure of an individual's assigned Social Security number as evidence which must be submitted by individual's declaring U.S. citizenship. This revision aligns with the use of an individual's Social Security number during the primary verification process. Relatedly, HUD is revising § 5.508(d) to include that the verification consent form must comply with Section 7 of the Privacy Act of 1974 given the collection of Social Security numbers.
Third, this final rule makes non-substantive changes, such as revising instances of “citizenship” to “U.S. citizenship” to be more specific and provide clarity, revising § 5.508(b) for clarity and to align closely with § 5.508 (b)(2), stating in § 5.516(a) “hearing” instead of “informal hearing” since public housing tenants are entitled to formalized grievance processes, and technical corrections throughout § 5.518 to correct grammatical errors and for consistency.
IV. Severability
Consistent with the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act, HUD has reviewed and responded to all public comments received in response to its notice of proposed rulemaking and acted within its statutorily delegated authority in the promulgation of regulations that are consistent with the Act. Nonetheless, if any provision of this final rule, or any provision of
24 CFR part 5
, is held to be invalid or unenforceable as applied to any action, that provision should be construed so as to continue to give the maximum effect to the provision permitted by law. If such holding is that the provision of this part is invalid and unenforceable in all circumstances, then HUD views each provision as severable from the remainder of this part and a finding that a provision is invalid should not affect the remaining provisions.
V. The Public Comments
The public comment period for the proposed rule ended on April 21, 2026. HUD received 16,238 comments. These comments were received from individuals, landlords, tenants, property owners (“owners”), housing authorities, housing cooperatives, non-profit housing organizations, non-profit organizations representing seniors or individuals with disabilities, housing associations, case managers for individuals experiencing homelessness, churches, law firms, etc. The public comments are discussed in various categories below. HUD notes that “tenant(s)” and “participant(s)” are used interchangeably throughout the summary and intended to reference participants under the covered programs of this rule.
A. Comments in Support of the Rule
1. General Support
Commenters expressed general support for the proposed rule and urged HUD to finalize and implement it, and stated variously that assistance should be limited to U.S. citizens and/or for people lawfully present in the United States. A commenter raised a grievance about the fairness of housing allocation by race and immigration status, disagreeing with rendering families
(
printed page 72980)
homeless on the basis of race while questioning why immigrants appear to receive housing, vouchers, or Section 8 assistance before Americans, veterans, or the elderly, and alleging that some recipients display signs of affluence. A commenter stated that the comment is not for or against the proposal, identifying as a law-abiding American, urging that immigrants come to the country legally, and arguing that illegal entry creates problems for low-income citizens and their families.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates commenters' support for its efforts to better align implementing regulations with Section 214, strengthen program integrity by requiring verification of all applicants and current participants, regardless of age, and protect limited housing resources for eligible US citizens and individuals with eligible immigration status.
2. Improves Statutory Alignment to Section 214 & PRWORA
Commenters argued that the proposed rule aligns HUD's regulations more closely with the text and purpose of Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act (
42 U.S.C. 1436a
), which prohibits HUD from making financial assistance available to persons other than U.S. citizens and specified eligible noncitizens in covered programs, and added that HUD's general rulemaking authority under
42 U.S.C. 3535(d)
permits the Secretary to promulgate the rules necessary to carry out that mandate. Commenters characterized the rule's core changes—requiring verification of status for all household members regardless of age, eliminating the “do not contend” option, and limiting proration to a temporary period pending verification—as better conforming the regulations to that statutory text and closing a longstanding loophole under which ineligible noncitizens can indirectly benefit from subsidies through prorated assistance in mixed-status households. A commenter added that the rule reflects reasoned, evidence-based rulemaking that centers Section 214 and PRWORA § 1642 and operationalizes verification through SAVE. A commenter maintained that the proposal reasonably relies on DHS's SAVE, which returns status information rather than deciding eligibility, and argued that using SAVE standardizes practice and should improve accuracy, uniformity, and timeliness across PHAs and owners.
A commenter urged HUD to remove the “do not contend” provision swiftly, describing a decades-long practice that left 200,000 existing tenants whose citizenship status has never been verified, and argued the statute specifically requires that assistance not be provided before eligibility status is “presented and verified,” so that a declaration not contending eligible status is the absence of verification rather than verification itself. The same commenter argued that making prorated assistance temporary is faithful to the statute and feasible today because verification through SAVE is now nearly instantaneous, whereas Congress authorized proration when verification was a manual, paper-driven process that could take days or weeks, leaving no justification for indefinitely continuing prorated assistance. A commenter also argued that codifying PRWORA reporting and extending it to private owners is long overdue, noting that PHAs were notified more than 30 years ago to begin using SAVE for citizenship verification and have been obligated since 2000 to report individuals present in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Responding to HUD's request for comment on severability, a commenter argued that the rule's provisions—elimination of the “do not contend” provision, removal of the age exemption, and universal SAVE verification—are substantially independent and should each be given effect to the maximum extent possible, and urged HUD to include a robust severability clause in the final rule.
To balance equity with statutory fidelity, a commenter recommended that HUD preserve temporary proration only while verification is pending, apply preservation assistance consistently for long-tenured households where allowed, and publish state-level projections to help PHAs plan rehousing supports. The same commenter asked HUD to clarify that secondary SAVE verification be completed within a target timeline such as 10 business days, and that assistance not be terminated or delayed while secondary verification is pending when acceptable documents are on file; to publish a verification workflow setting out the initial and secondary SAVE steps, evidence standards, and typical timelines; and to provide a privacy summary referencing the 2025 SAVE PIA/SORN updates explaining interagency data sharing and safeguards. A commenter contended that the safeguards in the rule—the temporary verification period and exemptions for certain vulnerable groups—mitigate concerns about family disruption or homelessness while the rule enforces the original intent of Section 214.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates commenters' support for its efforts to better align implementing regulations with Section 214. HUD is making preservation of assistance available only to the extent required by statute. HUD is electing to provide responsible entities with 30 days to request additional verification of immigration status where secondary verification is required. The rule provides for PHAs to elect to provide assistance before verification in § 5.512(b) consistent with the flexibility afforded in Section 214. The DHS-SAVE program maintains resources and tools on its website with considerable instruction and information on the use of SAVE. HUD encourages responsible entities to visit DHS's website:
https://www.uscis.gov/​save/​current-user-agencies
to access the tools and guides available to user agencies. HUD will consider what information it may provide to support PHAs' plans for rehousing transitions.
3. Improves Program Integrity
A commenter argued the rule strengthens program integrity by requiring verification for all household members, implementing SAVE as Congress intended, and limiting prorated assistance to the temporary verification period, so that federal housing subsidies are directed only to individuals who are legally eligible while preserving due-process protections for mixed-status families. A commenter characterized the rule as closing loopholes that have allowed federal housing assistance to flow to individuals whose eligibility has never been verified, including 25,000 deceased tenants living in HUD-subsidized properties, and urged HUD to stop fraud in taxpayer-subsidized housing and finalize the rule promptly. A commenter contended that HUD currently verifies immigration status through DHS's SAVE but does not require the same electronic verification for U.S. citizenship claims and supported requiring responsible entities to verify both citizenship and immigration status through SAVE using biographic data and a government-issued numeric identifier. A commenter, citing HUD's own Regulatory Impact Analysis that 97 percent of owners and 92 percent of PHAs have mixed-status families representing fewer than five percent of assisted households, argued the administrative burden of entering information into SAVE is an extension of processes most responsible entities already use rather than new infrastructure, and was not aware of a less burdensome alternative that would still close the statutory gaps.
Commenters supported the rule as a tool to reduce fraud, improve program
(
printed page 72981)
integrity, and protect limited housing resources through stronger documentation and verification standards. A commenter identified a specific residual loophole the rule does not reach: because live-in aides are not counted as “family members,” they are not subject to the rule, and the commenter's agency has live-in aides who may lack eligible immigration status and is uncertain how to designate their status on Form HUD-50058, with some flagged on the EIV-SAVE Tenant Matching Report as possible compliance gaps; the commenter also reported inconsistent guidance on the “I have eligible immigration status and am 62 years of age or older” declaration and asked HUD for definitive guidance, adding that the proposed rule and the Crosswalk of SAVE System Responses and Section 214 Eligibility promote transparency while maintaining Fair Housing compliance.
A commenter working in tax-credit and USDA farm-labor housing management identified a specific mechanism: households over the income limit add members to the household to reduce counted income by adding non-working members who show no recorded income because they cannot legally work but often work under the table, which lowers the household's counted income and qualifies it for subsidies—a pattern the commenter estimated at about 20 percent of the USDA households observed. A commenter who investigated welfare and food-stamp fraud argued that ineligible noncitizen parents receive aid for U.S.-born children while claiming no income, and identified a specific mechanism—parents using a minor child's or someone else's Social Security number for employment and failing to report those earnings, which keeps the child's benefits at the maximum and the household's HUD rent at the minimum—while seniors on small Social Security stipends wait up to five years for a rent-reduced home.
Commenters pointed to Home Forward, the housing authority in Portland, Oregon, alleging it prioritizes immigrants and refugees over Americans and maintains vacant subsidized units, and urged HUD to require every adult and child on a public-housing lease to provide immigration status and to address voucher fraud. A commenter argued that requiring documentation for all members, including children, prevents fraud and abuse and enhances national security and administrative integrity. A commenter recommended removing all noncitizens including those on Temporary Protected Status from eligibility, limiting all housing assistance to a maximum of three years, penalizing abuse with both incarceration and monetary fines equivalent to the amount fraudulently obtained, and removing equity-based eligibility guidelines.
A commenter argued the rule will help eligible families as landlords and managers who overlook American citizens in favor of ineligible tenants lose that opportunity, describing landlords charging roughly $1,200 per person, housing multiple people per unit, and not reporting the cash income. A commenter alleged a similar arrangement in San Diego County, alleging landlords collect about $1,500 per ineligible tenant in unreported cash while excluding citizens. Commenters supported vigorous enforcement, including monitoring and prosecuting responsible entity staff who circumvent the rule.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates commenters' support for its strengthening of program integrity by requiring verification of all applicants and current participants, regardless of age. HUD agrees that the final rule will protect limited housing resources through stronger documentation and verification standards. Section 214 provides for eligibility based on select immigration statuses, and HUD's implementing regulations must remain consistent with statutory requirements. As explained in the preamble to the proposed rule, the rule applies to family members receiving assistance and, as such, does not apply to live-in aides, foster adults, or foster children, who are not assisted family members. PHAs should reach out to their local HUD office for assistance with reporting on the Form HUD-50058. HUD notes that time-limiting housing assistance is beyond the scope of this rule, but HUD is undertaking separate rulemaking (
91 FR 10016
) to provide PHAs and multifamily housing owners with flexibility to implement work requirements and term limits.
4. Preserves Limited Resources for Eligible Citizens
Commenters supported the rule on the ground that federal housing assistance is a limited resource that should be reserved for households whose members are all eligible under federal law, arguing that long waiting lists mean prioritizing fully eligible households to ensure scarce resources reach those who meet program requirements. A commenter argued that when ineligible noncitizens can no longer access benefits even indirectly, those units become available to waiting lists filled with American citizens and legal residents, shortening wait times and reducing pressure on the private rental market. A commenter pointed to the Section 8 voucher program as already oversubscribed in most areas, with families languishing on waiting lists for years while mixed-status households receive partial benefits that could otherwise go to fully eligible applicants.
A commenter argued that ending indefinite prorated assistance is what frees units, reasoning that a household continuing to receive prorated assistance without full verification leaves that unit effectively unavailable to another fully eligible household on the waiting list, so a temporary verification period allocates housing more fairly and efficiently. A commenter tied the rule to lowering housing costs during what the commenter characterized as an unprecedented affordability crisis, citing reports from organizations such as the National Low Income Housing Coalition that millions of low- and moderate-income households are cost-burdened, spending more than 30 percent of income on rent or mortgage. A commenter argued that families are denied assistance daily because housing authorities cannot compensate rents that have risen with the market.
Commenters framed the competition for scarce units in terms of specific populations waiting for help—homeless citizens, veterans, the elderly, and people with disabilities—and named jurisdictions where they perceive the shortage most acutely, including Los Angeles and Southern California and East Boston. A commenter cited HUD data that nearly 8.46 million rental households met the worst-case-housing-needs designation—likely eligible for at least one HUD program but not receiving assistance—and that the market rate for a two-bedroom apartment rose nearly 40 percent over five years, to argue that this limited resource should go to eligible families. A commenter argued that a 5.1 million net increase in the foreign-born population from March 2022 to March 2024 coincided with increased rents and growth in housing demand—noting subsidized rents are typically discounted 60 to 70 percent below market and capped at 30 percent of tenant income—and that reserving assistance for eligible households eases that pressure. A commenter argued that subsidizing ineligible households is taxpayer money incentivizing unlawful entry rather than the economic contribution its defenders describe. A
(
printed page 72982)
commenter argued that mixed-status or fully ineligible families potentially at risk of losing housing must be weighed against citizens still waiting years for vouchers. A commenter cited a wait of three years and seven and a half months for a 30-percent-AMI apartment in an elderly LIHTC property in North Carolina.
Commenters argued the rule reinforces that housing programs were fundamentally intended for the American people and that eligible citizens and legal residents should not be displaced by ineligible households. A commenter argued that families made up entirely of citizens with a disabled member on SSDI, and descendants of American chattel slavery, should have priority for this housing over healthy noncitizen households, citing a waiting list decades long. A commenter cited being homeless with four children in 2004 and unable to obtain Section 8 or low-income housing despite urgent need, and supported the rule so that limited assistance reaches eligible families in crisis. A commenter alleged that in the commenter's area ineligible households occupy subsidized two-to-four-bedroom apartments renting around $3,000 per month while paying only $300 to $700 themselves, that citizens wait ten years or more for affordable units while immigrants reportedly obtain them in one to two years through expedited nonprofit assistance, and that unreported income lets these households qualify.
HUD Response:
HUD thanks the commenters for their support of the rule and acknowledgment that the most significant effect of this rulemaking would be to transfer housing assistance from mixed families, which contain some ineligible individuals, to fully eligible households who take their place. As HUD's Regulatory Impact Analysis explains, this transfer occurs because there are more individuals eligible for assistance than there is available assistance, and the estimated value of the assistance transferred to incoming fully eligible households ranges from $167 million to $218 million. HUD agrees that reserving this limited resource for households whose members are all eligible under federal law directs assistance consistent with Section 214.
5. Protects Taxpayer Funds and Improves Adherence to the Rule of Law
Commenters supported the rule on the ground that taxpayer-funded housing assistance should not flow to individuals who are not lawfully present, arguing that tax dollars are collected from citizens and should benefit citizens and eligible noncitizens rather than subsidize ineligible noncitizens. A commenter argued that taxpayers fund HUD's programs with the expectation that resources reach eligible American families, and that every day the rule is not in effect, assistance that could go to a waiting eligible family may go to ineligible noncitizens. Commenters argued the current allowance of assistance to mixed-status households is a pull factor that incentivizes illegal immigration, and that removing it protects the fiscal integrity of the programs. A commenter argued that for every ineligible person who receives state or federal dollars through programs such as Section 8 or Medicaid, a citizen in need loses out. Commenters asked HUD to confine assistance to citizens and lawfully present residents and to protect taxpayer dollars given significant cost growth. A commenter asked HUD to investigate two Los Angeles city council members the commenter alleged are diverting taxpayer money to ineligible recipients.
Commenters supported the rule as a matter of upholding the law, arguing that individuals who entered or remain in the country without legal authority should not receive housing subsidized by taxpayers, whether prorated or not, and that not following the law should carry consequences even if doing so causes hardship. Commenters distinguished legal immigration, which they said they support, from illegal immigration, framing the rule as fairness to citizens and to immigrants who completed the lawful process. A commenter argued that a legal citizen can readily prove status with a birth certificate or Social Security card without waiting months, and that legal citizens and lawful immigrants who need help are shut out because application lists are closed and funds have gone to ineligible noncitizens.
A commenter argued that lawful applicants undergo an extensive documented waitlist process and questioned why an ineligible household would face a lesser process. A commenter argued that public housing should be for those lawfully present the same way other federal resources are conditioned on legal status, analogizing that the government would not allow resources to further other civil violations such as fraud or criminal violations such as drug dealing, and giving the example that a homeless veteran who served the country should take priority over an undocumented household. A commenter urged HUD not to withdraw the proposed rule and to direct assistance to those most in need but deserving. A commenter argued that widespread circumvention of immigration laws over a long period has eroded the rule of law.
HUD Response:
HUD agrees that U.S. taxpayer funded housing assistance should be available only for eligible U.S. citizens and individuals with eligible immigration status as required by law and implemented in this final rule.
6. Increases Self-Sufficiency
Commenters supported the rule as consistent with values of self-reliance and work, arguing that assistance should encourage employment and self-sufficiency rather than long-term dependence. A commenter argued the rule promotes self-reliance and integration, that eligible immigrants meeting the criteria will still receive assistance, and that it restores confidence that taxpayer funds are used efficiently while encouraging legal pathways and compliance. A commenter argued that self-sufficiency is a core American value that should be expected of foreign nationals within the United States. A commenter supported reserving assistance for seniors, veterans, and people with disabilities and argued able-bodied recipients should work. A commenter framed removing assistance to ineligible households as freeing resources to subsidize families and homeless people rejoining the workforce. A commenter argued that declining to subsidize what the commenter described as “unlawful presence” is not unkindness but avoids enabling continued unlawful conduct.
HUD Response:
HUD thanks commenters for their support and agrees that U.S. taxpayer funded housing assistance should be available only for eligible U.S. citizens and individuals with eligible immigration status as required by law and implemented in this final rule.
B. Comments in Opposition to the Rule
1. Rule Would Not Create Any New Solutions
Commenters argued that the proposed rule is unnecessary because the existing proration framework already ensures that no federal housing subsidy is provided on behalf of household members who lack eligible immigration status, so the rule's stated integrity objective is already met and the rule is unnecessary. Commenters stated that section 2(a) of
Executive Order 14218
“Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Open Borders” is also satisfied because ineligible members receive no assistance and instead pay their own share of rent. Commenters further argued that the rule
(
printed page 72983)
conflicts with congressional intent because Section 214 contains no time limit on prorated assistance, and that HUD cannot point to statutory language authorizing the indefinite-proration bar it asserts. Further commenters asserted that the current system works and that no program-integrity problem justifies the change.
Commenters objected that, because ineligible members already receive nothing, the rule addresses no actual loophole and would produce no fiscal savings while imposing new costs. Commenters contended that because proration limits the subsidy to eligible members only, mixed-status households already receive a reduced subsidy and pay a correspondingly higher share of rent, so the rule would displace paying households without freeing any assistance for others. Commenters asserted that the rule contradicts the agency's own Regulatory Impact Analysis, which projects that the number of eligible individuals receiving assistance would fall from approximately 55,100 to 24,100—a reduction of more than 56 percent. They further drew on the RIA to argue the rule would raise costs, stating HUD would need an additional $311 million to $385 million to serve the same number of households. Commenters noted that pro-rating the assistance to only provide assistance to eligible individuals mirrors how other federal benefit programs, including SNAP, operate.
Commenters argued that household members have already attested to eligibility under penalty of perjury and the existing attestation system operates without a demonstrated problem, so a new documentation mandate duplicates existing safeguards while burdening housing agencies without added resources.
Commenters contended that the higher rents paid by mixed-status households let housing providers serve more families overall and offset the cost of assistance for others, many of them citizens, so eliminating those households would reduce, not expand, available assistance. Commenters disputed the premise that vacated assistance would simply be redirected, noting that in tight markets it cannot be, and citing the HUD Housing Choice Voucher dashboard showing California housing authorities using 104.2 percent of budget authority yet able to fund vouchers for only about 88.7 percent of authorized households. Commenters added jurisdiction-specific cost detail, noting that in 2024 nearly 80,000 people in about 20,000 mixed-status families in Oregon and nationally earned an average income well below program limits, and that where an agency cannot reissue vouchers after a family exits, each replacement household would require a higher subsidy—approximately $4,900 more per person on average.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees that the existing proration framework makes this rule unnecessary. An individual without verified eligible status living in a mixed household receiving long-term prorated assistance is benefitting from HUD financial assistance in a way that is prohibited by Section 214. Section 214 applies specifically to certain HUD financial assistance and prohibits the Secretary from making financial assistance available to persons other than U.S. citizens or specified categories of eligible noncitizens. Under HUD's current regulations, prorated assistance may continue indefinitely, so an individual whose eligible status has never been verified may reside in an assisted unit and benefit from HUD financial assistance on a long-term basis. The fact that assistance is prorated does not cure that result; it is the continued, unverified receipt of a HUD-subsidized benefit that Section 214 does not permit. This rule addresses that gap by making prorated assistance a temporary condition pending verification of the eligible status of all family members, where permitted by statute, and by requiring documentation and verification of citizenship and eligible immigration status. These changes bring HUD's regulations into greater alignment with Section 214 and are consistent with section 2(a) of
Executive Order 14218
.
HUD disagrees with the assertion that the rule is unnecessary because household members have already attested to eligibility. This assertion does not account for the operational reality that not all household members have previously claimed eligible status. Under current regulations, individuals can choose “not to contend” their status or may fall under past age exemptions, meaning their eligibility has never been formally addressed. The rule closes these gaps and establishes a timeline to give these individuals the time required to establish eligibility.
The current framework allows, but does not require, the request of additional documentation from individuals who submit a declaration of U.S. citizenship. The new requirements at
24 CFR 5.508
bring uniformity by requiring all individuals, regardless of age, who declare themselves to have U.S. citizenship to provide appropriate documentation, as well as a verification consent form to consent to responsible entities' review of submitted documents. This rule requires the responsible entity to review the evidence documents to verify citizenship.
HUD does not agree that the rule produces no benefit or that its costs are unjustified. As the RIA explains, the principal economic effect of the rule is to redistribute tenant subsidies from mixed families that contain ineligible individuals to households composed solely of eligible members, providing HUD the authority to reprioritize rental assistance for households with eligible citizenship or immigration status as required by law. Because there are more individuals eligible for assistance than there is assistance available, the assistance relinquished by exiting mixed families would be provided to fully eligible households on waiting lists. HUD acknowledges these transfer and cost implications, which the RIA identifies, including quantifiable upfront costs for responsible entities and tenants estimated at $17 million to $33 million. Under HUD's default fixed-budget scenario, any supplemental subsidy needed to preserve the identical number of assisted family members is held to zero in that scenario. The obligation to comply with Section 214 applies regardless of these transfer and fiscal effects.
2. Objections to Verification Methods
A. Verification Mechanics & SAVE Process Complexity
Commenters focused on the operational mechanics of the proposed verification requirements, arguing that requiring all household members to be verified through SAVE—including U.S. citizens and participants previously eligible to self-certify—would replace a streamlined process with a complex, multi-step one prone to error and delay. Commenters argued that the multi-step design multiplies the points at which an eligible citizen can be delayed or wrongly screened out, and that the added bureaucratic steps increase the administrative burden on both participants and program staff. Commenters asked the agency to retain the simpler existing process rather than adopt the two-stage requirement.
Commenters described the two-stage primary/secondary verification structure as inherently complicated and inconsistent. A commenter argued that when primary verification fails, secondary verification is not a single uniform process but varies by the document submitted and relies on PHA or owner staff to manually review documents, producing an overly long
(
printed page 72984)
process with inconsistent outcomes, delays, or denials, followed by a complicated appeals process. A commenter noted that responsible-entity staff would have to learn how SAVE works, master the distinction between primary and secondary verification, and handle and retain sensitive documents. A commenter argued that HUD's administrative-burden table ignores the effectively unquantifiable burden of dealing with SAVE's inevitable failure to return accurate results, which would generate a potentially enormous volume of administrative hearings and document-production demands on both agencies and low-income tenants that the analysis never accounts for.
Commenters objected that the rule eliminates the long-standing “do not contend” option and signed declarations of citizenship, replacing a workable attestation with a system that cannot deliver reliable citizenship results. A commenter argued that requiring persons aged 62 and older to submit at least one document for SAVE evaluation exceeds the statutory obligations of the Housing and Community Development Act, which expressly subjects those aged 62 and older to a different, less demanding verification standard.
Commenters also objected to the verification consent form itself, noting that it would function as notice to households that responsible entities must report suspected immigration violations to DHS. A commenter explained that renters who self-certify would have to sign both the existing declaration and a newly required verification consent form agreeing to submission of their information to SAVE, and that the form doubles as notification that responsible entities must inform DHS immediately whenever staff determine a household member is present in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Commenters challenged the proposed record-correction mechanism at
24 CFR 5.514(d)(4)
as inadequate, contending that a citizen falsely flagged by SAVE bears the burden of correcting the record and may be evicted on the basis of an erroneous result even while that result is being contested.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees that the requirements to utilize SAVE to verify individuals' status would be a novel operationally complex process. Responsible entities are already required to use the DHS-administered SAVE program to verify eligible immigration status and should therefore have familiarity with it. Comments that specifically object to the complexity of navigating a two-stage primary/secondary verification process, or comments that responsible entities will need to learn how to handle and process sensitive documentation, overlook that responsible entities must already be using these processes regularly for the verification of most eligible noncitizens in their programs.
HUD acknowledges that the requirement to verify more individuals' statuses in SAVE will increase administrative burden on responsible entities. The Regulatory Impact Analysis estimates that 19,660 U.S. citizens or eligible noncitizens in affected programs have not already provided proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status, and that 730 immigrants who previously chose not to contend their eligibility status would pursue verification. However, this verification is necessary to ensure that individuals are not benefiting from HUD financial assistance in a way that is prohibited by Section 214. Consequently, HUD cannot accept recommendation to retain an existing simpler process like accepting signed declarations in isolation.
The SAVE program also offers prospective, new, or current user agencies several trainings and customized tutorials to meet their specific needs, the information for which is easily accessible online at
https://www.uscis.gov/​save/​current-user-agencies
.
SAVE tutorials help users utilize SAVE correctly and efficiently and provide information about: SAVE and the verification process, SAVE CaseCheck, commonly used immigration documents and where to find immigration enumerators, common case responses, best practices for additional verification, managing cases, and administering SAVE accounts. Additionally, SAVE users are required to review the online tutorial and certify completion of the tutorial before they will be able to create new SAVE cases.
HUD agrees that secondary verification is not a uniform process but may vary, as the requisite documents depend on an individual's immigration status. SAVE is an evolving program that may be able to utilize certain information or documents in the future, so HUD is seeking to provide enough flexibility in its regulations to account for changes in SAVE's capabilities.
However, as noted, HUD is undertaking this rulemaking to better align its regulations with the wording and purpose of Section 214. Even if requiring verification of U.S. citizens and individuals aged 62 or older involved a modest increase in the operational complexity of the verification process, HUD believes it would be warranted to ensure that housing assistance is provided only to eligible individuals.
Finally, HUD disagrees that the consent form creates a new substantive reporting obligation. Rather, it informs applicants and participants of verification requirements and of circumstances in which information may be transmitted to DHS pursuant to existing laws and regulations. The fact that an individual is required to sign the verification consent form does not itself indicate that a responsible entity suspects that the individual has violated immigration law, nor does submission of information to SAVE constitute such a determination.
To commenters arguing that the “do not contend” option and signed declarations of citizenship should be maintained, HUD would note that the preamble to the proposed rule explains why HUD believes the option to not contend eligible immigration status is not consistent with the wording and purpose of Section 214. The preamble to the proposed rule also explains that HUD is requiring applicants and tenants to submit evidence of U.S. citizenship to responsible entities with any declaration of U.S. citizenship. This will better align HUD's regulations with the wording and purpose of Section 214, and it will better ensure that assistance is provided only to eligible individuals.
B. Housing as an Immigration Enforcement Tool, and Data Security & Personally Identifiable Information (PII) Exposure
Commenters objected that the rule, particularly in combination with the March 2025 HUD-DHS data-sharing memorandum, would impermissibly move HUD into immigration enforcement and conscript housing providers into a federal immigration-enforcement role that lies outside their statutory mission, expertise, and capacity. Commenters argued that proposed § 5.508(d)(4) would require housing staff to inform DHS whenever personnel determine that a household member is present in violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act, but that a housing authority's expertise is in housing, not immigration enforcement, and its staff are not equipped to make such determinations, both because of lack of expertise and a lack of resources. Commenters said that this determination requirement turns housing into an immigration enforcement instrument, exceeding HUD's role and twisting the intent behind Section 214.
Commenters objected specifically to the DHS reporting requirement in § 5.508(e)(2)(vi), arguing it would
(
printed page 72985)
convert providers into reporting agents and damage the provider-tenant trust essential to property management. Commenters argued the rule would force owners to become extensions of federal immigration enforcement, requiring owners and PHAs to immediately report undocumented household members under § 5.508(d)(4). Commenters warned that if participants believe disclosing family composition to their property manager may result in an immigration referral, they will withhold information or conceal household members, undermining effective property and program management.
Commenters argued the rule violates the Tenth Amendment by conscripting state and local agencies into federal immigration enforcement. They raised an anti-commandeering objection, arguing that by forcing public housing agencies to administer the re-verification process and comply with enhanced DHS reporting, the rule shifts the cost and implementation of federal immigration policy onto state and local agencies in a manner that contravenes the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.
Commenters argued that the new verification process creates serious privacy risks by expanding collection and cross-agency sharing of sensitive personal data. Commenters contended that DHS retains the personal information routed through SAVE for as long as a decade—even when it confirms citizenship—exposing tenants to lasting security, privacy, and misuse risks well beyond the initial verification, a concern documented in the voting-rights context. A commenter argued that a cohort of secretaries of state from twelve states has opposed SAVE's use on privacy grounds and that its use here conflicts with California laws protecting immigrants and privacy generally.
Commenters emphasized that the rule itself supplies no adequate safeguards for the data it would amass. A commenter argued that the rule is silent on how PHAs should reconcile the mandate with stricter state PII laws governing protected-information definitions, retention, and notice, and that providers need defined liability standards and safe-harbor protection when relying on federal verification outcomes outside their control. A commenter argued that proposed § 5.508(d)(3) affirmatively disclaims HUD responsibility for downstream use or disclosure despite the statute's command to protect such information “to the maximum degree possible,” exposing providers to legal and privacy risk over data practices beyond their control. A commenter argued that requiring responsible entities to collect, photocopy, and store sensitive biographic and government-issued data for every household member—and retain it for five years—increases the risk of identity theft and data breaches. Commenters argued that the rule undermines the Violence Against Women Act's housing protections—codified at
34 U.S.C. 12491
and implemented through
24 CFR part 5
—by forcing survivors' information into DHS systems, contrary to Congress's confidentiality intent.
Commenters warned that the custodians of this data have poor track records, citing a 2024 HUD Inspector General finding that HUD maintained a significant number of PII records with limited zero-trust controls, compounding the risk of entrusting more sensitive data to the agency, that four of the six resulting OIG recommendations remain outstanding, and that HUD OIG's December 2025 top-management-challenges report reiterated these information-security weaknesses. Commenters stated that broadening SAVE access beyond a small group of employees would require expanded staff access and comprehensive agency-wide training.
Commenters argued that the rule runs headlong into the Privacy Act's computer-matching provisions. A commenter argued that the rule identifies no computer-matching agreement authorizing HUD to compare participant data against the overhauled SAVE system, so that absent such an up-to-date agreement HUD's comparison of participant records violates the Privacy Act's computer-matching restriction—the definition of a “matching program” reaching any computerized comparison of automated systems of records. A commenter added that HUD's earlier cross-referencing of its data with SAVE to generate the EIV-SAVE tenant matching reports itself likely exceeded the uses tenants consented to.
Commenters stressed that these risks fall hardest on vulnerable tenants. A commenter argued that the accumulation of citizenship and immigration data in federal systems poses particular risks for people with disabilities, who may rely on others to navigate administrative processes and be less able to identify or contest erroneous data. A commenter argued that, given arrests of noncitizens at court hearings, of noncitizens married to citizens, and even of U.S. citizens, qualified participants will fear that sharing documentation with HUD exposes them to DHS.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees with commenters' contention that the rule newly requires housing agencies to share tenant data with immigration authorities, and with the contention that it affirmatively converts public housing agencies into immigration enforcers by requiring them to report household members they know are unlawfully present to DHS.
The verification the rule requires is limited to confirming eligibility for Federal housing assistance. Section 27 of the United States Housing Act of 1937, added in 1996, already requires HUD to furnish DHS with the name, address, and any identifying information of any individual whom HUD knows is not lawfully present in the United States. Section 27 further requires HUD to require that public housing agencies furnish such information. This is a longstanding requirement, and additional guidance was published in the
Federal Register
over twenty-six years ago (
65 FR 58301
). The guidance on this longstanding reporting mandate has made clear that any finding or conclusion of unlawful presence must be supported by a determination by DHS or the Executive Office for Immigration Review, so the concern that this reporting requires housing agencies to make legal determinations they are not equipped to make is unfounded.
Responsible entities do not make immigration determinations; they rely on DHS-administered SAVE to verify U.S. citizenship and immigration status. Furthermore, under proposed § 5.512(f), a responsible entity is not liable for any action, delay, or failure of DHS in conducting verification.
SAVE responses clearly indicate U.S. citizenship or immigration status which responsible entities can map to their eligibility categories. As noted above, the SAVE program also offers prospective, new or current user agencies several trainings and customized tutorials to meet their specific needs, the information for which is easily accessible online at
https://www.uscis.gov/​save/​current-user-agencies
.
SAVE tutorials help SAVE users utilize SAVE correctly and efficiently and provide information about: SAVE and the verification process, SAVE CaseCheck, commonly used immigration documents and where to find immigration enumerators, common case responses, best practices for additional verification, managing cases; and administering SAVE accounts. Additionally, SAVE users are required to review the online tutorial and certify to completing the review in
(
printed page 72986)
the SAVE system before they will be able to create new SAVE cases.
The reporting obligation identified by commenters is not a new enforcement role created by this rule because determinations of status for purposes of the Immigration and Nationality Act are the responsibility of the Department of Justice, not of any other agency. The final rule, however, does impose a new, parallel reporting obligation on Section 8 project-based rental assistance (PBRA) owners (as responsible entities) in the circumstances specified in 5.508(e)(2)(vi). Public housing agencies are already subject to the reporting requirement under section 404 of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA), as clarified in the 2000 Interagency Notice (
65 FR 58301
). Revised § 5.508(e)(2)(vi) provides that PHAs or owners, as applicable, may meet that requirement by conforming with applicable
Federal Register
notices, and proposed § 5.508(d)(4) requires the verification consent form to notify individuals of this longstanding obligation.
This final rule affirms the longstanding reporting requirement under PRWORA, ensuring applicants and existing households have notice of PHAs' obligation to comply with section 404 of PRWORA, and provide individuals with notice of this obligation on PHAs.
HUD acknowledges that this rulemaking will adversely affect some tenants and applicants for Section 214 covered programs, especially mixed families and ineligible noncitizens. HUD recognizes the concern that the verification requirement could discourage some potentially eligible citizens and noncitizens from applying; the RIA expressly acknowledges this possible reduction in take-up. HUD has taken steps to mitigate that effect: primary verification is conducted by the responsible entity through SAVE without requiring the applicant to assemble documents in advance, responsible entities must notify affected tenants of the requirement within 30 days of the effective date, and extensions of time to submit evidence are available under revised
24 CFR 5.508(g)(2)
.
HUD appreciates the concerns articulated by commenters about the security of individuals' personally identifiable information, and HUD agrees that responsible entities need to reduce exposure risks with good data security practices. Responsible entities will be creating more queries in SAVE, but their practices for safeguarding personally identifiable information should be well established since they have been using this system for years. The security protocols used by DHS to protect information submitted to SAVE are outside the bounds of this rulemaking. While responsible entities may establish access to SAVE through HUD, the results of queries created by responsible entities are stored in SAVE and maintained according to National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) retention schedules, not in a separate database created and maintained by HUD. Responsible entities utilizing SAVE to verify the immigration status of an individual submit required information directly to DHS, and responsible entities report to HUD their determinations about an individual's status on the basis of those SAVE queries.
Prior to this rulemaking,
24 CFR 5.508(d)(3)
already provided that the verification consent form must inform individuals that HUD is not responsible for the further use or transmission of evidence or other information by DHS. The final rule maintains an existing status quo on that point. The rule likewise makes no change with respect to the rights of survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. Furthermore, the final rule maintains existing regulatory provisions at
24 CFR 5.508(d)(3)
that limit release of evidence to DHS to the purpose of verifying an individual's U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status and not for any other purpose.
Commenters objecting to the lack of reference to a computer-matching agreement in this rulemaking misunderstand how responsible entities submit queries to SAVE. Responsible entities' use of SAVE is not a matching program under the Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1998 and does not require a computer-matching agreement. The 2026 EIV-SAVE tenant matching activity referenced by some commenters is distinct from the verification process established by this rule; that activity used a different methodology and is not the mechanism this rule adopts, under which responsible entities submit individual inquiries directly to DHS.
C. SAVE Operational Capacity/Delays
Commenters argued that SAVE remains untested and still under construction, and that relying on an unfinished program to determine housing eligibility will harm citizens and immigrants alike while creating massive administrative burdens inconsistent with HUD's mission and the rule's stated purpose. Commenters argued that SAVE was built to verify the immigration status of noncitizens, not the citizenship of U.S. citizens, and that pressing it into this new role is fundamentally unsound. Commenters stated that the system's known limitations and delays could wrongfully deny assistance to eligible citizens struggling to clear secondary-verification hurdles. A commenter argued that using a completely untested and unfinished SAVE system to determine housing eligibility violates participants' due-process rights under the federal and California constitutions.
Commenters emphasized that HUD's own preamble concedes SAVE cannot process the most common proof-of-citizenship documents—birth certificates and U.S. passports—and cannot review certain other citizenship documentation at all, forcing a significant number of HUD participants—including U.S. citizens—into documentary secondary verification, shifting burden onto participants and providers. A commenter argued that HUD lacks comprehensive citizenship records and does not capture all naturalized or derivative citizens, including many born before 1978. A commenter argued that even documented individuals face significant doubt about SAVE's ability to verify their status timely and accurately, especially for people who have changed their names, including women who took their spouse's name after marriage.
Commenters expressed serious doubts about SAVE's accuracy, citing a documented history of errors in the voting-rights context and reports from the Brennan Center and a 2018 U.S. Commission on Civil Rights documenting inaccuracy in the data sets underlying SAVE. Commenters asserted that HUD omitted any reliability figures for SAVE's citizenship function because DHS has not made them public, that reported error rates run at least 14 percent, and that the true rate is therefore unknown. Commenters warned that PHAs experienced SAVE's unreliability firsthand under HUD's 2026 EIV-SAVE tenant matching directive.
Commenters objected that HUD proposes undefined “manual processes” and “manual record searches” that will waste enormous PHA staff time and still produce inaccuracies, and that HUD expressly declined to set any deadline for completing secondary verification because of SAVE's limitations—leaving families in limbo, paying unaffordable high rent while they wait, with some evicted because they cannot pay the prorated amount. A commenter argued that existing errors in the current system
(
printed page 72987)
already produce harmful and likely unlawful HUD actions, and that expanding verification will increase wrongful denials, delays, and instability for vulnerable families.
Commenters emphasized that verification delays fall hardest on those least able to produce documents quickly, including participants with disabilities who face additional barriers in navigating various agencies to contest erroneous data. Commenters asserted that lower-income populations in general face difficulty in obtaining documents due to time, money, and transportation barriers. A commenter argued that survivors fleeing trafficking often cannot immediately access documentation—because withholding documents is a primary control tactic of traffickers—so verification delays will prolong homelessness and unsafe living conditions. A commenter argued that the rule removes the existing provision granting 30 days to appeal when secondary verification does not confirm status, that SAVE offers no appeal process, and that unlike current law—which stays PHA proceedings pending appeal—any termination or eviction would proceed while the participant scrambles to correct records; this risk would be compounded for larger households. A commenter argued that older adults forced through SAVE after removal of the age-62 exemption—facing technology, documentation, and mobility barriers—face heightened risk of wrongful termination, especially for many older U.S. citizens who have no birth certificate at all.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates the concerns expressed about SAVE's ability to verify citizenship. In instances where SAVE does not accurately identify an individual as a citizen in the primary verification stage, the responsible entity will collect additional documentation from the individual that establishes their status. This approach mitigates the consequence of any failure to immediately verify citizenship by requiring follow-up and review. However, HUD disagrees with commenters' characterizations of the potential for widespread verification errors in SAVE. HUD cannot substantiate claims that SAVE itself has a high error rate when verifying citizenship or eligible immigration status. Commenters may be conflating the possibility of systemic errors in SAVE with the possibility of problems with a specific method for utilizing SAVE data. Commenters likewise do not establish that SAVE would be more likely to fail at the primary verification stage for individuals who lack any documentary proof of citizenship.
Commenters have not provided evidence that SAVE's primary verification has consistent errors when full information is provided in the initial inquiry, nor do they present evidence that SAVE responses are consistently inaccurate at the secondary verification stage. Commenters cite industry letters that focused on the EIV-SAVE tenant matching directive, not SAVE itself, and the differences in methodology, as discussed in response to other comments, undermine commenters' contention that there would be widespread verification errors in SAVE itself. Even where SAVE is used for primary verification, instances without an automated data match should not lead to a wrongful denial because the responsible entity is (a) expected to submit a case for manual review as prompted when the system cannot generate an automated response, (b) allowed to request a manual review when an automated response appears incorrect or is unexpected, and (c) required to provide the family with the opportunity to request manual verification if they disagree with the automated response, and allow them to provide additional information and documentation.
To the extent that SAVE will be used for primary verification, the responsible entity should be able to quickly reconcile any data input errors by reviewing the documentation provided by the applicant or current tenant. Use of SAVE should not lead to a wrongful denial because the responsible entity is required to provide the family with the opportunity to provide additional information and documentation. Users may submit a case for additional verification if they received an unexpected response or have questions about the response. When SAVE is used for secondary verification, objections to undefined “manual record searches” incorrectly assume that responsible entity staff, rather than U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) staff, will be required to perform such manual review.
The rule does not establish a timeframe on the completion of the secondary verification process because the time required may vary depending on the complexity of an individual's particular immigration status.
Moreover, HUD estimates that responsible entities already are collecting the documentary evidence necessary thus not significantly increasing administrative burden. The Regulatory Impact Analysis estimates that only 1.05 percent of existing tenants have not provided proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status for another purpose. Where that documentation has already been collected, responsible entities still bear the additional administrative burden of creating an inquiry in SAVE, and perhaps following up on that additional inquiry by uploading the documentation already on hand. 5.514(d)(4) is meant to advise families that any records will need to be corrected with the issuing agency; should the family request a hearing, the responsible entity should duly consider all information and documentation provided in support. The verification of consent form for individuals declaring U.S. citizenship is a new requirement. However, applicants and tenants already provide consent for releases of information during the screening and admissions process, for example the forms HUD-9886 and 9887. HUD disagrees this will deter eligible applicants and has accounted for the light burden on current participants to review and sign the consent during their next annual or interim reexamination.
Comments that responsible entity staff lack expertise to distinguish immigration statuses or that staff lack training to create SAVE cases and interpret the results are concerning. Prior to this rulemaking, responsible entities were already required to use SAVE and to make determinations of whether individuals are eligible for assistance under Section 214. Responsible entities have been required to utilize SAVE to verify eligible immigration status since June 19, 1995, when the final rule implementing Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 (
60 FR 14816
) became effective. Responsible entities must provide adequate training to staff to make eligibility determinations as required by law. In addition, the rule would stagger deadlines for review of evidence of citizenship for current tenants, easing the logistical burden on the responsible entities.
HUD appreciates comments identifying the possible differential impact of the verification process on different individuals.
24 CFR 5.508
provides for extensions of time to submit evidence of citizenship or eligible status to accommodate such circumstances.
3. Rule Does Not Properly Balance Costs and Benefits
A. Nonprofit & Mission-Driven Provider Impact
Commenters representing nonprofit, faith-based, and mission-driven housing and service organizations argued that the verification requirements would fall
(
printed page 72988)
especially hard on providers operating with volunteer labor, thin budgets, and populations that are difficult to document. A commenter noted that nonprofit and charitable organizations are statutorily relieved under PRWORA from conducting eligibility verification of the federal public benefits they administer but argued that the notice nonetheless signals such organizations should heed the policy, undercutting the exemption in practice. A commenter representing affordable senior-housing providers stressed that mission-driven senior communities would have to collect documentation from HUD-assisted older adults who established eligibility years ago by declaration, diverting staff from tenant services.
A commenter representing Health Care for the Homeless providers quantified the burden, describing the rule as an expensive, time-consuming, unfunded mandate under which case managers—already responsible for obtaining client identification and documentation—would face substantial added work per client on top of existing caseloads. A commenter operating a community-integration service warned that its organization could not cover the expense of obtaining hundreds of discounted birth certificates and identification cards for the participants it serves. A commenter serving Puerto Rico noted that the requirements would impose disproportionate burdens on community-based housing intermediaries there, and a commenter serving low-income Californians argued that community organizations, social-services agencies, and legal-aid programs already overburdened by the housing and homelessness crisis would be pushed further. Commenters representing legal-services providers added that the resulting increase in evictions would divert and waste the resources of already-strained legal-aid and eviction-defense organizations, hindering their ability to serve clients.
Commenters representing nonprofit, community-based, and service-provider organizations argued that the new verification requirements would impose significant administrative strain on providers already operating with limited staff, reducing the capacity of housing clinics, service programs, and survivor-support organizations to serve their clients.
HUD Response:
HUD acknowledges that the rule would impose some administrative costs, as reflected in the Regulatory Impact Analysis, and it has weighed those costs in developing the final rule. Some additional administrative costs are inevitable to ensure that only eligible individuals receive assistance—for example, responsible entities will be required to obtain documentation of eligible status or to create additional inquiries in SAVE. To the extent that these additional costs are required to verify individuals' eligible status, HUD believes such costs are justified to ensure compliance with Section 214.
A potential source to lower the document costs is to use reduced or waived fees, if applicable in your state, when obtaining any of the required documents. In accordance with state law, some states already have reduced fees or no fees at all for certain categories of individuals. For example, those experiencing homelessness in Washington state can obtain their U.S. birth certificate with no fee. Likewise, those experiencing homelessness in Pennsylvania or California can apply for a birth certificate with fees waived. In addition, responsible entities are required to provide information on the changes in this rule once it becomes effective; this should help give tenants and applicants time before their annual recertification or application to secure the required documents needed. Also, responsible entities have the flexibility to give an extension of time to submit evidence of citizenship or eligible status (
e.g.,
a 30-day extension period, or up to 60 days, based on the circumstance of the individual case).
Finally, although charitable organizations are currently exempt under PRWORA, it does not relieve States or other governmental actors from the requirements to ensure that all relevant programs are in compliance with PRWORA. Additionally, this rule aligns HUD's requirements with Section 214, which prohibits the Secretary of HUD from making financial assistance available to any persons other than United States citizens or certain categories of eligible noncitizens in HUD's assisted housing programs.
B. Operational & Fiscal Burden on Housing Providers Leading to Decreased Housing Provided Overall
Commenters argued that the rule would impose a substantial and largely unfunded mandate creating administrative and fiscal burdens on public housing agencies and other housing providers, diverting scarce staff time and resources away from their core housing mission. A commenter drew an analogy to a February 2025 Executive Order and related federal efforts requiring states to re-verify immigration status for Medicaid and other programs, arguing that such re-verification mandates create administrative burdens for the agencies that must carry them out.
Commenters emphasized the operational strain of re-verifying entire assisted populations, arguing that the rule would require agencies to re-screen every household member—including U.S. citizens and long-tenured participants who established eligibility years ago by declaration—at each recertification, generating recurring work far beyond initial intake. Some commenters suggested this would constitute re-processing as many as millions of already-compliant households.
Commenters described the practical mechanics of compliance as a major operational undertaking, requiring agencies to revise their Administrative Plans and Admission and Continued Occupancy Policies (ACOPs), rebuild forms and notices, reprogram or reconfigure information systems, retrain staff, and stand up new document-collection and consent-tracking workflows before the rule could be implemented.
Commenters warned that the rule would increase processing time and slow leasing and lengthen vacancies, as households caught in re-verification, proration, or termination would leave units offline longer while agencies process hardship cases and turnover, reducing the housing actually available and cutting into program income. Commenters also said the more complicated implementation would increase paperwork, delays, and error rates without a demonstrated benefit.
Commenters argued that the added procedural steps would multiply informal hearings, grievances, and eviction proceedings, each of which consumes staff and legal-review time, so the rule would convert routine recertifications into contested, resource-intensive cases.
Commenters contended that HUD's regulatory impact analysis significantly understated the true administrative cost, arguing that it omitted the staff hours, system changes, legal review, and turnover costs the rule would impose and failed to account for the cost of upending existing eligibility frameworks, leaving the analysis unsupported. Commenters challenged HUD's characterization of the rule as reducing regulatory burden. Commenters argued that the rule contradicts the Administration's stated deregulatory goals by adding layers of administrative complexity rather than streamlining program operations. A commenter argued that departures impose significant turnover costs, since owners must refurbish, market, and re-
(
printed page 72989)
lease units and lose income during vacancy. A commenter contended that turnover requires staff time, unit turns, and recertification of new households, all straining budgets with no new funding. A commenter added that the economic analysis fails to meaningfully evaluate turnover costs for owners and expanded verification costs for smaller entities. A commenter asserted that turnover costs run $10,000-$20,000 just to evict and rehab an apartment, on top of administrative costs and rent loss.
Commenters argued that the RIA understates costs to housing providers by assuming repairs are the only turnover cost and omitting lost rent receipts, which a commenter estimated at $14.5-$18 million based on the family's rent share across 16,000 to 20,000 households. Commenters objected that HUD limited its analysis to local moving costs assuming no moving company and discounted tenant contest of eviction, ignoring the fearful environment of displacement. A commenter added that HUD failed to consider eviction and turnover costs for non-mixed-status families unable to produce required documentation.
A commenter maintained that if half the mixed families vacated, one authority would have at least 400 units vacant for an extended period, lowering its assessment score. A commenter added that certification changes must flow through TRACS, raising the volume of interim recertifications, subsidy corrections, and errors.
Commenters warned that agencies are already stretched thin, chronically understaffed and underfunded. Commenters representing agencies of varying size described disproportionate impacts on small, rural, tribal, and under-resourced agencies, which lack the dedicated staff, legal capacity, and systems to absorb the new verification, training, and compliance work. Commenters stressed that small and rural agencies operating with a single staff member or minimal capacity would be especially strained.
