of the least affordable markets in the nation, where affected families have extremely low incomes and could not remain housed without assistance. Commenters made parallel arguments for Santa Clara County, where 63 percent of roughly 22,000 served households are elderly or disabled and extremely low-income, Los Angeles County, especially for veteran households, Santa Cruz County, Santa Monica as one of the most expensive rental markets, Salem, Washington State, New York City, where 2.2 million residents live in poverty, and Oceanside. Commenters warned that California concentrates the highest-cost markets and largest immigrant population, so displaced families face the steepest re-housing barriers, with over 40 percent of California households already cost-burdened. Commenters urged jurisdiction-specific treatment for Puerto Rico, where a prolonged economic contraction deepens the shortage, requesting a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking and a territorial impact assessment. Commenters added that county governments and community-based partners would bear the fallout that HUD sheds.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates the market-specific data commenters provided regarding the affordability challenges facing families who may lose assistance under this rule. As explained in the proposed rule and in HUD's responses above, Section 214(d)(2) requires that assistance not be provided to individuals whose eligible status has not been verified, and this requirement applies uniformly regardless of local market conditions, cost burden, or the availability of comparable private-market housing. HUD acknowledges that families losing assistance in high-cost markets may face significant difficulty securing alternative housing, but responsible entities are not required to identify or provide such alternatives for families that do not qualify for continued or preservation assistance under §§ 5.516 and 5.518 following verification.
Regarding Puerto Rico, HUD did not propose, and does not believe the statute permits, territory-specific variation in the verification requirements of Section 214, which apply to all Section 214 covered programs nationwide, including in the territories. HUD has determined that a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking and separate territorial impact assessment are not necessary, as the Regulatory Impact Analysis and Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis accompanying this rule address the anticipated burden on responsible entities across all covered jurisdictions.
6. The Rule's Documentation Requirements Are Too Strict
A. Documentation Is Too Hard To Obtain
Commenters explained that many eligible U.S. citizens do not possess the documents the rule would require, because birth certificates and passports are commonly lost, were never issued, or were destroyed, and are burdensome to replace. Commenters observed that citizens born decades earlier, born at home, or born in jurisdictions with incomplete records may have no accessible birth record at all, and that replacing such records requires contacting the issuing jurisdiction and paying a fee. Commenters noted that older participants, participants who have moved across state lines, and participants who have experienced housing instability are especially likely to lack such records on hand. Commenters explained that documentation problems arise when a participant's records reflect a different name—for example after marriage or a legal name change—or when the participant was born in a different state, requiring cross-jurisdiction requests to reconcile the records. Some locations, like Puerto Rico, have geographical constraints that add additional burden to obtaining documents. Commenters argued that conditioning continued assistance on producing these documents would place eligible citizens at risk of losing housing for reasons unrelated to their actual eligibility.
Commenters offered local and national estimates on how many U.S. citizens lack ready access to citizenship documents: The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that approximately 3.8 million U.S. citizen adults lack proof of citizenship and an additional 17.5 million cannot easily obtain these documents, a figure also attributed to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, and one comment cited studies finding that over 14 percent of American citizens over 80 years old lack proof of U.S. citizenship in the voter-registration context. Commenters cited evidence that documentary-citizenship requirements fall unevenly by race and age, including estimates that 25 percent of African-American citizens and 18 percent of citizens over 65 lack a photo ID, arguing that comparable requirements elsewhere caused eligible citizens to lose coverage.
Commenters described practical barriers to producing documents, including limited access to the internet, to government offices, and to the identification needed to request vital records, particularly for participants in rural areas and for those without reliable transportation. Commenters noted that obtaining documents may require online systems, payment by credit card, or in-person visits that some eligible participants cannot readily complete. Commenters identified the monetary cost of obtaining required documents as a direct burden on eligible citizens, noting that birth certificates, passports, and other vital records carry fees that must be paid to the issuing jurisdiction costs could reach into the thousands of dollars for an affected family. Commenters added that these out-of-pocket costs fall on low-income households least able to absorb them. Commenters argued that imposing these costs on citizens who already qualify for assistance is unjustified and asked the agency to weigh the expense against the existing declaration process, which imposes no comparable cost.
Commenters maintained that these access barriers would translate into denials and delays for otherwise-eligible citizens and urged the agency to account for participants who cannot navigate document-request systems within the timeframes the rule allows. A commenter also stated that Medicare or other federal health-program cards should be usable only as supporting evidence of identity or residence.
HUD Response:
HUD acknowledges all the barriers identified by commenters and assessed in Section 6.2 of the RIA the costs to tenants and applicants associated with obtaining documentation to prove U.S. citizenship, or eligible immigration status. In recognition of the time and effort that may be involved in securing such documentation, the final rule adopts procedural safeguards that prevent terminations unrelated to eligibility. For example, before any denial or termination, the responsible entity must issue the notice required under proposed
24 CFR 5.514(d)
; an individual may pursue a records correction with the issuing or record-holding agency at any point during verification; and a family may request an informal hearing under proposed
24 CFR 5.514(e)
. A responsible entity may verify a tenant's status notwithstanding a name mismatch or record discrepancy where the individual provides sufficient documentation to reconcile the discrepancy.
Commenters raise several different types of difficulties that individuals may encounter in providing documentation, which should be distinguished—some may not have
(
printed page 73009)
ready access to documentation, whereas a much smaller number may not have an official birth certificate or other documentary proof of their status. For individuals who do not have ready access to documentation, the rule provides a window of time for families to request such documentation. Commenters do not offer evidence of how many eligible citizens lack any documentary proof of citizenship.
24 CFR 5.510
provides that acceptable documentation of U.S. citizenship may include other acceptable documentation as specified in HUD guidance. Should the need arise to specify additional documentation for these rare cases, HUD can issue additional guidance.
For non-mixed families, HUD is requiring responsible entities to communicate the documentary evidence requirements to current tenants/participants within 30 days of the rule's effective date so that currently assisted tenants/participants who have not submitted evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status required under § 5.508(b) may begin gathering any necessary documents in advance of their next annual or interim reexamination. As noted in 5.508(g), responsible entities may grant an extension of time to submit evidence where documents are unavailable and the family member is taking prompt and diligent effort to obtain such evidence. In acknowledgement of the barriers some individuals may face in obtaining documents, HUD is extending the flexibility to grant an extension by 30 days for a total of 60 days in the final rule, as described above. The final rule does not preclude a responsible entity from verifying participants' status due to name mismatches or record discrepancies, if the participant can provide the responsible entity with sufficient documentation reconcile the discrepancies. HUD acknowledges and appreciates the examples of individuals who may experience particular barriers providing the documents described in 5.510(b) and, as provided in 5.510(b)(6), will issue further guidance of other acceptable documentation. Finally HUD does not view Medicare or health-program cards as sufficient proof of eligibility.
B. Documentation Requirements Failed Elsewhere
Commenters drew on experience with comparable documentation requirements in other programs to argue that the proposed rule would produce similar harms, contending that citizenship-documentation mandates have previously caused eligible citizens to lose or be delayed in obtaining benefits. Commenters cited the experience under prior federal documentation requirements, in which eligible U.S. citizens—disproportionately low-income and elderly—encountered barriers to proving citizenship and lost coverage as a result, and argued that the same dynamic would recur under this rule. Commenters drew on named comparator programs: that after Medicaid added a paper-based citizenship-documentation requirement under the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, eligible citizens experienced enrollment delays and coverage losses; in a Government Accountability Office survey, half of the 44 responding states reported the requirement had reduced enrollment among eligible citizens. A housing-assistance provider reported handling nearly 13,000 birth-certificate requests since 2010 to help clients establish citizenship, illustrating the real administrative effort involved.
Commenters used these comparators to argue that the documentary requirement is likely to burden eligible citizens without achieving its stated purpose. Commenters cited evidence that documentary-citizenship requirements fall unevenly by race and age, including estimates that 25 percent of African-American citizens and 18 percent of citizens over 65 lack a photo ID, arguing that comparable requirements elsewhere caused eligible citizens to lose coverage.
HUD Response:
As stated above, HUD acknowledges that some applicants and tenants may face barriers in obtaining documentary evidence. The final rule requires responsible entities to provide notice of the documentary submission requirements within 30 days of the rule's effective date and provides for responsible entities to grant time extensions. Additionally, as noted above HUD will issue further guidance on acceptable documentation as provided for in § 5.510(b)(6). Unlike the paper-only comparator programs commenters describe, this rule provides for primary verification to be conducted by the responsible entity through SAVE, so that an applicant or tenant is not required to assemble documentation in advance and submits documentary evidence only where SAVE does not confirm status. HUD has determined that this rule balances the interests of affected parties and responsible entities while improving compliance with statutory obligations and aligning with policy goals.
7. Harm to Groups
A. Mixed-Status Families and the Loss of Prorated Assistance
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm immigrant and mixed-status families by displacing families already complying with existing law, contradicting national values toward immigrants, reducing the affordable-housing supply, chilling participation among eligible members, and undermining family unity. Commenters raised general concerns that the rule would harm immigrant and mixed-status families, including through fear, family disruption, and loss of housing.
Commenters pointed to prior policies—including the 1996 welfare-reform law (PRWORA) and the 2019 public-charge rule—as evidence that analogous measures produce measurable chilling effects that deter eligible members from seeking assistance, and cited
Executive Order 14012
's direction to remove such barriers.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule forces mixed-immigration-status households to choose whether to remove the ineligible member and break up the family, or keep the family intact and lose housing assistance for the entire household. Commenters stressed that the choice is immediate for thousands of households already relying on the program, regardless of how long they have participated in the program or whether other affordable housing is available to the family.
HUD Response:
HUD acknowledges the substantial volume of comments objecting that the rule forces mixed-status households to choose between separating the family and losing housing assistance and recognizes commenters' concern that this outcome is in tension with the stabilizing purpose of assisted housing. HUD notes that the rule and its Regulatory Impact Analysis do not require any family to separate; rather, they preserve a range of options for existing families that were receiving assistance under a Section 214-covered program, including temporary prorated assistance for mixed families while the eligibility of family members is being verified, and, for families that do not qualify for continued assistance, discretionary temporary deferral of termination of assistance for up to 18 months to allow additional time to arrange alternative housing. HUD reiterates that the rule's stated basis is aligning HUD's regulations with the eligibility limitation in Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980.
(
printed page 73010)
B. Harm to Children, Especially U.S.-Citizen Children
Commenters stated that removing a household's housing punishes children for the composition of their family, causing eligible U.S.-citizen children to lose assistance solely because another household member lacks eligible immigration status. Commenters emphasized that about 75 percent of mixed-status families consist of eligible children living with at least one ineligible parent, making separation unworkable. A commenter pointed to the agency's regulatory impact analysis and to the finding that approximately eighty percent of mixed-status families in HUD housing consist of eligible children and at least one ineligible parent.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm children, and U.S.-citizen children in particular, through eviction and homelessness. Commenters stated this would cause developmental and educational damage, and harm to mental-health, including anxiety, depression, and trauma. A commenter contended that housing instability disrupts schooling in ways children do not recover from, describing mid-year school changes, lost academic footing, and long-term harm to school continuity, employment, and mental health when families are forced to move. Commenters stated that HUD's own analysis acknowledges the rule risks conflicting with
Executive Order 13045
(Protection of Children from Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks) because of its adverse effects on child development. A commenter connected the rule to concrete health and child-welfare harms, citing research associating an eviction judgment with a substantially increased mortality risk and describing a voucher holder who relinquished assistance rather than lose a spouse providing medical care. Commenters warned that separation would push U.S.-citizen children toward the foster-care system when parents cannot both remain in the home and retain housing.
Commenters estimated 37,000 children would face eviction, and identified the reduction in assisted-housing supply as the mechanism driving increased child homelessness and poverty. Commenters stated that HUD's own estimates acknowledge that tens of thousands of affected participants are children and that the agency's analysis anticipates the resulting instability and its consequences for children's health and education. Commenters cited HUD's own analysis of the substantially similar 2019 proposal, withdrawn at the time, as estimating approximately 25,000 immigrant families would be evicted, including about 55,000 children who were themselves eligible for assistance. A commenter cited a Center on Budget and Policy Priorities figure of approximately 55,200 citizens and legal participants exposed to eviction or separation, including 35,400 citizen children. A commenter cited an estimate that more than 771,000 children live in households that could be affected, framing the developmental toll as a national-scale harm.
A commenter maintained that inadequate housing is itself a driver of family separation through the child-welfare system, citing evidence that inadequate housing was identified as a factor for roughly eleven percent of children who entered foster care and that homeless children enter foster care at many times the rate of their peers.
Commenters also contended that new documentation and proof-of-citizenship requirements would themselves jeopardize eligible children, including in households that struggle to produce records.
HUD Response:
These comments reflect a genuine and serious concern, and HUD does not take lightly the impact this rule will have on children in mixed-status households. As explained in the proposed rule, HUD acknowledges that this rulemaking will adversely affect mixed-status families, and that the most significant effect will be to transfer assistance from mixed-status to fully eligible households; an outcome that will fall in part on children in those households. This outcome follows from Section 214(d)(2), which does not permit HUD to provide continued assistance on behalf of an individual whose eligible status has not been verified, regardless of the age of that individual or of other household members and does not create an exception based on a family member's status as a child. As explained in HUD's responses above regarding preservation assistance, a family that does not qualify for continued assistance may seek temporary deferral of termination of assistance under § 5.518(b), and no termination may occur before completion of the informal hearing process under § 5.514(e); these protections apply to mixed-status families with children in the same manner as to other affected families.
HUD has considered the estimates cited by commenters, including the estimate that more than 771,000 children live in households that could potentially be affected by the rule. The actual effects will depend on the eligibility determinations of individual household members and the circumstances of each household. These estimates, however, represent the number of individuals who could potentially be affected by the changes and do not establish that all identified individuals will be evicted or lose housing assistance.
With respect to documentation burdens on U.S.-citizen children specifically, HUD notes that primary verification of citizenship will be conducted through SAVE not necessitating the collection of documents; however, to the extent that document submission is necessary, it is consistent with existing practice for many responsible entities, which already routinely collect identity documents such as birth certificates for other program purposes. HUD's Regulatory Impact Analysis estimates that approximately 20,000 mixed-status families received assistance as of December 2024, that children under 18 account for roughly 65 percent of the eligible family members in those households, and that families with children present, which HUD estimates likely leave assisted housing together rather than separate, represent approximately 16,000 (about 78 percent) of affected mixed-status families. HUD does not minimize this effect; as the Regulatory Impact Analysis explains, the net effect of the rule on homelessness is ambiguous, because any increase in homelessness among displaced mixed-status families may be offset by a decrease in homelessness among the fully eligible households, including formerly homeless households, who receive the reallocated assistance.
C. Harm to Specific Communities and Groups
Latino and Hispanic communities.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm Latino and Hispanic communities disproportionately and characterized its effect as discriminatory or racialized in impact. A commenter emphasized the disparate racial impact of the change, observing that mixed-status families are overwhelmingly families of color—on the order of 96 percent, with Latino families alone representing roughly 86 percent—such that more than 68,000 Latino participants would face separation or the loss of housing.
Commenters contended that the rule effectively penalizes Latino families for lawfully accessing subsidized housing to which eligible members are entitled. Commenters asserted that fear associated with the rule would deter
(
printed page 73011)
eligible members of Latino families from applying for or retaining assistance. Commenters maintained that the rule would increase eviction, homelessness, and displacement among Latino families.
A commenter maintained that the citizenship-status restrictions could result in increased racial profiling and discrimination targeting people of color and could deny U.S. citizens the ability to request housing assistance. A commenter requested that the agency not require U.S. citizens to prove citizenship as a condition of receiving support.
Black communities.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm black communities disproportionately, citing the number of black participants in mixed-status families who would be affected and barriers black U.S. citizens face in obtaining citizenship documentation.
Commenters stated that the rule would jeopardize housing assistance for an estimated 6,200 black participants in mixed-status families, and contended that black U.S. citizens face heightened barriers to obtaining citizenship documents, including older participants who may lack birth records, making them disproportionately likely to be harmed by new verification requirements.
AAPI communities.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities, citing their concentration in high-cost areas and multigenerational households, the number of AAPI households receiving assistance, and added barriers such as language access.
Commenters stated that a large number of AAPI households, cited as over 680,000, participate in public housing, Housing Choice Voucher, or project-based rental assistance programs, and argued that the rule would disproportionately affect AAPI families living in high-cost metropolitan areas and multigenerational, mixed-status households, compounded by language-access barriers.
Veterans.
Commenters, including one writing on behalf of veterans' legal clinic, argued that the proposed rule would harm veterans and their families who rely on assisted housing.
Persons with disabilities.
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm persons with disabilities by imposing new documentation burdens, creating barriers to accessible housing, straining disability-related fixed incomes, and increasing the risk of homelessness and institutionalization.
Commenters argued that tenants with disabilities face heightened barriers to completing the verification process, including mobility limitations that impede in-person document requests and cognitive or communication barriers that complicate navigation of federal systems. Commenters maintained that the added documentary steps would disproportionately burden disabled eligible citizens and could result in interruption of assistance where a tenant cannot complete the required steps within the timeframe allowed.
Commenters offered concrete illustrations of these barriers: one described beneficiaries who are elderly with dementia, who have developmental or psychiatric disabilities, or who have limited English, for whom obtaining and keeping identification is especially difficult.
Commenters stated that the rule's verification and documentation requirements would fall heavily on people with disabilities, including those for whom obtaining or producing records is difficult, and argued that some eligible tenants would lose assistance for inability to meet these requirements. Commenters contended that displacement would cost tenants their accessible or adapted units and that comparable accessible housing is scarce, creating barriers to relocation. Commenters asserted that tenants relying on SSI, SSDI, or similar fixed disability incomes could not absorb the loss of assistance without being pushed into poverty. Commenters maintained that the rule would increase eviction and homelessness among people with disabilities and, in some cases, force institutionalization for those with nowhere else to go.
HUD Response:
HUD recognizes the particular hardship this rule may pose for the communities and groups commenters identified, including Latino or Hispanic Americans, black Americans, AAPI participants, veterans, and participants with disabilities, including those in accessible or adapted units. As explained in the proposed rule and in HUD's responses above, Section 214(d)(2) does not permit HUD to provide continued assistance on behalf of an individual whose eligible status has not been verified, and this requirement does not vary based on a family member's race, national origin, disability, veteran status, or any other protected characteristic. HUD notes that families who do not qualify for continued assistance may seek temporary deferral of termination of assistance under § 5.518(b), and that no termination takes effect before completion of the informal hearing process under § 5.514(e), protections that apply equally to all affected participants.
HUD's regulations at § 5.502 require responsible entities to provide required notices and documents in a manner accessible to people with disabilities, consistent with
24 CFR 8.6
, and this rule does not alter that requirement.
HUD notes that veterans who are U.S. citizens or have eligible immigration status are not affected by this rule's verification requirements beyond the documentation and timing provisions applicable to all applicants and tenants, and that veteran family members without eligible status remain subject to the same preservation assistance protections, including temporary deferral of termination of assistance under § 5.518(b), available to other affected families.
D. Elderly Participants (Incl. Grandparents/Caregivers)
Commenters stated that eliminating the current exemption for individuals age 62 and older extends the verification obligation to household members previously excused from it. Commenters argued that the documentary requirement falls hardest on elderly citizens, who are least likely to have birth certificates or passports on hand and who face the greatest difficulty obtaining replacements. Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm elderly participants by disrupting caregiving and grandparent roles, straining fixed incomes, increasing homelessness among a fast-growing older population, and endangering the health of frail and vulnerable seniors. Commenters noted that many older tenants live on fixed incomes and face mobility, transportation, and technology barriers that make gathering documents especially burdensome. Commenters warned that these barriers place elderly eligible citizens at risk of losing assistance for administrative reasons unrelated to their eligibility.
Commenters stated that many elderly tenants are raising or caring for grandchildren and other kin, and argued that the rule would disrupt these caregiving arrangements and the households that depend on them. Commenters contended that seniors on fixed incomes would be forced to choose among rent, food, medication, and transportation, describing the loss of assistance as pushing basic needs out of reach. Commenters asserted that the rule would increase eviction and homelessness among seniors, whom they described as among the fastest-
(
printed page 73012)
growing segments of the homeless population. Commenters maintained that displacement would endanger the health of frail, disabled, or isolated elderly participants, with consequences including deteriorating health and increased mortality. Commenters argued that HUD's analysis understates the burden on older households, citing figures such as a large share of affected households headed by tenants over 62 and impacts spanning hundreds of counties. Commenters noted that multigenerational households and tenants with limited English proficiency would face added difficulty complying.
Commenters stated that the rule would eliminate both a longstanding documentation exemption and the Section 214 signed-declaration process available to tenants aged 62 and older, replacing them with documentation many cannot produce.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates commenters' attention to the particular circumstances of elderly participants, including those serving as caregivers for grandchildren or other family members. As explained in the proposed rule, HUD is removing the age-62 exemption currently reflected in §§ 5.508(b)(2) and 5.216(e) so that verification of citizenship or eligible immigration status applies uniformly to all applicants and tenants under Section 214 covered programs, regardless of age. HUD's rationale, as set forth in the proposed rule, is to bring its regulations into greater alignment with Section 214 and to make the verification process more uniform across the tenant population. With respect to practical burden, HUD notes that verification of eligible immigration status for noncitizens 62 and older will follow the same process already used for other noncitizens under this rule, and that primary verification of citizenship is conducted through collection and review of documentation under § 5.508(b), which responsible entities already routinely handle for other program purposes.
E. Survivors of Gender-Based Violence
Commenters argued that the proposed rule would harm survivors of gender-based violence by imposing documentation requirements that survivors fleeing violence cannot meet, conflicting with VAWA safety and confidentiality protections, and increasing the risk of homelessness.
Commenters noted that survivors of domestic violence may be separated from their identity documents or unable to access records held by an abuser, and that requiring documentary proof can expose survivors to additional risk. Commenters stated that survivors who have fled violence often leave without identity or immigration documents, and argued that the rule's documentation requirements would strip assistance from survivors unable to produce records. Commenters asserted that the loss of assistance would increase eviction and homelessness among survivors and their children. Commenters asked the agency to account for the circumstances of survivors who cannot readily obtain the required records.
Commenters contended that the rule conflicts with the safety and confidentiality protections extended to survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking, and trafficking, and warned that it could force survivors to remain with or return to an abuser to keep housing. Commenters contended that the rule conflicts with the protections Congress established for survivors under the Violence Against Women Act and the Trafficking Victims Protection Act. Commenters specified that survivors holding U-visas, T-visas, or VAWA self-petitions have documented status yet remain ineligible for HUD subsidy, so the rule would displace them from mixed-status households.
Additional commenters raised general concerns that the rule would harm survivors of gender-based violence, including their housing stability and ability to remain in contact with support services, without developing a further specific mechanism.
HUD Response:
HUD takes the safety of survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking, and trafficking seriously, and recognizes the particular difficulty this population may face in producing documentation. As explained in the proposed rule and in HUD's responses above, Section 214(d)(2) does not permit HUD to provide continued assistance on behalf of an individual whose eligible status has not been verified, and this rule does not create an exception based on a family member's status as a survivor of violence. HUD notes that families who do not qualify for continued assistance may seek temporary deferral of termination of assistance under § 5.518(b), and that no termination takes effect before completion of the informal hearing process under § 5.514(e). HUD's existing protections under
24 CFR part 5, subpart L
, implementing the Violence Against Women Act, including provisions governing confidentiality of information related to a survivor's status, are not altered by this rulemaking.
F. Formerly Homeless/Unhoused
Commenters explained that participants who have experienced homelessness frequently lack stable custody of identity documents, having lost or been unable to safeguard vital records during periods of instability. Commenters argued that requiring such participants to produce documentary proof would place newly or recently housed eligible citizens at risk of losing the assistance that stabilized their housing.
HUD Response:
HUD recognizes the particular difficulty that participants who have experienced homelessness may face in producing identity documentation and appreciates commenters raising this concern. As explained in the proposed rule and in HUD's responses above, primary verification of citizenship is conducted through SAVE, and responsible entities already routinely collect this type of documentation for other program purposes. HUD also lists multiple forms of documentation described in § 5.510. HUD notes that § 5.508(h), if granted, shall not exceed 60 days to submit required evidence where a family member certifies that the evidence needed is temporarily unavailable and that diligent efforts are being made to obtain it, and that responsible entities must notify individuals of their ability to pursue a records correction with any agency that issued or maintains relevant records at any point in the verification process, consistent with § 5.512(d).
8. Invest in and Strengthen Federal Housing Programs Instead
Commenters argued that the rule reflects misplaced priorities—spending on verification and enforcement machinery rather than on housing—and scapegoats immigrants for a systemic shortage. Commenters stated that the country faces a shortage of 7.1 million affordable rental units.
Commenters cited the administration's own budget requests proposing deep HUD cuts as evidence that housing stability is not a genuine priority, citing the FY2026 spending bill's partial funding to transition roughly 60,000 Emergency Housing Voucher families nationwide onto Tenant Protection Vouchers and the roughly 15,000 California EHV households at risk of eviction because that funding is insufficient. One commenter, writing as a local housing-authority commissioner in Florida, and others writing from Chicago and Los Angeles, urged that resources be redirected to maintaining and building housing in communities HUD had
(
printed page 73013)
previously failed; the Chicago commenter stated that thousands of public-housing units were demolished decades ago and that HUD never fulfilled its promise to build replacement housing. Commenters also invoked the 2019 defeat of a similar proposal, urging investment in federal housing programs rather than renewed scapegoating. Commenters contended that economists, housing authority officials, career HUD staffers, and policy experts agree the change will not lower housing costs and instead villainizes immigrants rather than the private-equity actors responsible for rising home prices and rents.
Commenters maintained that HUD should withdraw the proposal and instead work with Congress to make major new investments in the federal housing programs so that everyone has a safe and affordable place to call home. Commenters maintained that the proposed rule fails to address the root causes of unaffordability and would deepen the housing crisis rather than relieve it. Commenters framed the ask as a reallocation of existing funding toward assistance rather than verification, and several tied it to specific programs, urging continued growth of Housing Choice Vouchers, Project-Based Vouchers, the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (which the commenter urged be restored to match the 25 percent bond threshold changed by the One Big Beautiful Bill), HUD-VASH, HOME, CDBG, CDBG-DR, and homeownership programs. Commenters also grounded the demand in the depth of the affordability problem, noting that in no state can a full-time worker earning the minimum wage afford rent and that policies removing assistance from tens of thousands of households cut against federal efforts to reduce homelessness and improve long-term stability.
Commenters argued that the rule ignores the underlying shortage and that HUD should instead build and preserve affordable housing. One commenter offered concrete supply-side measures—eliminating parking minimums for new construction, simplifying entitlement and permitting to reduce delays, creating social housing and community land trusts, reshaping land-use and zoning rules toward mixed use, stabilizing fees, subsidies, and financing so building homes is less costly and more predictable, and strengthening tenant protections and preservation funding so tenants can stay housed. Another argued HUD should advocate for a larger budget so PHAs can operate and maintain existing units and construct new ones up to their Faircloth limit, and should seek repeal of the Faircloth limit to expand public housing. One commenter located the root cause in corporate acquisition of housing stock rather than immigrants, and another attributed Texas cost burdens (over half of Texas renter households cost-burdened (50.5 percent), more than a quarter paying above 50 percent of income (25.8 percent)) to persistently high interest rates, elevated construction costs, a reduced construction labor force, and stagnant federal funding, citing the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies' “America's Rental Housing 2026” report. A commenter argued that investing in immigrant-serving organizations and homeless harm-reduction organizations would be a better use of funds, and asked HUD to retain the existing mixed-status families rule and to support keeping families together.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees that the final rule reflects misplaced priorities. Rather, HUD believes that the final rule is consistent with the Administration's priorities concerning immigration-law enforcement, regulatory reform, and efficient administration of Federal programs. In particular, the rule is consistent with
Executive Order 14159
, “Protecting the American People Against Invasion,”
Executive Order 14165
, “Securing Our Borders,” and
Executive Order 14287
, “Protecting American Communities From Criminal Aliens,” which emphasize enforcement of the Nation's immigration laws and protection of public resources. The rule is also consistent with the Administration's broader regulatory reform and government-efficiency efforts, including
Executive Order 14222
, “Implementing the President's `Department of Government Efficiency' Cost Efficiency Initiative,” and
Executive Order 14238
, “Continuing the Reduction of the Federal Bureaucracy.” HUD believes that the proposed amendments further these objectives while bringing HUD's regulations into greater alignment with the statutory requirements of Section 214.
The rule is directed at who may receive assistance under existing programs, not at the size of the assisted-housing stock, and it therefore neither builds nor removes housing supply. As the Regulatory Impact Analysis explains, assistance no longer provided to mixed families is reallocated to fully eligible households already on program waiting lists. Building and preserving affordable housing is addressed through separate statutory authorities and appropriations, and nothing in Section 214 conditions its verification requirement on the pace of supply production. Accordingly, the availability of supply-side alternatives does not relieve HUD of its obligation under Section 214(d)(2) to verify eligibility before providing assistance. The Department nonetheless remains committed to pursuing, within its statutory authority and in coordination with Congress, regulatory and program improvements (such as through implementation of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act) that expand the supply of housing. Those efforts, however, are independent of, and do not displace, HUD's obligation under Section 214 to verify eligibility and to limit assistance to eligible persons.
9. Rule Is Contrary to Various Legal Requirements
A. Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act
Commenters argued that HUD's changes to the verification requirements for HUD participants exceed its authority under Section 214 and are inconsistent with the statute's express provisions. Commenters argued that Section 214 does not operate on individuals in the way the rule assumes and does not bar a household from assistance where one member is ineligible; instead, it directs prorated assistance so the family can remain together. Commenters grounded the conflict in the statute's operative language, arguing that the verification requirements apply with respect to financial assistance being or to be provided for the benefit of an individual, so a person not being or to be provided assistance falls outside the statutory verification requirement. Several read the verification text more narrowly than the rule: they argued the statute requires INS verification only for declarants younger than 62, so extending verification past that limit exceeds what the statute authorizes, and that Section 214 authorizes verification only by requiring presentation of documentation, giving HUD no basis to mandate SAVE searches of U.S. citizens.
Commenters also argued the statute assigns the verification-documentation decision to housing agencies and owners rather than to HUD, and that the Administration's immigration priorities cannot justify departing from Section 214's explicit terms.
They further argued that the age-62 declaration exemption is a deliberate choice by Congress that HUD may not override by rule. They argued the rule ignores Section 214's specific documentation exemptions for individuals aged 62 and older and for
(
printed page 73014)
children under 18, including a 1988 amendment expressly exempting older immigrants from the documentation requirements.
Commenters characterized the statute's use of “shall” as an imperative that leaves HUD no discretion to abandon the proration framework for mixed-eligibility families. Commenters stated that nothing in the statute requires eliminating ongoing prorated assistance for mixed-status households; it precludes only the provision of financial assistance to the ineligible member, which providers address by prorating the assistance. Commenters maintained that nothing in Section 214 mandates terminating assistance to an otherwise eligible household once proration has been applied, framing the change as a discretionary policy shift rather than a statutory mandate, and that the existing regulations already fulfill the purpose of Section 214 by ensuring no federal funds support ineligible members. Commenters argued that because Congress imposed no time limit on prorated assistance, HUD lacks authority to make it temporary, and that Congress knowingly permitted persons who decline an eligibility determination to reside in an assisted household, a choice HUD cannot reverse by rule.
Commenters also grounded arguments in case law, arguing that under decisions including
CMS Contract Management Services
v.
United States, 745 F.3d 1379, 1386 (Fed. Cir. 2014); Mertens

57 F.3d 270 (3d Cir. Ct. App. 1995), the statute's terms must be given their ordinary meaning and cannot be read to authorize what the rule does.
Commenters also invoked the rulemaking history, noting HUD's 1994 statement that Section 214 is specific about the special assistance to be provided to families with both eligible and ineligible members, at
59 FR 43900
,
