. They argued the proration framework reflects a deliberate policy choice by Congress that assistance may be provided to eligible members of mixed-status families so long as it is prorated, and that ending it contradicts HUD's prior interpretations and more than thirty years of sustained implementation. Commenters stated that, through Section 214, Congress intended to keep mixed-status families together, and that Congress enacted the prorated framework deliberately through the Housing and Community Development Act of 1987 as a compromise that limited new ineligible applicants while declining to break apart existing families. They added that if Congress had wished to end long-term prorated assistance it could have done so explicitly, and that HUD should not restrict statutory flexibility beyond what Congress authorized. A commenter contended that HUD may not make subjective legal determinations about the phrase for the benefit of that are not authorized by Congress or found in federal court rulings, and that HUD is neither a legislative nor a judicial body. Commenters added that even if the statutory language were ambiguous, the rule would still conflict with Congress's longstanding intent, established in the 1980 and later enactments, to allow mixed-status families to receive prorated assistance.
Commenters argued that the rule alters the regulatory definitions at
24 CFR part 5, subpart E
, that structure eligibility for mixed-status families, and does so in ways the statute does not require. They contended that many definitions in the current and proposed rule are inconsistent with Section 214, and that HUD lacks authority to delete or rewrite statutory definitions through this rulemaking.
Commenters argued the rule imposes a two-year disqualification on all members of a mixed household that exceeds the penalties Section 214 permits, and that, after
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
HUD's reinterpretation of these provisions receives no deference and must stand on the statute's text. They further argued the rule adopts non-statutory definitions of terms such as financial assistance and responsible entity, imposes penalties exceeding the statute including a two-year disqualification of all household members, and adds a new mandatory requirement to report individuals believed to be in violation of immigration law at 5.508(e)(2)(vi).
Commenters argued the elimination of the DHS and INS appeal procedures at § 5.514 independently violates the statute. Commenters argued that Section 214(d)(5) entitles a person whose assistance is denied or terminated on immigration-status grounds to a hearing with written findings and questioned how the rule complies with that requirement. They argued the informal hearing provided under § 5.514 is inadequate because it relies on the incomplete and untested SAVE system, leaving households unable to meaningfully contest an adverse determination, and that the rule provides insufficient timelines and disregards the practical barriers households face in responding.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees that the rule conflicts with Section 214. Section 214 prohibits the Secretary from making financial assistance available to persons other than U.S. citizens or specified categories of eligible noncitizens, and section 214(d)(2) provides that the Secretary “may not provide . . . assistance for the benefit of . . . [an] individual before documentation [of eligible immigration status] is presented and verified.” An individual without verified eligible status living in a mixed household receiving long-term prorated assistance is benefiting from HUD financial assistance in a way that is prohibited by Section 214. The rule brings HUD's implementing regulations into greater alignment with this text by requiring verification of the status of all applicants and recipients regardless of age and by treating prorated assistance as a temporary condition pending verification, “where permitted by statute.” The statute's proration provisions in section 214(c)(1)(A)-(B) are preservation-assistance provisions for families receiving assistance on February 5, 1988; this rule retains temporary prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination as the statute requires and does not abandon the framework Congress enacted.
As to the age-62 point, the preamble to the proposed rule explains that Section 214 conditions verification on the presentation of documentation and does not create a permanent, self-implementing exemption from status determination for older individuals; the current “do not contend” option, not the statute, is what produces no actual determination of status. HUD is retaining and modernizing the SAVE-based verification process it already uses for eligible immigration status and extending the same uniform process to declarations of U.S. citizenship, making verification more uniform for citizens and eligible noncitizens. Responsible entities remain the entities that collect and review documentation and submit information to SAVE, consistent with the statute's assignment of verification functions to housing agencies and owners.
HUD disagrees with commenters who say that the rule's definitions are inconsistent with the statute. HUD standardizes and updates language used in its definitions, but it intentionally did so consistent with the statute. By way of example, HUD replaces the obsolete “INS” definition with “DHS,” removes references to programs no longer in effect (the Rent Supplement and Section 235 programs, for which HUD notes no active contracts remain), standardizes the defined phrase “evidence of
(
printed page 73015)
citizenship or eligible status,” and adds a defined term “preservation assistance” that expressly includes the two statutory forms—prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination—implemented at §§ 5.516 and 5.518. Revised § 5.506(b) tracks the statute by providing at § 5.506(b)(3) that a family with at least one member of any age who has U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status is eligible for temporary prorated assistance under 5.520 pending final verification of other members.
Removing the outdated INS-appeal machinery in § 5.514 reflects the shift to SAVE while preserving an informal-hearing right.
The provision in
24 CFR 5.514(c)(1)(iii)
which terminates assistance of a family member who knowingly permitted another individual who is not eligible for assistance to reside (on a permanent basis) in the public or assisted housing unit of the family member for at least 2 years is a reasonable restriction on participation and is not inconsistent with statute.
HUD disagrees with the interpretation of § 5.508(e)(2)(vi) that it adds a new mandatory requirement to report individuals believed to be in violation of immigration law. It requires PHAs now notify tenants that they are required to notify DHS when a determination is made, consistent with the rules of this outlined in the proposed rule. There is no reporting requirement placed on tenants, and there is no requirement that PHAs or owners speculate on a tenant's citizenship status.
HUD disagrees with commenters that this rule removes the appeal process. This rule continues to provide the opportunity for informal appeal. The rule provides a meaningful process to contest determinations. HUD retains the statutory two-step verification structure: if primary verification through SAVE does not confirm status, the responsible entity must perform secondary verification and provide written notice that describes the primary-verification result, identifies the documentation or information needed, states deadlines, and informs the individual of the right to seek records corrections with the agency that issued or maintains the record at any time. The statute's reasonable-opportunity period (not to exceed 60 days) to submit further evidence is preserved. A family may then request an informal hearing under § 5.514(e), and, before any denial or termination, receives the notice required by § 5.514(d), which explains the reasons, the availability of proration pending final verification, and the criteria for preservation assistance.
The rule strengthens, rather than weakens, these safeguards relative to the outdated INS-appeal machinery it replaces, by adding the intermediate § 5.512(d)(1) notice and by allowing records correction at any point in the process. Assistance for applicants may be delayed during the informal-hearing process, but the hearing right and written-notice requirements remain intact, and existing tenants retain proration pending final verification.
B. Administrative Procedure Act—Arbitrary and Capricious
Commenters argued that the rule is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, asserting that HUD relied on inflated figures while omitting qualifying language and drew unsupported conclusions. Commenters argued the rulemaking record is procedurally deficient, analytically incomplete, and substantively insufficient to support the proposed changes under the standards the Administrative Procedure Act requires. They contended HUD's regulatory analysis does not quantify the costs it imposes or support its central assumptions, leaving the agency's conclusions without a basis in the record. They added that the regulatory impact analysis leaves its claimed benefits entirely unquantified and speculative, and that HUD disregards its own analysis predicting increased family homelessness.
Commenters argued that HUD's treatment of regulatory alternatives ignores that the existing regulations already comply with Section 214 and that the change would create substantial administrative burden and harm without justification. They contended HUD did not adequately weigh less burdensome alternatives or the reliance of currently assisted households before proposing to eliminate the prorated framework.
Commenters argued the changes are arbitrary and capricious because HUD substantially alters the eligibility verification process, including removing existing administrative provisions, without a reasoned explanation. They contended HUD mischaracterizes the prorated framework and offers a justification that does not support the departure from more than thirty years of consistent implementation. Commenters argued the rule reverses HUD's prior position without acknowledging or grappling with the earlier rulemaking record, contrary to the reasoned-explanation requirement.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates these comments but believes that these comments largely misunderstand or mischaracterize HUD's analysis. HUD believes that the proposed rule provides a reasoned explanation for its rulemaking and that both the proposed rule and the RIA show that HUD considered alternatives. The preamble in the proposed rule acknowledges that the rule would adversely affect some tenants, especially mixed families, and explains why HUD concluded that the reallocation of limited assistance to intended, fully eligible recipients justifies that cost.
The RIA analyzes regulatory alternatives, including grandfathering existing mixed families and applying the rule to new admissions only, limiting the change to households without children, and encouraging use of preservation assistance, and explains HUD's reasons for the chosen approach. Further, the proposed rule's preamble squarely addresses HUD's earlier construction, including the 1995 final rule's use of June 19, 1995 as the operative date, and explains why HUD now reads Section 214 to require verification of all members and to treat proration as temporary. That constitutes the reasoned explanation for a change in position that the record requires.
C. Administrative Procedure Act—Failure To Consider Reliance Interests
Commenters argued that mixed-status families have relied for decades on the prorated-assistance framework in arranging their housing and lives, and that HUD failed to account for those reliance interests before proposing to withdraw the framework. They contended that unwinding a longstanding policy on which households and housing providers have depended, without weighing that reliance, is a failure of reasoned decision-making. Commenters argued that reversing a longstanding policy requires a reasoned explanation acknowledging the change under
FCC
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.,
556 U.S. 502 (2009), and
Encino Motorcars, LLC
v.
Navarro,
579 U.S. __ (2016), that after
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2024), HUD's reinterpretation receives no deference, and that HUD ignored a less-disruptive alternative it had itself identified of grandfathering currently assisted families.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates these comments but again disagrees with the premise of the comments. HUD considered the position of currently assisted families. The preamble acknowledges that the rule would
(
printed page 73016)
adversely affect some tenants and applicants, especially mixed families, and the RIA devotes extended analysis to the effect on those households, including the number who may exit assistance, moving and eviction costs, and effects on homelessness. HUD did not treat existing participants as if the change were costless; it concluded that reallocating limited assistance to fully eligible households on waiting lists is warranted notwithstanding those effects.
As a threshold matter, reliance interests, however substantial, cannot override HUD's determination of what Section 214 itself permits. The reasoned-decision making requirement articulated in Fox and Encino Motorcars governs how an agency must explain a change in policy that falls within its discretion; it does not authorize an agency to perpetuate a practice that the statute does not permit simply because regulated parties or beneficiaries have come to depend on it. HUD has determined, based on the text of Section 214, that indefinite continued prorated assistance for mixed-status families is not a permissible reading of the statute. Because that determination concerns what the statute allows rather than a discretionary policy preference, commenters' reliance interests cannot supply a basis for retaining a practice the statute does not authorize. HUD's obligation to account for reliance interests is therefore properly addressed through the transition mechanisms discussed below, not through continuation of an ultra vires practice.
HUD also expressly identified and analyzed the grandfathering alternative. The RIA's Regulatory Alternatives section evaluates grandfathering all existing mixed families and applying the rule to new admissions only, under which mixed families would be replaced over time based on existing turnover trends, and evaluates continuing assistance to a subset of mixed families and encouraging preservation assistance to ease transition. In addition, the rule preserves transition mechanisms recognized by the statute—prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination of assistance (up to the statutory maximum deferral period)—which mitigate the disruption to families currently receiving assistance. Consideration and rejection of a less-disruptive alternative, with reasons, satisfies the obligation to account for reliance interests.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
Commenters argued the rule would newly require private housing providers to collect information, and that HUD improperly relies on an existing OMB control number to avoid a fresh information-collection review under the Paperwork Reduction Act. They contended the rule's paperwork-burden analysis understates the added burden the new collection imposes. They argued the rule imposes a new information collection whose burden HUD understates, that the added applicant-notice step at § 5.512(d)(1) compounds that burden without analysis, and that the notice itself is so convoluted that it defeats meaningful notice and comment.
HUD Response:
HUD satisfied its procedural obligations. The information-collection requirements were approved by OMB under control number 2577-0295, and the preamble sets out the estimated burden, including tabulations of one-time and annual reporting burden by program (for example, one-time Section 8 HCV burden of 11,990 respondents at 1.25 hours each). HUD explains that the added burden is relatively low because most existing tenants have already provided identity documentation for other purposes—an estimated 99 percent of existing U.S.-citizen tenants have already been verified—and because primary verification uses the same SAVE input for citizens and noncitizens. The notice step at § 5.512(d)(1) arises only when primary verification does not confirm status and is reflected in the burden estimate.
E. Regulatory Flexibility Act
Commenters argued the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires HUD to consider regulatory alternatives affecting small entities, and that HUD did not adequately do so before proposing the rule. Commenters said that HUD's minimal-impact assertion is baseless because all assisted families must undergo re-verification. They also argued the notice's added SAVE-notice steps at § 5.512(d)(1) compound burden without adequate analysis.
HUD Response:
HUD satisfied its procedural obligations. HUD certified that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, supported by data that in 2024, 92 percent of PHAs and 97 percent of housing owners had mixed families representing less than five percent of their assisted households, and that primary verification uses the same automated SAVE process for all declarants. HUD nonetheless invited comment on less burdensome alternatives. On the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, HUD determined the rule imposes no federal mandate on State, local, or tribal governments or the private sector within the meaning of UMRA. The rule was published for a 60-day comment period.
F. National Environmental Policy Act
Commenters argued that the rule would displace households and change occupancy across federally assisted housing at a scale requiring environmental review, and that HUD proceeded without the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) analysis the action requires. Commenters argued HUD's own NEPA regulations require review of socio-economic effects such as displacement and homelessness, that the action's intensity and context warrant an environmental impact statement, and that
Executive Order 12898
requires environmental-justice review of adverse effects on minority and low-income populations.
HUD Response:
As explained in the proposed rule, because the rule does not direct, provide for assistance or loan and mortgage insurance for, or otherwise govern or regulate, real property acquisition, disposition, leasing, rehabilitation, alteration, demolition, or new construction or establish, revise or provide for standards for construction or construction materials, manufactured housing, or occupancy, the rule is categorically excluded from environmental review under NEPA. In addition,
Executive Order 12898
was rescinded by
Executive Order 14173
on January 21, 2025.
G. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Commenters argued that the rule implicates the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act by shifting costs to state and local governments.
HUD Response:
Taking the statute as a whole, it is HUD's interpretation that an individual cannot elect to not contend eligible status. The declaration contemplated by the statute offers only two options: either the individual (i) is a U.S. citizen or (ii) has satisfactory immigration status. To better align HUD's regulations with Section 214, HUD is eliminating the option for individuals not to contend eligible status. The effect of this change makes the provision of proration found in
42 U.S.C. 1436a(b)(2)
temporary pending affirmative verification of eligibility or ineligibility of all family members. As for the PHA discretion in Section 214(i)(2), HUD does not interpret this provision to offer permanent discretion to PHAs as to whether or not to verify eligibility, as such an interpretation would contradict Section 214's
(
printed page 73017)
restriction of financial assistance to individuals with affirmatively established immigration status.
H. Fair Housing Act and the Duty to Affirmatively Further Fair Housing
Commenters argued that HUD failed to consider the rule's disparate impacts, including on U.S. citizens with disabilities who rely on ineligible household members for care. Commenters argued the rule would produce disproportionate harm to immigrant, Latino, and other protected communities without sufficient justification, in violation of the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on facially neutral policies that have a discriminatory effect. They argued the harm falls on families with children, implicating familial-status protections. Commenters expressly invoked the disparate-impact framework of
Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs
v.
Inclusive Communities,
576 U.S. 519 (2015), and its burden-shifting analysis, advanced an intentional-discrimination theory under the Arlington Heights factors, and argued that families with children are protected under the Act's familial-status provisions.
Commenters argued the rule would violate HUD's statutory obligation to administer its programs affirmatively to further fair housing, because HUD's own analysis predicts the greatest harm to families with children and to protected communities, the opposite of furthering fair-housing goals. They cited HUD's contemporaneous English-Only policy as further evidence that the agency was abandoning rather than advancing its fair-housing obligations.
Commenters, including local governments, argued the rule is inconsistent with commitments to affirmatively further fair housing and equitable access, and urged HUD to evaluate the disparate impacts before proceeding.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees with comments alleging that the rule violates the Fair Housing Act. The rule merely provides updates to procedures to verify eligibility for programs covered by Section 214. The Housing and Community Development Act establishes the statutory eligibility requirements for the covered housing programs. This rule does not restrict access to housing under these programs on the basis of any protected class. Establishing procedures to follow statutory guidelines has no bearing on the agency's statutory directive to affirmatively further fair housing since no person is being denied housing on the basis of a protected class.
I. Americans With Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act
Commenters argued that separating a tenant with a disability from a needed caregiver, or the loss of an accessible unit, would violate Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act. A commenter protected under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act argued that the rule would remove a household member who is an irreplaceable part of his support system, conflicting with the accommodation and integration obligations those statutes impose.
HUD Response:
The rule does not alter HUD's or responsible entities' obligations under the Americans with Disabilities Act or Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which continue to apply in full to the administration of Section 214 covered programs, including any reasonable-accommodation obligations. The rule verifies eligibility against the statutory citizenship and immigration-status categories and does not classify or disadvantage any individual on the basis of disability.
To the extent an individual member of a household does not have verified eligible status, the statutory eligibility restriction, not the individual's or a household member's disability, governs the availability of federal assistance. Eligible members retain prorated assistance pending final verification and remain protected by the preservation-assistance provisions the rule preserves.
J. Other Federal Statutes
Commenters argued the rule expands the collection and sharing of citizenship and immigration-status information in ways that raise conflicts with federal privacy protections. They further argued the rule's treatment of “federal public benefit” and related provisions is inconsistent with the governing federal definitions Congress enacted. Commenters developed the SAVE-related conflicts in detail, arguing that the overhauled SAVE system violates the Privacy Act by repurposing records in bulk without a valid routine-use basis and by failing the Act's data-accuracy obligations; that sharing Social Security Administration data with DHS violates the Social Security Act's disclosure restrictions at
42 U.S.C. 1306(a)
; and that the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, which created SAVE, did not authorize the system's expansion. They further argued that HUD lacks statutory authority to require owners and public housing agencies to make PRWORA reports to DHS and that compelling such reporting raises anti-commandeering concerns.
HUD Response:
The rule does not exceed HUD's authority or conflict with the federal information-sharing framework it relies on. Verification is performed through the DHS/USCIS SAVE program, which HUD already uses for eligible-immigration-status verification, and the rule requires each family member to sign a verification consent form authorizing responsible entities to collect and review status evidence and to release it to HUD and, for verification purposes, to DHS. The rule limits use of that information to verifying U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status. HUD's participation in SAVE is governed by a memorandum of agreement, and the reporting referenced in the rule tracks the existing PRWORA section 404 framework described in the 2000 Interagency Notice rather than creating a new sharing regime.
Because the rule builds on collections already approved under OMB control number 2577-0295 and on the established SAVE architecture, HUD does not agree that it repurposes records without basis or expands SAVE beyond its authorized function.
K. Constitution
Commenters argued the rule would force families to choose between remaining together and keeping their housing, burdening the constitutionally protected interest in family integrity the Supreme Court has recognized. They argued that denying benefits to eligible U.S.-citizen children based solely on a parent's status infringes those children's constitutional interest in familial integrity, and that the rule is unconstitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment as well.
Commenters argued that terminating housing assistance directly affects housing stability and the ability to remain housed, so doing so without adequate notice and hearing deprives households of a protected interest without due process. They argued the Fifth Amendment's guarantees extend to persons rather than citizens alone, so noncitizens household members are entitled to basic procedural protections, and that the process the rule provides falls short of both federal and state constitutional due-process requirements.
Commenters argued the rule violates the Fifth Amendment's equal-protection component by treating U.S. citizens who live with immigrant family members differently from other U.S. citizens, without adequate justification. They argued the rule discriminates against
(
printed page 73018)
Latino families on the basis of race, national origin, and familial status, and that official action reflecting a racially discriminatory purpose cannot stand. Citing
Plyler
v.
Doe,
457 U.S. 202 (1982), commenters argued that imposing severe burdens on children based on immigration status fails constitutional scrutiny. One commenter argued the rule is controlled by
Department of Agriculture
v.
Moreno,
413 U.S. 528 (1973), in which the Supreme Court struck down, on equal-protection grounds, a program provision excluding any household containing a particular disfavored member.
HUD Response:
The rule does not compel any family to separate. Rather, it implements Section 214's restrictions on providing Federal housing assistance to ineligible individuals, which also precludes allowing an individual without verified eligible status from living in a subsidized housing unit. Families may continue to live together, but they may not do so indefinitely while receiving Federal subsidies.
The rule also preserves transition protections—prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination of assistance—that give families additional time to make housing arrangements. Any effect on household composition results from the family's own choices in response to the statutory eligibility restriction, not from a governmental directive to separate.
As discussed more fully above, HUD disagrees with commenters that this rule impinges upon a family's due process rights. This rule continues to provide the opportunity for informal appeal and provides a meaningful process to contest determinations. The rule strengthens, rather than weakens, these safeguards relative to the outdated INS-appeal machinery it replaces, by adding the intermediate § 5.512(d)(1) notice and by allowing records correction at any point in the process. Assistance for applicants may be delayed during the informal-hearing process, but the hearing right and written-notice requirements remain intact, and existing tenants retain proration pending final verification.
HUD also disagrees that the rule violates equal protection requirements. The rule implements a line Congress itself drew. Section 214 restricts assistance to U.S. citizens and specified categories of eligible noncitizens; the rule verifies eligibility against those statutory categories and does not create a new classification. The distinction between eligible and ineligible persons is the statutory eligibility distinction, and the RIA explains the rule's purpose in program terms—targeting limited assistance to fully eligible households.
The rule applies uniform verification to all declarants regardless of age, race, or any other protected class, and does not single out any protected group for adverse treatment on a basis other than the statutory eligibility categories.
HUD also notes that
Department of Agriculture
v.
Moreno
is not relevant to this situation.
Moreno
involved a law which conditioned the provision of food stamps to households based on whether the members of the household were related. In
Moreno,
absent relation requirement, each individual would have been eligible for the benefit provided. Whereas this rule deals with households that contain individuals not independently eligible for assistance. Further, this rule clearly advances the government's interest of ensuring that assistance is only used on eligible members.
L. Conflict With Executive Orders
Commenters argued the rule conflicts with executive directives, including federalism requirements and directives concerning child and family welfare, because it would override state and local arrangements and produce family harms without the consideration those directives require. Commenters elaborated that the rule fails the deregulatory requirements of
Executive Order 14192
“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” which directs agencies to identify at least ten regulations for repeal and to offset new compliance costs, because HUD identified no offsetting regulations to remove; that it does not satisfy the cost-benefit and alternatives analysis required by Executive Orders 12866 and 13563; and that HUD wrongly claimed
Executive Order 13132
did not apply, skipping the required early consultation with State and local officials and the federalism summary impact statement. Commenters further argued that HUD improperly relies on
Executive Order 14218
as a justification for the rule, contending that an executive order cannot override the express terms of Section 214 and that courts have already enjoined portions of that order. One commenter also argued the rule does not comply with the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Division D, Title II, Section 242), which requires HUD rulemaking to follow
Executive Order 12866
and to allow at least 60 days for comment. A commenter objected that the rulemaking process, including the comment opportunity, was inadequate.
HUD Response:
This rule is exempted from
Executive Order 14192
, section 5(a).
Executive Order 14218
is valid justification as a reason for why HUD is considering this rule change at all. As explained in the proposed rule, HUD has fully complied with the requirements of Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 by providing the regulatory impact analysis and through coordinating with the Office of Management and Budget. This rule does not impose direct compliance costs on State and local governments, nor does it preempt state law, so the rule is in compliance with
Executive Order 13132
. Finally, the proposed rule was put out for 60 days of public comment.
M. Contract and PHA Legal Exposure
Commenters argued the rule would place PHAs in breach of their existing contracts, and that, because HUD would be making unauthorized legal determinations about the phrase for the benefit of, the rule invites litigation. They added that, with
Chevron
deference no longer available, HUD's reinterpretation of the governing statutes would be subject to prolonged legal challenge. Commenters argued that compelled evictions would breach existing tenant leases and that the rule is likely unenforceable because its drafting is ambiguous and defines eligible households inconsistently.
HUD Response:
The rule does not place responsible entities in breach. PHA and owner obligations under their HUD contracts, and the leases they administer, are subject to the federal eligibility and verification requirements of Section 214 and its implementing regulations; conforming those requirements to the statute does not create a contractual conflict. HUD retains the notice, secondary-verification, and informal-hearing procedures before any denial or termination and preserves prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination, so that terminations proceed only through the established process.
HUD also does not agree that the rule is unenforceably vague. The preamble defines operative terms and specifies the verification steps, deadlines, and hearing rights in the regulatory text, providing responsible entities with a clear compliance path.
N. Impermissible Retroactivity
Commenters argued that applying the new verification and eligibility requirements to families already residing in assisted housing would impose new legal consequences on past arrangements, displacing households that entered and remained in the program under the prior framework.
(
printed page 73019)
They contended that terminating or reducing assistance for currently assisted mixed-status households on this basis operates retroactively against settled expectations.
HUD Response:
The rule is not impermissibly retroactive. It changes the conditions on which assistance is provided going forward; it does not impose penalties or new legal consequences on past conduct. HUD's existing regulations already condition continued assistance on ongoing eligibility, verification, and recertification, and the rule operates prospectively from the effective date of any final rule. The rule also provides transition periods rather than immediate divestiture.
HUD also retains the statute's transition protections for existing households. Prorated continued assistance and temporary deferral of termination of assistance under
24 CFR 5.516
and
5.518
remain available to eligible families, and temporary deferral affords additional time to transition to other housing. Applying updated, prospective verification requirements to participants who must in any event undergo periodic recertification does not attach new consequences to completed transactions; it adjusts the terms of an ongoing benefit.
O. Conflict With State Law and State Preemption
Commenters argued the rule would place housing providers in conflict with state just-cause and tenant-protection laws by compelling terminations those laws do not permit. They contended it would also conflict with State limits on inquiring about or disclosing immigration status, exposing providers to liability under both Federal and State regimes.
HUD Response:
Congress has determined the requirements for who may reside in housing assisted with Federal programs. Section 214 prohibits Federal assistance to ineligible individuals, State or local law cannot override the Federal statute. Given the statutory requirement that Federal housing assistance only be provided to those with an eligible status, any terminations of assistance based on that would be considered just-cause and would be within the bounds of State and local law. Further, by enacting Section 214, Congress established a statutory framework requiring HUD to administer eligibility restrictions and immigration-status verification procedures. In carrying out these responsibilities, HUD possesses statutory authority to promulgate regulations necessary to implement the requirements of Section 214, including the authority to require disclosure of immigration status thus overriding State or local law should there be a conflict. At this juncture HUD does not foresee any conflicts between state and local laws, and this final rule. For example, California's Immigration Tenant Protection Act: AB 291 and AB 299 (2018), explicitly states that it does not prohibit a landlord from: (1) complying with any legal obligation under federal law, including, but not limited to, any legal obligation under any federal government program that provides for rent limitations or rental assistance to a qualified tenant, or a subpoena, warrant, or other order issued by a court; and (2) Requesting information or documentation necessary to determine or verify the financial qualifications of a prospective tenant, or to determine or verify the identity of a prospective tenant or prospective occupant. Civ.i Code §§ 1940.3(c)(1),(2). See also, Civ. Code § 1942.5(k). As such, this final rule does not conflict with California's Immigration Tenant Protection Act because it falls squarely under the exceptions as provided by the law.
10. Ideological Objections to the Rule
Commenters objected to the proposed rule on several ideological grounds. Some commenters characterized the proposed rule as cruel, inhumane, and counterproductive. Commenters asserted the rule is engineered to punish families rather than to reform administration, describing it as a radical overhaul that would harm thousands of families and dismantle protections for the most vulnerable, and framing it as an attempt to maneuver around constitutional protections while penalizing citizens with families. One characterized the administration's stated justification as pretext for pursuing immigration policy by denying immigrant families housing assistance they have long been entitled to and creating fear in immigrant communities. A commenter asked what purpose is served by punishing mixed-status families, many with pending citizenship, and stated the change would cause real hardship to thousands of citizens and their loved ones.
Commenters opposed to this rule also state their opposition due to their religious beliefs. Catholic commenters invoked the dignity of the person, the sanctity of the family, and the common good. A commenter stated that by forcing families to move, HUD would be denying them the ability to practice their faith in their own community. Commenters stated that the increased housing instability that the rule would generate would impact families' ability to practice their faith—one cannot keep the Sabbath, observe Ramadan, or gather for prayer without knowing where the family will sleep. Some commenters grounded their opposition in scripture and religious teaching, invoking the command to welcome the stranger, to shelter the homeless, and to love one's neighbor.
Commenters characterized the rule as advancing a racist and xenophobic agenda and objected that it targets immigrant families. Commenters objected that HUD's own framing dehumanizes immigrant families, pointing to public statements characterizing mixed families as fraudsters, illegal aliens, and ineligibles told to pack their bags. Commenters argued that the rule is a pretext for discriminating against a disfavored class and that the Secretary's public statements reveal a different purpose from general statutory alignment. One situated the rule within what it characterized as a broader, cross-agency agenda to target immigrants from majority non-white countries, tracing that agenda to named senior officials and prior HUD actions.
Commenters argued the rule scapegoats immigrant communities amid intensified enforcement. One pointed to expanded detention and deportation activity and cited deaths in immigration detention—32 in 2025 and at least 14 more in 2026—arguing the rule compounds already dangerous enforcement practices Commenters also objected that the government should not condition assistance on the immigration status of household members, calling the result a human-rights violation.
Commenters characterized the rule as unjust. One argued the change would add to an already large unhoused population and amounted to cruel and unusual treatment. Others objected that the rule is morally wrong, describing it as immoral, sinful, and indefensible and urging HUD to abandon it.
Commenters characterized the rule as shameful and disgraceful, calling it a stain on the agency and the country. Commenters objected that the rule disregards the inherent worth of the people it affects. Some argued the rule treats people as administrative categories rather than individuals. Commenters stated that treating one member's ineligibility as grounds to destabilize an entire household fails to treat people as moral agents deserving of dignity and urged HUD to act with compassion and basic decency, asking that families be treated humanely rather than displaced.
(
printed page 73020)
A commenter characterized the rule as unconscionable and contrary to American values, stating it would affect thousands of families that include American citizens and would force families to choose between housing and staying together. Others argued the rule betrays HUD's core mission and its public-service duty to house people in need and create strong, sustainable, inclusive communities and quality affordable homes, because it would increase homelessness rather than reduce it. A commenter argued the rule directly conflicts with HUD's mission to provide decent, safe, and affordable housing to the communities most in need, because it would impose significant administrative and financial burdens on public housing authorities while reducing assistance.
HUD Response:
HUD disagrees with the characterization of the rule as unjust, morally wrong, or shameful, intended to punish families, contrary to HUD's mission and statutory purpose, or a violation of a fundamental right. HUD takes seriously its responsibility to implement and enforce the law to ensure that Federal housing assistance funded by the U.S. taxpayer is used for the benefit of families who are eligible under U.S. law. To the extent that such housing assistance is currently used for the benefit of ineligible families, it is unavailable to eligible families who face many of the challenges asserted in these comments, ranging from homelessness to family separation to the lack of a community in which to establish roots, participate in public services, and achieve stability. Whether an individual is eligible for Federal housing assistance in the United States has no bearing on the inherent worth of that individual, and HUD rejects outright that the rule is a pretext for discriminating against a disfavored class.
HUD also respects the religious convictions reflected in these comments, but the eligibility restriction and verification requirement apply uniformly on the basis of citizenship or eligible immigration status and are not directed at any commenter's faith or religious exercise; nothing in the rule restricts any family's ability to practice its faith or to seek shelter from private, charitable, or faith-based sources.
11. Change Requests
A. Withdraw or Substantially Revise the Rule
Commenters urged HUD to withdraw or rescind the proposed rule in its entirety. Commenters urged HUD to reconsider the proposed rule and instead pursue approaches that maintain flexibility, ensure realistic timelines, conduct further impact analysis, and protect current participants; commenters added that prorated assistance should remain for families with ineligible members. Commenters stated that HUD advanced a nearly identical proposal in 2019, that it received over 30,000 public comments with approximately 95 percent in opposition, and that it was never finalized and was formally withdrawn by the Biden Administration in 2021 (in part as inconsistent with
Executive Order 14012
); they argued the current rule revives that withdrawn effort without grappling with the earlier rulemaking record.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates commenters' concerns about the impacts of the proposed rule and their recommendations that HUD withdraw, reconsider, or substantially revise the proposal. After considering the comments received, HUD has determined that withdrawing or fundamentally reconsidering the rule is not warranted.
Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 (
42 U.S.C. 1436a
) establishes restrictions on the provision of financial assistance based on citizenship and eligible immigration status. HUD has determined that the regulatory amendments adopted in this final rule further the Department's implementation of Section 214 by strengthening verification requirements and ensuring that HUD-assisted housing is provided in accordance with applicable eligibility requirements. The final rule also makes prorated assistance a temporary condition pending verification of the eligible status of all family members, where permitted by statute, rather than a status that may continue indefinitely, further aligning HUD's regulations with the wording and purpose of Section 214.
B. Request for Clarification of Rule Status
A commenter stated it is unclear whether the reported 60-90-day documentation requirements have been formally implemented or remain under consideration and requested clear guidance on whether the policies are currently in effect or still prospective, the anticipated timeline for any final rule, how existing households will be treated, and what protections, extensions, or accommodations will be available.
HUD Response:
The requirements described in the proposed rule were proposals and did not take effect upon publication of the proposed rule. Existing families remain subject to the requirements in effect until the applicable provisions of this final rule become effective. Therefore, any extensions or other protections available under HUD's current regulations will continue to apply until they are replaced by the provisions in this final rule.
The final rule establishes the requirements that HUD is adopting, including the applicable documentation, verification requirements, and the treatment of existing assisted households. HUD may issue additional implementation guidance, as appropriate, to assist responsible entities in implementing the final rule's requirements.
C. Extend Comment Period/Hearings/Consultation
Commenters requested that, at a minimum, HUD extend the public comment period and conduct public hearings in the regions most affected to allow full consideration of the impacts identified in HUD's own regulatory impact analysis and of less harmful alternatives.
HUD Response:
The proposed rule clearly identified the changes under consideration and the issues on which HUD sought public comment. HUD believes it provided interested parties with adequate notice and an opportunity to respond to the proposed rule.
The Administrative Procedure Act does not prescribe a minimum comment period, nor require HUD to extend a comment period. HUD believes that the 60-day period afforded the public a meaningful opportunity to submit data, views, and arguments regarding the proposed rule.
HUD received more than 16,000 comments during the 60-day comment period. The breadth of the public's participation supports HUD's position that the public had a meaningful opportunity to participate in the rulemaking process.
Further, the proposed rule builds substantially on an existing statutory and regulatory framework. Interested parties were not required to evaluate an entirely new regulatory framework within the 60-day period. Section 214 and HUD's implementing regulations already govern citizenship/immigration eligibility and verification. Many affected responsible entities already have experience with the underlying requirements. The rule's new requirements would build on existing verification procedures (including SAVE) and existing methods of calculated prorated assistance.
(
printed page 73021)
D. Substantive Changes
A commenter recommended specific implementation measures should HUD proceed: adopting a one-time status-evidence requirement per family member during continuous occupancy with an obligation to report changes; setting a secondary-verification service-level target (
e.g.,
10 business days) and clarifying that assistance is not terminated or delayed while secondary verification is pending when acceptable documentation is on file; publishing a verification workflow covering initial and secondary SAVE steps, evidence standards, and typical timelines; and providing a privacy summary referencing the 2025 SAVE PIA/SORN updates.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates the commenters' recommendations regarding implementation of the final rule and notes that the rule includes provisions that address several of the issues raised by the commenters.
First, HUD notes that § 5.508(a)(5) already provides that, for each family member, evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status is generally required to be submitted once during continuously assisted occupancy under a Section 214 covered program. The regulation further requires a family to immediately notify the responsible entity and submit evidence of the new status if a family member's citizenship or immigration status changes during occupancy.
Additionally, proposed § 5.512(d)(3) establishes a specific timeframe for secondary verification of eligible immigration status by requiring the responsible entity to request additional verification through SAVE within 30 days of notification of the results of primary verification.
With respect to the commenters' concerns regarding adverse action while secondary verification remains pending, § 5.514(b)(1)(i) in the rule provides that assistance to an applicant or tenant may not be delayed, denied, reduced, or terminated, on the basis of lack of U.S. citizenship or ineligible immigration status of a family member if the applicable verification process under §  5.512, including secondary verification under §  5.512(d), has been timely instituted but has not yet completed.
Regarding the commenters' recommendation that HUD provide additional information concerning the privacy implications of the verification process, specifically related to applicable Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) and Systems of Record Notices (SORNs), HUD recognizes the importance of protecting personally identifiable information used in the verification process and will comply with all applicable Federal privacy requirements. HUD will consider whether additional privacy-related information or guidance would be appropriate in conjunction with the final rule.
HUD may issue additional implementation guidance or technical assistance, as appropriate, to responsible entities in implementing the final rule's requirements.
E. Compliance Timeline & Transition Requests
Commenters argued that the rule's compliance timelines were operationally unrealistic and asked HUD to provide phased implementation, longer windows, and clearer guidance. A commenter characterized the proposed timeline for time-limited proration as operationally unrealistic, requiring agencies to track additional deadlines, communicate changes to households, and handle hardship cases on a monthly basis while managing existing program demands. A commenter argued that the timelines for documentation collection and verification are infeasible given the unprecedented scale of reverification, anticipated delays in obtaining official records, and PHA capacity constraints. A commenter contended that the rule pairs a highly complex notice with a 90-day compliance window and only a single 30-day extension, which families cannot realistically meet. The commenter further explained that because the compliance clock runs from the rule's effective date rather than from the date a family is actually notified, households could lose much of the window—or all of it—before they learn the requirement applies to them. A commenter objected specifically to requiring mixed households to certify eligibility within 90 days of adoption while other households wait until their next income certification, calling the disparity unjustified. A commenter emphasized that the 30-day notice period is insufficient and places significant operational strain on providers navigating complex verification while attempting to maintain tenant stability. A commenter argued the rule lacks clear implementation guidance for how PHAs should proceed when families cannot meet verification timelines or when terminations are delayed through the legal process.
Commenters requested a defined transition period before the rule takes effect. A commenter proposed a set of specific alternatives: delaying the effective date by at least six months to allow PBRA-assisted private property owners and PHAs to revise admissions and occupancy policies and procedures; tying verification timelines to each household's next annual reexamination rather than a fixed post-adoption deadline; permitting more than one 30-day extension; and allowing more than three six-month deferral periods before terminating assistance to mixed-status households. Commenters argued that the new responsibilities, combined with the 90-day compliance window following the effective date, would cause a significant shift in property management and operations with little room for error.
Commenters urged HUD to lengthen the compliance and relief timelines, asking for an implementation window of at least six months and for more generous extension and deferral allowances. Commenters argued that no rule of this magnitude should take effect in less than six months, given the time PHAs need to update internal controls and prevent wrongful terminations of eligible individuals. A commenter urged that PHAs be permitted to grant multiple 30-day extensions to accommodate bureaucratic delays and documentation costs. A commenter maintained that mixed-status households should be allowed more than three six-month deferrals to facilitate stable transitions and prevent abrupt loss of housing.
Commenters urged that the rule not take effect immediately upon finalization, asking HUD to provide an adequate implementation period, clear standardized guidance, and lead time before enforcement so agencies can revise admissions and occupancy policies. A commenter added that notification and documentation timelines should begin at each household's next annual reexamination so families have adequate time to gather records.
HUD Response:
HUD acknowledges commenters' requests for additional time and phased transition procedures and has structured the rule to provide a measured implementation period rather than an immediate cutoff. HUD believes that, to the extent the current regulations are not in compliance with Section 214, it is valuable to come into compliance as soon as practicable. There are individuals who will be harmed by unnecessary delay—individuals who are currently assisted by HUD programs may be ineligible for that assistance, while eligible individuals remain on waiting lists. In the interest of serving eligible families
(
printed page 73022)
as soon as possible, HUD chooses not to delay the effective date of this rule further than necessary. Although the rule becomes effective 30 days after publication, the effective date does not require all existing households to complete the new verification process on that date. The majority of households will have a year or more to submit evidence of U.S. citizenship. Accordingly, HUD determined that affected households and responsible entities will have sufficient time to comply with the new requirements, without requiring further delay the rule's effective date.
Under the notice provisions, responsible entities must give each tenant who has not submitted evidence of citizenship or eligible status the required Section 214 notification no later than 30 days after the effective date of the final rule. Under § 5.508(f)(2)(i), tenants in mixed families who have not previously submitted the required evidence must do so within 90 days of the effective date, while other affected tenants submit at their next annual or interim reexamination of income and household composition, in accordance with program requirements. HUD determined that an earlier submission deadline is appropriate for mixed families because changes made by this rule may affect a mixed-status family's continued eligibility for assistance before the family's next scheduled reexamination. Deferring submission of the required evidence until the next annual or interim reexamination could therefore result in assistance continuing beyond the point at which the family is no longer eligible under the applicable requirements. By contrast, for other existing tenants, HUD has determined that collection of the required evidence may appropriately be incorporated into the ordinary reexamination process, thereby reducing administrative burden on responsible entities and tenants. The differing timeframes thus reflect the different circumstances of these groups while allowing implementation to be staggered where appropriate.
HUD appreciates commenters' concerns regarding the interaction between the notice and documentation requirements. HUD has considered these concerns but declines to tie the 90-day compliance period to the date on which each individual family receives notice. Creating uniform periods measured from the effective date provides clear and administrable implementation deadlines for both responsible entities and mixed families. HUD encourages responsible entities to provide notice of Section 214 requirements as promptly as practicable following the rule's effective date. Responsible entities remain responsible for complying with the applicable notice requirements, and a family should not be adversely affected by a responsible entity's failure to provide required notice in accordance with the rule.
The rule also builds in transition flexibility at the individual level. Under § 5.508(g), responsible entities may grant a family additional time to submit evidence, regardless of how many family members are included in that extension. HUD acknowledges that some individuals may face barriers in obtaining documents and is, therefore, providing additional flexibility in this final rule for responsible entities to grant an extension of up to 60 days. For families that include ineligible members, temporary deferral of termination of assistance remains available under §§ 5.516 and 5.518: the initial deferral period may not exceed six months and may be renewed in six-month increments up to an aggregate of 18 months, affording additional time to arrange alternative housing.
Finally, the evidence requirement is a one-time obligation. Under § 5.508(f)(5), a family must submit evidence for a given family member only once during continuously assisted occupancy under any Section 214 covered program, so the transition burden described by commenters is an upfront cost of adjustment rather than a recurring requirement at every recertification.
F. Apply Prospectively Only/Grandfather Current Participants
Commenters requested that, should HUD proceed to a final rule, any new eligibility or verification requirements apply prospectively only—to future applicants and those on the waiting list—and not to current participants who relied in good faith on existing regulations, noting that a prospective-only approach is explicitly identified in HUD's own regulatory impact analysis as a regulatory alternative and the least harmful form of implementation, and adding that prospective application does not weaken the rule's deterrent effect on future applicants. Commenters warned that retroactive application would penalize participants who complied in good faith with existing regulations. A commenter asserted that HUD failed to meaningfully address the less-discriminatory alternative of grandfathering existing mixed-eligibility families and applying the rule only to new admissions.
A commenter recommended that verification focus on new applicants or members with unclear status and that documentation processes be streamlined to reduce administrative burden while preserving family unity and community stability.
Commenters requested that existing mixed-status households that have complied with current rules in good faith be grandfathered so they may remain together with prorated assistance, preserving assistance and avoiding destabilizing disruptions while any new requirements are phased in.
Commenters argued that the rule's requirement for existing tenants to produce citizenship or eligible-status documentation within 90 days (with any extension capped at 30 days) is not feasible, because vital-records offices, consulates, and other third-party record holders operate under processing backlogs that tenants cannot control; they asked that, if the rule is applied to current participants, verification instead occur at each family's next regular reexamination. Commenters added that there is no statutory requirement to apply new verification standards retroactively and that doing so is neither legally compelled nor equitable.
A commenter stated that prospective application reflects HUD's consistent historical practice over the 50-year history of the Housing Choice Voucher program—including when HUD imposed new restrictions on lifetime registered sex offenders, which were applied prospectively and grandfathered current participants—and that retroactively destabilizing compliant households is unprecedented in federal housing policy. A commenter further asked that HUD retain the age-62 exemption for current tenants who were age 62 or older as of the final rule's effective date, consistent with the 1987 statute and the reliance interests of elderly participants.
Commenters requested transition measures should HUD proceed, including phasing in requirements, setting the effective date no sooner than six months after publication, allowing adequate time for system updates and staff training with technical guidance and standardized compliance tools issued in advance of enforcement, continuing prorated assistance for up to one year while good-faith SAVE resolution efforts continue, and providing dedicated administrative or transition funding and administrative fee adjustments to cover implementation costs. One commenter recommended additional implementation safeguards: affirming that public housing agencies are housing providers and not immigration enforcement agencies, structuring secondary verification through a trained
(
printed page 73023)
third party, allowing agencies to rely on credible documentation and third-party letters where the data SAVE accesses contains errors, and providing standardized plain-language consent and notice forms in multiple languages explaining what information may be shared, when, and under what legal authority.
HUD Response:
HUD acknowledges these requests and notes that the RIA evaluated this alternative. The Regulatory Alternatives section analyzes grandfathering existing mixed families and applying the rule's provisions to new admissions only, under which mixed families would be replaced through existing end-of-participation trends over time. The RIA states that such a gradual option would fulfill the objectives of the rule while avoiding the transition costs borne by mixed families; given the low turnover rate, however, the RIA finds that grandfathering in existing mixed families would be expected to delay the transfer of assistance to fully eligible families by more than a decade.
HUD acknowledges commenters' references to prior HUD rulemakings in which requirements were applied prospectively or existing participants were grandfathered. The Department has considered those examples but does not believe they require the same approach here. The appropriate implementation framework depends on several factors, including the relevant statutory and regulatory framework, the Department's objectives, and circumstances of the particular rulemaking.
HUD also considered the commenters' recommendation to retain the existing age exemption for individuals who are 62 or older as of the final rule's effective date. HUD has discussed its rationale for eliminating the exemption elsewhere in the preamble. As explained in the preamble, the 1987 Housing and Community Development Act amended Section 214 to apply certain status-verification requirements to individuals younger than 62 years of age, and HUD's existing regulations at
24 CFR 5.216(e)
excluded participants age 62 or older as of January 31, 2010, from submitting certain information. This rule requires all applicants and tenants in Section 214 covered programs to submit evidence of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status regardless of age, consistent with the wording and purpose of Section 214. The extension of the verification requirement to individuals 62 years of age and older can be fulfilled using existing verification procedures, so retaining the exemption is neither compelled by Section 214 nor necessary to implement it in an orderly manner.
HUD recognizes that current participants may need time to obtain and submit required documentation and has considered these implementation concerns in establishing the final rule's effective date and compliance requirements.
HUD also considered commenters' concerns that some participants may experience difficulty obtaining documentation from vital-records offices, consulates, or other third parties within the prescribed period. For this reason, mixed-status families may have up to 150 days (90 days post effective date of the rule pursuant to § 5.508(f) plus a 60-day extension when applicable, pursuant to § 5.508(g)) to submit evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status. HUD believes these provisions provide an appropriate period for affected participants to establish eligibility while implementing the final rule in an orderly way within a defined timeframe.
G. Severability
Responding to HUD's request for input on severability, commenters argued that a general severability clause is insufficient and that HUD should specify which provisions it considers independently operable and what responsible entities' obligations would be under each partial-stay scenario. Others argued that because the rule repeatedly contravenes Section 214 it is not viable and should be withdrawn in its entirety rather than severed, while other commenters took the view that the provisions would operate independently if a portion were stayed.
HUD Response:
HUD appreciates the commenters' input and has taken it into consideration in drafting the severability clause for the final rule.
VI. Findings and Certifications
Regulatory Review—Executive Orders 12866 and 13563
Under
Executive Order 12866
(Regulatory Planning and Review), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and, therefore, subject to review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the order.
Executive Order 13563
(Improving Regulations and Regulatory Review) directs executive agencies to analyze regulations that are “outmoded, ineffective, insufficient, or excessively burdensome, and to modify, streamline, expand, or repeal them in accordance with what has been learned.”
Executive Order 13563
also directs that, where relevant, feasible, and consistent with regulatory objectives, and to the extent permitted by law, agencies are to identify and consider regulatory approaches that reduce burdens and maintain flexibility and freedom of choice for the public.
This rule was determined to be a “significant regulatory action” as defined in section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
(although not an economically significant regulatory action under section 3(f)(1) of the Executive Order). HUD has prepared a cost benefit analysis that addresses the costs and benefits of the rule. The cost analysis is part of the docket file for this rule.
Executive Order 14192
, Regulatory Costs
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” was issued on January 31, 2025. Section 3(c) of
Executive Order 14192
requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations. This rule is an immigration-related rule that is expressly exempt from the requirements of
Executive Order 14192
.
Environmental Impact
The rule does not direct, provide for assistance or loan and mortgage insurance for, or otherwise govern or regulate, real property acquisition, disposition, leasing, rehabilitation, alteration, demolition, or new construction or establish, revise or provide for standards for construction or construction materials, manufactured housing, or occupancy. Accordingly, under
24 CFR 50.19(c)(1)
, this rule is categorically excluded from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
).
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
) generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The regulatory amendments to HUD's noncitizen requirements will have only a minimal impact on small housing project owners, small mortgagees, and small housing agencies. The majority of PHAs and project (housing) owners have few mixed families, if any. In 2024, the share of PHAs where 95 percent or more
(
printed page 73024)
of their assisted households are non-mixed is 92 percent. The share is even higher for housing owners—97 percent of owners have mixed families representing less than five percent of their assisted households. At this time, HUD is unable to provide an accurate estimate of small PBRA owners because we do not always know whether there is a corporate structure behind an individual owner.
Further, the amendments will require primary verification of citizenship and eligible immigration status through the same process: Inputting information into SAVE for an automated response. A responsible entity's collection and review of appropriate documentation for U.S. citizenship will be limited to instances of secondary verification. As explained elsewhere in this preamble and in the Regulatory Impact Analysis for this rule, the burden on existing tenants, families, future applicants, and responsible entities is estimated to be low, even where existing individuals have not submitted any documentation for verification purposes. Some of the requirements could also be satisfied using existing procedures. For example, the rule will require that the eligible immigration status of all noncitizen in Section 214 covered programs, regardless of age, be verified through responsible entities utilizing the DHS/USCIS SAVE program. The extension of this requirement to individuals 62 years of age and older can be fulfilled by utilizing existing verification procedures. Furthermore, although the rule will revise eligibility for prorated assistance, current methods will be used to calculate the prorated assistance provided to an eligible family.
Notwithstanding HUD's determination that this rule will not have a significant effect on a substantial number of small entities, HUD specifically invites comments regarding any less burdensome alternatives to this rule that will meet HUD's objectives as described in this preamble.
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism
Executive Order 13132
(entitled “Federalism”) prohibits an agency from publishing any rule that has federalism implications if the rule either imposes substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments, and is not required by statute, or preempts State law, unless the agency meets the consultation and funding requirements of section 6 of the Executive order. This rule does not have federalism implications and does not impose substantial direct compliance costs on State and local governments nor preempt state law within the meaning of the Executive order.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) (UMRA) establishes requirements for Federal agencies to assess the effects of their regulatory actions on State, local, and tribal governments and on the private sector. This rule does not impose a Federal mandate on any State, local, or tribal government, or on the private sector, within the meaning of UMRA.
Paperwork Reduction Act
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
) (“PRA”), an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the collection displays a currently valid OMB control number. The information collection requirements contained in this rule have been approved by OMB under the Paperwork Reduction Act and assigned OMB control number 2577-0295.
HUD's current regulations do not require submission of any documentation for citizenship verification purposes, unlike eligible immigration status where HUD's regulations require submission of documentation for eligible status verification. This rule will change HUD's regulations to require each family member in tenant families who have not yet submitted evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status, and applicants who are declaring they have U.S. citizenship, to submit evidence in accordance with §§ 5.508 and 5.512 to responsible entities (mortgagors, project or housing owners, and PHAs). While this may impose some burden on existing tenants in HUD housing who have previously elected the “do not contend” provision, have submitted no documentation to date, have documentation proving their eligibility, and wish to continue to receive HUD assistance, the number of these existing tenants is low and the related burdens are thus relatively low, for tenants, families, and responsible entities.

PHAs already typically receive a birth certificate, passport, or some other identity verification document for deductions, program eligibility, and other purposes. Under this rule, responsible entities will also be required to collect and review citizenship evidence documents submitted by all applicants and tenants declaring to be U.S. citizens, and to review those documents to verify U.S. citizenship. Again, for Section 8 and Public Housing covered programs, responsible entities generally already receive and review this documentation for eligibility determinations and other purposes. As explained in the Regulatory Impact Analysis for this rulemaking, an estimated 99 percent of existing tenants who are U.S. citizens have been verified by PHAs (and owners). Finally, this rule will require that notification of Section 214 requirements, verification consent forms, notification of any failures to confirm primary verification, and notification of any denials or terminations of assistance be provided to applicants and tenants declaring to be U.S. citizens and noncitizen, as applicable.
