ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Antelope Valley College (AVC) has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Dr. Darcy L. Wiewall, Antelope Valley College, Department of Anthropology, 3041 W Ave. K, Lancaster, CA 93536, email
darcy.wiewall@avc.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of AVC, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains, representing at least one individual, have been identified from the Red Rock Canyon Rockshelter (CA-KER-147/AVC-12) site. The two lots of associated funerary objects are one lot of shell beads and one lot of flaked stone. The site located in Red Rock Canyon State Park on the western edge of the Mojave Desert, Kern County. The site was recorded by Alex Apostolides in 1963 and was designated trinomial CA-KER-147. This site was excavated by Roger W. Robinson, Antelope Valley College (AVC) in April 1973. The site was mapped, collected and tested under the auspices of the California Department of Parks and Recreation. Work at the site was initiated after a report of vandalism that included the disturbance of human burials. The project was designed to stabilize the vandalized area, discourage further vandalism, and determine the age, extent, and content of the site deposit. In 2009, Mark Q. Sutton, Roger W. Robinson and Jill Gardner published
“Excavations at the Red Rock Canyon Rockshelter (CA-KER-147), Western Mojave Desert, California”.
This is the final report published on the 1973 excavations. The publication states that the human remains recovered from the site were repatriated by State Parks in 2008. The site chronology was addressed by several means, including radiocarbon dating, obsidian hydration, and the use of temporally diagnostic artifacts such as projectile points, shell and glass beads, and ceramics. A radiocarbon assay of 630 ± 90 years BP was obtained on charcoal from a possible hearth. No hazardous substances are known to have been used to treat any of the human remains.
Human remains, representing at least one individual, have been identified from Bakersfield (CA-KER-676/AVC-176) site. The one lot of associated funerary objects are one lot of shell beads and shell fragments. The site located southwest of the city of Bakersfield, Kern County, was exposed by a storm in December 1977. Extensive local media coverage, including publication of the site's location and an invitation for public viewing, resulted in extensive vandalism. In March 1978, an emergency salvage excavation was conducted over a three-day weekend under the direction of Bob Schiffman (Bakersfield College) and Roger Robinson (Antelope Valley College). The human remains were transferred to Andy Greene, a Nüwa (Kawaiisu) elder living in Tehachapi, California. In 2025, Robinson returned collection materials to AVC, which included human remains and documentation, which permitted site provenience to be determined. There are no known publications or chronometric data from the site. No hazardous substances are known to have been used to treat any of the human remains.
Archaeologists have asserted that both the Kitanemuk and Kawaiisu peoples have continuously occupied and used areas on the northwestern and northern margins of the Antelope Valley for at least the past 2500 years BP. Ethnographic evidence documents that the Kitanemuk and the Kawaiisu were known to hunt, gather, and trade together, and they also intermarried. It is highly likely that the two territories overlapped. Linguistic sources demonstrate a strong continuous shared group identity between these ancestral populations and present-day Native American communities of Kitanemuk, Serrano and Tataviam descent. Traditional knowledge identifies the northwestern Antelope Valley as the ancestral homeland of Kitanemuk and Kawaiisu peoples since time immemorial. Based on this evidence and consultation with representatives of the Tejon Indian Tribe and Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (previously listed as the San Manuel Band of Mission Indians) and non-federally recognized California Tribes including the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians and the San Fernando Band of Mission Indians, these individuals are Native American.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice. The following types of information were used to reasonably trace the relationship: anthropological information, archaeological information, geographical information, folkloric, historical, kinship, linguistic, oral traditional, and expert opinion, including Tribal Traditional Knowledge.
Determinations
AVC has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of at least two individuals of Native American ancestry.
The three lots of objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a reasonable connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Tejon Indian Tibe.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
(
printed page 72900)
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after December 14, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, AVC must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. AVC is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

, and the implementing regulations,

Abstract of Information Available
Based on the information available, human remains representing at least 35 individuals have been reasonably identified at Arizona State University's Center for Archaeology and Society Repository (ASU). No associated funerary objects are present. The ancestors were excavated or collected between 1970-1973 from four known sites on Akun and Akutan islands in the eastern Aleutian Islands, Alaska, including Amatanan (49-UNI-00056)
(
printed page 72897)
(MNI=2), Chulka (49-UNI-00002) (MNI=20), Saa (49-UNI-00048) (MNI=10), Siskena (49-UNI-00008) (MNI=2), and one more from either Saa or Siskena. A clear coat of an unknown substance had been applied to some of the ancestral remains. The substance may be polyvinyl acetate, given that we know this substance was used by ASU's Laboratory of Physical Anthropology in the 1980s.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
BLM has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of at least 35 individuals of Native American ancestry.
There is a reasonable connection between the human remains described in this notice and the Native Village of Akutan.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Verde Valley Archaeology Center and Museum (VVAC) and the Museum of Northern Arizona (MNA) have completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Monica Buckle, Executive Director, Verde Valley Archaeology Center and Museum, 460 W Finnie Flat Road, Camp Verde, AZ 86322, email
director@verdevalleyarchaeology.org
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the VVAC and MNA, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified from the Dyck Cliff Dwelling. The 78 associated funerary objects are 58 textile fragments, 13 cordage fragments, two shell ankle bracelets, one gourd, one faunal bone, one ceramic sherd, one sample of tree bark, and one vegetal sample. No known potentially hazardous substances were used to treat the human remains or associated funerary objects.
The Dyck Cliff Dwelling is on private land owned by Paul Dyck at the time of excavation, in Yavapai County, Arizona. The site was occupied by the Southern Sinagua between A.D. 1050 and A.D. 1300. The dwelling was excavated by the Southwest Museum between 1962 and 1972. The collection was housed at the Southwest Museum for analysis and preparation of a report. In 1964, the Southwest Museum returned the burial to Paul Dyck, who then traded the burial to Clay Lockett, who then donated the burial to MNA. A total of 52 associated funerary objects were also donated to MNA but six objects were retained by Paul Dyck. The remaining collection at the Southwest Museum was transferred to the Paul Dyck Foundation Research Institute of American Indian Culture in 1986 and stored on his land in Arizona. The Paul Dyck Foundation donated the collection, including the six funerary objects from this burial, to the VVAC in 2014. Both the VVAC and MNA care for objects associated with the burial.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is clearly identified by the information available about the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
The VVAC and MNA have determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of one individual of Native American ancestry.
The 78 objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Hopi Tribe of Arizona.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
(
printed page 72898)
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after December 14, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the VVAC and MNA must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. The VVAC and MNA are responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,

, and the implementing regulations,

.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the California Department of Parks and Recreation intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of sacred objects and that have a known lineal descendant.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Dr. Leslie L. Hartzell, NAGPRA Coordinator, California Department of Parks and Recreation, P.O. Box 942896, Sacramento, CA 94296-0001, email
Leslie.Hartzell@parks.ca.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the California Department of Parks and Recreation, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 39 lots of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 39 lots of sacred objects are Abqo regalia and associated items, including missing or identified items.
California Department of Parks and Recreation records indicate that the sacred objects were taken from the ceremonial dance house at the Sulfur Bank Rancheria without permission. About 1958, the sacred objects were donated to the State of California Department of Natural Resources Division of Beaches and Parks, now the California Department of Parks and Recreation. Although the donation was made anonymously, in 1979, F.A. Riddell, State Indian Museum curator, identified A.E. Treganza as the donor. The sacred items are associated with Sarah Brigham who died in 1949 or before. These objects are integral to present-day religious traditions associated with the Maru beliefs. In 2023, the California Department of Parks and Recreation repatriated another group of sacred objects that were also taken from the ceremonial dance house at the Sulfur Bank Rancheria without permission and associated with Sarah Brigham, to lineal descendant Robert Geary. On December 24, 2002, the sacred objects were published in a Notice of Intent to Repatriation in the
Federal Register
(
67 FR 78508
, December 24, 2002) and that notice was amended on March 21, 2023 (
88 FR 17007
, March 21, 2023).
Determinations
The California Department of Parks and Recreation has determined that:
The 39 lots of sacred objects described in this notice are specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization.
Robert Geary is connected to the cultural items described in this notice.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after December 14, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the California Department of Parks and Recreation must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The California Department of Parks and Recreation is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to all requestors and any other consulting parties.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History (LACMNH) intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Amy E. Gusick, NAGPRA Officer, Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History, 900 Exposition Boulevard, Los Angeles, CA 90007, email
agusick@nhm.org
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the LACMNH, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 333 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 333 objects of cultural patrimony are flakes, shatter, manos, pestles, bowl fragments, metates, charcoal, projectile points, and historic artifacts. Between 2010 and 2012, Sapphos Environmental Inc. removed the cultural items from CA-LAN-360, an archaeological site at Vasquez Rocks in Agua Dulce, Los Angeles County, CA, ahead of construction of the Vasquez Rocks Natural Area Park and Nature Center. At the direction of the Los Angeles County Department of Parks and Recreation, the cultural material was deposited at the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History for curation.
In consultation with the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation and non-federally recognized California Indian groups including the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, these items were identified as culturally affiliated with the Serrano and Tataviam peoples based on Tribal Traditional Knowledge, genealogical information, geographical location within Serrano and Tataviam ancestral territory, and ethnographic, historical, and archaeological records.
Determinations
The LACMNH has determined that:
The 333 objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Morongo Band of Mission Indians, California and the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (previously listed as San Manuel Band of Mission Indians, California).
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after December 14, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the LACMNH must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The LACMNH is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.

DATES:

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the University of California, Berkeley, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 57 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 57 unassociated funerary belongings were removed from a family cemetery in Alameda County between 1950 and 1951 by Arnold Pilling, Cherie N. Gregoire, Michael Sitnik, Gordon L. Grosscup, and Mary Elizabeth Jane Hal and subsequently accessioned into the University of California Museum of Anthropology (Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology). The 57 unassociated funerary belongings are beads (three missing), a cross (grave marker), fastener, faunal remains, iron, marble, nail, pendant, porcelain fragments, potsherds, shells (three missing), and tiles.
Collections and collection spaces at the Phoebe A Hearst Museum of Anthropology were treated with substances for preservation and pest control, some potentially hazardous. No records have been found to date at the Museum to indicate whether or not chemicals or natural substances were used prior to 1960.
Determinations
The University of California, Berkeley has determined that:
The 57 unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Known lineal descendants (names withheld per request) are connected to the cultural items described in this notice.

. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The University of California, Berkeley is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to all requestors and any other consulting parties.

Title:
Market Development Division—Domestic Hemp Production Program.
OMB Number:

November 30, 2026.
Type of Request:
Extension and revision of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
The Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 Farm Bill) amended the Agricultural Marketing of 1946 and was signed into law December 20, 2018, as
Public Law 115-334
. Section 10113 of the 2018 Farm Bill amended the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (
7 U.S.C. 1621
et seq.
) by adding Subtitle G—Hemp Production. The law requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to promulgate regulations and guidelines to develop and oversee a program for the production of hemp in the United States. The Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018,
Public Law 115-334
(2018 Farm Bill) directs that this will include State and Tribal plans, and a USDA plan for those States, including territories of Indian Tribes, that choose not to submit their own plan. The 2018 Farm Bill amended the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (AMA) by adding Subtitle G (sections 297A through 297D of the AMA). Section 297D of the AMA requires the Secretary of Agriculture (Secretary) to promulgate regulations and guidelines relating to the production of hemp, including sections 297B and 297C, in consultation with the U.S. Attorney General. Additionally, section 297D of the AMA requires the Secretary to annually submit to the Committee on Agriculture of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry of the Senate a report containing updates on the implementation of this subtitle.
This is a request for the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to review the revisions and extend the expiration date of the HEMP PRODUCTION PRACTICES AND COSTS STUDY. This survey is necessary for the Secretary of Agriculture to meet authorities granted by, and meet reporting requirements under, section 297D of the 2018 Farm Bill. A description of the survey is below.
Hemp Production Practices and Costs Study
In brief, this survey—prepared by the University of Kentucky (UKY) under a cooperative agreement with the USDA Specialty Crops Program (SCP)—is a national, census-style effort designed to collect hemp production-practice and cost-of-production information from producers across all segments of the industry (fiber, grain, and floral). The survey supports rulemaking needs, Congressional reporting requirements, and analysis of production practices across the U.S. hemp sector. It also fulfills key data-collection objectives of the 2018 Farm Bill (
Pub. L. 115-334
) by closing longstanding information gaps and strengthening the quality of data available for federal decision-making.
Burden for Domestic Hemp Production Program
Estimate of Burden:
Public reporting burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 0.5 hours per response.
Respondents:
Individuals that represent a household, business, farm/ranch, or organization that is registered to grow hemp with a state, tribal, or USDA hemp program.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
4,010 (Total number of S/T/T and USDA licensees as of 09/2026).
Estimated Number of Responses:
4,019.
Estimated Number of Responses per Respondent:
1.
Estimated Total Annual Burden on Respondents:
2,010 hours.
Comments are invited on:
(1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
All responses to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will also become a matter of public record.
AMS is committed to complying with the E-Government Act of 2002 to promote the use of the internet and other information technologies, to provide increased opportunities for citizen access to Government information and services, and for other purposes.

printed page 72848)
A 60-day comment period is provided to allow interested people to respond to the notice.

I. Background
FDA is announcing the availability of a draft guidance for industry titled “Early-Phase IND Protocol Recommendations for Solid Tumors.” The purpose of this draft guidance is to provide recommendations to sponsors and clinical investigators developing early-phase trials, which include FIH protocols or protocols for drugs and biologic products with limited human experience, submitted under an IND to the appropriate disease-specific division located within OOD in CDER and OCE in CBER. This draft guidance is specific to solid tumors and does not address protocols for investigational drugs intended to treat hematologic malignancies.
This draft guidance is being issued consistent with FDA's good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The draft guidance, when finalized, will represent the current thinking of FDA on “Early-Phase IND Protocol Recommendations for Solid Tumors.” It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. .

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission has received a complaint and a submission pursuant to § 210.8(b) of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure filed on behalf of WobbleWorks Inc. on November 6, 2026. The complaint alleges violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (
19 U.S.C. 1337
) in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, and the sale within the United States after importation of certain handheld three-dimensional (“3D”) drawing devices. The complaint names as respondents: Guangzhou JER Education of China; MyFirst USA Inc. of City of Industry, CA; and MyFirst Tech Asia Pte. Ltd. of Singapore. The complainant requests that the Commission issue a limited exclusion order, cease and desist orders and impose a bond upon respondents' alleged infringing articles during the 60-day Presidential review period pursuant to
19 U.S.C. 1337(j)
.
Proposed respondents, other interested parties, members of the public, and interested government agencies are invited to file comments on any public interest issues raised by the complaint or § 210.8(b) filing. Comments should address whether issuance of the relief specifically requested by the complainant in this investigation would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) explain how the articles potentially subject to the requested remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the requested remedial orders;
(iii) identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the requested exclusion order and/or a cease and desist order within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) explain how the requested remedial orders would impact United States consumers.
Written submissions on the public interest must be filed no later than by close of business, eight calendar days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. There will be further opportunities for comment on the public interest after the issuance of any final initial determination in this investigation. Any written submissions on other issues must also be filed by no later than the close of business (5:15 p.m.)

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice; request for information.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces the Department of Justice's (“Department”) issuance of a memorandum titled “Guidance on Implementing English as the Official Language,” consistent with
Executive Order 14224
, titled
Designating English as the Official Language of the United States.
The Department invites public comments on the memorandum.
DATES:
Electronic comments must be submitted on or before January 11, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. OLP188 through the Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
The Department's general policy is to make all comments received from members of the public available for public viewing in their entirety on the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Therefore, commenters should be careful to include in their comments only information that they wish to make publicly available.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
James G. Meslener, Counsel, Office of Legal Policy, Department of Justice, 950 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20530; telephone: (202) 514-4601.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation
Interested persons are invited to provide comments or feedback by submitting written data, views, or arguments on the attached memorandum.
Please note that all comments received are considered part of the public record and made available for public inspection at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Such information includes personally identifiable information (such as your name, address, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter.
The Department may withhold from public viewing information provided in comments that it determines is offensive, that may adversely impact the privacy of a third party, or for other legitimate reasons. For additional information, please read the privacy notice that is available through the link in the footer of
https://www.regulations.gov
.
II. Discussion
On March 6, 2025, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14224
, titled “Designating English as the Official Language of the United States,”
90 FR 11363
. The Attorney General subsequently issued a memorandum to all Federal agencies about the implementation of
E.O. 14224
.
See
Memorandum from the Attorney General,
Implementation of
Executive Order No. 14,224
: Designating English as the Official Language of the United States of America
(July 14, 2025),
https://www.justice.gov/​ag/​media/​1407776/​dl
.
Per that memorandum, on September 1, 2026, the Attorney General issued to all Executive departments and agencies a memorandum titled “Guidance on Implementing English as the Official Language.” That notice was subsequently revised on October 22, 2026, in light of
Executive Order 14434
, “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,”
91 FR 63129
. The memorandum is attached as an appendix to this Notice.
Through this Notice, the Department is publishing the October 22, 2026, memorandum and invites public comment on it. As the memorandum states, after reviewing the comments, the Department will determine whether modifications are necessary or desirable, but the Department will not respond to the comments.
Daniel E. Burrows,
Assistant Attorney General, Office of Legal Policy.

MEMORANDUM FOR ALL EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
FROM: THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
SUBJECT:
Guidance on Implementing English as the Official Language
Background
On March 6, 2025, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14224
, titled “Designating English as the Official Language of the United States,”
90 FR 11363
. The Attorney General then issued a memorandum to all Federal agencies about the implementation of
E.O. 14224
.
See
Memorandum from the Attorney General,
Implementation of
Executive Order No. 14,224
: Designating English as the Official Language of the United States of America
(July 14, 2025),
https://www.justice.gov/​ag/​media/​1407776/​dl
.
To satisfy a directive from that memorandum, on September 1, 2026, the Attorney General issued a memorandum titled “Guidance on Implementing English as the Official Language.”
See
Memorandum from the Attorney General,
Guidance on Implementing English as the Official Language
(Sept. 1, 2026) (initial English Language Guidance). Thereafter, on October 2, 2026, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14434
, titled “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,”
91 FR 63129
. To ensure compliance with
E.O. 14434
, the Attorney General has revised the English Language Guidance as set forth below.
Before developing the initial English Language Guidance, the Office of Legal Policy (OLP) sought input and recommendations from Federal agencies about programs and policies to be implemented in an English-only format. OLP solicited feedback from several Department components and fifty-three Federal agencies. OLP received responses from twenty Federal agencies and one component.
The respondents provided OLP with valuable feedback concerning the implementation of
E.O. 14224
. The responses fell into the following categories: (a) actions taken to implement
E.O. 14224
; (b) notification of compliance with
E.O. 14224
; (c) background information on languages other than English being used or supported, with an explanation; (d) future plans to comply with
E.O. 14224
; and (e) “no input.” These responses assisted OLP in developing the initial English Language Guidance.
The below revised English Language Guidance incorporates the principles of
E.O. 14424
and other non-substantive revisions.
The Department seeks public comments on the English Language Guidance and, after reviewing the comments, will determine whether modifications are necessary or desirable. The Department will not respond to public comments.
Executive Departments and Agencies should update any relevant regulations that are inconsistent with
E.O. 14224
and these Guidelines.
Guidance Pursuant to
Executive Order 14224
, Titled “Designating English as the Official Language of the United States”
I. Introduction
[
1
]
Though not officially designated in the past, English has been our common language since before this Nation's founding. This fact is reflected in our Nation's governing documents, history and tradition, and daily interactions. Our shared national language has played an indispensable role in forming a cohesive society and ensuring consistency across government operations.
E.O. 14224
designated English as the official language of the United States. This English Language Guidance helps Federal agencies implement
E.O. 14224
by providing clear, practical guidelines on how to prioritize the English language in government operations.
[
2
]
The English Language Guidance also provides guidelines to assist agencies in determining when multilingual assistance may be required by law or necessary to
(
printed page 72924)
accomplish an agency's mission, and how to provide such assistance.
II. English Is the Sole Official Language
English is now the official language of the United States. Consequently, agencies should prioritize the English language over all other languages. After evaluating feedback from Department components and Federal agencies, the Department has identified opportunities where agencies should solely use English. For example, agencies should conduct official business, communicate with the public, develop forms and publications, administer programs, and provide services solely in English—unless, as explained further below, multilingual assistance is required by law or necessary to accomplish an agency's mission. The following is a non-exhaustive list of when agencies should solely use English:
a. official correspondence;
b. regulations, guidance documents, and policy statements;
c. public notices and announcements;
d. forms and applications;
e. Websites and digital services;
f. outreach and educational materials;
g. internal agency communications and training materials; and
h. super intelligence tools.
Agencies should strive to operate solely in English. For example, on August 17 of this year, the Department of Housing and Urban Development removed non-English languages from all departmental business and services. Feedback from Department of Justice components and Federal agencies revealed that websites and digital services are some of the quickest and most significant opportunities where an agency should prioritize English. In addition to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Departments of Homeland Security, Education, and Treasury have already begun removing materials from their website that were previously provided in languages other than English. The Department encourages other agencies to identify and remove non-English languages from their services.
Moving forward, agencies should promptly identify and review all multilingual assistance programs. Agencies should then determine whether multilingual assistance is required by law or necessary to accomplish an agency's mission. If multilingual assistance is neither legally required nor necessary to accomplish the agency's mission, then the agency should eliminate assistance in favor of English-only operations. If multilingual assistance is legally required or necessary to accomplish the agency's mission, then the English language version of any agency communication shall constitute the official and authoritative version unless otherwise required by law.
III. When and How To Provide Multilingual Assistance
Agencies should consult the below to determine when multilingual assistance may be required by law or necessary to accomplish an agency's mission and how to provide such assistance.
A. When Multilingual Assistance Is Required by Law
Agency feedback identified various instances where multilingual assistance is required by law. Agencies must provide multilingual assistance when it is required by law. Agencies should, however, only provide multilingual assistance to the extent that it is legally required. Examples of legal authorities that may require multilingual assistance are:
a. the Constitution;
b. federal statutes;
c. binding judicial orders;
d. binding regulations; and
e. international obligations having the force of law.
Furthermore, until recently,
Executive Order No. 13166
,
65 FR 50121
(Aug. 16, 2000) directed agencies to enhance access to federal programs for persons with limited English proficiency and required them to tailor guidance for recipients of federal funding under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. However,
E.O. 14224
rescinded
E.O. 13166
and thus multilingual assistance predicated on
E.O. 13166
is no longer legally required. Feedback indicated that most agencies have discontinued, or are in the process of discontinuing, multilingual assistance predicated on
E.O. 13166
. For example, several agencies reported that the recission of
E.O. 13166
allowed them to amend or fully remove their agency's Language Access Plans. Accordingly, agencies should continue evaluating whether multilingual assistance predicated on
E.O. 13166
is necessary to accomplish the agency's mission and if not, agencies should eliminate the assistance in favor of English-only operations.
B. When Multilingual Assistance Is Necessary To Accomplish an Agency's Mission
Multilingual assistance may be necessary when an agency determines that the inability to communicate in a language other than English would materially impair the agency's ability to carry out its statutory responsibilities, administer programs, protect the public, or deliver efficient government services. The following are instances where multilingual assistance may be necessary:
a. national security activities;
b. immigration enforcement activities;
c. law enforcement and security operations;
d. emergency preparedness and disaster response;
e. communications related to public health, public safety, or emergencies;
f. healthcare services;
g. surveys and data collection;
h. communications with foreign officials;
i. court proceedings; and
j. communications with crime victims or witnesses, or cooperating individuals.
For example, the Department of Homeland Security reported that given the security mission of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and the large volume of international travelers who may have limited English proficiency, the TSA will continue to utilize an automated helpline that is available in several languages. However, when an agency determines that multilingual assistance is necessary to accomplish the agency's mission, as in this instance, the agency should provide that assistance only to the extent needed to accomplish its mission.
C. How To Provide Multilingual Assistance
When multilingual assistance is legally required or necessary to accomplish the agency's mission, an agency should select the least burdensome and most cost-effective method available. When multilingual assistance is necessary to accomplish the agency's mission, such information should be translated accurately and include a clear disclaimer—in both English and the non-English language—that English is the official language and the authoritative version of all federal information.
Technological advances in translation services permit agencies to produce cost-effective methods for bridging language barriers and reducing inefficiencies with the translation process. For example, the Environmental Protection Agency and Department of Homeland Security are currently evaluating, developing, and testing superintelligence and machine translation programs that would allow them to more efficiently communicate with individuals who may have limited English proficiency. The Department encourages other agencies to consider the use of superintelligence and machine translation to communicate with individuals who may have limited English proficiency.
IV. Conclusion
This English Language Guidance is intended to equip agencies with practical guidelines to implement
E.O. 14224
, while complying with the law and upholding their core missions. The Department appreciates the agencies who provided critical feedback on how they have thus far implemented
E.O. 14224
. The Department looks forward to partnering with agencies to fully implement English as the official language of the United States.
Footnotes

                             The English Language Guidance is not intended to, does not, and may not be relied upon to create, any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person. Nothing in the English Language Guidance alters or supersedes any legal obligation imposed upon an agency.

AGENCY:

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or Agency) is announcing an opportunity for public comment on the proposed collection of certain information by the Agency. Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), Federal Agencies are required to publish notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed reinstatement of an existing collection of information, and to allow 60 days for public comment in response to the notice. This notice solicits comments on information collection associated with FDA's Voluntary Qualified Importer Program.
DATES:
Either electronic or written comments on the collection of information must be submitted by January 11, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments as follows. Please note that late, untimely filed comments will not be considered. The
https://www.regulations.gov
electronic filing system will accept comments until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time at the end of January 11, 2027. Comments received by mail/hand delivery/courier (for written/paper submissions) will be considered timely if they are received on or before that date.
Electronic Submissions
Submit electronic comments in the following way:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments. Comments submitted electronically, including attachments, to
https://www.regulations.gov
will be posted to the docket unchanged. Because your comment will be made public, you are solely responsible for ensuring that your comment does not include any confidential information that you or a third party may not wish to be posted, such as medical information, your or anyone else's Social Security number, or confidential business information, such as a manufacturing process. Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your comments, that information will be posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
If you want to submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made available to the public, submit the comment as a written/paper submission and in the manner detailed (see “Written/Paper Submissions” and “Instructions”).
Written/Paper Submissions
Submit written/paper submissions as follows:
Mail/Hand Delivery/Courier (for written/paper submissions):
Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852.
For written/paper comments submitted to the Dockets Management Staff, FDA will post your comment, as well as any attachments, except for information submitted, marked and identified, as confidential, if submitted as detailed in “Instructions.”
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the Docket No. FDA-2026-N-12575 for “Agency Information Collection Activities; Proposed Collection; Comment Request; Voluntary Qualified Importer Program.” Received comments, those filed in a timely manner (see
ADDRESSES
), will be placed in the docket and, except for those submitted as “Confidential Submissions,” publicly viewable at
https://www.regulations.gov
or at the Dockets Management Staff between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, 240-402-7500.
Confidential Submissions—To submit a comment with confidential information that you do not wish to be made publicly available, submit your comments only as a written/paper submission. You should submit two copies total. One copy will include the information you claim to be confidential with a heading or cover note that states “THIS DOCUMENT CONTAINS CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION.” The Agency will review this copy, including the claimed confidential information, in its consideration of comments. The second copy, which will have the claimed confidential information redacted/blacked out, will be available for public viewing and posted on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Submit both copies to the Dockets Management Staff. If you do not wish your name and contact information to be made publicly available, you can provide this information on the cover sheet and not in the body of your comments and you must identify this information as “confidential.” Any information marked as “confidential” will not be disclosed except in accordance with
21 CFR 10.20
and other applicable disclosure law. For more information about FDA's posting of comments to public dockets, see
80 FR 56469
, September 18, 2015, or access the information at:
https://www.govinfo.gov/​content/​pkg/​FR-2015-09-18/​pdf/​2015-23389.pdf
.
Docket:

https://www.regulations.gov
and insert the docket number, found in brackets in the heading of this document, into the “Search” box and follow the prompts and/or go to the Dockets Management Staff, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852, 240-402-7500.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Amber Barrett, Office of Operations, Food and Drug Administration, Three White Flint North, 10A-12M, 11601 Landsdown St., North Bethesda, MD 20852, 301-796-8867,
PRAStaff@fda.hhs.gov
.
(
printed page 72878)
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
), Federal Agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
and includes Agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
) requires Federal Agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed reinstatement of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, FDA is publishing notice of the proposed collection of information set forth in this document.
With respect to the following collection of information, FDA invites comments on these topics: (1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of FDA's functions, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of FDA's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques, when appropriate, and other forms of information technology.
Voluntary Qualified Importer Program
OMB Control Number 0910-0840—Reinstatement
This information collection supports implementation of FDA's Voluntary Qualified Importer Program (VQIP), a voluntary fee-based program that provides expedited review and import entry of human and animal foods into the United States. Program participants may import products to the United States with greater speed and predictability, avoiding unexpected delays at the point of import entry. Importers interested in applying can start their application (Form FDA 4041) by submitting a notice of intent to participate after setting up an account through the FDA Industry Systems (FIS) website at
https://www.access.fda.gov
,
which includes a VQIP Portal User Guide. To participate, importers must meet eligibility criteria and pay a user fee that covers costs associated with FDA's administration of the program. Consistent with section 743(b)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (
21 U.S.C. 379j-31(b)(1)
), FDA annually publishes a schedule of fees applicable to VQIP in the
Federal Register
.
Respondents to the information collection are persons that bring food, or cause food to be brought, from a foreign country into the customs territory of the United States (section 806 of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 384b
)) as a VQIP importer. A VQIP importer can be located outside the United States. Persons who may be a VQIP importer include the manufacturer, owner, consignee, and importer of record of a food, provided that the importer can meet all the criteria for participation.
To assist respondents with the information collection, we developed the guidance document entitled “FDA's Voluntary Qualified Importer Program” (November 2024), available at
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​guidance-industry-fdas-voluntary-qualified-importer-program
. The guidance document is prepared in a question-and-answer format and discusses eligibility criteria; includes instruction for completing a VQIP application; explains conditions that may result in revocation of participation as well as criteria for reinstatement; and communicates benefits VQIP importers can expect to receive under the program. The guidance also discusses preparation of the “Quality Assurance Program (QAP),” a compilation of written policies and procedures used to ensure adequate control over the safety and security of foods being imported. The November 2024 guidance revision clarified FDA's approach to VQIP inspections, allowed participants to add new foreign suppliers and foods to their existing VQIP programs throughout the year, and extended the deadline for submitting a notice of intent and application. The guidance document was developed and issued consistent with FDA good guidance practice regulations in
21 CFR 10.115
, which provides for public comment at any time.

Veterinary Feed Directive—
21 CFR 558.6
OMB Control Number 0910-0363—Extension
This information collection helps support implementation of FDA statutory and regulatory requirements. Section 504 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (
21 U.S.C. 354
) establishes a regulatory category for certain new animal drugs called veterinary feed directive (VFD) drugs. Our VFD regulation is set forth at § 558.6 (
21 CFR 558.6
). VFD drugs are new animal drugs, intended for use in or on animal feed, which are limited to use under the professional supervision of a licensed veterinarian in the course of the veterinarian's professional practice. An animal feed containing a VFD drug or a combination VFD drug may be fed to animals only by or upon a lawful VFD issued by a licensed veterinarian.
Distributors of medicated feed containing VFD drugs must notify FDA of their intent to distribute such feed via U.S. Postal mail, email, or fax and must maintain records of the receipt and distribution of all medicated feeds containing VFD drugs. Veterinarians issue three copies of the VFD: one for their own records, one for their client, and one to the client's VFD feed distributor. For third-party disclosures, FDA regulation requires that veterinarians include specific information on the VFD. A distributor may only distribute a VFD feed to another distributor for further distribution if the originating distributor (consignor) first obtains a written acknowledgment letter from the receiving distributor (consignee) before the feed is shipped.
We developed the guidance document “Guidance for Industry (GFI) #233 Veterinary Feed Directive Common Format Questions and Answers” (September 2016) (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​cvm-gfi-233-veterinary-feed-directive-common-format-questions-and-answers
) to provide guidance concerning the elements that must be included on the VFD and the elements that may be included on the VFD as described in § 558.6. The guidance also provides examples that illustrate how a common VFD format might appear.
Additionally, we developed the guidance document “GFI #120 Veterinary Feed Directive Regulation Questions and Answers (revised) (April 2024) Small Entity Compliance Guide” (
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​cvm-gfi-120-veterinary-feed-directive-regulation-questions-and-answers
) to aid industry in complying with the requirements of the 2015 VFD final rule.
Agency guidance documents are issued in accordance with our good guidance practice regulations in
21 CFR 10.115
, which provide for public comment at any time.

Abstract:
The Personnel Development Program (PDP) is a Federal program managed at the Office of Special Education Programs (OSEP) aimed at increasing the supply of qualified personnel in the field of special education. This program awards competitive grants to Institutions of Higher Education (IHEs) to support scholars who are preparing to provide special education and related services to children and youth with disabilities. Scholars who receive funding agree to work in the field of special education or related services for two years for each year of support they receive.
The information is collected through the web-based Personnel Development Program Data Collection System (PDPDCS) under the authority of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) (
20 U.S.C. 1462
) and the implementing service obligation regulations at
34 CFR part 304
, as well as reporting requirements under
34 CFR 75.110
. Through the PDPDCS, grantees, scholars, and employers report data electronically.
The PDPDCS enables OSEP to meet its Congressional mandate by providing reliable data to assess program efficiency, performance, and effectiveness. Data collected are used to evaluate grantees' compliance with PDP program requirements, report program performance on GPRA measures to Congress, track scholar enrollment in training programs and subsequent service obligation fulfillment, and to refer scholars to the Accounts Receivable and Bank Management Division (ARBMD) for repayment of part or all of the scholarship received, if the scholars are not fulfilling their obligations through service.

notice is hereby given that on October 30, 2026, Nasdaq PHLX LLC (“PHLX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at PHLX Equity 7, Section 3.
These amendments are effective upon filing. However, they will become operative on November 2, 2026.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​phlx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Exchange's transaction fees at PHLX Equity 7, Section 3. The Exchange proposes to streamline its schedule of credits to member organizations providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX, and to eliminate the supplemental credit to member organizations providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX .
First Change
Currently, the Exchange pays a credit to a member organization that provides liquidity on Nasdaq PSX through displayed quotes/orders. This credit currently has four separate tiers. The tiers are not labeled in the rule text, but this filing will refer to them as Tier 1 through Tier 4:
Tier 4
$0.0033 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.15% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month.
Tier 3
$0.0032 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.07% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month.
Tier 2
$0.0030 per share executed for Quotes/Orders entered by a member organization that provides 0.05% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month.
Tier 1
$0.0020 per share executed for all other Quotes/Orders.
The Exchange proposes to eliminate Tiers 2, 3, and 4. Therefore, the Exchange would pay a member organization providing displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX a credit of $0.0020 per share executed for displayed quotes/orders entered by a member organization—regardless of how much volume the member organization provides during the month.
Second Change
The Exchange currently pays a supplemental credit to a member organization that provides liquidity on Nasdaq PSX through displayed quotes/orders. This is a supplemental credit of $0.00005 per share executed for displayed quotes/orders entered by a member organization that: (i) provides 0.10% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the prior month; and (ii) provides 0.10% or more of total Consolidated Volume during the month. The Exchange proposes to eliminate this supplemental credit.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
3
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
4
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange's proposed changes to its schedule of credits are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In
NetCoalition
v.
Securities and Exchange Commission,
the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly,
(
printed page 72940)
regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .”
[
5
]
The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
6
]
Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of rebates and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds.
Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal reflects the Exchange's ongoing assessment of how to allocate its limited incentive resources in a competitive market and how to maintain a schedule of credits that is understandable and administrable for member organizations.
First Change
The Exchange believes that eliminating the three volume-based displayed liquidity credit tiers and retaining the existing $0.0020 per share executed credit for all displayed Quotes/Orders is reasonable because it will streamline the schedule and make the applicable credit easier for member organizations to understand and apply. The Exchange has limited resources to devote to incentive programs, and it is appropriate for the Exchange to periodically reallocate those incentives in a manner that best achieves its overall mix of objectives. The proposal is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because, after the change, each member organization that provides displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX will be eligible for the same $0.0020 per share executed credit for displayed Quotes/Orders, regardless of the member organization's monthly volume. Although member organizations that could have previously qualified for one of the eliminated higher tiers would receive a lower credit, those member organizations will remain eligible for the same displayed-liquidity credit as all other similarly situated member organizations, and any participant that views the Exchange's pricing as unattractive may route order flow to competing venues that offer more favorable pricing or less stringent qualifying criteria. Furthermore, because the eliminated credit tiers have experienced zero utilization for an extended period of time, the elimination serves primarily to streamline the Exchange's fee schedule without impacting any active participant behavior.
Second Change
The Exchange also believes that eliminating the supplemental displayed-liquidity credit is reasonable, equitable, and not unfairly discriminatory. The supplemental credit is an additional incentive layered on top of the displayed-liquidity credit described above and is available only when a member organization satisfies both a prior-month and current-month Consolidated Volume threshold. Eliminating that additional incentive will further simplify the fee schedule and allow the Exchange to allocate its limited incentive resources in the manner it believes best serves the Exchange's current needs. The change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because the supplemental credit will be eliminated in its entirety and will no longer be available to any member organization, while member organizations that provide displayed liquidity will remain eligible for the generally applicable displayed-liquidity credit. Moreover, any member organization that is dissatisfied with the elimination of the supplemental credit may route its order flow to competing venues that provide more favorable incentives or less stringent qualifying criteria.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In terms of inter-market competition, the Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive, or rebate opportunities available at other venues to be more favorable. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and with alternative trading systems that have been exempted from compliance with the statutory standards applicable to exchanges. Because competitors are free to modify their own fees in response, and because market participants may readily adjust their order routing practices, the Exchange believes that the degree to which fee changes in this market may impose any burden on competition is extremely limited.
First Change
In terms of intramarket competition, the Exchange does not believe that eliminating the three volume-based displayed-liquidity credit tiers will place any category of Exchange participant at a competitive disadvantage. The change will apply uniformly to all member organizations that provide displayed liquidity on Nasdaq PSX because the same $0.0020 per share executed credit will apply to all displayed Quotes/Orders. To the extent that the change reduces credits for member organizations that previously satisfied one of the higher volume thresholds, the Exchange believes any burden is limited by the voluntary and competitive nature of the Exchange's execution services, the availability of competing exchanges and off-exchange venues, and the ability of market participants to modify their order routing practices in response to credit changes. The Exchange therefore does not believe that the First Change will impair the ability of member organizations or competing order execution venues to maintain their competitive standing in the financial markets.
Second Change
The Exchange likewise does not believe that eliminating the supplemental displayed-liquidity credit will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In terms of intramarket competition, the supplemental credit will be eliminated in its entirety and will no longer be available to any member organization,
(
printed page 72941)
and member organizations that provide displayed liquidity will continue to be eligible for the generally applicable displayed-liquidity credit. In terms of intermarket competition, the change concerns an optional credit in a market where exchange execution services are subject to extensive competition from other exchanges and off-exchange venues. If the elimination of the supplemental credit is unattractive to market participants, they may adjust their order routing practices, and competing venues may modify their own fees and credits in response. Accordingly, the Exchange does not believe that the Second Change will impair the ability of members or competing order execution venues to maintain their competitive standing in the financial markets.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
7
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-PHLX-2026-71 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-71. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-71 and should be submitted on or before December 3, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

]

full_text:
