Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106841; File No. SR-KALSHIEX-2026-03]
November 6, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(7) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-7 under the Act,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 4, 2026, KalshiEX LLC (“Kalshi” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons. Kalshi also has certified the proposed rule change with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) under Section 5c(c) of the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”)
[
3
]
on November 4, 2026.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Description and Text of the Proposed Rule Change
Kalshi proposes to revise certain of its listing standards applicable to the underlying securities of perpetual security futures products listed on Kalshi (“Perpetual SFPs” and such underlying securities, “Underlying Securities”) to reduce the time to market for the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on certain covered securities following their initial public offering (“IPO”). The scope of this filing is limited solely to the application of the proposed rule change to Perpetual SFPs that may be traded on Kalshi. The text of the rule change is provided in Exhibit 4 to the filing.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The
(
printed page 72936)
self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
Kalshi is registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”) as a designated contract market (“DCM”) under the Commodity Exchange Act (“CEA”) and notice-registered with the Commission as a national securities exchange for security futures products pursuant to the notice registration provisions of Section 6(g) of the Act.
[
4
]
Under its notice-registration, Kalshi lists as security futures cash-settled contracts that convey exposure to the price of an underlying equity security, have no pre-specified expiration date and are designated as Perpetual SFPs in their respective contract specifications, pursuant to listing standard rules for security futures products that it has adopted under a separate rule filing under Section 19(b)(7) of the Act
[
5
]
and Rule 19b-7 thereunder
[
6
]
filed on September 18, 2026.
[
7
]
In light of anticipated trading interest, Kalshi plans to reduce the time to market for the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on certain covered securities following their initial public offering (“IPO”). To effect this plan, Kalshi proposes to adopt certain rule changes to the introductory language in Rule 14.3 and Rules 14.3(c) and 14.3(d) of Chapter 14 of the Kalshi Rulebook.
Description of Proposed Rule Change
Rule 14.3 of Kalshi's Rulebook sets forth the initial listing eligibility criteria for Underlying Securities of Perpetual SFPs listed on the Exchange. Rule 14.3 requires that an Underlying Security that is common stock satisfy several criteria at the time of initial listing in order to be eligible for a Perpetual SFP on the Exchange, including that the Underlying Security must (i) pursuant to Rule 14.3(a), be registered and listed on a U.S. national securities exchange and must be an “NMS security” as defined in Section 11A of the Exchange Act
[
8
]
and Rule 600(b) of SEC Regulation NMS,
[
9
]
(ii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(b), have a market capitalization of not less than $100,000,000,000 (one hundred billion U.S. dollars), (iii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(c), have an average daily value of transactions (“ADTV”) of not less than $450,000,000 (four hundred and fifty million U.S. dollars) over the six months immediately preceding the New Product Committee's review, except where the Underlying Security has been listed for trading for less than six months, in which case the Underlying Security must have an ADTV of not less than $1,000,000,000 (one billion U.S. dollars) over the prior month, (iv) pursuant to Rule 14.3(d), if the Underlying Security is a “covered security” as defined in Section 18(b)(1)(A) of the Securities Act of 1933,
[
10
]
have had a closing price of at least $3.00 for the previous five consecutive business days preceding the listing of a Perpetual SFP on such Underlying Security (or a closing price of at least $7.50 for the same period if the Underlying Security is not a “covered security”), (v) pursuant to Rule 14.3(e), have a public float of not less than 7,000,000 (seven million) shares, (vi) pursuant to Rule 14.3(f), have an estimated deliverable supply in excess of 20,000,000 (twenty million) shares, (vii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(g), have an issuer that is current in all periodic reporting obligations under Sections 13 or 15(d) of the Act,
[
11
]
and (viii) pursuant to Rule 14.3(j), have at least 2,000 security holders (whether of record or beneficial).
The initial eligibility criterion regarding trading volume history of potential Underlying Securities in Rule 14.3(c) is framed in terms of ADTV over the prior month, so does not contemplate Underlying Securities with exchange-trading histories of less than one month. Accordingly, under the current rule, if an IPO occurs on a given day, the earliest date that the Exchange could list a Perpetual SFP on such security would be one month following such date. The Exchange therefore proposes to amend Rule 14.3(c) to provide that, “where the Underlying Security has been listed for trading for less than one month, . . . the Underlying Security must have had a trading volume (in all markets in which it is traded) of at least 2,400,000 shares since the Underlying Security's initial public offering day.” The Exchange also proposes to include a definition of “initial public offering day” in the introductory language in Rule 14.3, which would define “initial public offering day” of an Underlying Security as “the first day on which the Underlying Security trades `regular way' on a national securities exchange.”
As proposed, this rule change would permit the Exchange to list a Perpetual SFP on an Underlying Security with a trading volume of 2,400,000 shares since its IPO, regardless of the length of time between the IPO and the New Product Committee's review of the Underlying Security, subject to satisfaction of all other initial eligibility criteria in Rule 14.3, as amended herein. This proposed amendment is consistent with the trading volume criteria adopted by securities options exchanges with respect to the eligibility criteria for underlying securities of securities options, which require such underlying securities to have had a total trading volume of 2,400,000 shares in the preceding twelve months without specifying a monthly ADTV requirement or any minimum lookback period.
[
12
]
Additionally, the minimum share price criterion in Rule 14.3(d) requires the market price per share of an underlying covered security to have been at least $3.00 for the previous five consecutive business days preceding the date on which the Exchange commences to list and trade a Perpetual SFP on such Underlying Security (the “five-day lookback period”). Under the current rule, even assuming adoption of the proposed amendment to Rule 14.3(c) discussed above, if an IPO occurs on a Monday, the earliest date the Exchange could list a Perpetual SFP on the relevant security would be the following Monday, with the market price determined by the closing price over the five-day lookback period from the Monday of the IPO through the following Friday.
The Exchange proposes to waive the five-day lookback period in Rule 14.3(d) for certain covered securities for the first three business days following their IPO and accelerate the listing of Perpetual SFPs on such securities by up to three business days.
[
13
]
As proposed, the
(
printed page 72937)
Exchange would permit, starting on or after the second business day following the covered security's IPO day (
i.e.,
not inclusive of the day of the IPO), the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on such security if it had a market capitalization of at least $3,000,000,000 (three billion U.S. dollars) based upon the offering price of its IPO. For example, under the proposed rule, if an IPO for a company with a market capitalization of $3 billion (based upon its offering price) occurs on a Monday, the Exchange could list a Perpetual SFP for trading on Wednesday, subject to the Underlying Security satisfying all other eligibility criteria in Rule 14.3, which could accelerate the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on IPO securities by up to three business days. This proposed amendment is also consistent with the listing standards of securities options exchanges, which have adopted parallel amendments to their rules in order to “provide investors the opportunity to hedge their interest in IPO investments in a shorter amount of time than what [was then] permitted.”
[
14
]
The Exchange submits that, like securities options on recently IPO'd securities, Perpetual SFPs on such securities will serve as valuable hedging tools to the trading community and help markets function efficiently by mitigating risks, thereby reducing volatility in the markets for such securities.
Other listing standards would apply, including the minimum $100,000,000,000 (one hundred billion U.S. dollars) current market capitalization requirement in Rule 14.3(b), which would be distinct from amended Rule 14.3(d) because it takes into account secondary trading after the IPO.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed amendments to Rule 14.3 are consistent with Section 6 of the Act and, in particular, further the objectives of Sections 6(b)(1)
[
15
]
and 6(b)(5)
[
16
]
of the Act insofar as they are designed to ensure the compliance of the Exchange and its members with applicable provisions of the Act and Commission and Exchange rules, to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and to promote just and equitable principles of trade. The Exchange further believes that the proposed rule changes are consistent with Section 6(h)(3)
[
17
]
of the Act which contains detailed requirements for listing standards and conditions for trading security futures products.
Section 6(h)(3)(C) of the Act
[
18
]
requires that Kalshi's listing standards for Perpetual SFPs be no less restrictive than comparable listing standards for options traded on a national securities exchange. For the reasons discussed above, Kalshi believes that the eligibility standards for Underlying Securities for Perpetual SFPs under the proposed rule change are no less restrictive than comparable listing standards for exchange-traded options. Since certain securities options exchanges have a comparable listing standard,
[
19
]
Kalshi believes that the proposed rule change meets the requirement of Section 6(h)(3)(C) of the Act.
As discussed above, the Exchange proposes to reduce the time to market for the listing and trading of Perpetual SFPs on Underlying Securities that are covered securities following their IPO if they have a trading volume of 2,400,000 shares since their IPO and market capitalization of at least $3 billion based upon the offering price. Taken together, the amendments would reduce the time to market for Perpetual SFPs on such securities, as Perpetual SFPs on such securities would be permitted to be listed and traded on Kalshi starting on or after the second business day following the IPO (not including the day of the IPO) if all listing criteria in Rule 14.3 are satisfied, including the $100 billion market capitalization requirement in Rule 14.3(b).
The proposed rule change would require IPO securities to have had a trading volume of 2,400,000 shares since their IPO to list Perpetual SFPs on such securities prior to such securities having one month of trading history, and would only waive the five-day lookback period for covered securities following their IPO if they have a market capitalization of at least $3 billion based upon their IPO offering price.
The proposed change with respect to the trading volume criteria is equally stringent as the trading volume requirement in Staff Legal Bulletin No. 15 (“SLB 15”),
[
20
]
except in that it does not require an Underlying Security to have a 12 month trading history. Specifically, SLB 15 itself notes that its requirement for a security underlying a security futures product to have an average daily trading volume of at least 109,000 shares for the preceding 12 months “is comparable to the requirement that a security underlying an option have a minimum monthly trading volume of 2.4 million shares for the preceding 12 months.”
[
21
]
The proposed change with respect to minimum share price would only waive the five-day lookback period for covered securities following their IPO if they have a substantial market capitalization of at least $3 billion based upon their IPO offering price. The Exchange believes that securities with such substantial market capitalizations at the IPO offering price are likely to satisfy the $3.00 market price per share five-day lookback period requirement. Further, the proposed market capitalization requirement of $3 billion based on the IPO offering price would ensure an objective qualification process for the waiver that would prevent market participants from being able to influence whether an IPO security qualifies for the waiver through trading in the security, which could be a concern if the threshold price was based on the market price of the shares following the IPO.
In accelerating the time to market for Perpetual SFPs on the types of large, high-profile IPO securities that would satisfy Exchange listing standards under the proposed amendments, the proposal does not materially change the listing process for Perpetual SFPs, nor does it propose to change any other eligibility criteria for Underlying Securities.
In addition, the Exchange represents that trading in IPO securities is subject to real-time market surveillance administered by the Exchange, with information sharing and coordination through its arrangements with the Intermarket Surveillance Group. The Exchange represents that these surveillances are designed to detect violations of Exchange rules and applicable federal law. Vigilant surveillance can help deter and detect violations of Exchange rules and the federal securities rules and regulations, and in so doing can help prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and
(
printed page 72938)
practices, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.
[
22
]
Finally, the proposed rule changes are established criteria used by securities options exchanges. The Exchange believes that the experience of those options exchanges establishes that the proposed rule changes, along with the other initial eligibility criteria in Rule 14.3, are designed to provide investor protection.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
Kalshi does not believe that the proposed rule changes will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In fact, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will promote competition by allowing Kalshi to list a broader array of single stock futures, without jeopardizing investor protection.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange has not solicited, and does not intend to solicit, comments on this proposed rule change. The Exchange has not received any unsolicited written comments from members or other interested parties.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The proposed rule change will become effective on November 19, 2026.
At any time within 60 days of the effectiveness of the proposed rule change, the Commission, after consultation with the CFTC, may summarily abrogate the proposed rule change and require that the proposed rule change be refiled in accordance with the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) of the Act.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views, and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
http://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
);
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include File No. SR-KALSHIEX-2026-03 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File No. SR-KALSHIEX-2026-03. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
http://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to File No. SR-KALSHIEX-2026-03 and should be submitted on or before December 3, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
23
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission

November 6, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 30, 2026, Nasdaq PHLX LLC (“PHLX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
(
printed page 72930)
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Equity 4 to remove all references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​phlx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
In September 2025 the Exchange added CORE FIX to its rulebook in Equity 4, in anticipation of making this new order entry protocol available to Exchange Participants in October of 2025.
[
3
]
In December 2025 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the first quarter of 2026.
[
4
]
In March 2026 the Exchange extended the implementation date for CORE FIX to the end of 2026.
[
5
]
In spite of its best efforts, the Exchange has been unable to generate interest in CORE FIX among Exchange Participants. Therefore, rather than deploy an order entry protocol that Participants are not even interested in testing, the Exchange proposes to abandon its plans to deploy CORE FIX.
[
6
]
This will allow the Exchange to better allocate its technological development resources. The Exchange notes that it will continue to offer all the order entry protocols that are currently available and operative on the Exchange—namely, OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX.
[
7
]
The Exchange proposes to eliminate all references to CORE FIX that are currently present in Equity 4. Specifically, these references are found in Rules 3100 (Limit Up-Limit Down Plan and Trading Halts on PSX), 3301A (Order Types), 3301B (Order Attributes), and 3307 (Processing of Orders).
[
8
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
10
]
in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade because it will ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the order entry protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX, which the Exchange will not deploy, will avoid confusion among Participants and other market participants regarding the protocols available for order entry. The proposed rule change will not alter the operation of the Exchange's market, the treatment of orders, or the rights or obligations of Participants; the Exchange will continue to offer the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols. Accordingly, the proposal will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and will protect investors and the public interest by providing clear and accurate information concerning the Exchange's order entry protocols.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issue; instead, its purpose is to ensure that the Exchange's rulebook accurately reflects the protocols that are available and operative on the Exchange. Removing references to CORE FIX will not deprive any Participant of an available order entry protocol, because CORE FIX has not been deployed on the Exchange. Participants will continue to be able to choose among the OUCH, RASH, FLITE, and FIX protocols based on their trading needs. Accordingly, the proposal will not impose any burden on competition, either among Exchange Participants or between the Exchange and other trading venues.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
11
]
and
(
printed page 72931)
subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
12
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-PHLX-2026-65 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-65. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-PHLX-2026-65 and should be submitted on or before December 3, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
13
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106838; File No. SR-NYSE-2026-54]
November 6, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on October 28, 2026, New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Rules 7.35 and 7.35A to change when the Exchange begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.35 (General) and Rule 7.35A (DMM-Facilitated Core Open and Trading Halt Auctions) to change when the Exchange begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to begin disseminating such information at the later of (A) 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time (“ET”), or (B) the earlier of (i) the time the Designated Market Maker (“DMM”) publishes the first pre-opening indication for the security pursuant to Rule 7.35A(d), or (ii) 10:00 a.m. ET.
As discussed below, the Exchange currently begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction at 8:00 a.m. ET, the same time applicable to all other Core Open Auctions, without regard to whether the underwriting syndicate has completed the IPO distribution process. This approach differs from that taken by at least one other national securities exchange, as described below. The Exchange believes that disseminating Auction Imbalance Information before the underwriting syndicate has finalized the distribution may result in information that does not reflect material aspects of the transaction and may therefore be misconstrued by market participants as indicative of the anticipated market for the security. The proposed change would better align the dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information with the liquidity formation process, thereby increasing transparency and reducing the potential for confusion, while preserving 8:00 a.m. ET as the earliest time such information may be disseminated, consistent with all other Core Open Auctions.
Background
Rule 7.35(c) governs the Exchange's dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information. Rule 7.35(c)(1) provides that Auction Imbalance Information is updated at least every second, unless there is no change to the information. Rule 7.35(c)(2) provides that Auction Imbalance Information is disseminated until the relevant Auction begins.
Rule 7.35A(e) governs the timing, content, and pricing of Auction Imbalance Information specifically for the Core Open Auction and Trading Halt Auction facilitated by a DMM.
Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(A) currently provides that, for the Core Open Auction, unless a security is halted, the
(
printed page 72932)
Exchange will begin disseminating Auction Imbalance Information at 8:00 a.m.
Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(D) further provides that the Exchange will not disseminate Auction Imbalance Information for the Core Open Auction if there is no “Opening Reference Price,” a term defined in Rule 7.35A(a). Rule 7.35A(e)(3) provides that the Imbalance Reference Price used in Auction Imbalance Information for the Core Open Auction is the Opening Reference Price, unless a pre-opening indication has been published, in which case it is the Opening Reference Price bounded by the pre-opening indication prices.
Historically, Rule 7.35(c)(3) provided that the Exchange would not disseminate Auction Imbalance Information at all for a security that was an IPO or Direct Listing and had not yet had its IPO Auction or Direct Listing Auction. In April 2020, in connection with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Exchange's Trading Floor operations, the Exchange adopted a series of temporary rule changes suspending this restriction so that Auction Imbalance Information would instead be disseminated for an IPO or Direct Listing in the same manner as for any other Core Open Auction.
[
4
]
This temporary relief was subsequently extended on several occasions.
[
5
]
In November 2020, the Exchange proposed to make this change permanent,
[
6
]
which the Commission approved in 2021.
[
7
]
As part of that filing, the Exchange deleted former Rule 7.35(c)(3) in its entirety such that an IPO or Direct Listing that had not yet had its IPO Auction or Direct Listing Auction would no longer be excluded from Auction Imbalance Information dissemination, and would instead be included in the same 8:00 a.m. dissemination applicable to Core Open Auctions generally. To enable the underlying calculation to function for a security with no trading history, the Exchange also amended the definition of the reference price used in that calculation to provide that, for an IPO that had not yet had its IPO Auction, the reference price would be deemed to be the security's offering price.
[
8
]
The current definition of Opening Reference Price in Rule 7.35A(a) does not include an IPO-specific value. As described further below, the Exchange proposes to add such a value as part of this filing.
Proposed Rule Change
As noted, the Exchange's current practice of disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction beginning at 8:00 a.m.,
i.e.,
at the same time as for any other Core Open Auction, differs from the approach taken by at least one other national securities exchange. Nasdaq, for example, does not begin disseminating its order imbalance indicator for an initial public offering until the beginning of the “Display Only Period” applicable to that security, and the subsequent “Pre-Launch Period” does not end until Nasdaq receives notice from the underwriter that the security is ready to trade.
[
9
]
In addition, once disseminated, the reference price used in Nasdaq's imbalance indicator for an IPO is the price closest to the issuer's actual initial public offering price.
[
10
]
As a result, Nasdaq's imbalance information for an IPO is not disseminated until information reflecting the completion of the underwriting syndicate's process is available.
By contrast, because the Exchange currently begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction at 8:00 a.m. ET, that information may be published before the underwriting syndicate has been finalized and before the DMM has issued a pre-opening indication reflecting the results of that process. At that stage, the information available to the Exchange, and therefore reflected in Auction Imbalance Information under the current approach, is limited. While the offering price generally would be known, along with Auction-eligible interest entered by market participants and electronically submitted Floor broker interest, the syndicate's distribution of the offering may not yet be complete, the underwriter may not yet have entered all interest intended to participate in the IPO Auction, and the DMM may not yet have received information from the underwriter relevant to determining the likely opening range for the security. In addition, because no pre-opening indication would yet have been published, the Imbalance Reference Price would be based solely on the offering price and would not reflect the DMM's assessment of the anticipated opening range. As a result, the imbalance, paired quantity, and related Auction Imbalance Information would reflect only a partial view of the interest ultimately expected to participate in the IPO Auction and would be measured against a reference price that has not yet been informed by the DMM's price discovery process. For a security with no trading history, the Exchange is concerned that Auction Imbalance Information disseminated under these circumstances may create confusion among market participants, who may reasonably view published imbalance information as representative of overall market interest when material aspects of the offering process remain incomplete.
The Exchange believes that disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction at the later of 8:00 a.m. ET or the earlier of the DMM's first pre-opening indication or 10:00 a.m. ET would address these concerns. A DMM's pre-opening indication is generally the mechanism by which an informed assessment of where an IPO security is likely to open is first made public. Under Rule
(
printed page 72933)
7.35A(d), a pre-opening indication identifies the security and the price range within which the Auction Price is anticipated to occur. It is disseminated through the securities information processor and the Exchange's proprietary data feeds so that it is available to all market participants simultaneously, and its publication requires supervision and approval of a Trading Official. A published indication must be updated if the anticipated Auction Price would fall outside the published range, the DMM generally must wait a prescribed period after publishing an indication before opening the security, and the Exchange will not permit a security to open outside the most recently published indication range.
[
11
]
Moreover, Rule 7.35A(d) does not prescribe an earliest time at which a DMM may publish a pre-opening indication. Accordingly, if a DMM receives sufficient information from an underwriter before 8:00 a.m. ET to formulate an anticipated opening range, the DMM could publish an indication before that time. Under the proposal, Auction Imbalance Information would nevertheless begin to be disseminated no earlier than 8:00 a.m. ET. In those circumstances, because the Imbalance Reference Price is bounded by the prices contained in a published indication, the first disseminated Auction Imbalance Information would already reflect the DMM's publicly disclosed assessment of the anticipated opening range. Because the indication would already be publicly available, market participants would have access to the DMM's anticipated pricing range before any Auction Imbalance Information is disseminated. The proposal therefore would not withhold from the market the information that the Exchange believes is most relevant to understanding where an IPO security is expected to open.
The Exchange believes that 8:00 a.m. ET is the appropriate floor for the dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information for IPO Auctions. Under Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(A), 8:00 a.m. ET is the time at which the Exchange begins disseminating Auction Imbalance Information for all other Core Open Auctions, and market participants and their systems are accustomed to receiving auction information beginning at that time. Retaining that start time for IPO Auctions preserves a uniform and predictable framework for the dissemination of Core Open Auction information across all securities rather than introducing an IPO-specific dissemination schedule. In addition, because the 8:00 a.m. ET floor can only defer, and never accelerate, the dissemination of Auction Imbalance Information relative to current practice, the proposal cannot result in information for an IPO Auction being disseminated earlier than it is today.
Similarly, the Exchange believes that 10:00 a.m. ET is the appropriate backstop. Because a DMM is not required to publish a pre-opening indication in every IPO Auction, the Exchange believes a time-based backstop is necessary to ensure that Auction Imbalance Information continues to be disseminated even where no indication is published. Absent such a provision, Auction Imbalance Information could potentially be withheld indefinitely solely because a pre-opening indication was not required under Rule 7.35A(d). The Exchange therefore believes that a fixed dissemination deadline promotes transparency while preserving the benefits of linking dissemination to the publication of a pre-opening indication where one is available.
In addition, 10:00 a.m. ET is thirty minutes after the commencement of Core Trading Hours, which is the point after which, under Rule 7.35A(a)(4)(A), an opening is considered a Delayed Opening for which the DMM should consult with a Trading Official. By that time, the Exchange believes the underwriter generally will have had a substantial opportunity to complete the syndicate's distribution of the offering and to enter interest intended to participate in the IPO Auction. The Exchange also believes that market participants would reasonably expect Auction Imbalance Information to be available at that stage of the opening process.
If no pre-opening indication has been published by 10:00 a.m. ET, the Exchange would begin disseminating the same Auction Imbalance Information currently disseminated for any Core Open Auction under Rule 7.35A(e)(2), including the total imbalance and its side, the paired quantity, and the Continuous Book Clearing Price calculated using all interest eligible to participate in the IPO Auction at that time, including Floor broker interest, plus the Imbalance Reference Price. Because no pre-opening indication would have been published, the Imbalance Reference Price would be the Opening Reference Price alone, which for an IPO that has not yet opened would be the security's offering price unbounded by an indication range. This is the same information the Exchange currently disseminates beginning at 8:00 a.m. ET. Accordingly, the proposal would modify only the timing of dissemination for an IPO Auction, not the content of the information disseminated. However, the Exchange believes that by 10:00 a.m. ET, such information is more likely to reflect the interest that will participate in the IPO Auction than information disseminated at 8:00 a.m. ET before the underwriting process has matured. In the absence of a published DMM indication, the Exchange believes that the offering price remains the most appropriate available reference point against which to measure that interest.
In short, the Exchange believes the proposal appropriately balances transparency and accuracy in IPO Auctions. Retaining 8:00 a.m. ET as a floor preserves the dissemination schedule applicable to all other Core Open Auction, while the 10:00 a.m. ET backstop ensures that Auction Imbalance Information will not be withheld indefinitely in the absence of a pre-opening indication. The Exchange therefore believes the proposal would improve the usefulness of Auction Imbalance Information and reduce the potential for investor confusion arising from the dissemination of imbalance data before the IPO price discovery process has sufficiently developed.
To effectuate these changes, the Exchange proposes to amend Rules 7.35 and 7.35A as follows.
First, the Exchange proposes to add new Rule 7.35(c)(3) to provide that, for an IPO Auction, the Exchange will begin disseminating Auction Imbalance Information at the later of (A) 8:00 a.m. ET, or (B) the earlier of (i) the time the DMM publishes the first pre-opening indication for the security pursuant to Rule 7.35A(d), or (ii) 10:00 a.m. ET. Once the Exchange begins disseminating such information, it will be disseminated in accordance with Rule 7.35A(e)(1)-(3) and updated as provided in Rule 7.35(c)(1).
Second, the Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.35A(e)(1)(A) to exclude an IPO Auction from the general rule that Auction Imbalance Information for the Core Open Auction begins disseminating at 8:00 a.m., and to cross-reference new Rule 7.35(c)(3) for the timing applicable to an IPO Auction.
(
printed page 72934)
Third, the Exchange proposes to amend the definition of “Opening Reference Price” in Rule 7.35A(a) to provide that, for an IPO that has not had its IPO Auction, the Opening Reference Price means the security's offering price. This amendment ensures that the Imbalance Reference Price calculation in Rule 7.35A(e)(3) functions as intended once Auction Imbalance Information begins disseminating for an IPO Auction under new Rule 7.35(c)(3), consistent with how the corresponding reference price for an IPO was defined before the rule's subsequent renumbering and restructuring, as described above.
The proposed change is limited to IPO Auctions and does not apply to Direct Listings, which are not priced through an underwritten offering and whose reference price under Rule 7.35A(d)(2)(A) does not depend on completion of a syndicate's book-building process. In addition, Auction Imbalance Information disseminated under the proposal would be available to all market participants in the same manner as for any other Core Open Auction.
Because of the technology changes associated with this proposed rule change, the Exchange will announce the implementation of this change by Trader Update. The Exchange is prepared to implement the proposed rule change no later than the first quarter of 2027.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
12
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
13
]
in particular, because it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest and because it is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes that aligning the timing of Auction Imbalance Information dissemination for an IPO Auction with the availability of the DMM's pre-opening indication, subject to an 8:00 a.m. ET floor and a 10:00 a.m. ET backstop, would promote just and equitable principles of trade and protect investors and the public interest by reducing the likelihood that market participants receive and rely upon Auction Imbalance Information that does not yet reflect material information about the offering process, such as the completion of the underwriting syndicate's process. The Exchange believes that the current practice of disseminating such information at a fixed time without regard to whether that process has concluded creates the potential for investor confusion regarding the reliability of the information disseminated, and that the proposed rule change would remove that potential source of confusion. As described above, the current rule was adopted and made permanent during the pandemic. With the passage of time, the Exchange is in a better position to fully appreciate the potential disadvantages of this approach to the investing public. The Exchange further believes that retaining the 8:00 a.m. ET floor and the 10:00 a.m. ET backstop appropriately balances the goal of disseminating more reliable information against the importance of timely transparency into the auction process: the floor ensures that Auction Imbalance Information for an IPO Auction is never disseminated earlier than for any other Core Open Auction, and the backstop ensures that such information is not withheld indefinitely absent a pre-opening indication.
The Exchange also believes that the proposed floor and backstop times are reasonably designed to protect investors and the public interest. The 8:00 a.m. ET floor is the same time at which auction information is first disseminated for every other Core Open Auction, and any pre-opening indication published earlier would already be publicly available through the securities information processor and proprietary data feeds. The 10:00 a.m. ET backstop coincides with the point, thirty minutes after the start of Core Trading Hours, after which the Exchange's rules treat an opening as delayed, and the information disseminated at that time in the absence of a pre-opening indication would be the same Auction Imbalance Information that is disseminated today. As a result, the proposal would not reduce the content of the information available to market participants; it would defer, by a defined and limited period, the initial dissemination of that information at a time when it is most likely to be unrepresentative.
Further, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system by more closely aligning the Exchange's practice with that of at least one other national securities exchange for a comparable product, thereby reducing a source of inconsistency that market participants may otherwise encounter when comparing the reliability of imbalance information for IPOs across trading venues.
[
14
]
Finally, the Exchange believes that amending the definition of Opening Reference Price to include an IPO-specific value is necessary and appropriate to ensure that the Auction Imbalance Information disseminated pursuant to the proposed rule change best reflects a defined and predictable reference price, consistent with the manner in which the Exchange previously defined the analogous reference price for an IPO before that provision was renumbered and restructured. The Exchange believes that this amendment removes impediments to and perfects the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system by ensuring that the rule operates as intended and does not leave the calculation of the Imbalance Reference Price for an IPO Auction undefined.
For the foregoing reasons, the Exchange believes that the proposal is consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is limited to the timing of Auction Imbalance Information dissemination for an IPO Auction and does not otherwise alter the manner in which DMMs or any other market participants interact with the Exchange.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intramarket competition, because the proposed timing would apply equally to all IPO Auctions on the Exchange, and the resulting Auction Imbalance Information would be made available to all market participants at the same time and in the same manner. The proposed rule change does not create any special or differential
(
printed page 72935)
treatment for any category of market participant.
The Exchange also does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on intermarket competition. To the contrary, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change may reduce a source of intermarket inconsistency by more closely aligning the Exchange's practice for IPO Auction Imbalance Information with that of at least one other national securities exchange, thereby facilitating more consistent expectations among market participants trading IPOs across multiple venues.
Accordingly, for the foregoing reasons, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change would impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
15
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
16
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
17
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file SR-NYSE-2026-54 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-54. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-54 and should be submitted on or before December 3, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
18
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Department of Justice
Drug Enforcement Administration
On January 19, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Troy R. Lehman, D.O., of Woodward, Oklahoma (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 1, at 1, 6. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. BL7481649, alleging that Registrant lacks state authority to handle controlled substances in Oklahoma and materially falsified his registration renewal applications.
Id.
at 2-4 (citing
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
,
824(a)(3)
).
On March 6, 2026, the Government submitted an RFAA to the Administrator requesting that the Agency issue a default final order revoking Registrant's registration. RFAA, at 3. After carefully reviewing the entire record and conducting the analysis as set forth in detail below, the Agency finds that Registrant is in default, finds that Registrant is without state authority, and finds that Registrant materially falsified his applications. Accordingly, the Agency grants the Government's RFAA and revokes Registrant's registration.
I. Default Determination
Under
21 CFR 1301.43
, a registrant entitled to a hearing who fails to file a timely hearing request “within 30 days after the date of receipt of the [OSC] . . . shall be deemed to have waived their right to a hearing and to be in default” unless “good cause” is established for the failure.
21 CFR 1301.43(a)
,
(c)(1)
. In the absence of a demonstration of good cause, a registrant who fails to timely file an answer also is “deemed to have waived their right to a hearing and to be in default.”
21 CFR 1301.43(c)(2)
. Unless excused, a default constitutes “an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
The OSC notified Registrant of his right to file a written request for hearing, and that if he failed to file such a request, he would be deemed to have waived his right to a hearing and be in default. RFAAX 1, at 5 (citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds him to be in default. RFAA, at 2.
[
1
]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
. Because Registrant is in default and has not moved to excuse the default, the Agency finds that Registrant has admitted to the factual allegations in the OSC.
21 CFR 1301.43(c)(1)
,
(e)
,
(f)(1)
.
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
at 1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to
21 CFR 1301.43(c)
,
(f)
, and
1301.46
. RFAA, at 3;
see also
21 CFR 1316.67
.
II. Lack of State Authority
A. Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. According to the OSC, the Oklahoma State Board of Osteopathic Examiners (Board) suspended Registrant from the practice of osteopathic medicine in Oklahoma on September 18, 2025. In addition, Registrant's Oklahoma osteopathic medical license expired by its own terms on June 30, 2026. RFAAX 1, at 3. Further, on October 31, 2025, Registrant's Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drug (OBNDD) license expired by its own terms. According to Oklahoma online records, of which the Agency takes official notice,
[
2
]
Registrant's OBNDD registration is inactive. OBNDD, Registrant Search,
https://obnddc.us.thentiacloud.net/​webs/​obnddc/​register
(last visited date of signature of this Order).
[
3
]
Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice medicine nor to handle controlled substances in Oklahoma, the state in which he is registered with DEA.
[
4
]
(
printed page 72914)
B. Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006). (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. § 802(21).”). The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Ashley Vermillion, N.P.,
91 FR 35270
, (2026);
Henry-Norbert O. Ndekwe, M.D.,
90 FR 15990
(2025);
Lawrence Rudolph, D.M.D.,
89 FR 79310
(2024).
[
5
]
Pursuant to Oklahoma's Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Act, “[e]very person who manufactures, distributes, dispenses, prescribes, administers or uses for scientific purposes any controlled dangerous substance within or into this state . . . shall obtain a registration issued by the Director of the [OBNDD], in accordance with rules promulgated by the Director.” Okla. Stat. tit. 63, § 2-302(A) (2026).
[
6
]
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant currently lacks authority to handle controlled substances in Oklahoma because his OBNDD registration is expired and his medical license was suspended, expired, and is now cancelled. As discussed above, a person must hold a valid OBNDD registration to dispense a controlled substance in Oklahoma. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to practice medicine and handle controlled substances in Oklahoma, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
III. Material Falsification
A. Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted.
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
. Accordingly, Registrant is deemed to have admitted to each of the following facts.
[
7
]
On September 17, 2001, Registrant applied for and was subsequently granted a DEA registration as a practitioner in Schedules II through V. RFAAX 1, at 4. On December 9, 2010, the Oklahoma State Board of Osteopathic Examiners (Board) issued an Order of Probation with Conditions, placing Registrant's Oklahoma medical license on probation until September 22, 2011.
Id.
Thereafter, Registrant applied to renew his DEA registration multiple times on the following dates: March 28, 2013; March 22, 2016; February 27, 2019; March 2, 2022; and March 31, 2025.
Id.
Each of the five renewal application forms contained Liability Question 3 which asks: “[h]as the applicant ever surrendered (for cause) or had a state professional license or controlled substance registration revoked, suspended, denied, restricted, or placed on probation, or is any such action pending?”
Id.
On each of the five renewal applications, Registrant answered “no” to Liability Question 3.
Id.
Registrant's “no” answers was false in light of the 2010 probation on his Oklahoma medical license.
Id.
Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant falsely answered Liability Question 3 on five renewal applications.
B. Discussion
A DEA registration may be denied, suspended, or revoked upon a finding that the applicant or registrant materially falsified any application filed pursuant to or required by the Controlled Substances Act (CSA).
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
.
[
8
]
To present a
prima facie
case for material falsification, the Government's record evidence must show (1) the submission of an application, (2) containing a false statement and/or omitting information that the application requires, (3) when the submitter knew or should have known that the statement is false and/or that the omitted information existed and the application required its disclosure, and (4) the false statement and/or required but omitted information is material, that is, it “connect[s] to at least one of [the section 823] factors that, according to the CSA, [the Administrator] `shall' consider” when analyzing “whether issuing a registration `would be inconsistent with the public interest.' ”
Frank Joseph Stirlacci, M.D.,
85 FR 45229
,
45238
(2020) (citing
21 U.S.C. 823
and
Kungys,
485 U.S. at 771). The Government must establish material falsification with record evidence that is clear, unequivocal, and convincing.
Kungys,
485 U.S. at 772;
Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45230-39.
First, the Government must prove that the applicant or registrant submitted an application for registration pursuant to the CSA.
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
;
see also
21 U.S.C. 822
(persons required to register);
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
(registration requirements).
Second, the Government must prove that the application contained a false statement or omitted information that
(
printed page 72915)
the application required, either of which may constitute a material falsity.
See, e.g., Emed Medical Company LLC and Med Assist Pharmacy,
88 FR 21719
,
21720
(2023) (applicant falsely answered “no” to Liability Question 3 on seventeen applications when the true answer was “yes”);
Richard J. Settles, D.O.,
81 FR 64940
,
64945-46
(2016) (applicant failed to disclose an interim consent agreement restricting his license based on findings that he issued controlled substance prescriptions without federal or state legal authority to do so). In making this assessment, the Agency will examine the entire application, including registrant's “yes/no” answers to the liability questions and any follow-up response(s).
Daniel A. Glick, D.D.S.,
80 FR 74800
,
74802
,
74808-09
(2015). To establish an omission, the Government must show both that omitted information existed and that the application required inclusion of that information.
See, e.g., Richard A. Herbert, M.D.,
76 FR 53942
,
53956
(2011) (omission of a probation which the application required to be identified);
Michel P. Toret, M.D.,
82 FR 60041
,
60042
(2017) (Voluntary Surrender Form alone is insufficient evidence to find material falsification based on registrant's “no” answer to the question regarding “surrender[s] (for cause)”).
Third, the Government must prove that the applicant or registrant knew or should have known that the statement is false and/or that the omitted information existed and the application required its disclosure.
See John J. Cienki, M.D.,
63 FR 52293
,
52295
(1998) (“[I]n finding that there has been a material falsification of an application, it must be determined that the applicant knew or should have known that the response given to the liability question was false.”);
Samuel Arnold, D.D.S.,
63 FR 8687
,
8688
(1998) (“It is also undisputed that Respondent knew that his Ohio dental license had previously been suspended.”);
Bobby Watts, M.D.,
58 FR 46995
,
46995
(1993) (“Respondent knew that the Tennessee Board of Medical Examiners had suspended his medical license on May 7, 1987, and had placed his state medical license on probation on May 2, 1988.”);
see also Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45236-37 & nn.22-23 (collecting cases).
Fourth, the Government must prove that the false statement and/or required but omitted information is “material.”
Kungys
holds that a statement is material if it is “predictably capable of affecting,
i.e.,
had a natural tendency to affect, the [Agency's] official decision,” or stated differently, “had a natural tendency to influence the decision.”
Kungys,
485 U.S. at 771-72. However, “[i]t makes no difference that a specific falsification did not exert influence so long as it had the capacity to do so.”
United States
v.
Alemany Rivera,
781 F.2d 229, 234 (1st Cir. 1985). As already discussed, materiality, for the purposes of the CSA, is tied to what the Administrator “shall” consider when determining whether issuance of a registration “would be inconsistent with the public interest.”
21 U.S.C. 823
;
Kungys,
485 U.S. at 771-72;
Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45234, 45238.
The Government has the burden of proof in this proceeding.
21 CFR 1301.44
. Here, the Agency finds based on clear, unequivocal, and convincing record evidence that the Government presents a
prima facie
case that Registrant submitted a materially false application.
21 U.S.C. 823
,
824(a)(1)
.
Registrant is deemed to have admitted that he applied to renew his DEA registration five times following Oklahoma's placement of Registrant's state license on probation in 2010. RFAAX 1, at 4. On each occasion, the renewal application contained Liability Question 3 which asked whether Registrant had surrendered (for cause) or had a state professional license or controlled substance registration revoked, suspended, denied, restricted, or placed on probation, or if any such action was pending.
Id.
Each renewal application clearly required Registrant to answer yes or no to Liability Question 3. Registrant answered “no” each time when the correct answer was “yes.”
Id.
Thus, Registrant falsified five renewal applications by failing to acknowledge his 2010 state license probation when he knew or should have known that the response given to the liability question was false each time he renewed his registration.
Id.
In addition, the falsities were material. Liability Question 3 is intended to obtain information relevant to conduct the analysis required by
21 U.S.C. 823
and
824
. Specifically,
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
and
(4)
require the Administrator to consider whether the applicant has had a state license or registration suspended, revoked, or denied by state authority, whether the applicant is authorized to dispense controlled substances under state law, and whether the applicant has committed acts inconsistent with the public interest. Further, the public interest factors require the Administrator to consider the recommendation of state licensing boards, the applicant's experience in handling controlled substances, the applicant's compliance with state laws related to controlled substances, and other conduct which may threaten public safety.
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)(A)
, (B), (D), (E). Liability Question 3, in other words, is tethered to provisions which the Administrator is required by statute to consider when reviewing applications for registration.
Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45238. Thus, a false answer to Liability Question 3 is material.
By omitting the 2010 probation of his state license, Registrant “deprived [DEA] of information potentially relevant to” the analysis that the Administrator is statutorily mandated to conduct.
Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45234-35;
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
,
824(a)
. Thus, omission of this information directly affected the public interest analysis that DEA was required to make when it reviewed his registration application.
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
,
824(a)
;
Stirlacci,
85 FR at 45238. Stated differently, the omissions were material because they were “predictably capable of affecting . . . [DEA's] official decision” regarding whether Registrant met “the requirements for” registration.
Kungys,
485 U.S. at 771.
In sum, the Agency finds clear, unequivocal, and convincing record evidence that Registrant's response to Liability Question 3 was materially false for failure to disclose the 2010 probation of his state medical license.
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
;
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
. The Agency further finds that the Government has established a
prima facie
case for material falsification, that Registrant did not rebut that
prima facie
case, and that there is clear, unequivocal, and convincing record evidence supporting revocation.
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
.
C. Sanction
Where, as here, the Government has presented a
prima facie
case showing that a registrant submitted a materially false renewal application, the burden shifts to Registrant to show why he can be trusted with a registration.
Morall
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
412 F.3d 165, 181 (D.C. Cir. 2005);
Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy, LLC
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
881 F.3d 823, 830 (11th Cir. 2018);
Garrett Howard Smith, M.D.,
83 FR 18882
,
18904
(2018). The issue of trust is a fact-dependent determination based on the circumstances presented by the individual practitioner.
Jeffrey Stein, M.D.,
84 FR 46968
,
46972
(2019);
see also Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy,
881 F.3d at 833. Moreover, as past performance is the best predictor of future performance, DEA Administrators have required that a registrant who has committed acts inconsistent with the public interest must accept responsibility for those acts
(
printed page 72916)
and demonstrate that the registrant will not engage in future misconduct.
Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy,
881 F.3d at 833;
ALRA Labs, Inc.
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
54 F.3d 450, 452 (7th Cir. 1995). Historically, the Agency has considered acceptance of responsibility, egregiousness, and deterrence when making this assessment.
See Michael Bouknight,
90 FR 31247
,
31250
(2025);
Sasha Melissa Ikramelahai,
90 FR 32017
,
32020-21
(2025);
Frank Joseph Stirlacci, M.D.,
85 FR 45229
,
45239-40
(2020). Acceptance of responsibility must be unequivocal.
Janet S. Pettyjohn, D.O.,
89 FR 82639
,
82641
(2024);
Mohammed Asgar, M.D.,
83 FR 29569
,
29573
(2018);
see also Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy,
881 F.3d at 830-31.
In addition, a registrant's candor during the investigation and hearing, if one is requested, is an important factor in determining acceptance of responsibility and the appropriate sanction.
See Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy,
881 F.3d at 830-31;
Hoxie
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
419 F.3d 477, 483-84 (6th Cir. 2005). Further, the Agency has found that the egregiousness and extent of the misconduct are significant factors in determining the appropriate sanction.
Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy,
881 F.3d at 833 n.4, 834. The Agency also considers the need to deter similar acts by a registrant and by the community of registrants.
Stein,
84 FR at 46972-73.
Here, Registrant did not timely request a hearing, and was therefore deemed to be in default.
21 CFR 1301.43(c)(1)
,
(e)
,
(f)(1)
; RFAA, at 1-4. To date, Registrant has not filed a motion with the Office of the Administrator to excuse the default.
21 CFR 1301.43(c)(1)
. Registrant has thus failed avail himself of the opportunity to refute the Government's case. As such, Registrant has not accepted responsibility for the proven violations, has made no representations regarding his future compliance with the CSA, and has not made any demonstration that he can be trusted with registration.
Moreover, the evidence presented by the Government shows that Registrant repeatedly supplied DEA with materially false information for over a decade in five renewal applications. This further demonstrates that Registrant cannot be trusted with the responsibilities of holding a controlled substances registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order the revocation of Registrant's registration.
[
9
]
Order
Pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(1)
and
(a)(3)
, I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. BL7481649 issued to Troy R. Lehman, D.O. Further, pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
, I hereby deny any pending applications of Troy R. Lehman, D.O., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Troy R. Lehman, D.O., for additional registration in Oklahoma. This Order is effective December 14, 2026.
Signing Authority
This document of the Drug Enforcement Administration was signed on November 3, 2026, by DEA Administrator Terrance C. Cole. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DEA. On June 26, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Traci B. Lujan, A.P.R.N., of Holladay, Utah (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 1, at 1, 4. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. ML5284815 CFR, alleging that Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Utah, the state in which [she is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
).
The OSC notified Registrant of her right to file a written request for hearing, and that if she failed to file such a request, she would be deemed to have waived her right to a hearing and be in default.
Id.
at 2-3 (citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds her to be in default. RFAA, at 2.
[
1
]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to
21 CFR 1301.43(c)
,
(f)
, and
1301.46
. RFAA, at 4;
see also
21 CFR 1316.67
.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted.
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
. According to the OSC, effective April 21, 2026, the Utah Division of Professional Licensing revoked Registrant's Utah Registered Nurse (RN) license, Registrant's Utah Advanced Practice Registered Nurse (APRN) license, and Registrant's Utah APRN controlled substance license. RFAAX 2, at 2. According to Utah online records, of which the Agency takes official notice,
[
2
]
Registrant's Utah RN, APRN, and APRN controlled substance licenses are all revoked. Utah Division of Professional Licensing License Lookup & Verification System,
https://secure.utah.gov/​llv/​search/​index.html
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice nursing, to practice as an APRN, nor to handle controlled substances in Utah, the state in which she is registered with DEA.
[
3
]
Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. 802(21).”).
[
4
]
The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Thomas Andr'e Endicott, D.D.S.,
90 FR 13892
(2025);
Gerald M. Baltz, N.P.,
87 FR 6749
(2022);
Paul E. Pilgram, M.D.,
82 FR 11058
(2017).
According to Utah statute, “[e]very person who . . . distributes, prescribes, dispenses, [or] administers . . . any controlled substance in Schedules I through V within [the] state . . . shall obtain a license issued by the [Division of Professional Licensing].” Utah Code Ann. § 58-37-105(2)(a)(i) (West 2026).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to handle controlled substances in Utah because Registrant's Utah APRN controlled substance license is revoked. As discussed above, an individual must
(
printed page 72913)
hold a Utah controlled substance license to dispense a controlled substance in Utah. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to handle controlled substances in Utah, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 824(a)
, I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. ML5284815 issued to Traci B. Lujan, A.P.R.N. Further, pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
, I hereby deny any pending applications of Traci B. Lujan, A.P.R.N., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Traci B. Lujan, A.P.R.N., for additional registration in Utah. This Order is effective December 14, 2026.

For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of DEA. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
Heather Achbach,
Federal Register Liaison Officer, Drug Enforcement Administration.
